en: The King said:
You have described the extensive lineage of the Moon and the Sun,
as well as the most wonderful history of the kings belonging to both dynasties.

O best of sages, please narrate to us the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu, who descended there by a portion of Himself into the lineage of Yadu, which was exceedingly righteous in character. Having descended into the family of Yadu, the Blessed Lord, the creator of all beings—
Tell us in detail those deeds which the Soul of the Universe performed.

Who, other than a killer of animals, would turn away from the chanting of the qualities of the Lord of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka)— a medicine for worldly existence that is sung by those whose thirst has ceased, and which is so pleasing to the ear and mind?

My grandfathers— Devavrata and the other great car-warriors (atirathas), who were like timingila fish— crossed the Kaurava army-ocean, which was otherwise impossible to traverse, using me as their raft, even though they had conquered the immortals in battle.
This body of mine, the seed for the progeny of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, has been consumed by the sparks from the weapon of Droṇa’s son.

O learned one, tell me of the heroic deeds of that Lord who, having assumed the discus, protected the womb of my mother when she had come to him for refuge; and of that illusory human (māyā-manuṣya) who, through his forms as the Supreme Person (puruṣa), Time (kāla), and the individual soul (jīva), bestows both death and immortality upon all embodied beings, internally and externally.
You have stated that Saṅkarṣaṇa, also known as Rāma, was the son of Rohiṇī;
how then could there be a connection with Devakī’s womb without a change of body?
And for what reason did the Blessed Mukunda go from his father’s house to Vraja?
Where did the Lord of the Sātvatas dwell together with his kinsmen?
While residing in Vraja, what did Keśava do, and what did he do in Madhupurī? And why did he slay his maternal uncle Kaṃsa, who was unworthy of such treatment?
Having assumed a human body, for how many years did he dwell with the Vṛṣṇis in the city of the Yadus? O Lord, how many wives did the Master have?
O Sage, tell me all of this and everything else regarding the deeds of Kṛṣṇa.

O omniscient one, you ought to relate this in detail to me, who am full of faith. This hunger, though extremely difficult to endure, does not afflict me as I drink the nectar of the narrations of Hari falling from your lotus-like mouth.
Sūta said:
O descendant of Bhṛgu, having thus heard these words of praise from Viṣṇurāta,
the venerable son of Vyāsa then [spoke].
Having paid homage to the deeds of Kṛṣṇa, which destroy the impurities of the Kali age,
the foremost of the devotees began to narrate them.
Śrī Śuka said:
O best of royal sages, your intellect has reached perfect resolution, since you have developed a steadfast devotion for the narrations of Vāsudeva. Indeed,
an inquiry concerning the narrations of Vāsudeva purifies three generations of men.
Just as the water from the feet of one who speaks, questions, or listens [purifies], so too the earth— oppressed by a vast burden of tens of millions of demon hosts disguised as arrogant kings—
went to Brahmā for refuge.
Having become a cow, distressed and with tears on her face, she approached the Lord and, weeping piteously,
related her misfortune to him.
Then Brahmā, having understood that, together with the gods and her, [approached the Lord].
The three-eyed one went to the shore of the ocean of milk;
having gone there, he, with a concentrated mind, worshipped the Lord of the World, the God of gods, Vṛṣākapi, the Supreme Person, with the Puruṣasūkta.
Having heard a voice uttered in the sky during his meditative absorption, the Creator spoke to the gods:

"O immortals, listen again to my words concerning Puruṣa; let it be carried out immediately and without delay. Long ago, the fever of the earth was taken up by the Supreme Person; you must now be born among the Yadus with your respective portions."
As long as that Lord of lords wanders upon the earth, diminishing its burden by His own power of time,
so that the Supreme Person, the Blessed Lord Himself, may be born in the house of Vasudeva for his pleasure, let the celestial women descend to take birth.
Ananta, a portion of Vāsudeva, the thousand-faced self-ruler,
will appear before [the Lord] as a deity desiring to do what is pleasing to Hari.
The divine Māyā of Viṣṇu is that by which the entire world is deluded.
"Commanded by the Lord as his partial expansion for the sake of the task, she shall come into being.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus instructed the hosts of immortals, the all-pervading Lord of the Prajāpatis—
Having comforted the Earth with these words, he departed for his own supreme abode.
Śūrasena, the lord of the Yadus, resided in the city of Mathurā and formerly enjoyed the territories of Mathurā and Śūrasena.
Thereafter, Mathurā became the capital of all the Yādava kings, where the Blessed Lord Hari is eternally present. Once, in that city, Vasudeva, known as Śauri, had performed his marriage ceremony.
On the journey, Kaṃsa, the son of Ugrasena, desiring to do what was pleasing for his sister, ascended the chariot together with Devakī and Sūryā;
surrounded by hundreds of golden chariots, he took hold of the reins of the horses.
As a dowry, he gave four hundred elephants adorned with golden garlands,
fifteen thousand horses, six hundred and thirty chariots,
and two hundred well-adorned, delicate female slaves.
Devaka, who was deeply affectionate toward his daughter, gave her a palanquin; at that time,
O dear one, as the bride and groom set out on their auspicious journey, conch shells, trumpets, mṛdaṅga drums, and kettledrums all resounded together.
On the road, the incorporeal voice addressed Kaṃsa, who was holding the reins:
"O ignorant one, the eighth child of this woman whom you carry shall be your slayer. Thus addressed, that wicked and sinful man, the defiler of the Bhoja lineage, [departed].
With sword in hand, he began to kill his sister and seized her by the hair; then Vasudeva, the most fortunate one, spoke to that cruel, shameless man of loathsome deeds, seeking to pacify him.
Śrī Vasudeva said:
You, whose virtues are praiseworthy by the brave and who bring glory to the Bhojas—
how could you kill a woman, your own sister, on the very day of her wedding?
O hero, death is born together with the body for those who possess birth;
whether today or at the end of a hundred years, death is indeed certain for all living beings.
When the body has reached its dissolution into the five elements, the embodied soul, helpless and following the lead of its past karma, departs.
Having attained another body, he abandons his former frame; just as one walking stands on one foot while moving with the other, so does the embodied soul,
following the course of its karma, leave one body for another like a caterpillar moving from one blade of grass to another.

Just as one whose consciousness is obsessed by a mental desire sees such a body in a dream, so too, reflecting in the mind upon what has been seen or heard, he— having lost his memory of his true nature— attains whatever it may be; for the mind, impelled by destiny and consisting of modifications, runs hither and thither among the five elements.
When this embodied soul enters into the modes of nature favored by Māyā, it is born together with them,
just as light is perceived as following the force of the wind when it passes through water or earth.
Thus, this person, following after passion for the modes of nature fashioned by his own māyā, becomes deluded;
therefore, one who is such should never practice malice toward anyone.

One who seeks his own welfare must indeed fear an enemy from another. This young sister of yours is helpless and like a daughter; you, who are compassionate toward the distressed, ought not to kill this auspicious woman.
Śrī Śuka said:
O descendant of Kuru, although he was thus being entreated with conciliatory words and various stratagems, that cruel man did not desist, for he remained devoted to his practice of cannibalism.

Perceiving that persistent insistence of his and reflecting upon it, Ānakadundubhi (Vasudeva) resolved upon this course of action to ward off the approaching time [of death]: "Death must be warded off by a wise man for as long as the power of his intelligence remains."
If he does not turn back, there is no fault on the part of the embodied soul.
Having offered my sons to death, I shall liberate this wretched woman. If a son were born to me, or if Death himself were to die, [then I would be saved].
Or rather, why should there not be the reverse? The course of the Creator is difficult to traverse.
One who has approached might turn back, and one who has turned back might fall again;
just as in the case of fire’s separation from or union with wood, there is no cause other than the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
"Indeed, even for a living being, the cause of the union with and separation from the body is thus difficult to comprehend.
Having reflected thus upon that wicked deed until he perceived the Self within himself,
Śauri (Kṛṣṇa) honored him with great respect.
With his lotus-like face serene, though his mind was pained, he laughed and spoke these words to the cruel and shameless man. Śrī Vasudeva said:
"O gentle one, you have no fear from her, for she is indeed one whose speech is not harsh toward the body.
I shall entrust her sons to you, from whom your fear has arisen.
Śrī Śuka said:
Knowing the essence of her words, Kaṃsa desisted from the killing of his sister-in-law;
Vasudeva also, being pleased, praised him and entered his home. Then, when the time had arrived, Devakī [gave birth], she who was all the deities.
And year by year, she gave birth to eight sons and one daughter.
Anaka-dundubhi, with great difficulty and overwhelmed by the fear of falsehood, handed over his first-born son, Kīrtimān, to Kaṃsa.
What is indeed unbearable for the virtuous? What is desired by the wise? What is an unworthy act for the miserly? And what is difficult to abandon for those who have mastered their selves?
Having seen that equanimity of Śauri and his steadfastness in truth, [the sages asked].
O King, Kaṃsa, with a satisfied mind, laughed and said this:
"Let this boy go back; indeed, I have no fear of him.
For it is ordained that my death shall come from the eighth pregnancy of you two."
Saying "So be it," Ānakadundubhi took his son and departed;
he did not welcome those words of the wicked man who had failed to conquer his own self.
As for Nanda and the other cowherds in Vraja, and their wives—none approved.

O descendant of Bharata, the Vṛṣṇis headed by Vasudeva, the Yadu women headed by Devakī, and all those who were their kinsmen, relatives, and friends— even those devoted to Kaṃsa— were indeed almost entirely divine beings belonging to both families.
Having arrived, the blessed Nārada informed Kaṃsa of this:
the Lord’s endeavor to slay the Daityas who were becoming a burden to the earth.
Upon the departure of the sage, Kaṃsa considered the Yadus to be gods.
Regarding Viṣṇu, who had entered the womb of Devakī for his own destruction,
Kaṃsa seized both Devakī and Vasudeva and confined them in his house with fetters;
out of fear that he might be born again, he killed each son of theirs as soon as he was born.
For generally on this earth, greedy kings, thirsting for their own lives, kill their mothers, fathers, brothers, and all their friends;
yet they do not realize that the self born here was previously slain by Viṣṇu.
He, possessed of great strength, personally subdued the great asura Kālanemi— who was being resisted by the Yadus—
as well as his father Ugrasena, the lord of the Yadus, Bhojas, and Andhakas,
and he devoured the Śūrasenas.
Śrī Śuka said:
[He was killed] by Pralamba, Baka, Cāṇūra, Tṛṇāvarta, Mahāśana,
Muṣṭika, Ariṣṭa, Dvivida, Pūtanā, Keśin, and Dhenuka.
Accompanied by other asura kings, such as Bāṇa and Bhauma,
the powerful Jarāsandha, taking refuge with the King of Magadha, wrought havoc among the Yadus.
Oppressed by him, they took up residence among the Kurus, Pañcālas, and Kekayas.
The Śālvas, Vidarbhas, Niṣadhas, Videhas, and Kośalas—
some of his kinsmen who followed him— waited upon him; yet, when six children had been slain by the son of Ugrasena, Devakī [remained].
The seventh [child] was indeed the abode of Viṣṇu, whom they call Ananta;
he became the embryo of Devakī, increasing both her joy and her sorrow.
The Blessed Lord, the Soul of the Universe, having perceived the fear arising from Kaṃsa, [entered the womb].
He commanded his own mistress, Yogamāyā, regarding the Yadus who were his own masters:
"Go, O auspicious Goddess, to Vraja, which is adorned with cowherds and cattle;
Rohiṇī is the wife of Vasudeva, and she resides in Nanda's Gokula."

Moreover, other [demons] who are agitated by Kaṃsa dwell in various hiding places. Therefore, having drawn out from Devakī’s womb my own abode known as Śeṣa, which is her embryo, place it within the womb of Rohiṇī.
Then, O auspicious one, I shall attain the state of being the son of Devakī through a portion of My own self;
you shall become Yaśodā, the wife of Nanda. Human beings will worship you, the sovereign goddess who grants all desires and boons.
With offerings of incense, oblations, and sacrificial gifts, men on earth bestow names and establish shrines for her who grants all desires and boons—
calling her Durgā, Bhadrakālī, Vijayā, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Kumudā, Caṇḍikā, Kṛṣṇā, Mādhavī, and Kanyakā; Māyā, Nārāyaṇī, Īśānī, Śāradā, and Ambikā—
because he draws forth the embryo, they call him Saṅkarṣaṇa on earth.
He is called Rāma because he delights the world, and Balabhadra because of his preeminent strength.
Having been thus instructed by the Blessed One, and having accepted His words with "So be it" and "Om," he circumambulated Him, went to the cowherd settlement, and acted accordingly.
When the embryo had been transferred by Yoga-nidrā from Devakī to Rohiṇī, the citizens cried out, "Alas! The fetus has miscarried!
Even the Blessed Lord, the Soul of the Universe who grants fearlessness to His devotees, [remained there].
A portion of Himself entered the mind of Ānakadundubhi;
bearing the splendor of the Supreme Person and shining like the sun,
He became manifest, difficult to approach and exceedingly invincible to all beings.

Then the goddess Devakī, with a concentrated mind, bore that auspiciousness of the world— the portion of Acyuta who is the soul of all and has become her very self— just as the quarter of the sky holds the moon which brings joy to the mind.
That Devakī, who was the dwelling place for the abode of the entire universe, no longer shone intensely.
In the house of the lord of the Bhojas, Sarasvatī was confined like a flame of fire; she was like a virtuous woman in the presence of one who is wicked in knowledge.
Seeing her, whose inner radiance surpassed all others, illuminating the palace with her pure smile, Kaṃsa—
"He said: 'This Hari, the stealer of my life-breath, has surely taken refuge in my heart-cave, since I have never before been such as this.
What must I do quickly regarding him today, so that, being dependent on his purpose, he does not destroy my prowess?'"
The killing of a woman, a sister, or one who honors her elders destroys fame, prosperity, and longevity at all times. Indeed, he who lives by extreme cruelty is already dead while still alive;
when his body perishes, men curse him, and he, identifying with the physical form, will certainly go to blind darkness.
Having thus withdrawn from that most terrible state, the Lord himself remained there, intent upon enmity toward Hari and awaiting his birth;
whether sitting, reclining, standing, eating, or wandering the earth.
Contemplating Hṛṣīkeśa, he saw the entire world as consisting of Him alone. Then Brahmā and Śiva, having arrived there along with sages such as Nārada,
and together with the gods and their attendants, praised the Bull among men (Vṛṣabha) with hymns.
He whose vow is truth, who is devoted to truth, who is the triple truth; He is the source of truth, established in truth,
the truth of truth, and the guide of cosmic order and truth.
We have taken refuge in You, whose nature is Truth.
You are the primordial tree: having a single path, two fruits, three roots, four tastes, five kinds [of wood], six essences, seven barks, eight branches, nine eyes, ten leaves, and two birds.
You alone are the source of this existing world; you are its presence and its grace.

Those whose minds are veiled by your *māyā* perceive you as manifold, whereas the wise do not. You, the conscious Self, assume various forms for the welfare of the world of moving and non-moving beings.
They bring happiness to the virtuous and repeatedly cause misfortune for the wicked;

O lotus-eyed one, those who have fixed their minds upon You— the abode of all existence— through meditative absorption, cross the ocean of worldly existence, which is as vast as it is difficult to traverse, by means of the boat of Your feet, using the hoof-print of a calf as their vessel.

Having yourselves crossed over this terrible ocean of worldly existence, which is so difficult to traverse, O radiant ones, you who possess abundant friendship have here [offered] the boat of your lotus feet.
Having placed [us] there, you have departed, O Lord who bestows grace upon the virtuous;
while others, O lotus-eyed one, consider themselves liberated,
yet their intellects remain unpurified due to their lack of devotion toward You.
Having ascended with great difficulty to the highest station,
they then fall back down below, disregarding Your feet;
but such is not the case, O Mādhava, for Your devotees who have bound their affection to You never fall away from the path.
Protected by you, O Lord, they wander fearlessly upon the heads of the hosts of Vināyakas;
for the sake of the stability of embodied beings, you resort to pure goodness (*sattva*),
a form that is the means for attaining their ultimate welfare.
O Creator, if this world were not Your own nature, then people would not strive for Your worship through Vedic rituals, yoga, austerity, and meditative absorption.
You, who effect the cleansing of the distinction between knowledge and ignorance,
are inferred by the manifestations of the modes; for it is by You that a mode is made manifest, or that which manifests a mode.
O Lord, Your names and forms cannot be defined by qualities, births, or actions, for You are their witness; yet,
O God, whose path is inferred by mind and speech, people indeed perceive You through ritual action when they hear, chant, remember, and contemplate [Your glories].
Your names and forms are auspicious; however,
one whose mind is absorbed in Your lotus feet is no longer subject to worldly existence during their activities.
"By good fortune, O Hari, the burden of this earth has been removed from you, the Lord who takes birth for that purpose; by good fortune,
it is now marked with your most beautiful footprints."
We shall behold the earth and the heavens graced by Your compassion; O Lord, we can conceive of no cause for Your becoming other than Your own pastime,
since birth, dissolution, and even maintenance are brought about by ignorance within You, the Self who is the refuge of fearlessness.
O Lord, having assumed incarnations as a fish, a horse, a tortoise, a man-lion, a boar, a swan,
a king, a brahmin, and among the gods,
you protect us and the three worlds just as you do now.
"O best of the Yadus, remove the burden of the earth; salutations to you!
By good fortune, O Mother, the Supreme Person has entered your womb;
the Lord himself, by his own portion, for our welfare."
“Let there be no fear for the Lord of the Bhojas who is about to die;
your son shall become the protector of the Yadus.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus praised the Supreme Person, whose nature is beyond this world,
the gods, placing Brahmā and Śiva at their head, returned to heaven.
Śrī Śuka said:
Then there was a most auspicious time, endowed with all excellent qualities;
for it was the very birth-star of Aja, when the constellations, planets, and stars were propitious.
The quarters of the sky became serene, and the heavens shone with the rising of pure clusters of stars.
The earth was filled with cities, villages, cow-pens, and mines abounding in auspiciousness;
the rivers possessed clear waters, and the lakes displayed the beauty of lotuses; the forest ranges were resonant with the humming of swarms of bees and clusters of blossoms.

A pure wind blew, pleasant to the touch and carrying holy fragrances; and the sacrificial fires of the twice-born blazed there peacefully. The minds of the virtuous, who were enemies of the asuras, became serene.
As that unborn one was being born, the kettledrums resounded simultaneously;
the Kinnaras and Gandharvas sang, the Siddhas and Cāraṇas offered hymns of praise,
and the Vidyādharīs danced with joy along with the Apsarases.
Filled with joy, the sages and the gods released flowers;
the clouds thundered softly over the ocean as Janārdana was being born in the thick darkness of midnight.
Viṣṇu, who dwells within the heart of all, appeared in Devakī, who was like a goddess,
just as the full moon appears in the eastern quarter.
That wonderful child, with lotus-like eyes and four arms, held weapons such as the conch and the mace.

Vasudeva beheld Him who bore the Śrīvatsa mark, whose neck was adorned with the Kaustubha gem, and who wore yellow garments as beautiful as a dense rain-cloud; whose thousand locks of hair were embraced by the luster of His precious vaidūrya crown and earrings; and who shone brilliantly with magnificent waist-bands, armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments.
Then, his eyes wide with wonder upon beholding Hari as his son, Ānakadundubhi,
overwhelmed by the festive joy of Kṛṣṇa’s descent, leaped up and joyfully gave ten thousand cows to the brāhmaṇas.
Then, recognizing him as the Supreme Person, he offered praise with his body bowed low, his mind composed, and his palms joined in reverence.

O descendant of Bharata, Śrī Vasudeva, who knew His power and was free from fear, spoke to Him as He illuminated the lying-in chamber with His own radiance: "You are known to me; you are the Supreme Person Himself, beyond material nature."
He whose nature is the bliss of pure experience and who perceives all intellects—
He alone, having first created this world consisting of the three qualities by means of His own material nature,
is subsequently perceived as if He had entered it, though He has not entered.
Just as these unmodified elements, together with the modified ones,
possessing diverse potencies and existing separately, indeed produce the Virāṭ;
having come together and brought it forth, they appear as if they have entered into it.
Since they already exist [within you], their manifestation here [in the external world] does not occur;

thus, although You exist through the qualities that are perceivable by the intellect and characterized by inference, there is no perception of those qualities because of the absence of obscuration. For You, the reality of the Self, who are the Self of all and all-pervading, there is neither "outside" nor "inside."
The ignorant person, who determines that he exists within the perceivable qualities of the self as something distinct from it, does not possess that correct understanding;
for, without a refutation [of his error], the person continues to take up what has already been abandoned.
O All-pervading Lord, from You come the birth, maintenance, and dissolution of this world.
They speak of You as being effortless, devoid of qualities, and changeless;
yet this does not contradict Your nature as the Lord and Brahman,
for it is figuratively attributed to You through Your association with the qualities.
For the maintenance of the three worlds, You indeed assume Your own white complexion through Your own Māyā; for the sake of creation, You assume a red hue augmented by the quality of passion (rajas).
O Lord of all, at the end of the age, you have descended into my house with a dark complexion due to *tamas*, desiring to protect this world;
you shall slay the armies led by millions of demon commanders known as Kṣatriyas.
"But this one, O Lord of the Gods, was unrighteous; having heard that you had slain his elder brothers,
he sought to kill you when you were delivered by men into his hands."
"Having heard this, he is now approaching with weapons raised.
Śrī Śuka said:
Then, beholding his own son who possessed the marks of a Great Being (mahā-puruṣa), [the king...]
Frightened of Kaṃsa and greatly amazed, Devakī ran toward him.
Śrī-Devakī said:
"That form which they call the unmanifest and primordial..."
The Brahman is the light, devoid of qualities, changeless,
pure existence alone, without distinction, and effortless;
you are that very Viṣṇu, the lamp of the inner self.

When the world has perished at the end of two parārdhas, when the gross elements have merged into the primordial element, and when the manifest has returned to the unmanifest by the force of time, You alone remain, known as the "Residueless" (Aśeṣa).
This very time belongs to You, O Lord whose bond is the Unmanifest.
They say that by which the universe acts is "activity" (ceṣṭā),
consisting of the great cycle from the blink of an eye up to the end of a year;
I take refuge in Him, the Sovereign Lord, the abode of security.
A mortal, terrified by the serpent of death, fled through all the worlds but found no place free from fear;
yet having now reached Your lotus feet by chance, he sleeps in peace, for death departs from him.
Therefore, as You are the remover of the terror of Your servants, protect us who are frightened by the terrible son of Ugrasena.
"And do not let this form of Yours, the abode of meditation, become visible to those who see with the eyes of flesh. O Madhusūdana, let that wicked man not know of Your birth in me;
for my mind is unsteady, and I am terrified because of You, Kaṃsa."
O Soul of the Universe, withdraw this extraordinary form of Yours,
endowed with four arms and graced by the splendor of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
For at the end of the night, You, the Supreme Person, are the universe itself within Your own body, according to its capacity.
"He who nourishes me has now entered my womb; oh, how that is indeed a mockery of the world of men!
The Blessed Lord said: "In a previous creation, during the era of Svāyambhuva Manu, you yourself were Pṛśni."
Then this sinless Prajāpati named Sutapas,
when you two were indeed commanded by Brahmā to create progeny,
restrained the aggregate of your senses and performed supreme austerity.
Enduring the qualities of the seasons— rain, wind, heat, cold, and time—
with their minds purified by the restraint of breath,
subsisting on withered leaves and air, they remained with tranquil hearts.
Desiring their boons from me, they strove to worship me;
thus, as you two performed that most difficult and intense austerity for twelve thousand divine years, you were absorbed in my own self.

"O sinless ones, at that time I was well-pleased by this form of yours, and I, the king of givers of boons, manifested myself because I was constantly meditated upon in your hearts with austerity, faith, and devotion,
desiring to grant your wish."
When it was said, "Choose a boon," you replied, "A son like us has been chosen by you. Yet,
though you were a husband and wife who took no pleasure in worldly objects and were childless,
you did not choose liberation from me, being deluded by the divine illusion (*deva-māyā*).
"When I have departed, you two, having obtained a boon and your heart's desire fulfilled, shall enjoy worldly pleasures after giving birth to a son equal to me—
provided that you do not see anyone else in the world who is your peer in character, nobility, and virtues."
"I was your son, known as Pṛśnigarbha;
then once again, from Kaśyapa and Aditi,
I became known as Upendra and Vāmana because of my dwarf stature."

"In this third birth, O virtuous ones, I was indeed born from you two again with that very same body; what I have spoken is the truth. This form has been shown to you so that I may remember my previous births."
Knowledge of Me does not arise in any other way through a mortal form;
by constantly meditating upon Me with the feeling of being My sons and with the feeling of being Brahman, you two, having developed such affection, shall attain My supreme destination.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord Hari became silent; by His own internal potency (ātma-māyā), while his parents were looking on, He instantly became an ordinary infant.
Then, impelled by the Blessed One, Śauri took his son from the lying-in chamber;
when he desired to go outside, at that moment the goat—

Then, by that Yogamāyā who had been born as the wife of Nanda, all the citizens at the gate— whose cognitive functions and perceptions were withdrawn— were made to sleep; and all the gates were closed, difficult to pass, with massive door-panels secured by iron bolts and chains.
When Vasudeva, the carrier of Kṛṣṇa, arrived, those rivers withdrew of their own accord, just as darkness vanishes before the sun.
The rain-cloud poured down with a low rumbling, while Śeṣa followed behind, warding off the water with his hoods.
Even as Indra rained repeatedly, the Yamunā flowed on, her waves foaming with the speed of a deep torrent.
The river, agitated by hundreds of terrifying whirlpools, gave way like the ocean did for the Lord of Śrī;
and having approached Nanda’s cowherd settlement, Śauri found those cowherds there fast asleep with slumber.
Having placed his son on Yaśodā’s bed and taking her daughter, he returned home;
then Vasudeva placed the girl on Devakī’s bed.
Having fastened the iron shackles upon his feet, he remained there as before, concealed;
and Yaśodā, the wife of Nanda, perceived that a child had been born, yet she did not recognize its true nature,
being exhausted by sleep and deprived of her memory.
Śrī Śuka said:
All the gates of the inner and outer quarters were closed as before.
Then, hearing the sound of the child, the household guards arose.
They quickly approached and reported to the King of the Bhojas that very birth from Devakī’s womb, which he had been anxiously awaiting;
rising swiftly from his bed, agitated by the thought, "This is the moment," he was overwhelmed with distress.
He went quickly to the maternity chamber, stumbling along with his hair disheveled.
The noble lady, distressed, spoke piteously to her brother:
"O auspicious one, this is your daughter-in-law; you ought not to kill a woman."

"O brother, many children, like unto fire, have been destroyed by you who were impelled by fate; let at least one daughter be given to me. Indeed, O Lord, I am your younger sister, now wretched and my sons have been slain."
"You ought to grant this final offspring to me, your slow-witted wife.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, while she was weeping most piteously, he took his daughter into his arms.
When entreated for her, that wicked man rebuked her and snatched her from his hand.
Having seized his own sister’s newborn daughter by the feet,
he whose affection was uprooted for the sake of his own interest dashed her against the surface of a stone.
Leaping up from his hand, that goddess immediately ascended into the sky;
she became invisible as the younger sister of Viṣṇu, possessing eight great arms equipped with weapons,
adorned with divine garlands, garments, unguents, and jewel ornaments.
Bearing bows, spears, shields, swords, conchs, discs, and maces,
and being praised by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Kinnaras, and Uragas who presented him with vast offerings, he spoke these words.
"O dull-witted one, what is the use of killing me? Surely he who was born to bring about your end has already been born.
Let that former enemy kill me wherever he may be; do not harm these wretched ones in vain.
Having spoken thus to him on earth, the divine goddess Māyā—
He indeed came to possess many names among those who have many names.
Having heard what was spoken by her, Kaṃsa was greatly astonished;
releasing both Devakī and Vasudeva, he spoke with humility.
"O sister! O brother! Alas, by me—a sinner—your many children have been slain like those of a man-eater. Indeed, I am a wicked man who has abandoned compassion and forsaken my kinsmen and friends."
"O Brahman, to what worlds indeed shall I go when I die, even while still breathing? Even a god speaks falsehood, not only mortals;
for it was through his confidence that I, a sinner, killed the children of my sister."
"Do not grieve, O highly fortunate ones; your sons are experiencing the results of their own actions. Living beings, subject to destiny, do not remain forever in one place.
Just as terrestrial creatures on this earth come and go, so it is with them."

This Self does not undergo transformation within these [bodies] in the same way that the earth does; yet for those who do not know it thus, there is a sense of duality, from which arises the misconception of the Self,
as well as union with and separation from the body, and the cycle of worldly existence does not cease.
Therefore, O blessed lady, do not grieve for your sons, even though they were slain by me; for everyone helplessly reaps the fruit of their own actions.
As long as one lacks self-vision, one considers oneself, "I am struck" or "I shall strike."
"As long as that ignorant one, identifying with them, persists in the state of oppressor and oppressed, [so long shall this continue].
O virtuous ones, compassionate toward the distressed, forgive my wickedness.
Having spoken thus, his face bathed in tears, the brother-in-law then grasped the feet of his sister.
Trusting in the words of the girl, He released them from their fetters,
demonstrating His friendship to Devakī and Vasudeva; and Devakī, her anger appeased, was filled with remorse for her brother.
Vasudeva, laughing, released him and said to him:
"O illustrious one, it is exactly as you say regarding embodied beings:
the notion of 'I' arises from ignorance, and from that comes the distinction between 'self' and 'other'."
Possessed by grief, joy, fear, hatred, greed, delusion, and pride,
those of dualistic vision do not perceive the One Being as it destroys one being after another through its various manifestations.
Śrī Śuka said:
Kaṃsa, having been thus addressed by the pure words of the gratified Devakī and Vasudeva, was granted leave and entered his home. When that night had passed, Kaṃsa summoned his ministers.

He related to them all that which had been spoken by Yoga-nidrā. Having heard what their master had said, the enemies of the gods— the sons of Diti, who were ill-informed and filled with indignation toward the deities— spoke to him.
"If it be so, O King of the Bhojas, then today we shall slay the infants— both those less than ten days old and those over ten days— in the cities, villages, cowherd settlements, and elsewhere.
What will the gods, who are cowards in battle, achieve with their efforts?"
With minds constantly agitated by the twanging of your bow and being struck on all sides by the volleys of arrows you discharge,
those who desire to live cast everything aside and flee for their lives.
Some of the gods, wretched and with palms joined in supplication, had laid down their weapons;
some, with their lower garments and topknots disheveled, cried out, "We are afraid!
[The Lord said: "You have not forgotten your weapons and missiles, nor are you without chariots; why are you overcome by fear?"
"You slay those who are averse because their minds are attached elsewhere, who have broken their bows, and who do not fight.
What is the use of gods who are heroes only in safety and boast without combat? Or what is the use of Hari, who dwells in seclusion, or of Śambhu, who is a forest-dweller?"
Of what use is Indra, whose prowess is meager, or even Brahmā, who is occupied with asceticism?
Nevertheless, we consider that the gods must not be neglected because of our status as their rivals.
Therefore, employ us, your devoted followers, in uprooting that very source of their power.

Just as a disease in the body that is neglected by men cannot be treated once it has taken root, so too this great enemy, the aggregate of the senses, when neglected, becomes powerful and cannot be moved. For Viṣṇu is indeed the root of the gods, wherein resides eternal dharma.
For him, Brahman, cows, and Brahmins, as well as austerity and sacrifices accompanied by sacrificial fees, constitute his wealth.
Therefore, O King, we are destroying with all our might the Brahmins who discourse on the Veda, the ascetics devoted to sacrifice, and the cows that yield the oblation.
The brāhmaṇas, the cows, the Vedas, austerity, truthfulness, self-restraint, tranquility,
faith, compassion, forbearance, and sacrifices— these are the bodies of Hari.
For He is indeed the presiding lord of all the gods, the enemy of the demons, and the one who dwells within the heart.
All the deities, including the Lord (Īśvara) and the four-faced Brahmā, have him as their root.
Indeed, the means for his destruction is the harming of the sages.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, having deliberated with his evil counselors, the wicked-minded Kaṃsa,
that demon enveloped by the noose of Time, considered the killing of brāhmaṇas to be for his own benefit;
he then dispatched those who delight in slaughter to carry out the massacre of the virtuous people.
Entering their homes, He encountered the Dānavas in all directions, who could assume any form at will; for they were of a rajasic nature, their minds deluded by tamas,
and having drawn near to their own death, they practiced hostility toward the virtuous.
"Longevity, prosperity, fame, virtue, the higher worlds, and even blessings— all such auspicious things as well as all other excellences of a man are destroyed by transgressing against the Great One.
Śrī Śuka said:
But Nanda, his mind vast, having experienced great joy at the birth of his son,
bathed, purified himself, and adorned himself; then, having summoned brahmins learned in the Vedas,
he had them recite benedictions for the birth-rite of his son.
He caused the worship of the ancestors and the gods to be performed according to the prescribed rites; likewise,
he gave two million well-adorned cows to the Brahmins,
as well as seven mountains of sesame seeds covered with heaps of jewels, gold, and fine garments.
By means of timely bathing and purification, by sacraments, austerity,
and sacrifice, by gifts, contentment, and the knowledge of the self regarding material objects, [the body] is purified;
meanwhile, the Brahmins, Sūtas, Māgadhas, and bards uttered words of auspiciousness.
The singers sang and the kettledrums and war-drums resounded repeatedly.
The settlement of Vraja had its gates, courtyards, and interiors of the houses swept and sprinkled with water,
and was adorned with variegated banners, flags, garlands, cloth, sprouts, and arched gateways.
The cows, the bull, and the young calves were smeared with turmeric oil;
they were adorned with various minerals, peacock feathers, garlands, garments, and golden necklaces,
and were further embellished with costly clothes, ornaments, tunics, and turbans.
O King, the cowherds arrived with various offerings in their hands; and the cowherd women,
having heard of the birth of Yaśodā’s son, were filled with joy and adorned themselves with garments, ornaments, collyrium, and other finery.
With faces like lotuses possessing filaments of fresh saffron,
their broad hips and swaying breasts moving as they hurried along with offerings,
the gopīs wore polished jewel-earrings and golden neck-ornaments around their throats.
Clad in variegated garments, with showers of flower-garlands falling from their topknots onto the path,
the women of Nanda’s household shone as they walked along,
adorned with bracelets and graced by the beauty of swaying earrings, breasts, and necklaces.

Offering these blessings, saying "Protect [him] for a long time," they sprinkled the child with turmeric powder, oil, and water, and sang his praises. Various musical instruments were played during that great festival.
When Kṛṣṇa, the infinite Lord of the universe, arrived at Nanda’s cowherd settlement,
the cowherds, filled with mutual joy, splashed one another with curds, milk, ghee, and water, smeared one another, and pelted each other with fresh butter.
The high-minded Nanda gave clothing, ornaments, and cattle-wealth to them, as well as to the charioteers, bards,
panegyrists, and others who lived by their learning;
with a noble heart, he honored each of them with whatever they desired, as was appropriate.
For the purpose of worshipping Viṣṇu and for the prosperity of her own son,
the highly fortunate Rohiṇī, welcomed by Nanda the cowherd,
wandered about adorned with divine garments, garlands, and neck-ornaments.
From that time forward, O King, Nanda’s Vraja became possessed of all prosperity; by virtue of Hari’s residence there, it became a playground for Lakṣmī through his own divine qualities.
Having appointed the cowherds to the protection of Gokula, He departed for Mathurā.
O best of the Kurus,
having heard that his brother Nanda had arrived to pay Kaṃsa’s annual tax, Vasudeva learned that the tribute had been paid to the king and went to his place of release.
Seeing him, he rose up suddenly like a body that has regained its life-breath;
filled with joy and overwhelmed by love, he embraced his most beloved with both arms.
Having been honored and seated comfortably, he respectfully inquired after his well-being.
O Lord of the People, with his mind fixed upon his two sons, he said this:
"By good fortune, O brother, although you were advanced in years, childless, and had turned away from the desire for offspring, progeny has now been obtained."
"By good fortune, you have been encountered today— though wandering in this wheel of worldly existence and subject to rebirth— as one whose sight is difficult to obtain and who is so dear to behold.
The dwelling together of dear friends, whose deeds are as varied as a painted scene, does not last for long."
Just as rafts are swept away by the current of a river,
is that great forest where you now dwell, surrounded by your friends, free from disease, abundant in water, grass, and creepers, and favorable for cattle?
"O brother, is my son with his mother in your Vraja?
Thinking you to be his father, is he being cherished by both of you? Indeed, the three goals of life for a man are ordained and experienced through friends."
"When they are suffering, the three goals of life (tri-varga) do not serve any purpose.
Śrī Nanda said:
"Oh, so many sons of Devakī have been killed by Kaṃsa!"
The one remaining youngest daughter also went to heaven.
Indeed, this person who has not seen the ultimate end and for whom the unseen is supreme is deluded;
he who knows the true nature of the Self, which is beyond the unseen, is not bewildered.
Śrī Vasudeva said:
"The annual tribute has indeed been paid to the king, and we have seen you all.
You should not remain here for much longer, for there are many portents occurring in Gokula."
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus addressed by Vasudeva, Nanda and the other cowherds took leave of him and departed for Gokula in carts yoked with oxen.
Śrī Śuka said:
On the way, Nanda reflected that the words of Vasudeva could not be false;
apprehensive due to the arrival of these portents, he went for refuge to Hari.
Sent by Kaṃsa, the terrible Pūtanā, the slayer of infants,
wandered through cities, villages, cowherd settlements, and other places, killing children.
In those places, there were no rites such as the hearing of sacred texts that could have warded off the demons.

For there, the female demons (yātudhānīs) were indeed performing [rites] against the Lord of the Sātvatas. Then, on one occasion, that Pūtanā, a wanderer through the sky, having assumed a female form by her illusory power (māyā), entered Nanda’s cowherd settlement, moving according to her own will.
Her hair was entwined with *mallikā* flowers,
her waist was constricted by her broad hips and breasts,
she was elegantly dressed, and her ears were adorned with ornaments.
Her face was adorned with locks of hair shimmering with luster;
she captivated the minds of the women of Vraja with her charming smiles and glances cast from the corners of her eyes.
The gopīs perceived Him, whose hand was like a lotus,
as if they were seeing the goddess Śrī herself in embodied form, come to behold their husband.
At that time, a child-seizing spirit (bālagraha), searching for children by chance in the house of Nanda, encountered the Lord, who is the end of all that is unreal.
She saw the child, whose own innate splendor was concealed, lying upon the bed like a fire placed within ashes.

Recognizing her as the demoness Bālakamārikā, the Soul of all moving and non-moving beings closed His eyes and placed that infinite one upon His lap, just as one who mistakes a rope for a snake might take hold of a sleeping serpent.
Seeing her with such a sharp mind and exceedingly amorous gestures— like a sword sheathed within its scabbard—

the two mothers stood watching as they were overwhelmed by the splendor of that excellent woman. At that moment, [the demon] offered his breast, which was fierce and possessed of indigestible potency.
Then, seizing the infant’s terrible fang,
the Blessed One pressed it firmly with both hands and,
filled with wrath, drank from it along with its very life-force.
"Release me! Release me! Enough! she cried out as her entire vital essence was being crushed;
opening her eyes wide, repeatedly tossing her feet and arms, her limbs drenched in sweat, she wept aloud.
By the sound of her cries, which possessed an exceedingly deep and violent force, the earth with its mountains and the heavens with its planets shook.
The netherworlds and the directions trembled, and people fell upon the earth fearing the stroke of a thunderbolt.
Thus distressed, the night-stalker,
losing her life-breath, threw back her hair and gaped at him with her hands and feet.
Having extended his own form within the cow-pen,
O King, he fell down like Vṛtra struck by the thunderbolt;
even as he was falling, his body [crushed] the trees within a distance of three gavyūtis.

O King of kings, he crushed it; that was a great wonder. [The demon] had a mouth with fierce fangs as large as plow-poles, nostrils like mountain caves, breasts like massive boulders, a terrifying appearance, and disheveled reddish hair.
Seeing that body— with eyes as deep as blind wells, terrifying with its rising sandbanks,
arms and legs bound together like embankments, and a belly like a lake devoid of water—
the cowherd men and women were struck with terror.
But first, their hearts, ears, and heads were pierced by the sound of that [thunder],
and the cowherd women, overcome with agitation, quickly approached and seized the child who was playing fearlessly upon her breast.
Yaśodā and Rohiṇī together provided complete protection for the child from all sides by means of such methods as waving cow-tails and bathing the infant with cow-urine and then with cow-dust.

And the cowherd women performed a protection ritual by applying [cow-dung] with the names [of Kṛṣṇa] upon their twelve limbs; having touched water, they then separately applied it to their own limbs and hands, and subsequently performed the ritual placement of the seed-syllables (*bīja-nyāsa*) upon themselves and upon the child.

May Aja protect your feet; may Maṇimān protect your knees, and Yajña, the Infallible, your thighs. May Hayāsya protect the region of your hips, Keśava your belly, and Īśa, the Lord, your heart; may Ina protect your neck.
May Viṣṇu be at my back, Urukrama at my right arm, Īśvara at my face, and Hari with his discus and club be in front;
may the slayer of Madhu, bearing his bow and sword, be at both your sides.
May Śaṅkha protect the corners, may Urugāya protect the upper part,
Tārkṣya the ground, and Haladhara-Puruṣa everywhere. May Hṛṣīkeśa protect the senses, and Nārāyaṇa protect the vital breaths.
May the Lord of Śvetadvīpa protect the heart; may the Lord of Yoga protect the mind.
May Pṛśnigarbha protect your intellect, and may the Supreme Lord protect the self. May Govinda protect you while playing, and may Mādhava protect you while sleeping.

May Vaikuṇṭha protect you as you walk; may the Lord of Śrī protect you as you sit; and may the Eater of Sacrifice, who strikes fear into all malevolent spirits, protect you as you eat. May the ḍākinīs, the yātudhānīs, the kuṣmāṇḍas, and those who are the seizers of children [be subdued].
The bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, yakṣas, rakṣasas, and vināyakas; Koṭarā, Revatī, Jyeṣṭhā, Pūtanā, Mātṛkā, and the rest;
as well as those who cause madness and epilepsy, who harm the body, the vital breaths, and the senses.
May all those great portents seen in dreams, as well as the elders and the child-seizing spirits,
perish— all of them terrified by the utterance of the name of Viṣṇu.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, while his protection was ensured by the cowherd women bound to him by affection,
the mother, having nursed her son at her breast, laid him down to rest.
At that moment, Nanda and the other cowherds arrived from Mathurā at Vraja.
Beholding the body of Pūtanā, they were struck with great amazement:
"Surely he has become a sage, or perhaps he was a master of yoga;
for that very portent which Ānakadundubhi foretold has now been witnessed."
Having cut that corpse with axes, the inhabitants of Vraja threw it far away,
limb by limb, and cremated it while wrapped in wood.
As the body was burning, its smoke was as fragrant as aguru.

Having been used by Kṛṣṇa, Pūtanā— the demoness who killed the children of the world and subsisted on blood— was instantly cleansed of her sins upon rising; even though she gave her breast to Hari with the intent to kill him, she attained the supreme destination.

How much more so, then, for one who with faith and devotion offers his dearest possession to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul— just as His mothers, being devoted to Him, offer everything? [He does this] with His two feet, which abide in the hearts of His devotees and are worthy of worship by those honored by the world.

Even that female demon attained heaven— the destination of one’s own mother— by stepping upon her body and suckling at her breast; what then need be said of the cows who were the foster-mothers, having drunk the milk from breasts enjoyed by Kṛṣṇa?
The Blessed Lord, the son of Devakī, who bestows all things including absolute liberation, drank their milk, which flowed from them due to maternal affection for their sons; and they, in turn,
cast unceasing glances upon Kṛṣṇa as their son.
O King, the cycle of worldly existence, which arises from ignorance, is no longer possible for them.
Having caught the fragrance of the smoke from the straw mats, the inhabitants of Vraja returned to the settlement, asking, "What is this? From where does it come?"

Having heard from the cowherds there the account of Pūtanā’s arrival and so forth, as well as her death and the child’s well-being, they were filled with great wonder. Then Nanda, noble-minded, took up his son who had returned from the dead.
O best of the Kurus, having smelled his head, he attained supreme joy. That mortal who hears with faith this wonderful childhood account of Kṛṣṇa’s liberation of Pūtanā attains devotion to Govinda.
The King said: O Lord, by whichever incarnation the Blessed Hari, the Supreme Controller,

performs deeds that are pleasing to the ear and delightful to the mind for us— by hearing which, O Master, one’s discontent departs, one becomes free from thirst, and the quality of goodness (sattva) of a person is purified without delay.
If you consider devotion to Hari and friendship with His attendants to be the very essence of life,
then please speak of other wonderful deeds of Kṛṣṇa as well—
deeds performed while He resided in the human world, conforming to the ways of that species.
Śrī Śuka said: Once, during the conjunction of the birth asterism, while the women had gathered for the festive bath marking the occasion of his rising,
the virtuous Satī performed the ceremonial consecration of her son amidst the sounding of musical instruments, songs, and the chanting of mantras by the twice-born.
Nanda’s wife, having had her bath and other rites performed by the brahmins who had offered auspicious benedictions and were well-honored with food,
clothing, garlands, and desired cows, gently laid him down as he was overcome by sleep; meanwhile,
the wise woman, her mind eager for the birth-ceremony, continued honoring the residents of Vraja who had gathered there.
She did not hear the crying of her son; weeping herself because he desired the breast, she lifted her feet toward him.

Struck by the feet of the infant lying on the ground—feet as soft as young sprouts of the *ano'lpaka* plant—the cart overturned, its various vessels of precious metals and base metals shattered, its wheels and axles displaced, and its pole broken.
Seeing this, Yaśodā and the other women of Vraja who had assembled for the birth-ceremonies,
as well as Nanda and the others, were overwhelmed by the sight of the wonder.
"How indeed did the cart overturn itself?
asked the boys of the cowherds and cowherd girls whose minds were unsettled.
"This was undoubtedly kicked over by this weeping child with his foot," they said.
The cowherds did not believe him, thinking his words were those of a child;
they did not know that the strength of that boy was immeasurable.
Taking her crying son, Yaśodā, fearing a malevolent spirit (*graha*), [acted].
After the brahmins had performed the rite of auspiciousness with Vedic hymns, he suckled at her breast;
meanwhile, the powerful cowherds had established her, along with her equipment, as before.
Having offered oblations, the brahmins worshipped her with curd, unbroken grains, *kuśa* grass, and water.
"Those who are free from malice, falsehood, hypocrisy, envy, violence, and pride—
the blessings of those of truthful character have not been rendered fruitless.
Having spoken thus, he took up the boy with mantras recited from the Ṛg, Sāma, and Yajur Vedas.
Having been consecrated with waters containing purifying herbs by the best of the twice-born,
and having had the benediction for prosperity recited, Nanda the cowherd, with a composed mind,
offered oblations into the fire and gave food of excellent quality to the brahmins.

For the sake of his sons' prosperity, he gave away cows endowed with every excellence, adorned with garments, garlands, and golden necklaces; and those cows were then employed by the disciplined brāhmaṇas who were conversant with the mantras, as well as the blessings they pronounced.
Those [merits] will clearly never bear fruit at any time.
Once, while fondling her son who had climbed onto her lap,
the virtuous woman was unable to bear the weight of the infant, which felt like a mountain peak.
Placing him on the ground, the cowherd girl was struck with wonder and oppressed by the weight;
she meditated upon the Great Person and resumed her worldly duties.
Then a demon named Tṛṇāvarta, a servant of Kaṃsa, was dispatched.
In the form of a whirlwind, it carried away the child who was sitting there,
enveloping all of Gokula and stealing away their vision with its dust,
while shaking the intermediate and main quarters with an exceedingly terrible sound.
For a moment, the cow-pen became shrouded in dust and darkness;
Yaśodā did not see her son because she had laid him down there.
Deluded, no one could perceive either themselves or others.
Afflicted by the pebbles hurled by Tṛṇāvarta,
and seeing her son’s path amidst that rain of dust from the fierce whirlwind, his mother,
remembering him with exceeding compassion, fell to the ground and lamented like a cow whose calf has died.
Hearing that crying, the cowherd women there, their minds deeply distressed and their faces filled with tears,
wept because they could not find the son of Nanda; meanwhile, Tṛṇāvarta, having subsided his speed, took the form of a whirlwind and carried him away.
Traveling through the sky, Kṛṣṇa was unable to proceed because he bore such a heavy burden;
thinking that stone to be his own weight due to its great mass,
the child held it by the neck and was unable to let go of that wonderful infant.
With his throat seized, rendered motionless, and his eyes bulging out,
the demon let out an indistinct cry and fell lifeless in Vraja along with the child.
As he fell from the sky onto a rock, all his limbs were shattered into a terrifying sight.
Just as when a city is pierced by the arrow of Rudra, the women gathered together and saw [the city] weeping;
they took [the child] and presented him to his mother, filled with wonder at Kṛṣṇa hanging from his chest—
him who had been carried off by the man-eater, yet was now safe, released from the jaws of death by traveling through the sky.
The cowherd women and the cowherds, led by Nanda, having regained him, attained the highest joy, saying:
"Oh, how truly wonderful! This child was brought back to life after being taken away by a demon;
indeed, the wicked, murderous one has been destroyed by his own sin, while the saintly man is liberated from fear through equanimity."
What austerity have we performed, or worship of Adhokṣaja, or works of public utility, sacrifices, gifts, or kindness toward living beings,
that this child has returned even after having passed away?
"By good fortune, you have arrived, bringing your own kinsmen!
Having seen many wonders in the great forest,
Nanda the cowherd was filled with amazement and once again honored the words of Vasudeva.

Once, the beautiful woman, overflowing with affection, took the infant onto her lap and, her breasts flowing with milk, caused him to drink from them; meanwhile, his mother gazed upon her son’s radiant smile as he had nearly finished drinking.
O King, as she was licking her mouth, this was seen by her as she yawned:
the sky, heaven and earth, the assembly of lights, the quarters of space, the sun, moon, fire, wind, and oceans;
the continents, mountains, their daughters, the forests, and all beings, both stationary and moving.
O King, suddenly beholding the universe, she, whose eyes were like those of a young fawn, became seized with trembling; closing her eyes, she stood utterly amazed. Śrī Śuka said:
O King, Garga, the family priest of the Yadus and a man of great austerity,
being urged by Vasudeva, went to the cowherd settlement of Nanda.
Upon seeing him, [Nanda] was exceedingly pleased and rose with palms joined in reverence.

Having honored the sage with the thought that he was Adhokṣaja himself, preceded by prostrations, and having delighted him with kind words as he sat comfortably after being offered hospitality, he said: "O Brahmin, what may we do for you, who are already fulfilled?"

O Blessed One, for householders whose minds are dejected, even a great disturbance is conducive to their ultimate welfare, and never otherwise; that which is the direct path of the luminaries is knowledge beyond the reach of the senses.
By that which has been imparted by you, a person knows both the higher and the lower;
for you are the best among those who know Brahman, and it behooves you to perform the purificatory rites for these two children, since among men a Brāhmaṇa is the spiritual preceptor by birth.
Śrī Garga said:
"I am the preceptor of the Yadus and have always been renowned throughout the world; therefore, you should consider this son, consecrated by me, to be the son of Devakī."
The evil-minded Kaṃsa, having heard the words of Devakī’s daughter, reflected: "O Ānakadundubhi, the eighth pregnancy of Devakī cannot possibly be a female child. Thus he thought.
"Alas! If he has gone there without hesitation, then that would be a calamity for us.
Śrī Nanda said:
"He was unobserved in this secluded place, even by my own people in the cowherd settlement."
"Perform the purificatory rites for the twice-born, preceded by the recitation of benedictions.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus requested, the brāhmaṇa [performed] that very thing which he himself desired to do.
In secret, the sage Gūḍha performed the naming ceremony for the two boys.
Śrī-Garga said:
"This son of Rohiṇī indeed delights his friends with his virtues."

He will be called Rāma because of his superior strength; they know him as Bala because he is not distinct from the Yādavas, and they also call him Saṅkarṣaṇa. Indeed, there were three castes for him as he assumed forms according to the age.
"Once white, then red, and likewise yellow, he has now attained blackness. Previously born as the son of Vasudeva,
this glorious one is known by those who possess true knowledge as Vāsudeva."
"Your son has many names and forms corresponding to his qualities and deeds; I know them, but people do not.
This delighter of the cowherds and the cattle will bestow the highest good upon you."
"By means of this, you shall easily cross over all difficulties.
O Lord of Vraja, in former times, when there was no king and the virtuous were oppressed by bandits, they were protected by this [mantra] and, flourishing, conquered those bandits."
Those fortunate men who feel affection for him are not overcome by enemies,
just as the Asuras cannot defeat those who take the side of Viṣṇu. Therefore, this son of Nanda is equal to Nārāyaṇa in his qualities.
"Protect [the child] with focused attention through your splendor, fame, and majesty.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus instructed himself, and after Garga had departed for his own home, [the Lord entered the womb].
Nanda, filled with joy, considered himself fulfilled in all his desires.
As a short time passed, Rāma and Keśava began to play about in Gokula,
crawling on their knees and hands.
Dragging their pair of feet along,
crawling through the mud of Vraja with beautiful lowing sounds,
they followed the people with hearts delighted by those cries.
Appearing as if bewildered and terrified, they approached their parents;
their mothers, out of affection, embraced their two sons— who were beautiful with the mud-paste smeared upon their limbs— holding them with both arms.
Having given their breasts to the two who were drinking from them, they experienced great joy upon gazing at the faces of the two infants, adorned with charming smiles and tiny teeth,
as they displayed the playful gestures of boys so lovely to behold for women.
Within the cow-pen,
the women— having abandoned their homes— watched with joy and laughter as the two boys were being pulled hither and thither by calves who had seized their tails.

There, even the two mothers were unable to restrain their own two sons— who had wandered far off while playing— from horned beasts, fire, fanged creatures, swords, water, birds, and thorns, nor could they perform the domestic duties for them.
O royal sage, in a short time, Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa attained full mastery over their minds; in Gokula,
they began to walk with ease, their knees not yet touching the ground as they stepped with their feet.

Then the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, together with Balarāma and his companions— the boys of Vraja— played with the women of Vraja, bringing them great joy. The gopīs beheld the charming childhood frolics of Kṛṣṇa.
While his mother was listening, they gathered together and said:
"Sometimes, letting out his calves at an improper time, he laughs aloud; then, by means of various clever thefts, he eats sweet curd and milk as if it were stolen."
Intending to eat the monkeys, he distributes them; yet if he does not eat, he breaks the vessel.
When no goods are obtained, he becomes angry at his household and departs after reviling his children. He devises a stratagem using a stool, a mortar, and other such items within reach of his hand.

For, at that time when the gopīs were intensely preoccupied with their household duties, He who knows the secret, having placed His own body— which was like a lamp providing light— within the vessels on the carrying-pole, revealed it as a hidden flaw in the darkness of the house. (BhP 10.8.30.2–4)
Thus, out of audacity, he indulges in urination and other acts upon the dwelling;
having fashioned his deeds through fraudulent means, he remains there like a handsome beast.
In this manner, he is gazed upon by the women with eyes full of fear and faces graced with beauty.
Her meaning having been explained, she smiled and did not wish to reproach him.
Once, while those cowherd boys, headed by Rāma, were playing,
they reported to their mother that Kṛṣṇa had eaten clay.
Taking Kṛṣṇa by the hand and reproaching him, Yaśodā, wishing for his welfare, spoke to him whose eyes were wide with fear and agitation:
"O you of unsubdued self, why have you eaten clay in secret?"
"Indeed, these boys of yours say so, and even this elder brother of yours;
O Mother, I have not eaten them—everyone is falsely accusing me.
If my words are true, then look directly at my mouth."
When he was thus told, "Open [your mouth]," the Blessed Lord Hari,
whose sovereignty is unimpeded, being a playful human child, opened his mouth. There she beheld the entire universe— the moving and the stationary, the sky, and the directions.
The terrestrial globe with its mountains, continents, oceans, wind, fire, moon, and stars;
the wheel of luminaries, water, fire, air, and space; the sense organs born of the *vaikārika* [sattva], the mind, the subtle elements (*mātrā*), and the three qualities (*guṇas*).

Seeing this wondrous variety—the distinctions of living beings, time, nature, karma, latent impressions, and subtle bodies—within the body of his son whose mouth was wide open, he entered Vraja along with himself and fell into doubt:
"Is this a dream? Or is it the illusion of a god? Or alas, is it a delusion of my own intellect?"
Moreover, whatever innate spiritual power belongs to this very child of mine,
which is not within the range of conjecture and cannot be directly grasped by thought, mind, action, or speech—
whatever it rests upon, by whom it is perceived, and from whence it arises— that state, so difficult to conceive, I bow down to.
"He is my husband, he is my son; I am the virtuous wife of the Lord of Vraja and the mistress of all wealth.
These gopīs and gopas, along with the cattle, are mine—He by whose illusory power (māyā) I have such a deluded mind; He is my ultimate refuge.
When the gopī had thus realized the truth, that Lord [appeared].
The all-pervading Lord manifested His Vaiṣṇavī Māyā, consisting of maternal affection for a son;
immediately her memory was lost, and that cowherd woman, placing her child upon her lap, became as she had been before, her heart overwhelmed by the thickening of intense love.
His majesty was being sung by the three Vedas, the Upaniṣads, Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and the Sātvata doctrines; he regarded Hari as his own son.
Śrī Rājā said:
O Brahmin, what did Nanda do that resulted in such great and ultimate welfare,
and why did the highly fortunate Yaśodā drink from whose breast Hari drank?
Why did the parents not recognize the noble deeds performed by Kṛṣṇa as an infant?
Even today, poets sing of that which removes the impurities of the world.
Śrī Śuka said:
Droṇa, the foremost of the Vasus, together with his wife Dharā—
Regarding the instructions he was about to give, he spoke to Brahmā:
"When we two have been born upon this earth, may there arise in us supreme devotion toward Hari, the Great God and Lord of the Universe, by which one may cross over worldly misery."
Having been told "So be it," the illustrious and highly renowned Droṇa was born in Vraja;
he became known as Nanda, and that Dharā became Yaśodā.
Then, when Janārdana had become their son, there arose devotion toward the Blessed One.

O descendant of Bharata, the love between the cowherds and cowherdesses for the couple was exceedingly great. To fulfill the command of Brahmā, the omnipresent Lord Kṛṣṇa dwelt in Vraja with Balarāma and, through His own divine play, brought them joy.
Śrī Śuka said:
Once, while the household maidservants of Yaśodā, the wife of Nanda,
were occupied with other tasks, she herself churned the curd.
She sang those various songs concerning His childhood exploits that had been sung here,
remembering them at the time of churning the curd;
she wore a linen garment tied with a cord upon her broad hips.
With her pair of breasts flowing with milk from maternal affection for her son, the fair-browed woman trembled;
her bracelets on her arms jingled from the exertion of pulling the rope, her earrings swayed,
and her face was perspiring as the *mālatī* flowers fell from her loosened braid as she churned.
Approaching his mother as she was churning curd while desiring milk for her child, Hari took hold of the churning-stick and, bringing her joy, forbade her.
As she looked at his smiling face with affection, her breasts flowing with milk, he climbed onto her lap and she suckled him.
Leaving him unsatisfied, she fled away with speed while the milk was being poured out and placed upon the fire.

Then, his anger aroused, he bit the vessel of curd-mash with his teeth, its lower lip quivering and red; having broken it with a stone, he feigned tears and, entering a secluded spot, devoured the fresh butter.
Having brought out the well-boiled milk and re-entering, she saw the curd-pot;

seeing it broken, she laughed at the deed of her own son, yet she did not see him there. She found him perched upon the top of the mortar, sitting on its lid and giving as much as he desired to the monkey.
Having seen the fresh butter, his eyes suspicious due to the thought of theft, he later approached his son slowly.
Seeing her with a staff in hand, he quickly descended from there and fled like one afraid.
The gopīs pursued Him whom even the minds of yogis— minds impelled by austerity— are not able to enter;
yet His mother followed behind, her gait faltering under the weight of her broad, swaying hips, she of the slender waist.
Following the flowers that had fallen from her loosened hair-tie due to his speed,

she touched him as he ran away in guilt; with her own hand, she wiped the collyrium-stained eyes of the weeping boy who was looking up at her with eyes agitated by fear, and seizing him by the hand, she threatened him.
Abandoning her staff and perceiving her son to be afraid, she who is affectionate toward her children—
though she was well aware of his prowess— intended to bind him with a rope.
He, for whom there is neither inside nor outside, neither before nor after;
Having considered Him— the unmanifest Adhokṣaja, who is both the prior and the posterior, the exterior and the interior of the universe, and who is Himself the universe— to be a mere mortal child,
the cowherd woman bound Him with a rope to a mortar, as if He were an ordinary being.

As that rope was being tied around his little son who had committed a transgression, it became two finger-breadths too short; therefore, the cowherd woman joined another rope to it. When that one was also insufficient, she joined yet another to it.
Even that rope which Yaśodā took to bind Him was always two finger-breadths too short;
thus, as she continued to fasten the ropes of her own house while the cowherd women looked on with smiles, she herself became smilingly amazed.
Seeing his own mother, her limbs perspiring and the garlands in her hair disheveled,
Kṛṣṇa was filled with compassion for her exhaustion and bound himself. Indeed, O dear one, Hari has thus demonstrated his submissiveness to his servants.
Even by his own will, Kṛṣṇa has brought this entire world, including its lords,
under his control; neither Viriñca, nor Bhava, nor even Śrī— who rests upon his very limbs—
attained such grace as that which the Gopī obtained from him, the giver of liberation.

This Blessed Lord, the son of the cowherd girl, does not bring such ease to embodied beings as He does here to those possessed of devotion— unlike the ease found by the wise who regard Him as their own self.
Meanwhile, while His mother was preoccupied with household chores, the Lord Kṛṣṇa—
He saw first the two Arjunas, the Guhyakas who were the sons of Dhanada;
they had previously been reduced to the state of trees due to the curse of Nārada for their arrogance.
Known as Nalakūvara and Maṇigrīva, they were endowed with great splendor.
The King said: O Blessed One, please tell me the cause of that curse;
what was that censurable act by which the celestial sage fell into darkness?
Śrī Śuka said:
Having become attendants of Rudra, the two sons of the Giver of Wealth,
arrogant and intoxicated with pride, were sporting in the delightful grove of Kailāsa by the river Mandākinī.
Having drunk the intoxicating wine of Varuṇa, their eyes rolling with intoxication,
they wandered through the flowering forest accompanied by women who sang in their praise; then, entering the Ganges, they sported amidst the groves of lotuses.

The two of them sported with the young women like two elephants with their female mates. And by chance, O descendant of Kuru, the divine sage Nārada, the blessed one, saw the two gods there and perceived that they were intoxicated.

Seeing him, the goddesses were ashamed; fearing a curse, they quickly put on their garments, though the two Guhyakas remained naked. Seeing those two sons of the gods, intoxicated by wine and blinded by the pride of their beauty, [the sages cursed them].
For the sake of bestowing grace upon those two, [the Lord], about to pronounce a curse, sang this.
Śrī Nārada said:
"Indeed, for one who relishes objects of enjoyment, there is no other cause for the delusion of the intellect than the quality of passion (rajas)."
Where pride, arrogance, noble lineage, and the like prevail; where women, gambling, and liquor are common;
and where animals are slaughtered by merciless ones who have not conquered their own selves, imagining this body to be free from old age and death, though it is perishable.

Even that which is designated as "divine" is ultimately known as worms, excrement, and ashes; what does one who harms living beings know of his own self-interest for the sake of such things, since hell awaits him?
Is the body truly one's own, or does it belong to the giver of food, or even to the mother who bore it?
Whether from one's mother, father, a powerful buyer, fire, or even a dog—
since this body is common to all and its origin and dissolution are unmanifest,
what wise person, except for the wicked, would claim it as their own and kill living beings?
For one who is wretched and blinded by the intoxication of wealth, poverty is the supreme ointment.
A poor man regards all living beings through the analogy of his own condition.
Just as a person whose body has been pierced by a thorn does not desire that pain for another being, so too does the poor man feel for others.
Having attained equality with the living entities (jīvas) through his external marks, yet not pierced by the thorns [of worldly objects],
being poor and free from the arrogance of "I," he is liberated here from all intoxications;
whatever hardship he encounters by chance is indeed his supreme austerity.
For one who is perpetually poor, whose body is emaciated by hunger, and who longs for food,
the senses wither away and even the impulse to violence ceases.
It is precisely for such a poor man that saintly persons, who perceive all with equanimity, become suitable companions.
Through the virtuous, one diminishes that thirst and thereby becomes purified from afar.
What is the use of those pillars of wealth— unvirtuous, relying on the wicked, and objects of indifference— to those who are even-minded and seek the feet of Mukunda?
Therefore, I shall remove the intoxication of darkness from these two who have lost self-control; they are blinded by the pride of wealth, intoxicated by the wine of Varuṇa, and enslaved by women.
For though they are the sons of a world-guardian, they are now submerged in ignorance.
Those two, being extremely intoxicated with pride, did not realize that they were naked;
therefore, it was fitting that they should become stationary beings. However, by my grace, they shall possess memory even in that state, through my favor.
Having obtained the presence of Vāsudeva, when a hundred divine autumns have passed,
they will again attain the celestial realm, having regained their devotion.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having spoken thus, that divine sage departed for the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa;
meanwhile, Nalakūvara and Maṇigrīva remained as the twin Arjuna trees.
To fulfill the word of the sage, the foremost of the devotees of the Lord, Hari acted accordingly.
He went slowly to the place where the twin arjuna trees were;
"The celestial sage is most dear to me, since these two are the sons of the Lord of Wealth;
therefore, I shall accomplish that which was sung by that Great-Souled One."
Thus, while Arjuna and the twins were away, Kṛṣṇa went toward them;
by the mere entry of His own self, He dragged that mortar which had fallen among the animals, following after it as He pulled it out with His childlike strength.
When their leg-bindings were suddenly loosened by Dāmodara,
the two trees— whose trunks and branches trembled violently due to his supreme prowess— fell down with a fierce roar.
There, two Siddhas, whose bodies were radiant with supreme splendor like two fires produced from the friction of *kujā* wood,
approached Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of all worlds, and bowed their heads to him.
With palms joined in reverence, the two stainless ones spoke thus:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O great yogi, you are the primordial Supreme Person. The Brahmins know this entire universe, both manifest and unmanifest, to be your form."
You alone are the Lord of the body, the self, and the senses of all living beings;
You alone are the imperishable Lord Viṣṇu, the Blessed Time. You are the Great One, the subtle primordial nature (prakṛti), consisting of the qualities of passion, goodness, and darkness.
You alone are the Supreme Person, the presiding overseer who knows all fields and their transformations.
You are ungraspable by the graspable transformations— the qualities born of nature—
who here, being shrouded by those very qualities, could possibly know You who are eternally established?
Salutations to You, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the Creator; salutations to Brahman, whose majesty is concealed by the qualities that are the self-luminous radiance of Your own nature.
To You, whose incarnations are known even though You are bodiless, appearing within embodied forms.
With those various incomparable and unsurpassed heroic powers that are unattached within embodied beings,
you have now descended with a portion of your essence for the prosperity and the dissolution of all the worlds; you are the Lord of all blessings.
Obeisances to the supremely auspicious one; obeisances to the supreme blessing!
Obeisances to Vāsudeva, the peaceful one, the lord of the Yadus!
O Earth, please grant permission to us two, who are but servants following in Your footsteps.
By the grace of the Lord, the sage, we have obtained the vision of Him;
our speech is engaged in reciting His qualities, our ears in His stories, our hands in His service, and our minds at Your feet.
May my memory be fixed upon the prostration of the world at Your feet, which are the abode of all; may my sight be directed toward the vision of the virtuous who have become Your own forms.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus praised by the two of them, the Blessed Lord, the Master of Gokula,
who was bound to the mortar with a rope, laughed and spoke to the two Guhyakas. The Blessed Lord said:
