This was already known to me long ago by the compassionate sage, that through his words, the downfall of us two— who were blinded by the intoxication of wealth— was an act of grace.
This is especially true for saintly persons who possess equanimity of mind and whose very selves are dedicated to Me.
"From seeing us, bondage shall cease for a person, just as it does for the eyes from seeing the sun.
Therefore, O Nalakūvara, you two who are devoted to Me, go to his abode;
the supreme state desired by you both has been attained within Me."
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus addressed, the two of them circumambulated him and bowed down again and again;
then, taking leave of the one who had bound the mortar, they departed toward the northern direction.
Śrī Śuka said:
O best of the Kurus, having heard the sound of the two trees falling, the cowherds headed by Nanda arrived there, apprehensive due to the fear of a thunderbolt.
There on the ground they saw the twin Arjuna trees;
not understanding the cause of their falling,
they wandered about until they saw the boy bound with a rope, dragging the mortar.
"Whose is this? From where has this wonder arisen? Is it a portent? asked the timid children.
"It was by him," they said, pointing to the one standing in the middle who was dragging the mortar that had fallen crosswise; "we have seen even two men."
They did not accept what he had said, thinking, "That cannot be possible," for some among them were of doubtful mind regarding that uprooting of the two trees by the child.
[Others saw him] dragging the mortar, bound with a rope, as his own son.
Seeing this, Nanda’s face broke into a smile and he released his hold; sometimes the Blessed One danced like a child, encouraged by the cowherd women,
and at other times he sang loudly, bewildered and under their influence like a wooden puppet.
Sometimes, when commanded, he carries a stool, a measuring rod, or sandals;
and he makes gestures such as waving his arms, thereby bringing joy to his own people while demonstrating to the world that he is subject to the will of his servants.
The Blessed One brought great joy to Vraja with his childhood antics.
Hearing the cry, "O sir, buy some fruit! Acyuta, who bestows all fruits, quickly took some grain and went forth seeking fruit.
The seller of fruit, seeing his two hands devoid of grain,
filled them with fruits; and as her basket of fruit was thus filled,
she saw Kṛṣṇa on the riverbank and called out to him, who had broken the Arjuna tree.
When Rohiṇī-devī, though summoned, did not approach her two sons as they were playing intensely with other children due to their absorption in play,
she sent Yaśodā, who was deeply affectionate toward her son.
While her son was playing excessively with the other boys along with his elder brother, Yaśodā, her breasts flowing with milk from maternal affection for her child, called out to Kṛṣṇa:
"Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa, O lotus-eyed one! Dear child, come and drink from my breast."
"Enough with these diversions; you are weary from play and exhausted by hunger, my dear son.
O Rāma, come quickly, my child, along with your younger brothers, you delight of the family!
Having already taken food this morning, you ought to eat now."
"O descendant of Daśārha, the lord of Vraja is waiting for you while he is about to eat.
Come, bring us pleasure; let us go to our own homes, O boys!
Son, your limbs are covered in dust; come and take your bath."
"Today is your birth-star; give cows to the Brahmins, being pure.
Look, look at your friends, groomed by their mothers and well-adorned!
You too, having bathed and taken your meal, should sport about, well-decorated."

O King, having thus perceived her son to be the crown of all, Yaśodā’s mind became bound by affection; taking Acyuta along with Rāma by the hand, she led them to her own hut and performed the birth rites.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having experienced great portents in the Bṛhadvana forest, the elder cowherds,
headed by Nanda, gathered together and deliberated upon the affairs of Vraja.
There, a cowherd named Upānanda, who was superior in both knowledge and age, spoke.
Knowing the truth regarding place, time, and purpose, and acting for the pleasure of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, we who desire the welfare of Gokula must depart from here;
for great portents are approaching that will cause the destruction of the children.
This boy, though released by some means from the child-killing Rākṣasī,
surely fell upon the fire by the grace of Hari;
yet he was carried away through the sky by a whirlwind and led to safety from that calamity by the Daitya.
Having fallen there upon a stone slab, he was rescued by the lords of the gods;
that the boy did not die after finding himself between two trees—
whether it was he or anyone else— that too was the protection of Acyuta.
"Before this ominous portent of ill omen reaches Vraja from here,
we shall take the children and depart elsewhere with our followers to the forest named Vṛndāvana, a fresh grove suitable for cattle."

"Let us go this very day to that place where the cowherds, cowherd-maidens, and cows find their refuge, and where the sacred mountain is covered with grass and creepers. Harness the carts without delay;
if it pleases you, let the herds of cattle go on ahead."

Having heard that, O King, the cowherds, their minds focused on a single purpose, exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! They gathered their respective families—elders, children, women, and all their belongings—and set out with their equipment fully prepared.
Having loaded the cattle onto carts, the cowherds— vigilant and with bows in hand— placed the herds at the front, filled their horns on all sides,
and set out together with the family priest amidst the great sound of musical instruments.
The gopīs, mounted upon their chariots, their fresh breasts radiant with saffron, wearing golden neck-ornaments and fine garments,
sang of Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes with great affection.
Likewise, Yaśodā and Rohiṇī were seated together in a single cart.
Eager to hear stories concerning Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, they departed;
having entered Vṛndāvana, which brings happiness at all times,
they established their dwellings there with wagons arranged in the shape of a half-moon.

O King, beholding Vṛndāvana, Govardhana, and the sandy banks of the Yamunā, Rāma and Mādhava felt the highest delight. Thus, bestowing affection upon the inhabitants of Vraja through their childhood antics, they remained there.
In due time and by their own destiny, the two cowherd boys became keepers of calves;
not far from the land of Vraja, accompanied by the cowherd children and equipped with various playthings, they tended the calves.
In one place they played the flute, in another they threw stones; in some places with their feet and tinkling bells, and in others with artificial bulls,
acting like bulls and bellowing, they fought with one another.
Imitating the cries of living beings, they moved about like ordinary mortals.
Once, while Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma were tending the calves with their own companions on the bank of the Yamunā, a demon arrived, desiring to kill them.
Seeing him in the form of a calf, having joined the herd of calves, Hari,
showing him to Baladeva, slowly approached as if bewildered;
Acyuta then seized him by his two hind legs along with his tail.
Having whirled him around, he hurled him onto the tip of a wood-apple tree, and his life departed.
That massive-bodied demon fell down as the wood-apples were being dropped.
Seeing this, the astonished boys exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!"
And the gods became thoroughly satisfied, raining down flowers;
those two, having become cowherd boys— the sole protectors of all the worlds—
wandered about tending the calves after their morning meal.
One day, having gone near a body of water to let their respective calves drink, they all drank the water themselves.
There, the boys beheld a great being standing.
There,
the great demon named Baka, assuming the form of a crane,
arrived suddenly and, being powerful with a sharp beak, swallowed Kṛṣṇa like a mountain peak shattered by a thunderbolt and fallen.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa seized by the great crane, Balarāma and the other boys became senseless,
like the senses deprived of the life-breath.
[Then they saw] that son of a cowherd, the father of the Teacher of the World, burning the base of the crane's palate like fire.
The crane, however, being excessively enraged, immediately vomited up the bone and again attempted to strike with his beak.
As he was attacking, the Lord of the virtuous seized the crane—the friend of Kaṃsa—by the two mandibles with His arms;
while the children looked on, He who brings joy to the inhabitants of heaven effortlessly tore him apart like a blade of vīraṇa grass.
Then the inhabitants of the celestial realm showered the enemy of Baka with *nandana* jasmine and other flowers;
they praised him with the sounds of drums and conch shells, and seeing this, the cowherd boys were filled with wonder.
Having recovered from Baka’s mouth, the boys, headed by Rāma, rejoiced like the group of senses regaining the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Embracing Him upon His arrival at that place, they were filled with bliss; leading the calves back to the cow-pen, they sang of those events.
Hearing this, the cowherds and cowherd girls were struck with wonder, and honoring their most beloved friend, they gazed at him with thirsty eyes as if he had returned from the dead out of longing.
"Oh, alas! This child has encountered many deaths;
surely he must have previously committed some offense against them, since he is in fear of them. Yet, even so, those of terrible aspect do not overcome him."
Having approached him with the intent to kill, they perish like moths in a fire.
Oh, the words of those who know Brahman are never untrue! For that which the venerable Garga said has been experienced exactly so.

Thus, Nanda and the other cowherds, joyfully recounting the stories of Kṛṣṇa and Rāma and enjoying themselves, did not experience the suffering of worldly existence. In this way, through their childhood pastimes, the two spent their youth in Vraja.
By means of hiding places, bridge-constructions, leaping like monkeys, and other such methods—
Śrī Śuka said:
Having risen early in the morning from Vraja, he once set his mind on grazing in the forest along with his companions and the calves.
Awakening them with his beautiful sound from the horn, Lord Hari emerged, preceded by His calves;
along with Him came thousands of affectionate boys, carrying smooth sticks, canes, horns, and flutes.
Placing their respective calves before them—numbering more than a thousand each—they went forth with great joy.
Having formed groups of their own calves with countless calves of Kṛṣṇa, they grazed them about here and there, sporting with the playful activities of children,
using fruits, sprouts, clusters of blossoms, peacock feathers, and mineral pigments.
Though adorned with glass, guñjā berries, gems, and gold, they did not even notice their ornaments;
stealing each other's carrying-baskets and such, they threw them at those they recognized from afar.
And those standing there, laughing from a distance, gave them back again.
If Kṛṣṇa had gone far away to behold the beauty of the forest, they would have rejoiced by touching him, each saying, "I first! I first!
Some played flutes while others blew horns.
Some were singing along with bees, others warbling with cuckoos;
some were running with partridges, others walking with noble swans; some were perching with cranes, and others dancing with peacocks.
Dragging the young monkeys, climbing trees with them,
playing with them, and leaping among the leafy branches;
together with frogs, they crossed rivers overflowing with flowing water.
Laughing at their own reflections and shouting back at their echoes,

those who had accumulated a mass of merit— having attained the service of the Supreme Deity through the experience of the bliss of Brahman characteristic of the virtuous, yet still relying on *māyā*— played together with the Divine Child.
The dust of whose feet is unattainable even by self-controlled yogis after many births of arduous effort—
that very same one has now personally become the object of my vision.
How can the good fortune of the inhabitants of Vraja be described?
Then, a great demon named Agha descended, unable to endure their joyful play—
that which is constantly awaited within by even the immortals who drink nectar and desire their own lives.
Seeing the children headed by Kṛṣṇa, Aghāsura— directed by Kaṃsa and accompanied by Baka and his younger brother Bakī— thought:
"This one is indeed the cause of the destruction of those two, my brothers."
"I shall slay these two along with their army when they have made my friends like sesame seeds and water; then the inhabitants of Vraja will have lost their lives.
For what concern is there regarding bodies once the life-force has departed? Indeed, those who possess breath are the true sustainers of progeny."
Having thus resolved, that wicked one assumed a massive python’s body, as long as a *yojana* and as thick as a great mountain;

with its mouth wide open like a cave, he then lay across the path, desiring to swallow [the travelers]. With the mountains for his lower lip and the clouds for his upper lip, with the caves for the interior of his mouth and the mountain peaks for his fangs, he remained there.
With its mouth filled with darkness, its tongue as the extended path, its breath like a harsh wind, and its gaze hot as a forest fire,
[the serpent] saw him in that state; perceiving him to be the very splendor of Vṛndāvana,
they all playfully imagined him to be the gaping maw of a great python.
"O friends, tell me: does this mass of being standing before us not resemble the gaping maw of a serpent ready to swallow us?
Truly, it is like a dense cloud reddened by the rays of the sun, appearing as the upper jaw."
The lower lip is like a riverbank, reddened by its own reflection;
it rivals the two nostrils on the left and right, which resemble the hollows of trees.
Behold also these high peaks, which are like his fangs.
This path strewn with arrows roars against my tongue;
this darkness that has entered within them also dwells within my mouth. Behold, this forest heat and harsh wind appears like my very breath.

"Even though he has the foul stench of the creatures burnt by him, like the smell of raw meat within, why does he not devour us who are settled here? If he is indeed such [a predator], he will perish in an instant like the crane. Seeing the face of the crane's enemy [the cat] approaching, they laughed and departed with slaps of their hands.

Having heard this mutual falsehood spoken by those ignorant of Him, and having reflected upon it, the Rākṣasa— who dwells in the hearts of all beings— realized that what was said was not untrue, though it appeared to be so.
Just as the Blessed One set his mind upon restraining his own kinsmen,
the infant calves along with their mother entered the interior of the demon’s belly; they were not swallowed,
for the Rākṣasa was waiting for the arrival of Baka’s form while remembering his own slain beloved.
Seeing them— those who had no other protector, fallen from his own hand, wretched, and like fodder for the fire in the belly of Death— Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of fearlessness to all, [acted].
Afflicted by compassion and amazed by what fate had ordained,
he thought: "What purpose is there here in the life of this wicked man,
or in the continued injury to these virtuous ones?"
Reflecting deeply on how this duality might come to pass, Hari, who perceives everything without exception, understood and entered its mouth;
then, the gods, their vision obscured by clouds, cried out "Ha! Ha! in fear.

And those demons, such as Kaṃsa and others, who were the kinsmen of Agha, rejoiced upon hearing that. But the imperishable Lord Kṛṣṇa, wishing to crush him who sought to pulverize Him along with the boy and the calf, suddenly expanded His neck.

Then, as Atikāya’s path was blocked and he wandered here and there with his vision lost, the vital air (prāṇa) within his body became obstructed; bursting through the crown of his head, it emerged outside.
By that very [force], when all his life-breaths had departed, he saw his calves and friends as deceased.
Having raised him up with his glance, the Blessed Lord Mukunda emerged once more from his mouth, accompanied by him.

A great, wondrous light, arising from the coils of the fat serpent and blazing the ten directions with its own radiance, waited in the sky for the Lord's departure; then, while the gods looked on, it entered into that light.
Then, exceedingly delighted, the celestial nymphs honored him with flowers, the gods with dances,
and the musicians with songs and instrumental music.
The brahmins [offered] hymns and the attendants the sounds of "Victory!";

hearing those wonderful sounds of praise, excellent music, songs, and the various festive auspicious cries of "Victory! and so forth, the low-born one (Kṛṣṇa) quickly arrived from his own abode and, upon seeing the lord of the earth, was filled with wonder.

O King, that wonderful, dried-up python skin in Vṛndāvana became a cave-like playground for the residents of Vraja for many days. This was a deed performed by Hari in his childhood, whereby he liberated himself from the serpent.
Seeing this in the childhood stage of Mṛtyu, the boys in Vraja were struck with wonder and said:
"This is not surprising for the Supreme Creator, the source of all high and low, who manifests as a human child through His illusory power—
that even Agha, whose sins were washed away by the touch of Him, attained equality with the Self, a state so difficult for the wicked to achieve."
O dear one, since even a mental image of His limbs placed within [the heart] once bestows the destination of the devotees of the Lord,
how much more so when He Himself has entered within— He who has cast aside all illusion through the direct experience of eternal self-bliss?
Śrī Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, having thus heard the wonderful life-story of his own father, which was given by the god among the Yādavas, the King—
his mind captivated by that very merit— again questioned the son of Vyāsa.
Śrī Rājā said:
O Brahman, how could that which was performed by Hari during His childhood be experienced at a different time? For the children sang of what had been done by Hari in His paugaṇḍa stage.
O Great Yogin, O Guru, tell me this; my curiosity is great.
"Surely this is the illusory power (māyā) of Hari himself, and not otherwise.
O Teacher, we, though merely kṣatriyas, are the most fortunate in the world;
for from you we repeatedly drink the holy nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s stories."
Śrī Sūta said:
Thus questioned, that son of Bādarāyaṇa had all his senses captivated by the infinite Lord who was thus brought to mind.
Having regained his outward vision with great difficulty, he slowly replied to him, O best among the supreme devotees of the Lord. Śrī Śuka said:
Well asked, O most fortunate one, O best of devotees, that you,
though hearing the stories of the Lord repeatedly, still desire to hear them anew.
This is the very nature of the virtuous who possess the essence— that even for those whose speech, hearing, and minds are directed toward His purpose, they remain ever-thirsting.

O King, listen attentively as I tell you this secret; for masters may indeed speak even their secrets to a devoted disciple. Listen to the virtuous news of Acyuta, which, though it concerns women and libertines, seems ever new at every moment.
Having thus protected the cowherd boys from the mouth of Death,
the Blessed One led them to the riverbank and spoke as follows:
"O friends, how delightful is this riverbank, perfect for our play, with its soft and pure sands!"
"Filled with trees shimmering with the echoes of the humming of bees attracted by the fragrance of blossoming lotuses,
we shall eat here, for our hunger has grown intense during the day;
meanwhile, O calves, drink water nearby and graze slowly on grass."
Saying "So be it," they had the children drink milk, tethered the calves on the grassy sward,
and unfastening their carrying-baskets, they ate joyfully together with the Blessed One.
All around Kṛṣṇa, circles of many rows of kings were gathered.
With their faces turned toward Him and their eyes blossoming with joy, the boys of Vraja sat together in the forest and shone like petals upon the pericarp of a lotus.
Some ate with flowers, some with petals, some with sprouts, shoots, or fruits; others used young leaves, bark, or even stones as their vessels.
All of them showed one another their respective preferences for various foods.
Laughing and making others laugh, they descended together with the Lord;
he carried a flute against his belly and a horn and a staff under his arms,
held a smooth morsel of food in his left hand, and had its fruits upon his fingers.
Standing in the midst of his own circle of friends, making them laugh with his own jests,
the enjoyer of sacrifice indulged in childhood sports while the world of heaven looked on. O descendant of Bharata, thus did they enjoy themselves among the calves, their minds fixed on Acyuta.
The calves, however, lured by the grass, entered deep into the interior of the forest.
Seeing them terrified with fear, Kṛṣṇa spoke to dispel their dread: "O friends, do not despair; I shall bring back the calves."

Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa went into the mountain caves, groves, and thickets searching for his calves, with a morsel of food still in his hand; the lotus-born Brahmā, the creator, entered within that very place, seeking the Lord who appeared as a child through his illusory power.
Standing in the sky, he who had previously hidden the calves and the cowherd boys elsewhere so that they might see his other charming majesty as well,
was filled with supreme wonder upon seeing the powerful Lord's liberation of the demon Aghāsura.
Then, not seeing the calves, Kṛṣṇa returned to the riverbank and searched everywhere in the forest for both the calves and the cowherd boys; yet,
though he was the knower of all things, he did not see the calves or the herdsmen anywhere within the deep forest.

Kṛṣṇa suddenly arrived at everything that had been prepared according to the ritual injunctions. Then Kṛṣṇa, the Lord and creator of the universe, assumed a dual form in order to bring joy to his mothers and to Kaṃsa.

As long as [He] has the diminutive body of a cowherd boy with calves; as long as He possesses hands, feet, and so forth; as long as He has a staff, horns, a bamboo flute, leaves, and a crest; as long as He has ornaments and garments; as long as He has character, virtues, name, form, and age; and as long as He has His pastimes and other activities—[so long shall I remain].
Everything was pervaded by Viṣṇu; the unborn Lord, whose form is everything, shone like his own body.
Having himself warded off his own calves—the cows who were his very self—with his own calves who were his own self, the Soul of All entered the cowherd settlement, sporting with his own pastimes.
Having led each of those calves away separately and settled them in their respective stalls,
O King, He became the very self of each one and entered each of those dwellings.
Their mothers, rising in haste at the sound of the flute, lifted Him up with their arms and embraced Him tightly.
Considering the nectar-like flow of milk from her breasts, moistened by affection, to be the supreme Brahman, she nourished her sons.
Then, Mādhava was cherished with royal massages, baths, ointments, ornaments, protective rites, forehead marks, and food;
thus delighting them with his own conduct, he departed at nightfall when the hour of Yama had arrived.

Then the cows, having quickly approached the cow-pen, were reunited with their respective calves who had been summoned by the sounds of "hum"; licking them repeatedly, they caused the milk flowing from their udders to be drunk. In this [pastime], the motherhood of the cows and the gopīs was characterized by an abundance of affection beyond ordinary measure.
As before, even among these [other] children of Hari, there was no [manifestation of] *māyā*; yet,
day by day for a year, the creeper of affection of the inhabitants of Vraja toward their own children gradually increased beyond all bounds, whereas toward Kṛṣṇa it grew as if unprecedented.
Thus, protecting himself by means of his own self under the pretext of being a cowherd boy, he,
the protector of calves, sported for a year in the forest and the cow-pen.
Once, while tending the calves, he entered the forest together with Rāma.
When five nights of three watches each had passed, completing the year, the unborn Lord [Kṛṣṇa] was there;
then, as the cows wandered from afar toward the cow-pen with their calves,
they saw grass upon the summit of Govardhana Hill while grazing.

Then, seeing that, overcome by affection for him and forgetting his own self, that herd of cows—having lost sight of their own difficult path—went with speed toward the tears [of the calf], lowing "huṅ" sounds; they had two legs, humps, and necks, with upturned faces and tails.
Having come together, the cows, though themselves mothers of calves, allowed their calves to suckle from them.
As if swallowing their own limbs and licking the milk from their udders, the cows— driven by the pain of being blocked, the exhaustion of their efforts, shame,
and great distress— arrived after the hardship of the difficult path and beheld their calves with the young bulls.
Their hearts flooded with the nectar of love born from beholding Him, their passion awakened and their anger gone,
those elders lifted the children onto their arms, embraced them, and smelled their heads, thereby attaining supreme joy.
Then the cowherds, now advanced in years, were perfectly satisfied by the embrace of their grandchildren.
Having slowly emerged from their hardship with tears flowing as they remembered him,

Balarāma observed the moment-by-moment intensity of longing in the ocean of love of the people of Vraja; seeing that even toward their children whose breasts were no longer being nursed, they were moved by causeless affection, he reflected.
"What is this wonder, as it were, regarding Vāsudeva, the Self of all?
An unprecedented love for Him increases within the people of Vraja and their children.
Who is this woman? From where has she come? Is she divine, or a human woman, or perhaps an Asurī?"
"Generally, the illusory powers (*māyā*) of my Lord are such that nothing else can delude even me.
Having reflected thus, the descendant of Daśārha (Kṛṣṇa) beheld with his divine vision all the calves, along with their keepers, as being Vaikuṇṭha itself.
"Neither these lords of the gods nor these sages are [the source]; you alone shine, O Lord, even while appearing as the locus of differentiation.
How can you say, according to the Veda, that everything is separate from you? When he had spoken thus, Balarāma understood the account related by the Lord.
Just then, the Self-born Brahmā arrived, measuring time by his own lifespan, which lasts for but a moment.
He beheld Hari playing as before for a year, together with everyone; indeed, all the boys who were in Gokula, along with the calves,
had fallen asleep upon my illusory bed and have not yet awakened.
"From here, these others—deluded by my *māyā*—have come from somewhere else;
they are exactly as many as those who were sporting there with Viṣṇu for a year.
Having thus meditated for a long time upon these distinctions, that Self-born One [Brahmā]...
"Which ones are true and which are not?"— it was impossible for him to know this in any way.
Thus, while Viṣṇu— who is beyond delusion and the deluder of the entire universe— was causing confusion,
the demon too was himself utterly deluded by his own *māyā*.
Just as darkness vanishes in the night at sunrise, or as the light of fireflies disappears in the day, so too does the great power of other māyās perish within the self of one who is engaged in yoga.
At that very moment, while Aja was looking on, all the cowherd boys [disappeared].
They appeared dark as rain clouds, dressed in yellow silk garments,
four-armed, with conch shells, discs, maces, and lotuses in their hands;
they wore crowns, earrings, necklaces, and forest garlands.
Their arms were adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark, armlets, gems, conch shells, and bracelets; they shone with anklets, bangles, waist-bands, and finger-rings;
and from their feet to their heads, they were covered with fresh garlands of *tulasī*.
With soft glances from all their limbs, offered by those of great merit, smiles as bright as moonlight, and sidelong looks tinged with red,
they were like the Creator and the Protector through the qualities of *rajas* and *sattva*, as if for their own purposes.

He is worshipped individually by all beings, from the self (Ātman) down to a blade of grass, including those with form and those moving or stationary, through various offerings such as dance and song,
and by means of the powers of *aṇimā* and others, as well as the sovereign glories beginning with *ajā*.
She was attended by the twenty-four principles beginning with the Great Principle (mahat),
which were surrounded by Time, inherent nature, latent impressions, desire, action, and the modes of nature—
all of whom had their own powers destroyed by her majesty and appeared in embodied forms.
The unborn [Lord] thus beheld all those whose forms consist solely of the essence of truth, knowledge, infinity, and bliss,
and whose vast majesty remains untouched even by the vision of the Upaniṣads.
By whose light all this world, including the moving and the unmoving, shines;
from him, with his eleven senses paralyzed by the surge of intense curiosity,
Brahmā became silent, like a puppet-girl within a city of clay.

Thus, when the Lord is inconceivable, His own majesty is self-evident, and He is the Supreme who cannot be measured by the limited cognition of others—when even one who is not the Master becomes bewildered, wondering "What is this? at the sight of Him; ||| BhP_10.13.057/4 tasminn eva tadā prabhau bhagavati pratyakṣato dṛṣṭavati BhP_10.13.057/5 śrī-śuka uvāca | śrī-śuka said: ||| BhP_10.13.057/6 atha tatraiva saṅkarṣaṇo bhagavatā kṛta-saṁvid ātmānam āviścakāra ||| BhP_10.13.057/7 Then, right there, Saṅkarṣaṇa, having received a signal from the Blessed One, manifested Himself. ||| BhP_10.13.057/8 tam āgatam abhipretya bhagavān ādi-pūruṣaḥ BhP_10.13.057/9 pratyudgamya parirabhyopasṛṣṭam abhinandya ca ||| BhP_10.13.057/9 Perceiving that he had arrived, the Blessed One, the Primeval Person, went out to meet him, embraced him, and greeted the one who had approached. ||| BhP_10.13.057/10 pṛthivyām upaveśyātha pāda-saṁvāhana-kriyā BhP_10.13.057/11 cakre tasyācyutaḥ sārdhaṁ rāmeṇāmalayā girā ||| BhP_10.13.057/10 Then, having seated him upon the earth, Acyuta performed the service of massaging his feet together with Rāma and with pure speech. ||| BhP_10.13.057/11 tasmai bhagavān āsanam upadiśya kṛta-saṁvidaḥ BhP_10.13.057/12 saṁviveśa yathā-nyāyam upasaṁsṛṣṭam ātmavān ||| BhP_10.13.057/11 Having offered a seat to him, the self-controlled Blessed One sat down according to custom with Saṅkarṣaṇa, who had already received his signal. ||| BhP_10.13.057/12 atha tatra mahā-bhāgaḥ kaścid brahma-vic-chikhāmaṇiḥ BhP_10.13.057/13 upasaṁśrāvayan viprān upāsīno 'bhyagāyata ||| BhP_10.13.057/12 Now, a certain highly fortunate crest-jewel among the knowers of Brahman, sitting nearby and instructing the brāhmaṇas, began to sing. ||| BhP_10.13.057/13 śrī-brahma-vic-chikhāmaṇir uvāca | The crest-jewel among the knowers of Brahman said: ||| BhP_10.13.057/14 ya eṣaḥ sākṣād akṣeṣu tiṣṭhan sarvendriyair api BhP_10.13.057/15 na ceṣṭate na karmāṇi bibharti ||| BhP_10.13.057/14 He who, dwelling directly within the senses, does not act through any of the sense-organs nor does He perform actions. ||| BhP_10.13.057/16 ya eṣo 'ntar-hṛdaye 'ñjasaiva ti
Having realized this, the Supreme Being suddenly withdrew the curtain of Māyā from Aja;
then, having regained his senses, who [Aja] arose like one returning from the dead and,
opening his eyes with great difficulty, spoke this along with himself.

Immediately looking all around, he beheld before him Vṛndāvana, the beloved of all, filled with trees that provide sustenance for people; there, even men, deer, and other creatures who are by nature fierce enemies, lived together in harmony.
There, like friends, they bore the burden of his hunger, thirst, fatigue,
and other such states; and he, the non-dual Brahman, the supreme, infinite, and unfathomable consciousness, enacted the drama of childhood within the lineage of the cowherds.
As before, searching all around for his calves as if they were friends,
the Supreme Lord Brahmā saw one calf with a mouthful of grass in its hand;
seeing this, he quickly descended from his own chariot.
Having cast his body upon the earth like a golden staff,
and having touched the pair of His feet with the tips of their four crowns,
they bowed down and performed a consecration with the fine waters of their joyful tears.
Rising again and again, he fell at the feet of Kṛṣṇa after a long time,
remaining there as he remembered over and over again the greatness he had previously witnessed.
Then, slowly rising and wiping his eyes, he gazed up at Mukunda with his neck bowed low.
With palms joined in reverence, humble, composed, and trembling with a voice faltering from emotion,
the illustrious Brahmā said: "I bow to You, O Worthy of Praise, whose body is like a cloud and whose garment is the lightning."
To Him whose face shines with a crest of *guñjā* berries and peacock feathers,
who bears the beauty of the marks of wild garlands, mouthfuls of grass, a bamboo staff, and a horn, and whose gentle feet are the source of all cattle; to Him, the protector of the animals.

O Lord, no one is capable of even mentally comprehending within their heart this divine form of Yours, which is composed of Your own will and not of material elements; how much less so can anyone grasp it directly, since it is the very experience of Your own bliss?
Therefore, casting aside the effort toward such knowledge, let us simply bow down.

O Unconquered One, those who remain steadfast in their respective stations and live by constantly vocalizing Your message— which has entered their ears through the Vedas— with body, speech, and mind, have effectively conquered even You within the three worlds.
O All-pervading Lord, for those who cast aside devotion— the path to the highest good— and strive only for the attainment of pure knowledge,
nothing remains for them but toil.

O Infinite One, O Acyuta! Just as those who merely thresh the outer husks of grain do not obtain the rice within, so too, although there were many yogīs here in this world, they attained Your supreme goal only after awakening through devotion alone—devotion offered to You by means of their own duties performed with their efforts dedicated to You, and brought forth through the narrations of Your glories. O Lotus-eyed One, they reached that highest state.
Nevertheless, O Infinite One, Your majesty, whose qualities are immeasurable, can be understood by those whose inner selves are pure;

for You are changeless, self-experienced, formless, and the very Self that is realized as non-different from the knower—indeed, not otherwise. Who indeed is capable of measuring the qualities of You, whose nature is the modes of material energy, even though You have descended out of compassion?
By those well-measured moments of time, the dust of the earth, the mist in the sky, and the radiance of the stars are all determined.

Therefore, observing Your compassion with keen insight, one who lives while experiencing the ripening of his own deeds and offers obeisances to You with heart, speech, and body— he alone is the heir to the state of liberation.
O Infinite One, O Supreme Self, O Illusionist who employs *māyā*, I see my own unworthiness even before You;
for having spread out Your illusory power (*māyā*) to behold Your own majesty, how small I was, like a spark in a fire!
Therefore, O Acyuta, forgive me, who am born of the mode of passion (*rajas*), ignorant, and one who imagined a lord separate from You.

"He whose eyes are blinded by the dense darkness of the pride of the unborn (Brahmā) deserves my compassion, for he has me as his protector. "But where am I— my body being only seven spans in height, confined within the pot-like cosmic egg enveloped by the elements of fire, water, earth, and the great egoity that moves through space?"
Where is such greatness of Yours— whose movement through the atoms of countless cosmic eggs occurs on the path of the wind within the pores of Your hair—
compared to the lifting of Your feet while still in the womb? O Adhokṣaja, it is not even fit to be mentioned before You.

"O Infinite One, is there even a little within your belly that can be described as 'existent' or 'non-existent'? The statement that Brahmā emerged from the lotus-stalk of the navel of Nārāyaṇa at the time of the dissolution of the three worlds in the universal ocean is certainly not false; however, O Lord, I have not emerged from you."
You are indeed Nārāyaṇa, for you are the Self of all embodied beings, the sovereign Lord, and the witness of the entire world.
O dear one, the term "Nārāyaṇa" is derived from the fact that men (nara) are the source of waters (aya), and that too is true; it is not Your own illusory power (māyā).
If that world-body of Yours were situated within the water, then You Yourself would be the manifest universe.
O Blessed One, was it not seen by me at that very moment?
Or was it truly well-seen within my heart at that very moment? Why has it vanished from view again so suddenly?

In this very incarnation of the manifestation of Māyā, You have indeed revealed the illusory nature of this entire manifest universe— both its external, clearly visible aspects and its entirety within Your mother’s womb—
in such a way that all this appears with its own self-nature within Your belly.
All that [was seen] even here in you; how could this have been without your *māyā*?
This very day, even without you, why was the illusory nature of yours not demonstrated to me?
You were alone at first, and then all the friends and calves of Vraja appeared.
There were as many four-armed forms as there are universes, all of which were worshipped by me along with all those beings;
yet only those very same universes remained, while that immeasurable, non-dual Brahman alone was left over.
To those ignorant of Your path, You manifest Yourself as the Self within the non-Self, spreading forth Your illusory power (*māyā*).

O Lord, just as I am the creator of the universe, you are its ordainer, and the three-eyed Śiva is its end; likewise, O Sovereign, though you are unborn, you manifest births among the gods, sages, humans, animals, and even aquatic creatures.
O Creator, these births are for the sake of subduing the wicked who are intoxicated by pride, and for the sake of bestowing grace upon the virtuous.
O Infinite One, O Blessed Lord, O Supreme Self, who in these three worlds knows Your incarnations, O Lord of Yoga?
Where, how, how many, and when do You expand Your *yoga-māyā* while sporting?
Therefore, this entire world is unreal in its essential nature.
That which appears like a dream, devoid of intellect and consisting of manifold sufferings,
though arising from Māyā, shines as if real only within You, the infinite one whose body is eternal bliss and consciousness.
You alone are the one Self, the ancient Person, the Truth, self-luminous, infinite, and primordial;
eternal, imperishable, ever-blissful, stainless, full, non-dual, liberated from all limiting adjuncts, and immortal.
Such as You are, they perceive You—the Self of even all embodied beings—as the very Self of their own selves.
Those who possess the excellent eye of the Upaniṣads obtained from their guru and the Sun cross over, as it were, the ocean of worldly existence.
To those who do not know the Self as the Self, the entire manifold world appears as born from that very [Self];
yet by means of knowledge, it dissolves once again, just as the appearance and disappearance of a serpent's coils occur upon a rope.
O Knower of Truth, bondage to existence and liberation from it are known as ignorance and knowledge; they are two names for these states and nothing else exists apart from them.
When the eternal, pure, and supreme Self is contemplated, these two appear like day and night in the sun.
Having realized You as the Self and the Supreme, and the Supreme as the very Self...
The Self, moreover, is to be sought within; alas, how great is the ignorance of the ignorant!

O Infinite One, while You exist within, the virtuous abandon that which is not You and seek You alone. Indeed, even if it were a non-existent serpent within, would the wise go for a real jewel that exists there? How much more so for You?

Nevertheless, O Lord, only one who is favored by even a tiny fragment of the grace of Your two lotus feet truly knows the reality of the greatness of the Blessed One; no other can know it, even if they search for a long time.
Therefore, O Protector, let that great fortune be mine—whether in this life or in another, even among the animals.
By whom, though I am but one among the people of this world, I have come to serve the sprout-like feet of Your Majesty.

Oh, how exceedingly blessed are the cowherd women of Vraja, who with great joy drank the nectar of Your breast-milk— O Lord, for whose satisfaction even the sacrifices performed by You in the form of a calf are not sufficient even today!
"Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune for Nanda the cowherd and the inhabitants of Vraja, that their friend is the Supreme Bliss, the Perfect, Eternal Brahman!
O Acyuta, let alone the greatness of their good fortune!"
"Alas, we eleven are indeed most fortunate,
for we drink repeatedly from the goblets of our senses this nectar-wine of the honey flowing from Your feet, O Śarva and the other gods!"
That birth in this forest is indeed a source of great fortune, whatever it may be,
since even here in Gokula there is the sprinkling of the dust from the feet of the Lord;
for my entire life is the Blessed Mukunda himself.
Even today, the dust of whose feet is sought after by the Vedas— O Lord,
does Your Honor grant it to these inhabitants of Ghoṣa?
Our minds, wandering elsewhere, are bewildered as to where we might find any fruit other than You, who are the fruit of all fruits.
Even Pūtanā, along with her kin, was offered by the gods to You as if out of devotion to Your form;
for those whose abode, wealth, friends, beloved ones, self, sons, life-breath, and hopes are all for Your sake— for them, lust and other passions are merely thieves, and their home is but a prison.

O Lord, as long as those people do not [worship] Your feet, O Kṛṣṇa, so long does the fetter of delusion remain; though You are beyond all worldly manifestation, You nevertheless imitate it on this earth in order to spread the mass of bliss for those who have taken refuge in You.

Let those who know already know; what is the use of much speaking? O Lord, the majesty of Your mind, body, and speech is not within the range of my perception. Grant me leave, O Kṛṣṇa; You know all, for You are the all-seeing.
You alone are the Lord of the worlds; this world is offered unto You.
O Śrī-Kṛṣṇa, who brings delight to the lotus-like Vṛṣṇi clan, and who causes the increase of the earth, the gods, the twice-born, the cattle, and the oceans!
O dispeller of the darkness of false dharma, O enemy of the demons who afflict the earth, O Arhat, O Blessed One, may you endure until the end of the kalpa and the sun; salutations unto You!
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus praised the Infinite One, circumambulated him three times, and bowed at his feet,
the Creator of the World departed for his own abode, which he had desired.
Then, having taken leave of them, the Blessed One [dismissed] those who were previously stationed there.
He brought the calves to the riverbank as before, to his own former friend. O King, though a full year had passed for the Lord of their lives and their inner self,
the boys— struck by Kṛṣṇa’s illusory power— considered it to be only half a moment.
What is there that those whose minds are deluded by *māyā* do not forget in this world— [that] by which the entire universe is deluded and constantly forgets its true self?
And his friends said to Kṛṣṇa, "Welcome to you who have come with such great speed!"
"Even a single morsel brought here was not eaten; let it be eaten properly.
Then Hṛṣīkeśa, laughing, ate together with the children, and showing them the python's hide, he returned from the forest to Vraja.
His body was variegated with peacock feathers, flowers, forest products, and minerals;
he was enriched by the festive sounds of his loud flute, leaves, and horn;
and while tending the calves, his pure fame was sung by his followers.

He whose sight was a festival for the eyes of the gopīs entered the cowherd settlement; the children in Vraja sang, "Today this great serpent has been slain by this son of Yaśodā and Nanda, and we have been saved from him."
The King said:
"O Brahmin, how can such love for Kṛṣṇa—who is born of another—arise, which has never before occurred even toward one's own offspring? Please explain this."
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, for all living beings, one's own self alone is most dear;
other things, such as children and wealth, are dear only because they belong to that self.

O king of kings, O best of the royal order, the affection that embodied beings feel for their own respective selves is not matched by the attachment they hold toward sons, wealth, homes, and the like. This is true even for those men who maintain the doctrine that the body is the self.
The body is not as dear as those who follow it;
for if the body were possessed of the sense of "mine," then it would not be as dear as the self. Indeed, even while this body decays, the hope for life remains exceedingly strong.
Therefore, one's own self is the most beloved of all embodied beings;
for the sake of that self alone is this entire world of moving and non-moving things. Know this Kṛṣṇa to be the Self of all selves.

For the welfare of the world, He too appears here as if possessing a body through His illusory power (māyā). To those who know the reality here, everything that is stationary or moving is the form of the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa; there is no other substance whatsoever here.
The essential nature of all things resides in the Lord;
even of Him, Kṛṣṇa the Blessed One is the essence—what then could be said of that which is not His form?
Those who have taken refuge in the boat of the sprout-like feet of Murāri, the Great Abode of holy fame, [attain liberation].
The ocean of worldly existence is but a cow’s footprint compared to that supreme state; for those who have attained it, there are no more misfortunes.
All this that I was asked by you here has been narrated to you;
that which was performed by Hari in his childhood has now been proclaimed in his youth.

Hearing this account of Murāri’s deeds performed with his friends— which destroy all sins— and his eating of grass-blades, as well as his other manifest forms and his hymns of praise to Aja (the Unborn), a person attains all their goals by listening to and chanting it.
Thus, through these childhood pastimes, the two of them passed their youth in Vraja.
By means of hiding places, bridge-constructions, monkey-leaps, and so forth—
Śrī Śuka said: And then, while they were in the beauty of their childhood years in Vraja...
Those two, esteemed by the cowherds,
while tending the cows together with their friends,
made the sacred Vṛndāvana exceedingly beautiful with their footprints.
Then Mādhava, endowed with strength and surrounded by cowherds chanting his own glory, blew his flute;
placing the cattle before him, he entered the flower-bearing forest, desiring to sport there—
a place crowded with bees, deer, and birds of sweet song, and possessing lakes of water as vast as the great mind.

Perceiving that the place was perfumed by the wind carrying the fragrance of hundred-petaled lotuses, the Blessed One set His mind upon enjoying Himself there. Beholding the trees there—whose branches were touching His feet with the beauty of their reddish sprouts and the great weight of their fruits and flowers—the Primeval Person, the First Man, looked at His elder brother as if smiling with joy and said: bhagavān uvāca: "O elder brother, look! These forest lords touch Your crown with the splendor of their reddish shoots, which bear the heavy burden of abundant fruit and flowers. The Blessed One spoke: "Behold these forest trees, O elder brother; they touch Your crest with the beauty of their reddish sprouts and the great mass of their fruits and blossoms. Seeing the trees whose tips brushed against His head with the glory of their crimson new leaves and the profusion of their fruits and flowers, the Original Puruṣa, as if smiling with delight, addressed His first-born brother.
The Blessed Lord said:

Ah! These trees, who have taken birth as plants, bow down with their crests—taking up Your lotus feet, which are worshipped by the best of gods and immortals and are worthy of offerings of flowers and fruits—in order to destroy the darkness within themselves.
These [sages] are devoted to you; singing your glory, which is the sacred ford for all the worlds, they follow the path of the Original Person.
Indeed, these hosts of sages are for the most part your foremost followers.
Even in the forest, those whose souls are devoted to You do not abandon their pure Lord, though He remains hidden;
O Praiseworthy One, these peacocks dance with joy,
and the does gaze upon You with eyes that express their love, just like the gopīs.
And with hymns of praise, flocks of cuckoos sang for him who had come to their home:
"Blessed are we forest-dwellers, for such indeed is the nature of the virtuous. "Blessed is this earth today, along with its grasses and creepers, by you—"
The trees and creepers touched by His feet, the rivers, mountains, birds, and deer by His compassionate glances,
and even the Gopīs between His arms— yet Śrī herself yearned for that which was within His two arms.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, with a delighted mind, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by his followers, took pleasure in tending the cattle in the beautiful Vṛndāvana, along the banks of rivers and on the ridges of the mountain.
In one place, while his devoted followers were singing along with bees blinded by intoxication, he himself sang;
on the road, accompanied by Saṅkarṣaṇa, his own deeds were being sung by them. In another place, he conversed with a parrot that was prattling with sweet words.
In some places he mimicked the cuckoo as it warbled sweetly; in other places he echoed the cries of the black swans;
and in some places, making the peacock laugh, he danced along with its dance.
In some places, with a voice as deep as a rain-cloud, he affectionately called by name the cattle grazing at a distance— a sound pleasing to the cows and the cowherds—
and likewise summoned the cakoras, krauñcas, cakravākas, bhāradvājas, and peacocks.

Like one who is terrified of tigers and lions, he would follow after the living beings [in fear]. At times, when the noble one was exhausted from play, he would himself rest him upon his lap as a pillow and soothe him with the massaging of his feet and other such services.
While they were dancing, singing, leaping about here and there, and fighting with one another,
the two cowherds took each other by the hand and laughed as they praised their play.
At times, exhausted by the fatigue of wrestling, they would rest upon beds of tender leaves.
Taking shelter at the foot of a tree, he lay down with the calves of the cowherds as his pillow; some massaged the feet of that great soul,
while others, their sins destroyed, fanned him with whisks.
Others, O Great King, whose minds were moistened with affection, sang slowly of the other charming deeds of that Great Soul which were suited to Him;
thus, He whose own nature was concealed by His own *māyā*, imitated the state of being a cowherd's son through His activities.
With the sprout-like feet cherished by Ramā, he sported with the cowherds like one of them, acting like a commoner though his conduct was that of the Lord.

A cowherd named Śrīdāmā, a friend of Balarāma and Keśava, along with Subala, Stoka-kṛṣṇa, and other cowherds, spoke this out of love: [Note: The provided text contains three numbered segments; the translation above corresponds to the first two segments as they form a continuous narrative unit.]
"O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one! O Kṛṣṇa, destroyer of the wicked!
Not far from here is a very great forest crowded with rows of palm trees;
there, abundant fruits fall and have fallen."

They exist, but they have been imprisoned by the evil-minded Dhenuka; O Rāma, O Kṛṣṇa, that demon of exceeding prowess has assumed the form of a donkey and is surrounded by many other kinsmen whose strength is equal to his own.
Therefore, O slayer of enemies, because men are afraid of him who has made human beings his food, that place is not frequented by them; it is abandoned by herds of beasts and flocks of birds,
yet fragrant fruits remain there, such as have never been eaten before.
"Indeed, this fragrant scent spreads in all directions;
O Kṛṣṇa, give those [garlands] to us whose minds are enticed by the fragrance. O Rāma, there is a great longing for them; go, if it pleases you."
Having thus heard the words of their friend, and desiring to do what was pleasing to their friend,
the two Lords laughed and went, surrounded by the cowherds, to the palm grove;
there Balarāma entered, making the palm trees tremble with his arms.

With great force, like a rutting elephant, he caused the fruits to fall. Hearing the sound of the falling fruits, the demon-donkey rushed toward the surface of the earth, making the mountains tremble.
Having quickly approached from the opposite side, the powerful and wicked one struck Balarāma on the chest with both feet;
letting out a cry of pain, the villain fled away. Then, regaining his composure, the assailant stood at a distance, enraged.
O King, in his rage, he threw down the demon's other two feet toward Bala;
seizing him by the ankles with one hand, he whirled him around and hurled him onto the tip of a palmyra tree, from which he lost his life due to that spinning.
Struck by him, the great palm tree, with its massive trunk, trembled and broke, shaking those standing nearby; it fell upon another, and that one upon yet another.
By Balarāma’s effortless discharge, they were struck down like the carcasses of wild asses.
All the palm trees trembled as if shaken by a great wind.
This is not surprising in the Blessed One, the infinite Lord of the universe,
in whom this world is woven like a cloth upon its threads, my dear.
Then all the kinsmen of Dhenuka, who had become jackals and were enraged because their relative had been killed, rushed toward Kṛṣṇa and Rāma.
O King, as they fell upon them, both Kṛṣṇa and Rāma dealt with them effortlessly.

He cast those who had seized his hind legs onto the king of grasses (the *tṛṇarāja*). The earth, strewn with heaps of fruits and the lifeless bodies of the Daityas, shone like the sky filled with clouds topped by palm trees.
Having heard of that great feat of theirs, the gods and others showered rains of flowers, played musical instruments, and offered hymns of praise. Then,
their fear gone, men began to eat the fruits of the *tāla* trees.
And the cattle wandered for grass in the forest where Dhenuka had been slain;
Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes are like lotus petals and whose hearing and praise are meritorious,
returned to Vraja with His elder brother, being extolled by His attendant cowherds.
Him, whose locks were sprinkled with the dust of cows and bound with peacock feathers, whose beautiful smile was accompanied by eyes lovely with wild flowers,
and who played the flute while his fame was sung by his followers;

The cowherd women, their eyes longing for a sight of him, came together; having drunk the nectar of Mukunda’s face with the bees of their eyes during the day, those women of Vraja abandoned the distress born of separation.
Having received that respectful welcome, he entered the cow-pen with bashful smiles and humility, as they cast sidelong glances at him;
Yaśodā and Rohiṇī were both devoted to their sons, and he was likewise devoted to them.
According to their desire and according to the time, they bestowed supreme blessings upon them;
their fatigue from the journey was removed there by means of bathing, massaging, and other such services.
Having put on beautiful lower garments and being adorned with divine garlands and perfumes, they sat there.
Having eaten the delicious food offered by their mother and being cherished,
they lay down upon an excellent bed and slept happily in Vraja.
Thus did the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, wandering about Vṛndāvana, at times—
O King, having gone to the Yamunā with his friends, he left Balarāma behind.
Then the cows and the cowherds, afflicted by the heat of the summer and tormented by thirst,
drank her foul water, which was corrupted by poison.
O best of the Kurus, having touched that water which was like poison, all those whose minds were struck by fate fell lifeless at the edge of the water.
Seeing them in such a state, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the masters of yoga, [acted].
With a glance that rained down nectar, he restored his masters to life. Their memories fully regained, they rose from the edge of the water and,
looking at one another, were all filled with great wonder.
O King, they considered that sight of Govinda’s favor to be like one's own resurrection after drinking poison and passing away. Śrī Śuka said:
Seeing Draupadī defiled by the black serpent, the omnipresent Lord Kṛṣṇa, seeking her purification, caused that snake to depart. Śrī-rāja said:

O Brahmin, how did the Blessed One seize the serpent within the bottomless water? Tell me, O sage, how he—who dwelt for many ages—remained there; for such was the power of that Lord, the Infinite, who acts according to His own will.
Who could ever be satiated while enjoying this nectar of the noble deeds of the cowherd?
Śrī Śuka said:
On the Kālindī there was a certain pool belonging to Kāliya, [filled] with the fire of his poison.
In that [ocean], as the milk is being boiled, birds flying overhead die upon being touched by the wind from the waves of poison,
which is laden with droplets;
likewise, all creatures dwelling on its shores, both stationary and moving, perish.
Beholding him whose venomous power was of fierce velocity, and that river made turbid by him, Kṛṣṇa— the incarnation for the restraint of the wicked— climbed a very tall kadamba tree.
Having tightened his belt, he slapped his arms and fell into the serpent-pool; by the force of that fall of the essence of men,
the mass of water in the pool, which had been breathing out poison from the serpents agitated by the shock, was stirred.
Leaping across the couch, with waves terrifying from the venom of his poison, he rushed for a hundred bow-lengths; what is that to the one of infinite strength?
As He was sporting in the lake, [the world was shaken] by the churning of His staff-like arms.
O dear one, hearing the roar of that elephant of supreme prowess and perceiving it to be an assault upon his own abode, the serpent,
unable to endure it, rushed toward him.
They beheld him, who was beautiful to behold, delicate, and of deep, pure white complexion; bearing the Śrīvatsa mark and wearing yellow garments; with a face made lovely by a gentle smile;
playing fearlessly, his feet like the interior of a lotus.
Biting him in his vital spots with his arm in rage, he covered him;
seeing him encircled by the coils of the serpent and rendered motionless,
his dear friends, the cowherds, were deeply distressed.
With their own selves, friends, wealth, wives, and desires dedicated to Kṛṣṇa,
they fell down, their intellects bewildered by grief, sorrow, and fear;
the cows, bulls, and heifers, crying out in extreme distress, collapsed as well.

With their eyes fixed upon Kṛṣṇa, they stood as if terrified and weeping. Then, in Vraja, three kinds of most terrible portents arose— on the earth, in the sky, and within the self— foreboding imminent danger.
Seeing them, the cowherds, led by Nanda, were agitated with fear;
they knew that Kṛṣṇa had gone to tend the cattle without Rāma.
Not knowing the truth, and perceiving those ill omens, they concluded that his death had occurred.
With their lives centered on Him and their minds fixed on Him, though afflicted by pain, grief, and fear,
all of them— including children, the elderly, and women— O dear one, lived like beasts; yet, wretched as they were, they departed from Gokula, longing for a sight of Kṛṣṇa.
Seeing them thus dejected, the Blessed Lord Mādhava Balarāma,
who knew the prowess of his younger brother, merely smiled slightly and said nothing.
Searching for their beloved Kṛṣṇa by following the footprints that had indicated his location, they—
Following the path marked by the characteristics of the Lord, they went to the bank of the Yamunā.

O dear one, they proceeded quickly along the way, observing here and there the footprints of the Lord of the Universe— imprinted with the lotus, barleycorn, elephant-goad, thunderbolt, and banner— and interspersed with the tracks of other cattle.
Having observed from nearby that Kṛṣṇa was motionless at the edge of the lake, encircled by the coils of a serpent within the inner pool,
and seeing the cowherd boys of dull intellect and the cattle all around him, [he approached].
Distressed by the supreme agony of the one who was crying out,
the gopīs, whose minds were deeply attached to the infinite Lord,
remembered His friendship, His smiles, His glances, and His words.
When their beloved was swallowed by the serpent, they were tormented by intense grief;
they beheld the three worlds as empty, deprived of their dear one. Then they saw Kṛṣṇa’s mother entered into her offspring.
Sharing the same agony, their tears flowing as they grieved, they sat together recounting various stories of the beloved of Vraja,
their eyes fixed upon Kṛṣṇa’s face like those who are dead.
Seeing Nanda and the others— who had their very lives centered on Kṛṣṇa— about to enter that lake,
the Blessed Lord Balarāma, who knew the power of Kṛṣṇa, forbade them; thus he beheld his own Gokula, whose only refuge was Kṛṣṇa.
Perceiving that he, along with his wives and children, was deeply distressed on his account, and following the path of mortals,
he remained for a moment and then rose from the coils of the serpent.
His body being thus expanded,
the serpent’s own coils were distressed; enraged, he raised his hoods and remained there, hissing from the mouths of his breaths which were like pits of poisonous fire.
With fixed eyes and a face like a flaming torch, he gazed at Hari;
[the Lord] was licking his two lips with his forked tongue,
while his gaze possessed the fire of exceedingly fierce venom.
Playing, he circled around him just as the king of birds does;
the other, too, wandered about, watching for an opportunity.
Thus, his strength was exhausted by this wandering, and his shoulders were drooping.
Bowing down, the Primal Lord mounted upon their broad heads;
his lotus feet, turned deep red by the touch of the multitude of jewels upon their crowns, danced as he, the teacher of all arts and sciences, moved.
Beholding him then prepared to dance,
the wives of his Gandharvas, Siddhas, Munis, Cāraṇas,
and Devas joyfully played mṛdaṅgas, paṇavas, and ānakas, and sang.
They suddenly approached him with offerings of flowers and hymns of praise;
however, O dear one, whichever head of the hundred-headed one did not bow down,
that very one he crushed with blows from his feet, wielding a harsh staff.

As his life-force was exhausted, the serpent, wandering about, vomited blood from his mouth and emitted a most foul stench from his nostrils; he fell into a state of extreme agony as venom poured from his eyes onto his heads.
Whatever rose upward as he hissed loudly in rage,
he made it descend with a dancing step;
thus, like a man of old, he became subdued as if worshipped by flowers.
O King, with his thousand hoods shattered by that wondrous *tāṇḍava* dance, vomiting profuse blood from his mouths and with his limbs broken,
he remembered the Ancient Person, the Teacher of all moving and unmoving beings.
With his mind, he went to that Nārāyaṇa,
the refuge, who was oppressed by the excessive burden of the world within his womb, while the canopy of his hoods was crushed by the blow of Kṛṣṇa’s heel.
Seeing the serpent, his wives approached him in distress, their garments, ornaments, and hair-braids loosened; then,
with deeply agitated minds, they placed their children before him.

Placing their bodies upon the ground, the virtuous women bowed down to the Lord of Beings; with palms joined in reverence, desiring liberation from the sins of their husband, they sought refuge in the Protector.
The wives of the Nāgas said:
"Indeed, this punishment is just for him who has committed an offense;
Your incarnation is for the purpose of subduing the wicked."

You look with equal vision even upon the sons of Your enemy; You bestow self-restraint as a blessing, for this punishment inflicted by You upon the wicked is indeed a favor granted to us, removing our very impurities.

That this embodied being has been turned into a venomous serpent is considered by you to be nothing but a favor, even though it was your own anger. What great austerity must he have performed in the past, free from pride yet bestowing honor upon others,
or what dharma characterized by compassion for all people, that you, the soul of all living beings, are so pleased with him?
O Lord, we do not know whose power it is that has been granted the privilege of touching the dust of Your feet—

that power by the desire for which Śrī performed penance as a woman, having abandoned all desires and observed her vows for a very long time, and for which neither the heights of heaven nor universal sovereignty was desired.
Those who have taken refuge in the dust of his feet do not desire the status of Brahmā, nor sovereignty over the waters, nor the perfections of yoga, nor even liberation from rebirth.
Therefore, O Lord, this serpent-king—who is born of darkness and under the sway of anger—has attained that which is difficult for others to reach;
for him who wanders in the wheel of worldly existence, whatever he desires becomes manifest. Salutations to You, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, the Great Soul.

Obeisances to You, the abode of all beings, the Being, the Supreme, the Supreme Self; to the ocean of knowledge and realization, the Brahman of infinite power; obeisances to You who are beyond the modes and changeless, yet also to Your form composed of the material elements.
To Kāla, whose navel is time, the witness of the divisions of time;
to the universe, its observer, its creator, and the cause of the universe;
to the Self of the elements, the subtle elements, the senses, the vital breaths, the mind, the intellect, and the subconscious impressions.
Salutations to the infinite, subtle, and immutable Supreme Knower, who, through the conceit of the three modes of nature, remains hidden from the experience of one's own self,
yet conforms to various doctrines and possesses the power of both the signified and the signifier.

Obeisances to the source of all authority, to the Seer, the origin of the scriptures; obeisances again and again to the Veda, which consists of both the path of worldly engagement and the path of renunciation. Obeisances to Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, the sons of Vasudeva.
Salutations to Pradyumna, to Aniruddha, and to the Lord of the Sātvatas.

Salutations to the lamp of the qualities (*guṇa*), who veils the self of the qualities; who is characterized by the functioning of the qualities, yet is the seer of the qualities and possesses self-awareness.
Salutations to you, Hṛṣīkeśa, who abide in the unmanifest, for the perfection of all that is manifest; salutations to you, the sage whose nature is silence.
Salutations to you, the knower of the goal of both the high and the low, the sovereign overseer of all.
To the non-universal and the universal, to the witness of this world, and to its cause—

to You, O All-pervading Lord, who through Your qualities bring about the birth, maintenance, and dissolution of this universe, yet remain effortless, unconditioned by time, and the sustainer of power.
Awakening each being to their respective natures, You, whose movements are never in vain, act for the sake of their contemplation; these very forms of Yours exist within the three worlds.
Whether they be peaceful, restless, or born of delusion,
those who are peaceful are dear to You; for now, You have come to protect the virtuous and to sustain those who strive to uphold dharma.
An offense committed by one's own offspring must be forgiven once by a father;
O peaceful-souled one, you ought to forgive me, a fool who did not know you. O Blessed One, show favor to this serpent as he is giving up his life.
"O Lord, grant us our husband, who is the very life-breath of us women who are worthy of your compassion. By your command, ordain what we, your maidservants, must perform;
for by practicing with faith that which you ordain, one is indeed liberated from all fear."
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus praised by the wives of the serpent, the Blessed One released him,
who was unconscious with his head shattered by the trampling of His feet.
Having regained his senses and vital breath, Kāliya, sighing with difficulty and dejected, spoke to Hari, Kṛṣṇa, with joined palms after much effort. Kāliya said:
O Lord, we are indeed wicked by nature, possessing long-standing resentment due to our association with darkness;

for it is difficult to abandon one's innate disposition, O Protector, which consists in grasping at what is unreal. O Creator, this entire universe was fashioned by You through the emission of the *guṇas*.

O Blessed One, we are serpents there, possessing diverse natures, powers, vigor, origins, seeds, dispositions, and forms, and being of great pride by birth; how can we, deluded ourselves, abandon Your māyā which is so difficult to cast off?
"For you, O omniscient Lord of the universe, are indeed the cause therein;
whether you intend to show favor or to exercise restraint, please ordain that for us.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard these words, the Blessed One, who had assumed a human form for a specific purpose, said:
"O serpent, you must not remain here; go to the ocean without delay.
This river is being enjoyed by cows and men, along with their own kinsmen, children, and wives."

That mortal who remembers this instruction of mine to you, and recites it at both twilights, shall incur no fear from you. He who, having bathed in this pleasure-grove of mine, satisfies the gods and others with water offerings—
Having fasted and remembering me, one should worship me; thus one is liberated from all sins.
Having abandoned the island of Ramaṇaka, he has taken refuge in this lake;
out of fear of him, Suparṇa will not eat you, who are marked by my foot.
The venerable sage said: O King, having been liberated by the Lord Kṛṣṇa of wondrous deeds,
he joyfully honored Him, and the wives of the serpent also paid him respectful homage.

Having worshipped the Lord of the World, whose banner bears Garuḍa, with divine garments, excellent flower garlands, and priceless jewels, as well as with divine fragrant ointments and a great wreath of blue lotuses, he propitiated Him.
Then, being pleased and granted permission by Him, he circumambulated and bowed down to Him;
accompanied by his wife, friends, and sons, he went to the island within the ocean.
At that very moment, the Yamunā became free of poison, her waters turned to nectar.
Through the grace of the Blessed One, who had assumed a human form for his pastimes,
the King said:
"How did Kāliya abandon the serpent-dwelling of Raṇaṅka?"
"What improper act has Suparṇa committed that he alone should be punished?
Śrī Śuka said:
"There was a monthly offering here consisting of the tribute brought by the serpent folk."
O mighty-armed one, the tree-deity was previously appointed as the lord of the Nāgas;
at every change of the moon, all the Nāgas offer their respective shares for their own protection to the high-souled Suparṇa.

O King, the serpent Kāliya, son of Kadrū, intoxicated by the power of his venom, disregarded Garuḍa and himself devoured that offering. Hearing this, O King, the Blessed One, the beloved of the Lord, became enraged.
Desiring to strike him down, the one of great speed rushed toward Kāliya. As he was charging with force, the serpent— whose weapons were his venom,
who possessed many upraised hoods, whose teeth were his arms, and whose fierce eyes hissed with a terrible tongue— sprang up and bit Garuḍa.
The son of Tārkṣya, filled with wrath,
possessing fierce speed, and the seat of Madhusūdana,
cast him aside with his left wing, which shone like gold.
He of fierce prowess struck the son of Kadru;
Kāliya, violently agitated by the blows of Suparṇa’s wings,
entered the lake of the Yamunā, which was inaccessible and difficult to approach.
Once there, Garuḍa, though forbidden by Saubhari, forcibly seized his desired prey— a water-dweller— as he was hungry;
for he had seen the fish, who were wretched and miserable, being devoured once their lord had been killed.
Out of compassion, Saubhari, while ensuring the safety of those there, said:
"If Garuḍa enters here and devours the fish, he shall immediately be deprived of his life; I speak this as the truth."
Kāliya alone, and no other serpent, knew that;
terrified of Garuḍa and driven out by Kṛṣṇa, he took up residence there.
[Then they saw] Kṛṣṇa emerging from the lake, adorned with divine garlands, fragrances, and garments.

Upon perceiving that place strewn with great clusters of jewels and adorned with Jāmbūnada gold, all the cowherds rose up as if their very lives had returned; their souls filled with intense joy, they embraced one another with affection.
O descendant of Kuru, Yaśodā, Rohiṇī, Nanda, the cowherd women, and the cowherds, having met with Kṛṣṇa, found their desires fulfilled; even the withered trees were revived.
And Balarāma, embracing Acyuta and recognizing His majesty, laughed aloud.
Placing him on his lap with love, he gazed at him again and again;
the cows, the bulls, and the heifers attained supreme joy.
Then the brahmins and the elders, accompanied by their wives, approached Nanda.
They said, "By good fortune, Your Majesty’s son has been released from the grip of Kāliya. O Kṛṣṇa, grant gifts to the twice-born for the sake of his liberation.
O King, Nanda, with a joyful mind, then ordered cows and gold to be given.
The highly fortunate Yaśodā also, having regained her lost child,
embraced him and placed him on her lap, repeatedly shedding a stream of tears.
O King of kings, they spent that night there, exhausted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue.
The cows, dwelling in the cow-pen, were staying by the banks of the Kālindī.
At that time, a forest fire arising from the pure woods surrounded the entire cow-pen at midnight while they were asleep and proceeded to consume it.
Then, rising up in agitation and burning with distress, the inhabitants of Vraja went for refuge to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord who had assumed a human form through His illusory power.
"Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! O most fortunate one! O Rāma of immeasurable prowess!"

This most terrible fire is indeed devouring us, your own followers; O Lord, protect us, your friends, from this fire of Time which is so difficult to cross. We are unable to abandon Your feet, which grant freedom from all fear.
Thus, observing the distress of his own kinsmen, the Lord of the universe,
Ananta, who wields infinite power, drank up that fierce fire.
Śrī Śuka said:
Then Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by his kinsmen whose hearts were filled with joy,
entered Vraja, which was adorned by the cowherd community, while being celebrated in song;
thus did he sport in Vraja through the illusory power of his guise as a cowherd.
The summer season did not become excessively dear to embodied beings;
yet, due to the qualities of Vṛndāvana, it appeared like spring,
for there Keśava himself dwells in person together with Rāma.
There, the chirping of crickets was drowned out by the roar of waterfalls;
it was perpetually adorned with groves of trees moistened by the spray of those falls,
and by breezes from rivers, lakes, and springs that carried the pollen of white, red, and blue lotuses.
There, in that place of excessive lushness, no forest fire born of the summer heat or the sun ever occurs for the forest-dwellers;
there, the rivers with their deep waters and waves at the banks, along with the sandy shores, flow all around with liquid mud;
and there, neither the rays of the fierce-rayed sun nor the virulent poisons seize the moisture of the earth or its verdant grass.
The glorious forest was in full bloom, filled with various deer and birds crying out,
with peacocks and bees singing, and cuckoos and cranes warbling;
there the Lord Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Balarāma, prepared to play.
Making the flute resound, surrounded by cowherds and herds of cows,
Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and the other cowherds— adorned with ornaments made of young sprouts, peacock feathers, clusters of flowers, garlands, and mineral pigments— danced, fought, and sang.
While Kṛṣṇa was dancing, some sang and others played upon flutes, cymbals, and horns; others offered praise. These were gods disguised as cowherds, appearing in the form of cowherd boys.

O King, they praised Kṛṣṇa and Rāma like spectators praising an actor; and sometimes, wearing side-locks of hair like crows' wings, the two of them played at wrestling with whirling, leaping, hurling, slapping, and pulling.
While others were dancing in some places, O Great King, the two singers themselves, acting as musicians, praised them repeatedly, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!
In some places they struck with *bilva* fruits, in some with water-pots, and in some with handfuls of *āmalaka* berries.
Sometimes by means of touching the eyes while blindfolded, sometimes by acting like deer or birds,
sometimes by croaking like frogs, and with various other jests;
at times by means of a swing, and at times by imitating the movements of kings.
Thus the two of them wandered through the forest with games well-known in the world—
among rivers, mountains, mountain valleys, groves, woodlands, and lakes—
while Rāma and Kṛṣṇa tended the cattle with the cowherds in that forest.
The demon Pralamba, in the form of a cowherd, approached with the desire to seize him;
although the Lord, the descendant of Daśārha, was all-knowing and omniscient,
He consented to that friendship while contemplating his slaughter.

There, having summoned the cowherds, Kṛṣṇa, the expert in pastimes, said: "O cowherds, let us play by forming pairs as is fitting. Thereupon, the two leaders among the cowherds, Rāma and Janārdana, formed a pair.
Some were engaged with Kṛṣṇa, while others were with Balarāma;
they performed various games characterized by being the rider and the mount,
wherein the victors mounted and the defeated carried them.
Carrying, being carried, and tending the herds of cattle,
they went to the banyan tree named Bhāṇḍīraka with Kṛṣṇa at their head,
along with Rāma, Śrīdāman, Vṛṣabha, and the others.
