O King, during that game, Kṛṣṇa and the others carried those who were defeated;
however, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa was himself defeated and carried Śrīdāmā,
while Bhadrasena carried Vṛṣabha, and Pralamba carried the son of Rohiṇī.
Considering Kṛṣṇa to be irresistible, that foremost of the Dānavas carried him away as fast as possible beyond Avarohaṇa; yet he continued to carry him,
who possessed the weight of the king of mountains, the earth.
The great asura, his speed gone, assumed his own form; adorned with golden ornaments,
he shone like a cloud illuminated by lightning and the moon.
Beholding that form moving freely in the sky—
its eyes blazing, its brow furrowed, its fangs formidable,
its crest of hair flaming, and adorned with bracelets, crown, and earrings— [he was struck with awe].
At that wonderful splendor, the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) was slightly startled; then,

regaining his composure and becoming fearless, Bala struck the enemy on the head with a firm fist— just as the lord of the gods struck a mountain with the speed of a thunderbolt— thereby rescuing himself as if from one who was carrying him off like a merchant's caravan.
Struck, his head instantly shattered, vomiting blood from his mouth and deprived of consciousness,
the asura fell with a great roar, lifeless, like a mountain struck by the weapon of Indra.
Seeing Pralamba slain by the powerful Balarāma, [the demons were terrified].
The cowherds were filled with great wonder and cried out, "Excellent! Excellent!
Uttering blessings, they praised him who was worthy of such honor, their hearts overwhelmed with love as they embraced him as if he had returned from the dead.
When the wicked Pralamba was slain, the gods were supremely relieved;
they showered Balarāma with garlands and exclaimed, "Excellent!
Excellent! Śrī Śuka said:
While the cowherds were absorbed in their play, their cows, wandering far away and grazing at will,
entered a thicket out of greed for grass. The goats, cows, and buffaloes continued to enter from forest to forest.
Thirsting from the forest fire, they entered the Īṣīkā forest while crying out.
At that time, Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and the other cowherds, not seeing their animals, were filled with remorse; though they searched, they did not know the whereabouts of the cows.

With their livelihood lost and their minds bewildered, they all followed the path of the cows by means of the grass cut by their hooves and the hoofprints marked upon it; they searched for their own herd, which had strayed into the Muñja forest and was crying out.
Having reached that place, thirsty and exhausted, they turned back;
then, summoned by the Lord with a voice as deep as a thundercloud,
they heard the resonance of their own names and, filled with great joy, responded with cries of their own.

Then, from all sides, a great forest fire arose by chance, bringing destruction to the dwellers of the woods; fanned by the driver’s fierce torches, it licked at everything, both stationary and moving. Seeing that approaching conflagration on every side, the cowherds and the cows were struck with fear.
And they, having sought refuge with Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, spoke to them just as people afflicted by the fear of death seek refuge with Hari:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O great hero! O Rāma of unfailing prowess!
You ought to protect us who have sought refuge and are being consumed by the forest fire."
"O Kṛṣṇa, surely Your kinsmen do not deserve to be thus distressed. For we, O Knower of all duties, have You as our protector and are devoted solely to You.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard the piteous words of his kinsmen, the Blessed Lord Hari said, "Close your eyes; do not fear. When they had closed their eyes, saying "So be it," the Blessed One [emitted] a fierce fire.
Having drunk them with his mouth, the Lord of Yoga released them from their distress with great effort. Then, opening their eyes, they were led back to Bhāṇḍīra;
hearing this, they were struck with wonder, seeing themselves and the cows liberated.

Having observed Kṛṣṇa’s yogic power, manifested through his yoga-māyā, and seeing their own safety from the forest fire, they considered him to be immortal. Then, at the close of day, Janārdana, together with Rāma, turned the cows back.
Making the flute resound, he entered the cow-pen while being praised by the cowherds;
at the sight of Govinda, the cowherd girls experienced supreme bliss,
for in his absence even a single moment had seemed like a hundred ages to them.
Śrī Śuka said:
The cowherds related to the women that wonderful deed of the two of them— their own deliverance from the forest fire— and also the slaying of Pralamba.

The elder cowherds and the cowherd women, having heard that, were struck with wonder and considered Kṛṣṇa and Rāma— the foremost of gods— to have returned to Vraja. Then the rainy season set in, which brings forth all living beings.
With its radiant horizon and the vault of the sky resounding with thick blue clouds accompanied by lightning and thunder, the firmament,
its light obscured, shone like Brahman endowed with qualities.
When the proper time arrived, the rain-cloud began to release with its own rays that wealth consisting of water which had been drunk up by the earth for eight months;
great clouds, accompanied by lightning and shaken by fierce winds, appeared.
For those seeking liberation, his pleasing and life-sustaining grace was like compassion itself; the earth, emaciated by austerity yet nourished by the Lord, became exceedingly vast,
just as the body of one who performs optional penance expands upon attaining its fruit.
At the onset of night, fireflies shine in the darkness but not the planets;
just so, in the Kali age, heretics flourish through sin but not the Vedas.
Having heard the roar of the rain-cloud, the frogs uttered their voices.

Just as Brahmins remain silent when their religious observances have ended, so too did the small rivers, which had gone astray and were drying up, lie still; for the body, wealth, and prosperity of a man who lacks self-mastery are likewise subject to such states.
Green with young grass and red with indragopa insects,
the earth— shaded by the *ucchilīndhra* mushrooms— became like the very goddess Śrī incarnate for men.
The fields, abundant with crops of young grass, brought joy to the farmers.
All those dwelling on land and in water, who were proud and ignorant that [all things] are subject to destiny, felt remorse; by resorting to the fresh water,
they assumed beautiful forms, just as one does by serving Lord Hari.
The ocean, joined by the rivers, was agitated with waves driven by the wind,
like the mind of an unrefined yogi when smeared by desire and the pairs of qualities (*guṇas*). The mountains, though struck by the torrents of rain, did not tremble.
Being overwhelmed by calamities, the paths of those whose minds were fixed on Adhokṣaja became obscured; for they were overgrown with weeds, neglected, and left unrefurbished.
Likewise, the Vedas, though being studied by the twice-born, fell into disuse over time.
Among the clouds, the friends of the world, the lightnings— fickle in their affection— did not maintain stability, just as lustful women do not remain steady toward virtuous men.
And in the sky, Indra’s bow appeared devoid of its string, even though it was held by one who possesses all virtues.
Just as the quality-less *puruṣa* does not shine when the manifestation of the qualities (*guṇa-vyatikara*) is active,
nor does the moon shine when covered by clouds radiant with its own moonlight,
so too the *puruṣa* does not shine when illuminated by the light of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃ-mati*).

Delighted by the festival of the arrival of the clouds, the crested peacocks rejoiced; those weary of the heat in their homes were as joyful at the arrival of Acyuta as they were at the coming of the rains.
Having drunk water with their feet, the trees assumed various forms.

O dear one, like cranes exhausted by their pursuit of desires, they dwelt in lakes whose shores were not yet tranquil, having previously been worn out by austerities; they were like villagers with wicked intentions dwelling in homes where worldly duties remain unfulfilled.
As the Lord rained down, the bridges were broken apart by the floods of water,
just as the paths of the Vedas are destroyed in the Kali age by the false arguments of heretics;
and driven by the winds, the clouds released their nectar into all living beings.
Just as the lords of the people receive the blessings offered by the twice-born at the proper times,
so did Hari, accompanied by Balarāma, enter that most excellent forest— abounding in ripe dates and rose-apples and surrounded by cows and cowherds— to enjoy himself.

The cows, though slow-moving due to the great weight of their udders, ran swiftly when called by the Blessed One out of affection, their teats streaming with milk. The forest-dwellers were delighted by the rows of forest trees dripping with honey.
From the sound of the mountain's waterfalls, nearby caves became visible;
and in some places, as he rained down upon the hollows of trees and within the caves,
the Blessed One took rest and enjoyed himself, subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits.
Accompanied by Saṅkarṣaṇa, he ate the rice with curd that had been brought on a stone slab near the water,
together with the cowherds who were to be fed;
they lay down upon the grassy meadow and chewed with their eyes closed.
Seeing the satisfied bulls, calves, and cows, whose exhaustion from carrying their own milk had vanished, and beholding that splendor of the rainy season which brings happiness at all times,
the Blessed Lord worshipped it, augmented as it was by his own power.
While Rāma and Keśava were thus dwelling in that Vraja,
autumn arrived— cloudless, with clear waters and gentle breezes;
through the emergence of lotuses, the waters returned to their natural state by the grace of autumn.

Just as autumn removes from the sky the clouds, from the earth the mixture of living beings, and from the waters the impurity of mud, so does devotion to Kṛṣṇa remove the inauspiciousness from the minds of those in the stages of life who have fallen away through the practice of yoga.
Having surrendered all their waters, the clouds shone with pure luster,
like peaceful sages who have abandoned all desires and are liberated from sin. The mountains released their water, yet in some places they did not release even a drop of auspiciousness.
Just as the wise may or may not bestow the nectar of knowledge at the proper time,
so too those who move in shallow waters do not perceive the water diminishing; likewise, foolish men with families do not realize that their lifespan wastes away day by day.
Just as those who move in deep waters find distress from the autumnal sun,
so too did the poor, wretched householder with uncontrolled senses suffer;
yet, little by little, they abandoned the mud, the dry land, and the plants.
Just as the wise remain steady in their lack of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and other non-self entities, so the ocean became silent with its waters stilled upon the arrival of autumn; likewise,
when the self has properly ceased [its worldly activity], the sage completely desists from the scriptures.
Just as farmers protect their fields from water with firm embankments,
so do yogis restrain their leaking knowledge by means of the vital breaths; and just as the moon removes the heat produced by the rays of the autumnal sun for all living beings.
Mukunda removed from the women of Vraja the consciousness born of identification with the body.
The sky shone, free of clouds and filled with the pure stars of autumn,
like a mind endowed with *sattva* that perceives the meaning of the *Śabdabrahman*.
Just as the moon with its unbroken orb shines in the sky surrounded by hosts of stars, so did Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Yadus, shine upon the earth surrounded by the circle of the Vṛṣṇis;
and he embraced the forest breeze, which was equally cool and warm, laden with flowers.

The people abandoned their distress, while the cowherd women did not, for their hearts had been stolen by Kṛṣṇa; the cows, deer, birds, and women became filled with longing, like the actions of the Lord manifested through the fruits of autumn.
At the rising of the sun, the lotuses bloomed with great joy, except for the night-lily;
and the worlds, O King, were free from fear because of the monarch, just as they are when free from robbers.
In the cities and villages, there were great festivals with first-fruits offerings and sensory delights.
The earth, rich with ripened crops, shone intensely through the two phases of Lord Hari.
Merchants, sages, kings, and those who had performed ritual ablutions went forth and obtained their wealth,
just as perfected beings (siddhas) imprisoned by the rains receive their own portions when the proper time arrives.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, accompanied by his cows and cowherd boys, Acyuta entered the water, which was as clear as autumnal water and scented by the breeze from the lotus ponds.
The Lord of Madhu, having plunged into the mountains, lakes, rivers, and forests resounding with blossoming groves,
powerful bees, and flocks of birds, tended his cows along with his cowherd boys and sounded his flute.
Hearing that flute-song which awakens the memory of [their beloved], the women of Vraja were stirred by the rise of longing.
O King, some among them, remembering the deeds of Kṛṣṇa, began to describe him to their friends in his absence; however,
their minds being distracted by the force of passion, they were unable to do so.
Wearing a crest of peacock feathers on his head, a *karṇikāra* flower on his ears, a garment tawny like gold, and the Vaijayantī garland,
he filled the holes of his flute with the nectar of his lips while surrounded by throngs of cowherds.

O King, having heard that sound of the flute— which was His own song of praise and which captivated the hearts of all living beings— the women of Vraja entered the forest of Vṛndāvana, where He delights in His own feet; describing it thus, they all called out to Him.
The gopīs said: O friends, we do not know of any greater fruit for those endowed with eyes than this— that you two, along with your companions, have driven the cattle into the forest.
Those who have drunk in the faces of the two sons of the Queen of Vraja— which are not served by the flute— and which release affectionate side-glances;
and those who behold them in their variegated attire, adorned with garlands of mango sprouts, peacock feathers, clusters of blossoms, blue lotuses, and water lilies.

In the midst of the assembly of cowherds, they shone brilliantly like two preeminent actors upon a stage; and somewhere they were singing. "What auspicious thing has this flute performed for the Gopīs?
Even the nectar from the lips of Dāmodara belongs to the Gopīs."

O friend, Vṛndāvana spreads the fame of the earth; for when he himself partakes of the remaining essence, the rivers shed tears of joy, as do the trees, whose bark bristles with thrill like noble men.

Beholding Govinda’s flute— which has attained its splendor from the lotus feet of Devakī’s son— and which causes intoxicated peacocks to dance, all living beings on the mountain ridges cease their activities.
Blessed are these female deer, though their intellects are dull, who,
upon hearing the sound of the flute of Nanda’s son as he assumes his various guises, have come together with the male deer.
They offered worship through their affectionate glances upon beholding Kṛṣṇa, whose form and character were a festival for women,
and having heard the distinct song of his whistling flute.

The goddesses, seated in their celestial chariots, their hearts pierced by the god of love, their flower-adorned braids falling loose, and their garments disarrayed, were utterly bewildered; and the cows too [were captivated] by the flute-song issuing from Kṛṣṇa’s mouth.
The young calves stood with their ears pricked up, drinking the nectar [of Govinda's voice], while taking mouthfuls of milk from the flowing udders;
they touched Govinda within themselves with their eyes, their lashes moist with tears.
"O Mother, surely the birds and the sages in this forest are mostly [liberated],
for they have ascended the branches of the trees with beautiful sprouts and listen to that sweet flute-song uttered by Kṛṣṇa as He gazes upon them."
At that time, with their eyes closed and all other speech silenced,
the rivers listened to the song of Mukunda; having understood it, the force of their currents was broken by the god of love, as indicated by the formation of whirlpools.
The offerings of lotuses seize the pair of feet of Murāri, which are embraced by the waves acting as his arms;
having seen the cattle of Vraja along with Rāma and the cowherds in the heat of the sun, [they offer them shade].
As he moved along, playing his flute and inspiring love, a cloud— arisen from the rows of flowers blooming with increased affection— formed a parasol over his friend with its own body.
The Pulinda women were filled with joy by the saffron from the lotus feet of the Wide-Strider,
which was adorned upon the breasts of their beloveds and had become like mere grass in comparison to the pain of longing caused by the memory of beholding Him.
Smearing it upon their faces and breasts, they abandoned that mental anguish.
"Ah! This mountain is indeed a preeminent servant of Hari, O women, since he experiences such joy from the touch of the feet of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa."
He increased the pride of those two, along with their herds of cows,
as they led the cattle through the forest with cowherds, providing them with water, fresh grass, caves, and tubers and roots— O noble one!
By the sweet-toned sounds of the flute, the friends among the embodied beings were rendered motionless; among the youths, there was horripilation—
an extraordinary sign produced by the noose of yoga.
Thus describing these various pastimes of the Blessed One as he wanders in Vṛndāvana, the gopīs, speaking among themselves, became absorbed in that very state. Śrī Śuka said:

In the first month of the winter season, the young girls of Nanda’s cowherd settlement observed the vow of worshipping Kātyāyanī while subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya). Having bathed in the waters of the Kālindī at dawn when the sun had just risen, they remained by the water's edge.
O King, having fashioned a sand image of the Goddess,
they worshipped it with fragrant scents, garlands, offerings, incense, and lamps,
as well as with various other gifts such as sprouts, fruits, and rice grains.
"O Kātyāyanī, O Mahāmāyā, O Mahāyoginī, O Sovereign Lady!
O Goddess, make the son of Nanda-gopa my husband; salutations to you! Reciting this mantra, those maidens performed their worship.
In this manner, for one month, the maidens, their minds fixed on Kṛṣṇa, observed their vow;
they worshipped Bhadrakālī, praying, "May the son of Nanda become our husband.
At dawn, having risen, they stood with their arms linked together by their respective clans.

As they went daily to bathe in the Kālindī, they sang aloud of Kṛṣṇa. Once, having arrived at the riverbank and laid aside their garments as before, they sported joyfully in the water while singing of Kṛṣṇa.
The Blessed One Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the masters of yoga, understanding their intention, went there surrounded by his companions to accomplish that task;
taking their garments, he quickly climbed a *nīpa* tree.
Laughing along with the laughing children, he spoke these words in jest:
"O young women, come here and take back each of your own garments as you please;
I speak the truth, for this is not a joke, since you have all been emaciated by your vows."
"Never before have I spoken an untruth, and you all know this well; O slender-waisted ones, accept it either one by one or all together.
Seeing that playful jest of his, the gopīs were overwhelmed with love.
Ashamed, they looked at one another and, overcome with laughter, did not emerge.
While Govinda was speaking thus, their minds captivated by his jesting,
they remained submerged up to their necks in the cool water and, trembling, said to him:
"O sir, show us honor! We know you as the beloved son of Nanda-gopa, the glory of Vraja; give us garments, for we are trembling with desire.
O Śyāmasundara, we are your maidservants; let us do whatever you command."
"O knower of dharma, give us our clothes; otherwise, we shall report this to the king.
The Blessed Lord said:
"If you are my maidservants, you will do as I have told you."
"Come here and take back your own garments, O girls of pure smiles;
if you do not, I shall not give them away—what can the angry king do?
Then, from that reservoir, all the girls emerged, trembling with cold.

Covering their private parts with their hands, they rose up, distressed by the cold. Seeing them, the Blessed One, gratified by their pure devotion, placed his garments upon their shoulders and spoke with a smile.

"Since you, though firm in your vows, plunged into the water while naked, this indeed was an offense against the gods. Joining your palms above your heads, offer salutations to dispel this sin; having done so, take up your lower garments.
When Acyuta had spoken thus, the women of Vraja considered their bathing naked to be a lapse from their vow.
Desiring the fulfillment of all their past deeds, they bowed down before Him who had directly manifested as the deer that removes all faults.
Seeing them thus prostrate, the Blessed Lord, the son of Devakī,
being moved by compassion, bestowed garments upon them, thereby gratified by their devotion.
They were firmly mocked and made to feel ashamed; they were teased and made to act like children at play,
and even their garments were stripped away from them.
Delighted by the company of their beloved, they felt no envy;
having put on their own garments and prepared for union with their dearest, their hearts were captivated and they did not move, their eyes cast down in bashfulness.
Having understood their resolve to touch his feet, the Blessed One Dāmodara spoke to those women who were firm in their vows:
"O virtuous ladies, your intention to worship me has been perceived."
That which has been approved by me is indeed destined to come true. For those whose minds are absorbed in Me, desire does not lead to further desire;
just as parched or boiled grains are generally no longer capable of producing seed.
"O young women, you have attained perfection; by my grace, you shall enjoy these nights.
For the sake of which these virtuous ladies performed this vow of worshipping the Noble One.
Śrī Śuka said:

Thus instructed by the Blessed One, the young maidens, having attained their desire, entered Vraja with difficulty while meditating upon His lotus feet. Then the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, was surrounded by the cowherds.
Having gone far from Vṛndāvana with His elder brother while tending the cows,
He saw that under the scorching heat of the midday sun, the trees were providing shade for themselves as if they were holding parasols; seeing this, He spoke to the inhabitants of Vraja.
O Stokakṛṣṇa, O Aṃśu, Śrīdāman, Subala, Arjuna,
Viśāla, Vṛṣabha, Ojasvin, Devaprastha, and Varūthapa—
behold these highly fortunate ones, whose lives are dedicated solely to the welfare of others.
Enduring wind, rain, heat, and cold, they protect us;
oh, how excellent is their birth, for all living beings depend upon them!
Indeed, like a virtuous person, those who seek their help never turn away empty-handed.
With leaves, flowers, fruits, shade, roots, bark, and wood;
with fragrant resins, ashes, bones, and sprouts—they fulfill their desires.
Such is the fulfillment of the purpose of birth for embodied beings here among other embodied beings.
"Always practice what is beneficial through one's life-breath, wealth, intellect, and speech"—
thinking thus, he went to the Yamunā through the midst of trees with drooping branches, laden with an abundance of sprouts, clusters, fruits, flowers, and leaves.
There, O King, having caused the cows to drink water that was well-purified, cool, and auspicious,
the cowherds themselves then drank the water to their heart's content;
and while grazing the cattle at will in her grove, O King, they remained there.
Approaching Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, afflicted by hunger, they spoke as follows. The gopas said:
"O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one! O Kṛṣṇa, destroyer of the wicked!"
"This hunger indeed afflicts us; you ought to provide a remedy for its pacification.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus addressed by the cowherds, the Blessed Lord, the son of Devakī, [acted].
Being pleased with his devotee, the wife of a brāhmaṇa, He spoke as follows: "O brāhmaṇas who discourse on the Veda, proceed to the sacrificial ground of the gods;
for there the descendants of Aṅgiras are performing a sacrificial session (sattra) out of a desire for heaven."
"Having gone there, O cowherds, beg for rice, sent forth by us,
while proclaiming the names of the Blessed One and of me, the Noble One.
Thus instructed by the Blessed One, they went and begged accordingly.
With palms joined in reverence, they fell prostrate on the ground like staffs before the brāhmaṇas and said: "O gods upon earth, listen! We are the executors of Kṛṣṇa’s command;
know that we, the cowherds urged by Balarāma, have arrived—may prosperity be yours!"
"O best of men, Rāma and Acyuta, who are grazing their cows nearby, are hungry and desire rice from you.

O brāhmaṇas, if you have faith, give rice to these two seekers, for you are the most excellent knowers of dharma. [This is the fruit] of the animal sacrifice, the Sautrāmaṇī, and the initiation ceremony."
"Indeed, one does not incur fault by eating the food of anyone other than one who is initiated [for sacrifice]," yet even while hearing this request of the Blessed One, they did not listen;
for they were of petty desires, performers of many rituals, childish, and conceited as if they were elders.
Place, time, distinct substances, mantras, ritual procedures, officiating priests, sacrificial fires,
deities, the sacrificer, the sacrifice itself, and religious duty— all of which consist of Him—
that Supreme Brahman, the Lord Adhokṣaja, is directly manifest.

O scorcher of enemies, those mortals of dull intellect, viewing them with human eyes, did not believe; for they neither said "Yes" nor "No" to what was said. Returning thus disappointed, the cowherds spoke accordingly to Kṛṣṇa and Rāma.
Having heard that, the Blessed One, the Lord of the universe, smiled and spoke again to the cowherds, demonstrating the ways of worldly convention:
"Inform my wives that I have arrived along with Saṅkarṣaṇa."
"Those who have dwelt within me with devotion will gladly give you food.
Then, having gone to the hall of the wives and seen them seated there, beautifully adorned,
the cowherds bowed to those virtuous wives of the twice-born and spoke these words with humility.
"Obeisances to you, the wives of the brāhmaṇas; please attend to our words.
We have been sent here by Kṛṣṇa, who is grazing the cows not far from this place. Accompanied by Rāma and the cowherd boys, he has gone a long distance away."
"Let food be given to him who is hungry, along with his followers.
Hearing that Acyuta had arrived, those who were constantly eager for his sight became filled with excitement,
their minds captivated by talk of him.
Taking four kinds of food rich in many qualities in their vessels,
they all rushed toward their beloved, just as rivers flow toward the ocean;
though they were being restrained by their husbands, brothers, kinsmen, and sons.
In the forest grove of the Yamunā, adorned with fresh *aśoka* shoots, the women— whose hearts were fixed on the Lord of Excellent Renown through long-standing devotion—
beheld Him wandering there surrounded by cowherds along with His elder brother.
Dark-complexioned, with a golden halo, wearing forest garlands and a garment of deerskin, and adorned with minerals and coral ornaments,
he has one hand placed upon the shoulder of Anavrata while with the other he brandishes a lotus.
Then, with their eyes— their ear-ornaments having mostly heard of the joy of the beloved's lotus-face, with its smiles, cheeks, and curls like blue lotuses— they immersed their minds in Him.
O King, having drawn him within and embraced him for a very long time, they abandoned their distress according to their desires, just as wise men cast off suffering;
thus, having renounced all other hopes, they attained their goal through the desire to behold the Self.
Having perceived them, the Seer of all things spoke with a smiling face:
"Welcome to you, O highly fortunate ones; please be seated. What may I do for you? For it is indeed appropriate that you have come here out of a desire to see us."
Indeed, those who are wise and perceive their true self-interest certainly practice unswerving and uninterrupted devotion toward Me, who am dear to the Self,
just as they do toward their life-breath, intellect, mind, own body, wife, children, wealth, and so forth.
Since they became dear through contact with him, who indeed could be more dear than he? Therefore, O twice-born ones, go to the place of sacrifice for the gods;
as householders, you shall complete your own sacrificial session together with them.
The wives said:
"O All-pervading Lord, you ought not to speak such cruel words;
please make your promise true at the very root of your feet."
We have obtained this garland of *tulasī* cast down by His feet, which we carry upon our hair, having utterly transcended all kinsmen;
neither husbands, nor parents, nor sons take it from us.
Neither brothers, kinsmen, nor friends, much less others, can help us; therefore, O subduer of enemies, since our souls have fallen at your feet,
provide for us no other refuge.
The Blessed Lord said:
Your husbands, fathers, brothers, sons, and others shall not be displeased with you;
the worlds, accompanied by me, and even the gods approve of you.
"O dear ones, the embrace of the body here does not lead to true joy or passion for men; rather,
by fixing your minds upon Me through hearing, seeing, meditating, and chanting My glories, you shall attain Me before long."
"Therefore, do not return home merely because of our proximity.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having been addressed thus, those wives of the twice-born returned once more to the sacrificial enclosure.
Free from envy, they completed the sacrificial session (satra) together with those women.
Among them, one who had been separated from her husband embraced the Blessed One as she had heard of him in her heart and abandoned her body, which was bound by the results of karma.
The Lord Govinda, the Master, having fed the cowherds with that very same fourfold food, ate himself as well; thus did He,
whose human form was a divine play, dwell within the world of men.
He took delight in the cows, cowherds, and gopīs, enchanting them with his beauty, speech, and actions.
Then, O brahmins, those who had committed an offense felt remorse as they recalled how they had rejected the request of the two Lords of the Universe, who were appearing in the guise of men.
Seeing the extraordinary devotion of the women toward the Lord Kṛṣṇa, and seeing themselves devoid of it, they were filled with remorse and censured themselves:
"Fie on our threefold birth! Fie on that vow! Fie on our great learning!"

"Fie on our lineage! Fie on our ritual skill! For we, though twice-born and teachers of men, have turned away from Adhokṣaja and are deluded by our own self-interest. Surely the illusory power of the Blessed One bewilders even yogis, since we, who are gurus to humanity, are so infatuated with our own welfare."
"Oh, behold the boundless devotion even of these women toward Kṛṣṇa, the teacher of the world,
which has severed the death-traps known as home! They possess neither the purificatory rites of the twice-born nor do they dwell under a guru."
We possess neither austerity, nor inquiry into the self, nor purity, nor auspicious rituals;
nevertheless, we lack firm devotion to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the lords of yoga, whose fame is supreme— even though we are endowed with the purificatory sacraments and other such refinements.
"Indeed, for us who were deluded by our own interests and intoxicated by the desires of household life—oh!
the Goal of the virtuous has reminded us through the words of the cowherd boys;
otherwise, how could He, whose every desire is fulfilled and who is the Lord of those who grant even liberation, have done so?"
What use have we, who are themselves objects of His lordship, for this mockery of the Lord? That He should abandon others and repeatedly resort to one whose feet She longs to touch—
that prayer of His is intended only to delude people, serving as a pretext to conceal His own faults.
Place, time, distinct substances, mantras, rituals, officiating priests, the sacred fires,
the deity, the sacrificer, the sacrifice, and dharma— all of which consist of Him;
He alone is the Lord Viṣṇu himself, the Master of the Lords of Yoga.
"We have indeed heard that he was born among the Yadus, yet being deluded, we did not recognize him. Salutations to that Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa of unimpeded intellect,
by whose illusory power our minds are bewildered and we wander upon the paths of karma."
"May that Primal Person indeed forgive our transgression, for we whose natures were deluded by His own *māyā* did not recognize His true majesty.
Thus, remembering their own sin, they had committed an offense against Kṛṣṇa.
Desiring to see Vraja, they were afraid of Kaṃsa and did not move from that place.
Śrī Śuka said:
The Blessed Lord, accompanied by Baladeva, remained right there.
Seeing the cowherds making preparations for a sacrifice to Indra,
the Blessed One— the soul of all and the seer of all— though already aware of it,
bowed with humility and questioned the elders led by Nanda.
"O father, please tell me: what is this agitation that has come upon you?
What is the fruit, for whom is it intended, or by what means is this sacrifice accomplished?
O father, speak of this to me, who am eager to hear, for my desire is great."

Indeed, there is nothing here that must be hidden from the virtuous who are devoted with their whole being, for they perceive no distinction between self and others, and harbor neither enmity nor indifference toward one another; even a neutral person should be avoided like an enemy.
One who acts as a friend to oneself is called a true friend.
This person performs actions both knowingly and unknowingly;
for the wise man, there may be success in his actions, whereas such success does not come to the ignorant man.
"Among those, has the yoga of action been considered by you? Or perhaps the worldly path? Please tell me properly as I ask. Śrī Nanda said:
The Lord Parjanya is Indra, and the clouds are his own bodily forms;
they pour down the water that delights and sustains all living beings. O dear one, we and others alike [worship] him, the Lord and Master of the rain-clouds.
With substances perfected by that seed, men perform sacrifices with rituals;
they subsist on its remnants for the sake of attaining the fruits of the three goals of life.
For men who exert human effort, the rain-cloud is the bringer of the fruit.
That man who, out of desire, hatred, fear, or greed, should abandon this dharma handed down through traditional succession, will certainly not attain what is auspicious. Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard the words of Nanda as well as those of the other inhabitants of Vraja,
Keśava, inciting anger toward Indra, spoke to his father.
The Blessed Lord said:
A living being is born by means of karma and is dissolved by karma alone;
happiness, misery, fear, and security are attained through karma alone.
If there were some Lord who [bestowed] the fruits of the actions of others, [then this would not be so].
He too serves only his own creator, for he is not the master of one who is not his creator.
What can Indra do here for living beings who follow their own respective karmas?
He is powerless to alter what is ordained by the nature of men.
For a person is dependent on their own nature and thus follows that nature;
all this world, including gods, asuras, and humans, is established in its own nature.
Having obtained various high and low bodies through the power of karma, a living being eventually casts them off.
An enemy, a friend, a neutral party, action itself, the guru, and the Lord—
therefore, one who abides in his own nature and performs his own duty should fully worship action. Indeed, that by which one proceeds directly is his very deity.

He who subsists upon another while depending on one thing for his livelihood finds no security from that other, just as an unchaste woman finds no security with paramours. A Brahmin should conduct himself through sacred knowledge, and a Kṣatriya through the protection of the earth.

A Vaiśya should live by the means of livelihood (vārtā), while a Śūdra should live by service to the twice-born. Agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and money-lending are said to be the fourfold vārtā; among these, we are constantly engaged in the occupation of cattle-tending.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the causes of maintenance, creation, and dissolution;
by rajas the manifold universe is produced, and the diverse world arises from their mutual interaction.
Impelled by rajas, the clouds rain waters everywhere.
"By those very [means] the subjects achieve their goals; what will Mahendra do?
We have no cities, provinces, villages, or houses; O dear one, we are forest-dwellers who always reside in woods and mountains."
"Therefore, let the sacrifice be commenced with cows, Brahmins, and fire;
let this sacrifice be accomplished with those materials required for the Indra-sacrifice.
Let various cooked foods be prepared, including soups, milk-rice, and other delicacies."
Let the *saṃyāva*, cakes, and fried pastries be taken, as well as the milk from all the cows; let the fires be properly offered by the Brāhmaṇas who discourse on the Veda,
and let food of many qualities and gifts of cows be given to them.
And from others—such as horse-dealers, outcasts, and the fallen—one should give according to their merit.
Having given fodder to the cows, let an offering be presented to the mountain. Then, well-adorned, having eaten, and being anointed with unguents and dressed in fine garments, [they should proceed].
Perform circumambulations of cows, brāhmaṇas, fire, and mountains;
this is my opinion, dear one, which you should carry out if it pleases you.
This sacrifice is dear to me and to cows, brāhmaṇas, and mountains alike.
Śrī Śuka said: Having heard what was spoken by the Lord, who is the soul of time and who desired to destroy the pride of Indra, Nanda and the others accepted those words, saying, "Well said."
And so they carried out everything exactly as Madhusūdana had instructed.
Having caused the mountain-dwellers and the twice-born to recite benedictions,
they respectfully offered oblations with those materials and provided fodder for the cows.
Placing their cattle-wealth at the front, they circumambulated the mountain; and having mounted well-adorned carts yoked with oxen,
the cowherd women sang of Kṛṣṇa’s heroic deeds along with the blessings of the twice-born.
But Kṛṣṇa, assuming another form that inspired confidence in the cowherds,
spoke with a massive body, saying, "I am a mountain," and accepted abundant offerings.
Together with the people of Vraja, he offered obeisances unto Him, the Self of all selves.

"Oh, behold! This mountain, having taken on a form, has bestowed its grace upon us. He, who can assume any form at will, slays those forest-dwellers who disregard mortals; let us bow down to him for the protection of ourselves and our cattle."
Having thus performed the sacrifice to the mountain, the cows, and the twice-born as impelled by Vāsudeva, those cowherds, together with Kṛṣṇa, returned to Vraja. Śrī Śuka said:

O King, having realized that his own worship had been thwarted by the cowherds led by Nanda and headed by Kṛṣṇa, Indra became enraged. He summoned the host of clouds known as Sāṃvartaka, which brings about the end of all things.
Indra, enraged, urged his speech and spoke words of contempt for the Lord:
"Oh, how great is the pride and arrogance of these cowherds who dwell in the forest! Having taken refuge in Kṛṣṇa, a mere mortal, they have committed an offense against the gods."

Just as people, having abandoned the science of logic (*ānvīkṣikī-vidyā*), seek to cross the ocean of worldly existence by means of solid boats made of ritual action— boats that are merely nominal— [so too do they approach You].
[They approach] one who is talkative, childish, stubborn, ignorant, yet who considers himself a scholar.

"Taking refuge in the mortal Kṛṣṇa, these cowherds have done me an offense. Shake off the arrogance born of pride in their wealth from those who are puffed up by Kṛṣṇa; lead these cattle to their destruction!"
"And I, mounting the elephant Airāvata, followed to Vraja with hosts of Maruts of great speed, desiring to destroy Nanda’s cowherd settlement. Śrī Śuka said:
Thus commanded by Maghavan, the clouds, their bonds released,
began to overwhelm Nanda’s cowherd settlement with torrents of rain through their sheer power,
flashing with lightning and thundering with the roar of storm-clouds.
Driven by fierce gusts of wind,
clouds incessantly released showers of water as thick as pillars;
drenched by these floods of water, the earth could no longer be seen, nor its elevations and depressions.
Afflicted by the intense downpour and the violent wind, the cattle trembled;
and the cowherds and cowherd-maidens, distressed by the cold, went for refuge to Govinda. Oppressed by the rain, they covered their heads and children with their own bodies.
Trembling, they approached the feet of the Blessed One and said:

"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O most fortunate one! O Lord, you who are affectionate toward your devotees, it behooves you to protect Gokula, which has you as its protector, and us gods, from the wrathful [Dānava]."
Seeing them rendered unconscious, being struck by a rain of stones and a violent wind,
Lord Hari, the Blessed One, considered it to have been wrought by the enraged Indra. Indeed,
there was a rain of stones accompanied by an extremely fierce wind, blowing from all directions.
Since our sacrifice has been thwarted by us, Indra rains down for our destruction;
therefore, I shall properly effect a remedy through the yoga of the self.
Out of the folly of those who consider themselves lords of the world, I shall destroy that darkness which is the intoxication of opulence.
For the gods who are endowed with the nature of goodness have no cause for astonishment at the Lord;
rather, the humbling of the pride of the wicked by Me serves to bring about their pacification.
Therefore, this cowherd settlement is my refuge, has me as its lord, and is my own possession.

"I shall protect [them] by means of my own yoga; this is the vow I have undertaken. Having said this, Viṣṇu took up Govardhana Hill with one hand and held it up effortlessly, as a child holds a mushroom.

Then the Blessed One said to the cowherds: "O mother, O father, O inhabitants of Vraja, enter the mountain cave with your cows and wealth as you please. You need have no fear here of being struck down by the falling mountain from my hand."
"Enough with this fear of wind and rain; indeed, a shelter for that has been provided for you.
Thus comforted in their minds by Kṛṣṇa, they entered the pit along with their wealth, their cattle-pens, and their dependents, each according to the space available.
Having abandoned the distress of hunger and thirst as well as his desire for comfort, while being watched by those inhabitants of Vraja,
he held up the mountain and did not move from his spot for seven days.
Hearing of that power of Kṛṣṇa’s yoga, Indra was greatly amazed.
Deprived of his support and his resolve shattered, he warded off his own clouds.
Hearing that the sky was cloudless with the sun risen, and that the fierce wind and rain had ceased, the upholder of Govardhana spoke to the cowherds:
"Depart! Cast away your fear, O cowherds, along with your women, wealth, and children! The wind and rain have ceased, and the rivers have mostly subsided.
Then those cowherds set out, each taking his own herd of cattle.
The carts, the equipment, and the women, children, and elders moved slowly;
meanwhile, the Lord, the Master, while all living beings looked on, playfully restored that mountain to its former place as it had been before.
The residents of Vraja, overwhelmed by the force of their love,
approached Him with embraces and other gestures; and the gopīs, filled with affection, honored Him with joy.
With curd, unbroken grains of rice, and water, they offered auspicious blessings.
Yaśodā, Rohiṇī, Nanda, and Rāma— the best among the strong—
embraced Kṛṣṇa and, overcome with affection, bestowed their blessings upon him.
In the heavens, the hosts of gods, Siddhas, Sādhyas, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas,
being delighted, offered praises and released showers of flowers, O King;
and conchs and kettledrums resounded in the sky, impelled by the gods.
O King, the lords of the Gandharvas, headed by Tumburu, sang [His praises].

Then, O King, Hari, surrounded by His devoted cowherds and accompanied by His army, returned to His own cow-pen. The cowherd women went along, joyfully singing of His various deeds that touch the heart.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having witnessed such deeds of Kṛṣṇa, those cowherds, who did not understand His true power, approached Him in great astonishment and spoke.
Since these deeds of the boy are indeed so exceedingly wonderful,
how could he deserve a birth among common folk that is so self-contemptible? For he, though but a seven-year-old child, [performed this] with ease by means of one hand alone.
How did he, bearing the best of mountains like a king of elephants bearing Mount Puṣkara,
drink the breast of the immensely powerful Pūtanā with his infant mouth while her eyes were closed, taking her life along with it as time consumes the body?
As he was crawling on his hands and knees, an ox, rushing downward, fell upon him;
while he was crying out, the overturned vehicle struck him with its forefeet.
Then, as he sat upon a one-year-old calf being carried away through the air, [he cried out].
He who, by the Daitya, was seized by the throat and rendered distressed by Tṛṇāvarta; who, on one occasion, was bound to a mortar by his mother for stealing the *dhaiyaṅgava* butter;
and who, while passing between the two Arjuna trees, struck them down with his arms.
While herding the calves in the forest, accompanied by Rāma and surrounded by the boys,
he tore apart with his two arms the enemy Baka, who desired to kill him, from the mouth;
[he likewise tore apart] the one who had entered among the calves in the form of a calf with the intent to slay them.
Having killed [the demon], he playfully felled the wood-apple trees with it;
and having slain the donkey-demon and his kinsmen,
the powerful one made the palm forest safe, filled with ripe fruit.
Having caused the fierce Pralamba to be slain by Balarāma, who is endowed with great strength,
he liberated the cattle of Vraja and the cowherds from the forest fire. Then,
having subdued the most venomous serpent-king and rendered him free of pride, he released him from the lake.

Having forcibly driven out the Yamunā, he rendered its waters poisonless. And how is it that there is such an irrepressible affection for him among all of us inhabitants of Vraja, O Nanda, and even in your son; how can this be innate?
Where is a seven-year-old boy, and where is the upholding of the great mountain? Therefore, O Lord of Vraja, doubt arises in us regarding Your son.
Śrī Nanda said:

"O cowherds, hear my words; let your suspicion concerning this child depart. Regarding this boy, Garga Muni told me that he indeed assumes three complexions, taking on different forms according to the age."
"Once white, red, and yellow, he has now assumed a black hue. Previously born in some place as the son of Vasudeva,
this glorious one is proclaimed by the wise as Vāsudeva."
There are many names and forms belonging to your son, corresponding to his qualities and activities; I know them, but other people do not.
This delighter of the cowherds and the cattle will bring about your ultimate welfare.
"By means of this, you shall easily cross over all difficulties.
O Lord of Vraja, in former times, when there was no king and the virtuous were oppressed by bandits, they protected one another and, flourishing together, conquered those bandits."
Those men who feel affection for this most illustrious one are not overcome by enemies, just as the Asuras cannot prevail over those who take the side of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, O Nanda, this boy is equal to Nārāyaṇa in his qualities.
"There is no cause for wonder regarding his deeds due to his splendor, fame, and majesty"—
having thus directly instructed me, Garga returned to his own home;
I consider Kṛṣṇa, the performer of effortless deeds, to be a portion of Nārāyaṇa.
Having heard these words of Nanda, which were sung by Garga, the inhabitants of Vraja were filled with joy; they honored Nanda and, their astonishment having vanished, they likewise honored Kṛṣṇa.
While the god Indra was raining down thunderbolts, stones, rain, and winds out of anger at the disruption of his sacrifice—

Seeing the cattle, their keepers, and the women sinking down, He took pity on them; smiling, though appearing weak, He uprooted a mountain with one hand as easily as a mushroom, and bearing it, He rescued the cowherd settlement. May Indra, who was terrified by the pride of Mahendra, be pleased with us, the cows.
Śrī Śuka said:
When Govardhana Hill had been lifted and Vraja protected from the downpour,
Surabhi and Śakra themselves came from Go-loka to Kṛṣṇa.

Approaching Him in a secluded place, feeling ashamed for having previously treated Him with contempt, he touched the feet of Kṛṣṇa— who possesses immeasurable splendor— with his crown, which was as radiant as the sun; for he had now witnessed and heard of the Lord's true majesty.
With his pride as the lord of the three worlds destroyed, Indra spoke this with palms joined in reverence:
Indra said:
Your abode is composed of pure goodness (*sattva*), peaceful, filled with austerity, and free from the qualities of passion (*rajas*) and ignorance (*tamas*).

This flow of the material qualities is composed of *māyā*; there is no binding attachment to them for You. O Lord, how then could those causes of it—greed and the like, which are the marks of the ignorant—exist in You?
Nevertheless, the Blessed One bears the rod of punishment for the protection of dharma and for the restraint of the wicked.
You are the father, the guru, and the sovereign lord of the worlds; you are insurmountable Time who has taken up the rod of punishment.
Out of compassion, You strive through forms assumed by Your own will to shake off the pride of those who consider themselves lords of the universe.
Those like me, who were arrogant enough to claim lordship over the world, shall quickly cast off that intoxication upon seeing You, the fearless one, at the appointed time.
Abandoning the path of the noble, those devoid of self-respect follow the pursuits of the wicked; such is indeed Your instruction.

Therefore, O Lord, You ought to forgive me, who am intoxicated by the pride of power, who have committed an offense against You, and who am ignorant of Your majesty. O Lord, may my mind never again become so deluded as to be unrighteous.

O Adhokṣaja, this incarnation of Yours here on earth is for the destruction of the commanders of armies who have brought about a heavy burden upon the world, and for the welfare of those who follow Your feet,
O Lord. Salutations to You, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, the Great Soul.
Obeisances to Vāsudeva, to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Sātvatas; obeisances to Him who assumes a body by His own will, whose form is pure knowledge;
obeisances to the All, the Seed of all, the Self of all beings.

O Blessed One, this was done by me through the winds that destroy the cow-pen and cause desolation, while the sacrifice was being obstructed by you, who are full of pride and fierce anger; yet, with my pillars shattered and my efforts rendered futile, I have been graced by you, O Lord.
"I have come for refuge to You, the Lord, the Guru, and the Self.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus was the Blessed Kṛṣṇa glorified by Maghavan.
With a voice as deep as a thundercloud, smiling, he spoke these words. The Blessed Lord said:
"O Maghavan, out of favor toward you, I brought about the destruction of your sacrifice."

For the sake of constant remembrance of me, I deprive of all prosperity that person who, being excessively intoxicated by the glory of Indra and blinded by the pride of power and wealth, does not see me standing with staff in hand; yet, for whomsoever I desire to show favor, I do not deprive him of his prosperity.
"Go, O Śakra; may it be well with you. Carry out my instruction:
remain in your respective offices, disciplined and free from pride.
Then the wise Surabhi, having offered her salutations to Kṛṣṇa, spoke.
Having addressed the Lord in the form of a cowherd along with her own offspring,
Surabhi said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O great yogin, O soul of the universe, O source of the universe!"
O Acyuta, with You as our Lord of the world, we have found our protector.
You are our supreme deity; O Lord of the universe, You are Indra to us. For the welfare of cows, brahmins, gods, and those who are virtuous, please become manifest.
"Urged by Brahmā, we shall consecrate you as Indra.
O Soul of the Universe, you have descended to remove the burden of the earth.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus addressed Kṛṣṇa, Surabhi [offered] her own milk;
Indra, urged by the celestial sages and the mothers of the gods, [offered] waters from the celestial Gaṅgā drawn by the trunk of Airāvata.
They sprinkled the descendant of Daśārha and addressed him as "Govinda.

Tumburu, Nārada, and others—Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas—having arrived there, sang the glory of Hari which removes the impurities of the world; and the celestial women, filled with joy, danced gracefully.
The leaders of the hosts of gods praised him and showered him with rains of wonderful flowers;
the three worlds attained supreme bliss, and at that time the cows yielded milk flowing like rivers.
The rivers became floods of various flavors, and the trees began to drip honey.
O descendant of Kuru, when Kṛṣṇa was consecrated as king, the medicinal herbs ripened without being cultivated, the mountains bore jewels, and all these things—
even those that were cruel by nature— became free from enmity, my dear.
Having thus consecrated Govinda, the lord of the cows and Gokula,
Śakra, permitted by him, departed for heaven surrounded by the gods and others.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Having fasted on the eleventh day and worshipped Janārdana,
Nanda entered the waters of the Kālindī on the twelfth day to bathe.
A servant of Varuṇa, an asura, seized him and led him into the presence [of his master].
Disregarding the forbidden hour, Kṛṣṇa and Rāma entered the water at night;
not seeing them, the cowherds cried out, "Kṛṣṇa! Rāma!
Upon hearing this, the Blessed Lord saw that his father had been seized by Varuṇa.
O King, having gone into his presence, the powerful lord of the world-protectors, who grants fearlessness to his own people,
beheld Hṛṣīkeśa who had arrived;
having honored him with great worship, he spoke, for the sight of him was a great festival to him.
Śrī Varuṇa said:
O Lord, today my body has been purified; this very day my purpose has been attained, O Blessed One, for those who take refuge at Your feet have reached the further shore of the path.
Obeisances unto You, the Blessed One, the Absolute Truth, the Supreme Self,
wherein no illusion is heard of— the conceptualization of the creation of the world—
due to my ignorance, my delusion, and my lack of knowledge regarding what ought not to be done.
"This father of yours has been brought here; therefore, you ought to forgive him.
O Kṛṣṇa, O all-seeing one, you ought also to show me your favor.
O Govinda, who are so affectionate toward your father, let this father of yours be taken back."
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus propitiated, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of lords,
took his father and departed, bringing joy to his kinsmen.

But Nanda, having seen that super-sensory grandeur of the world-protectors and their deference toward Kṛṣṇa, was amazed and spoke to his kinsmen. And those cowherds, O King, with minds full of curiosity, considered him to be the Lord.
"Will our Lord not grant us His own subtle state?"—
perceiving this thought of His own people, the Blessed One, the all-seeing, Himself reflected upon this out of compassion for the fulfillment of their resolve.
"Indeed, the people in this world, wandering through high and low states of existence due to ignorance, desire, and karma, do not know their own true destination.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed Lord Hari, who is possessed of great compassion, [acted].
He revealed his own realm to the cowherds, which is beyond darkness—
that eternal, infinite light of Brahman, which is truth and knowledge,
and which the sages perceive when their minds are concentrated and the material qualities have subsided.
Led by Kṛṣṇa to the Brahma-lake, they were submerged and then raised up;
there they beheld the world of Brahmā, where Akrūra had previously gone.
Having seen it, Nanda and the others were filled with the bliss of supreme joy.
And there they were greatly amazed to see Kṛṣṇa being praised by the Vedic meters.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
The Blessed Lord also spent those nights when the mallikā jasmine flowers were in full bloom in autumn.
Having observed this, He, relying upon His internal potency (yoga-māyā), set His mind on sporting.
Then the moon, the king of stars, rose over the quarters, anointing the face of the eastern direction with his most auspicious reddish rays;
he appeared like a beloved lover who, after a long absence, emerges to dispel the sorrows of his beloved.
Seeing the moon with its full orb,
which resembled the face of Ramā and was as red as fresh saffron,
and seeing that forest colored by its tender rays;
He sang in a sweet tone, enchanting to those with beautiful eyes; hearing that song which increases the god of love, the women of Vraja, their minds captivated by Kṛṣṇa,
came to where their beloved was, their movements unnoticed by one another and their earrings swaying as they ran.
Some, filled with longing, went toward him, leaving their milking unfinished;
others went after having placed the milk on the fire and before removing the *saṃyāva* porridge from the oven;
some went after setting aside the food they were serving, and others after giving milk to drink to their infants.
Some, desiring to serve their husbands, set aside their own food; others smeared themselves with unguents, wiped them away, or applied collyrium to their eyes;
and some, with their garments and ornaments disarrayed, went into the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
Though they were being restrained by their husbands, fathers, brothers, and kinsmen,
those gopīs, whose hearts had been stolen by Govinda and who were utterly deluded, did not turn back.
Some gopīs remained inside their houses, unable to find a way out.
Absorbed in meditation upon Kṛṣṇa, they closed their eyes and visualized Him;
shaken free of all impurity by the intense heat of the unbearable separation from their beloved,
and having exhausted all [other] auspicious merits through the bliss obtained from the embrace of Acyuta during their meditation.
Even though they associated with Him— the Supreme Self— with the notion that He was their lover,
they immediately cast off their bodies composed of the material modes, their bonds being utterly destroyed.
Śrī Parīkṣit said:
O sage, they know Kṛṣṇa as the supreme beloved, but not as Brahman;
how, then, could there be a cessation of the flow of the modes for those whose intellects are fixed on the modes?
Śrī Śuka said:

This was told to you previously, how even the King of Cedi attained perfection despite being an enemy of Hṛṣīkeśa; how much more so those who are dear to Adhokṣaja! O King, the manifestation of the Blessed Lord is for the sake of the ultimate welfare of human beings.

Those who constantly direct desire, anger, fear, affection, a sense of identity, and even friendship toward Hari— the immutable, immeasurable, and qualityless one whose very self consists of the qualities— indeed attain absorption in Him.

"You should not feel such astonishment toward the unborn Lord Kṛṣṇa, the master of the lords of yoga, for by him all this is liberated. Having seen those women of Vraja approaching his presence, the Blessed One—
The Blessed Lord, the best among those who speak, spoke, enchanting them with the elegance of his words: The Blessed Lord said:
"Welcome to you, O highly fortunate ones! What pleasing service may I do for you?"
"Tell me whether all is well with Vraja, and state the reason for your arrival.
This night is terrible in form and frequented by fierce creatures;
return to Vraja, O slender-waisted women; you must not remain here."
"Your mothers, fathers, sons, brothers, and husbands are searching for you, not seeing you; do not feel anxiety for your kinsmen.
Behold the blossoming forest, illuminated by the rays of the full moon."
"O virtuous women, go now to that cowherd settlement adorned with the beauty of tree sprouts swaying in the playful breeze of the Yamunā; do not delay. Your husbands desire to hear from you;
the calves and children are crying, so give them milk and milk the cows."
Or rather, because of your deep affection for me, your hearts have been restrained;
you have indeed come here, and it is fitting that living beings take pleasure in me.
For the devoted service of a husband without guile is the supreme duty of women.
He brings welfare to his kinsmen and provides for his offspring.
Even if he is ill-behaved, unfortunate, aged, dull-witted, diseased, or even poor,
a husband who is not a sinner must not be abandoned by women who desire worldly well-being.
For noble women, an extramarital affair is everywhere despised; it leads not to heaven, brings ill repute, yields meager results, is fraught with hardship, inspires fear, and is universally loathed.
Yet, through hearing, seeing, meditating upon, and chanting the glories of Me, devotion toward Me arises.
"Therefore, do not return home merely because of our proximity.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard these unpleasant words spoken by Govinda, the gopīs—

Despondent and with their resolutions shattered, they fell into an insurmountable anxiety; with their faces cast down, they sighed, their bimba-like lips drying with grief as they scratched the earth with their feet.
With tears that had soaked their garments, they stood silent, bearing a heavy burden of great sorrow, as they wiped away the saffron from their breasts.
They gazed upon their beloved, who was speaking as if he were someone other than dear to them.
Having turned away all other desires for the sake of Kṛṣṇa,
those deeply devoted women wiped their eyes, which were impaired by weeping,
and spoke with voices faltering due to agitation.
The gopīs said:
O All-pervading Lord, you ought not speak such cruel words to us,
who have abandoned all sense objects and taken refuge at the base of your feet.

O You who are difficult to restrain, please favor Your devotees; do not abandon us, just as the primordial Person, the Lord, favors those seeking liberation. For, my dear friend, [this service] consists of attending upon one's husband, children, and friends.
"O Knower of Dharma, you have stated that this is the specific duty of women;
let it be so, for you are the Lord who stands at the very foundation of instruction. You are indeed the dearest one, the kinsman, and the very Self of all embodied beings."
For the wise find delight in You, their own eternal Self; what need have they for wives, sons, and the like, which bring only suffering?
Therefore, be gracious to us, O Supreme Lord, and do not cut us off from You.
O lotus-eyed one, the hope long held by me for you has finally been fulfilled;
my mind, which had been drawn away from home by worldly pleasures, now enters into you with ease, as do my hands when they take up the work of service.
Your feet do not move even a step from the soles of Your feet;
how then shall we go to Vraja, or what indeed shall we do? O dear one, sprinkle us with the full vessel of the nectar of Your lips.

O friend, if we do not reach the state of Your feet through meditation, our bodies will be consumed by the fire born of separation; otherwise, that fire of the heart’s passion produced by Your smiles, glances, and sweet songs will consume us.

O lotus-eyed one, ever since we touched the sole of Your foot— which is dear to the forest-dwellers and which Lakṣmī has been granted a moment’s respite upon— it has never again come directly before anyone else.
Alas, though we have been delighted by you, we are unable to remain here;
for even Śrī, having obtained a place upon your chest— which is cherished by your servants— longed for the dust of your lotus feet along with Tulasī.
For whom even the exertion of other gods is rendered futile by her mere glance, so too have we taken refuge at the dust of Your feet;
therefore, O destroyer of afflictions, be gracious to us at the base of Your feet.
Having reached this state and abandoned their dwellings, they have fixed their hope upon worshipping you;
O Ornament of Men, grant the service of servitude to those whose souls are scorched by the intense longing born from beholding your beautiful smile.

Beholding Your face veiled by Your locks of hair, the beauty of Your earrings upon the regions of Your cheeks, the nectar of Your lips, Your smiling glance, and the pair of Your staff-like arms granting fearlessness;
"May we become handmaidens to Your chest, the sole beloved of Śrī!
O Lord, what woman in the three worlds would not falter from the noble conduct of those who are utterly infatuated by the sweet, melodious, and long notes of Your flute-song?"
Beholding this form, the good fortune of the three worlds,
for which the cows, birds, trees, and deer bore horripilation,
it is evident that you have been born as the remover of the fear and suffering of Vraja.

O God, the primordial Person and protector of the world of the gods, place Your lotus-hand upon us, O friend of the distressed; place it upon our scorched breasts and upon our heads, for we are Your maidservants.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard their lamentation, the Lord of the masters of yoga,
though finding delight in the Self alone, smiled and compassionately brought pleasure to the gopīs.
Accompanied by those women whose faces blossomed at the sight of their beloved, the infallible Lord Acyuta—
whose noble deeds were celebrated and who possessed the radiant luster of a broad smile like jasmine flowers— shone like the moon surrounded by stars;
while being sung to, he sang aloud as the leader of hundreds of groups of women.
Wearing the Vaijayantī garland, he wandered about, adorning the forest;
having entered the riverbank of cool sands, which was frequented by the gopīs and filled with the joy of its rippling waters and the breeze scented with the fragrance of night-lotuses.
By stretching out his arms for embraces, by the grasping of their thighs, the loosening of their waist-knots, the touching of their breasts, and the playful strikes of his fingernails;
by his jesting, glances, and smiles, he delighted the beautiful women of Vraja while exalting the Lord of Love.
Thus, they received honor from the high-souled Blessed Kṛṣṇa.
For those proud women considered themselves superior to all others on earth;
seeing their intoxication with such good fortune and their arrogance, Keśava vanished right there in order to quell it and to show them grace.
Śrī Śuka said:
When the Blessed One had suddenly vanished, the women of Vraja,
not seeing him, were tormented like female elephants who have lost their herd-leader.

With their gait, affectionate smiles, amorous glances, charming conversations, and playful movements, the women had their hearts captivated by the Lord of Ramā; becoming absorbed in Him, they mimicked His various gestures.
Through His walking, smiling, looking, speaking, and other acts, the forms of the Beloved became firmly established within those who loved Him.
"Here I am," thus did those women, whose very selves were absorbed in Kṛṣṇa’s playful pastimes, announce themselves.

Singing loudly of Him alone, they searched from forest to forest together like madwomen. They questioned the trees—the lords of the forest—who, though existing within all beings, are as pervasive as the sky.
"O Aśvattha, Plakṣa, Nyagrodha, Kurabaka, Aśoka, Nāga, Punnāga, and Campaka trees, have you seen the son of Nanda? He has departed, having stolen away our hearts with his smiles and glances of love."

O Tulasī, auspicious one, beloved of Govinda’s feet, has that Acyuta— who is exceedingly dear to you and whose smile removes the pride of proud women— been seen by you as he wanders with his circle of friends? O younger brother of Rāma, [has he been seen] whose smile takes away the arrogance of the haughty?
"O *mālatī*, was the *mallikā*, the *jāti*, and the *yūthikā* seen by you?
Has Mādhava departed, bringing joy to you with the touch of his hand?
[The trees replied: "The *cūta*, *priyāla*, *panasa*, *āsana*, *kovidāra*, *jambū*, *arka*, *bilva*, *bakula*, *āmra*, *kadamba*, and *nīpa* [trees]."

May those others who exist for the sake of others along the banks of the Yamunā proclaim the path of Kṛṣṇa to us whose souls are bereft of Him. O Earth, what austerity have they performed, that you shine with your body covered in horripilation from the festival of the touch of Keśava’s feet?
O wife of the deer, did you come here with your limbs embraced by the one born from my foot, or by the stride of the Wide-Strider (Urukrama), or perhaps by the body of the Boar-form?
O friend, as Acyuta spreads for you the perfect bliss of his glance,
the fragrance of the jasmine garland belonging to the Lord of the Family— stained by the saffron from the breasts of his beloved as she clings to his body— wafts here.
O trees, here He dwells, having placed His arm upon the shoulder of His beloved, holding a lotus in His hand,
followed by the swarms of bees intoxicated with the scent of the *tulasī*— He who is accompanied by Balarāma. Pay Him homage!

Or what does he delight in as he moves about with affectionate glances? Ask these creepers; they have been embraced by the arms of the Lord of the Forest and surely now bear horripilation from being touched by his fingernails—oh, how wonderful!
Thus the gopīs, distressed in their search for Kṛṣṇa, spoke words like those of a madwoman;
being absorbed in Him, they imitated His various pastimes.
One of them, acting like Pūtanā, drank from the breast of another who was acting like Kṛṣṇa.
Another, acting like a child, wept as he struck her with his foot;
another, acting like a Daitya, he carried off while she was absorbed in the thought of him being a young Kṛṣṇa.
One girl, pulling at his feet, rolled about on the ground with the sounds of her tinkling ornaments.

Two of them acted like Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, while some others protected [the calves]; another struck at the one acting as a calf, and there was yet another who acted like a crane. She called out to Kṛṣṇa, who followed her as she went far away.
Some, sounding their flutes while playing, praised her, saying, "Excellent!
Another, placing her own arm upon one of them as they moved along, said with her mind fixed on him, "I am Kṛṣṇa; behold my graceful gait."
"Do not fear the wind and rain; I have provided protection against them.
Having said this, with one hand he raised up their garment while they were struggling;
then, O King, having climbed up and stepped upon it with one foot, he seized the other by the head.
"Go away on this inauspicious day; indeed, I am born as the punisher of the wicked. Thereupon, one [of them] said: "O cowherds, look at the fierce forest fire!
Quickly close your eyes; I shall provide for your safety immediately."
There, a certain slender woman, already bound with another garland at the mortar,
said, "I bind this breaker of vessels who steals the fresh butter," and being terrified,
she covered her face with her beautiful eyes and feigned fear.
Thus questioning Kṛṣṇa, the creepers and trees of Vṛndāvana beheld in that forest region the footprints of the Supreme Soul;
"Clearly these are the footsteps of the high-souled son of Nanda."

Indeed, the women were seen following His path ahead by various footprints marked with banners, lotuses, thunderbolts, goads, barley-corns, and other signs; beholding those footprints closely mingled with the footprints of their brides, they spoke in distress.
Whose footprints are these, left by one who has walked with the son of Nanda,
her forearm resting upon his shoulder like an elephant-cow beside a male elephant? Surely the Blessed Lord Hari, the Supreme Controller, has been propitiated by this woman.

"O blessed ones! How fortunate are those groves which Govinda, being pleased, abandoned us for and led to in secret! Ah, those dust-particles from Govinda’s lotus feet—which Brahmā, Śiva, and the goddess Ramā bear upon their heads to dispel all evil!"
These footprints of hers cause us great agitation,
for she alone has carried off the gopīs and enjoys the lips of Acyuta in secret; indeed, her footprints here are not seen because they have surely been covered by sprouts of grass.
The Beloved lifted up his beloved, whose well-formed soles were weary;
"O Gopīs, behold these footprints of Kṛṣṇa, the lover, who is burdened by the weight of carrying his bride. These footprints are deeply impressed as he carries the young woman.
31. Here the beloved was lowered by the Great-Souled One for the sake of flowers;
32.1. Here the gathering of blossoms was performed by the lover for the sake of his dear one;
32.3. Behold these two footprints, left as he stepped forward upon his entire foot.

In this place, the lover surely performed the dressing of his beloved's hair; while adorning her with crest-ornaments, he must have sat here. Though he was self-satisfied and finds delight only in the Self, he took pleasure with her, remaining entirely undisturbed.

Displaying the wretchedness of lustful men and the wicked nature of women, the gopīs wandered about thus, deprived of their senses; for Kṛṣṇa had left the other women in the forest and led away that particular gopī.
And she then considered herself the most excellent of all women, thinking:
"Leaving behind the cowherd girls, my beloved is pursuing me out of desire.
Then, having gone to a certain part of the forest, she spoke haughtily to Keśava.
"I am unable to move; take me wherever your mind desires.
Thus addressed, he said to his beloved, "Mount upon my shoulder.
Thereupon Kṛṣṇa vanished, and that bride was filled with remorse.
"Alas, O Lord, O Beloved, O Consort! Where are You? Where are You, O mighty-armed one?
O Friend, show Your presence to me, Your wretched maidservant.
Śrī Śuka said:
Searching for the path of the Blessed One, the cowherd women, not far from him,
beheld their friend who was distressed and bewildered by separation from her beloved. Having heard what she related, as well as her attainment of honor from Mādhava, they [approached].

Due to their wickedness, they felt both contempt and supreme astonishment. Then, as long as the moonlight was still visible, they entered the forest; but perceiving that it had entered into darkness, the women turned back.

With their minds fixed on Him, their speech devoted to Him, their movements centered on Him, and their very selves absorbed in Him, they sang only of His qualities and did not remember their own bodies. Returning again to the sandy bank of the Kālindī, they meditated upon Kṛṣṇa.
Gathered together and longing for his arrival, they sang of Kṛṣṇa. The gopīs said:
"By Your birth, Vraja has attained supreme victory; for here indeed Indirā (the Goddess of Fortune) dwells eternally."
O Beloved, look! Your devotees in every direction, their lives surrendered to You, are searching for You.

O Lord of Love, with Your glance that steals away the splendor of the interior of a lotus blooming in an autumn pond, You treat these women—who are Your bond-slaves without price—as if they were commoners; O Giver of Boons, is this not execution for one who strikes down those who are already His?

O Ṛṣabha, we have been protected by You again and again from the danger of poison, drowning in water, predatory beasts, Rākṣasas, rain, wind, lightning-fire, and even from the bull-demon Vṛṣamaya who threatened us on all sides.
Indeed, You are not merely the son of a cowherd woman, but the witness of the inner self of all embodied beings.
Requested by Vikhanas for the protection of the universe, You, O Friend, have appeared in the lineage of the Sātvatas.

O Bull among the Vṛṣṇis, bestower of fearlessness, place Your lotus hand—which grants all desires—upon our heads, for we have approached Your feet out of fear of worldly existence; O Beloved, grant us the grasping of Your glorious hand.
O Hero who destroys the suffering of the people of Vraja, whose smile shatters the pride of Your own kinswomen; O Friend, favor us, Your maidservants, and show us Your beautiful lotus-face,
which draws away the sins of prostrate beings, follows those who graze upon the grass, and is the abode of Śrī.
Place Your lotus feet, resting upon the hoods of the serpent, upon our breasts; cut away the fever of desire within our hearts.
O lotus-eyed Hero, with Your sweet voice and charming words that delight the minds of the wise, satisfy us—who are bewildered by these ritual injunctions—with the nectar of Your lips.

The nectar of Your stories, praised by the wise, is the life-giver for those scorched by suffering; it removes all impurities, is auspicious to hear, and is full of splendor. Those people who on this earth recite these extensive accounts are truly great givers.
Your smiling, Your loving glances, and Your pastimes are the very essence of auspicious meditation.
O deceiver, those secret intimacies that touch our hearts truly agitate our minds.
O Lord, when you move from Vraja to graze the cattle,
our minds fall into a state of distress, thinking, "O Beloved, your lotus-like feet must be pained by the stones, grass, and sprouts."
At the close of day,
O Hero, as You display Your lotus-face covered by dark locks of hair and shrouded in thick pollen, You repeatedly instill the god of love within our minds.
You are the granter of desires to those who bow before You, worshipped by the Lotus-born Brahmā, the ornament of the earth, and the one to be meditated upon in times of distress.
O Our Delight, O Destroyer of Suffering, place Your most peaceful lotus feet upon our breasts;
O Hero, grant us the nectar of Your lips, which increases amorous joy, destroys grief, is beautifully kissed by Your resonant flute, and causes men to forget all other attachments.
While you wander through the forest during the day, even a mere moment seems like an eon to those who do not see you;
yet for the dull-witted who gaze upon your curly locks and your beautiful face, it is as if their very eyes were made of stone.
O Acyuta, they have come to you at last, having utterly transcended their husbands, sons, kin, brothers, and relatives.
