O Deceiver, even women who know the ways of the world are deluded by Your song; who would abandon You when You meet them in secret at night?
Seeing Your broad chest—the very abode of Śrī—Your smiling face, Your loving glances, and the awakening of love within their hearts, their minds are repeatedly bewildered by intense longing.

O dear one, the manifestation of You, the destroyer of sins, is sufficient for all auspiciousness to the inhabitants of Vraja and the forest; yet, please withdraw even slightly from us, whose souls long for You, so that there may be an end to the pain in the hearts of Your own kin.
[For] that well-formed lotus-foot of Yours [is placed] upon our breasts...
Terrified, O Beloved, we slowly place our feet upon these harsh thorns;
therefore you wander through the forest—does that not cause you some pain? Yet the minds of us who live for your sake continue to roam [only] after you.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, thus the gopīs, longing for the sight of Kṛṣṇa, sang aloud, lamented in various ways, and wept with melodious voices.
To them appeared Śauri, his lotus-face smiling,
wearing yellow garments and garlands— the manifest destroyer of even the God of Love himself.
Beholding their dearest beloved arrived, those women’s eyes blossomed with joy.
All those bodies rose up simultaneously, like the vital breath returning to its source.
One woman joyfully grasped Śauri’s lotus-hand with her own lotus-palms;
another placed his arm, adorned with sandalwood paste, upon her shoulder.
One slender woman took the chewed betel from his mouth with her joined palms;
another, tormented by love, placed his lotus feet upon her breasts; and one, overwhelmed by the intensity of her love, knit her brows in a frown.

Another, biting her lips, seemed to strike him with the casting of her side-long glances; another, with unblinking eyes, took delight in his lotus-face and was not satiated, even though she had drunk it in, just as the virtuous are never sated by his feet.
One woman, having placed him within her heart through the aperture of her eyes and closing them,
stood with her limbs bristling with joy, embracing him like a yogi immersed in bliss;
all of them were satisfied by the supreme festival of beholding Keśava.
Just as people who have attained a wise man cast off the fever born of separation,
so too the Lord Acyuta, surrounded by those women whose sorrows were dispelled,
shone forth even more brilliantly, my dear, like the Supreme Person accompanied by His potencies.
Taking them with him, the Lord entered the sandy bank of the Kālindī—

a place auspicious and free from the darkness of night, where the gloom was dispelled by the mass of rays from the autumnal moon, and which was filled with bees drawn to the fragrance of the wind carrying the scent of blooming *kunda* and *mandāra* flowers.
The sands were made soft and strewn by the movement of Kṛṣṇā’s hands;
their heart-pains were shaken away by the joy of seeing Him, and they reached the end of their desires, just as the Vedas reach their goal through the realization of Brahman.
With their own upper garments, marked by the saffron from her breasts, they prepared a seat for their own kinsman.
Seated there, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign whose throne is established within the hearts of the masters of yoga,
shone as he entered the assembly of the gopīs, honored by them and bearing a form that was the sole abode of the splendor of the three worlds.
Having greeted him— who kindles the god of love— with smiles, playful glances, and the arching of his eyebrows, they paid him homage.
Having praised Him by touching His feet and hands upon their own limbs, they spoke somewhat indignant.
The Śrī-gopīs said:
"He who reciprocates with one who worships him; he who does otherwise is the opposite."
"O venerable one, please tell us properly: why is it that some do not serve both [the Lord and the devotees]?
The Blessed Lord said:
"Those friends who serve one another do so because their efforts are directed solely toward their own self-interest."
Therein, neither friendship nor righteousness exists for the sake of self-interest, for that is not otherwise;
yet those who are compassionate serve even one who does not serve them, just like parents.
O slender-waisted ladies, in this world, both righteousness and friendship are beyond reproach.
Even those who worship Me do not truly worship Me; how much less so those who do not worship?
For they are self-delighting, their desires already fulfilled, ungrateful, and hostile toward their gurus.
But I, O friends, do not abandon even those living beings who worship Me, for the sake of following the conduct of those very people.
Just as a poor man, upon losing wealth he had acquired, remains absorbed in thought of it and perceives nothing else,

so too, O women, because you have abandoned worldly life and the Vedas for my sake, I have concealed myself from you while I was manifesting before you, so that you might continue to follow me; you should not feel resentment toward that which is dear to me, for you are my beloveds.
"O gods, even with your entire lifespan, I am not able to fully describe the virtuous deeds of you who are united with the faultless;
for you have severed the chains of the household, which are so difficult to break, and having worshipped me, let that merit return to you through your goodness.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus heard the exceedingly charming words of the Blessed One, the gopīs abandoned the fever born of separation, their blessings being fulfilled by His very limbs.
Thereupon, Govinda began the rāsa-dance with those who were devoted to Him.
Accompanied by beloved jewel-like women with their arms interlaced one with another,
the Rāsa festival commenced, adorned by a circle of gopīs,
with Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, standing in the midst of every two of them.

As soon as they entered and were grasped by the neck by the women who drew them close to themselves, the sky became crowded with hundreds of celestial chariots belonging to the gods and their wives, whose hearts were seized by intense longing.
Then the kettledrums resounded and showers of flowers fell;
the lords of the Gandharvas, together with their wives, sang His stainless glory. So too did the bracelets, anklets, and girdles of the women.
A tumultuous sound arose from those who were with their beloveds in the circle of the *rāsa* dance.
Therein, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, shone exceedingly with them,
like a great emerald in the midst of golden jewels.

The wives of Kṛṣṇa— by the placement of their feet, the shaking of their arms, their smiles, the play of their eyebrows, their waists that were breaking under the sway of their swaying breasts, their earrings rolling upon their cheeks, and the beads of sweat on their faces— the knots of their braided hair and their waist-bands became loosened.
Singing of him, they shone like flashes of lightning within a circle of clouds;
those sweet-voiced ones, who delight in pleasure, sang loudly while dancing,
their hearts gladdened by the touch of Kṛṣṇa, and by his song this entire world was pervaded.
One woman sang the musical scales unmixed with Mukunda;
being pleased, he honored her, saying, "Excellent! Excellent!
She sang that very *dhruva* melody, and he bestowed great honor upon her.
One woman, exhausted from the *rāsa* dance, with her bracelets and jasmine garlands loosened, took hold of the shoulder of the wielder of the mace who was standing at her side;
there she grasped Kṛṣṇa’s arm, which rested upon one shoulder and bore the fragrance of blue lotuses.

Smelling the sandalwood paste applied [to her], his hair standing on end with joy, he kissed the cheek of one woman whose face was adorned by the radiance of earrings swinging during her dance; pressing his own cheek against hers as she offered him the chewed betel nut.
One woman danced and sang, her anklets and waist-bells tinkling; standing by his side, she placed the auspicious lotus-hand of Acyuta upon her breasts when she grew weary.
Having obtained Acyuta as their beloved, the gopīs found him who is the exclusive favorite of Śrī.
With their arms clasping his neck, they sang as they carried him away—
the beauty of their faces enhanced by the heat from their cheeks, which were adorned with earrings and lotuses in their ears— accompanied by the musical sounds of their bracelets and anklets.
The gopīs danced together with the Blessed One in the rāsa assembly, where bees sang as they hummed from the garlands fallen from their own hair;
thus, through embraces, the touch of His hands, affectionate glances, unrestrained amorous play, and laughter.
The Lord of Rāma sported with the beauties of Vraja, like a child playing with his own reflected images.

O best of the Kurus, their senses overwhelmed by the joy of contact with His limbs, the women of Vraja— whose garlands and ornaments had fallen away— were unable to properly adjust their hair, their silken garments, or the cloths upon their breasts.
Beholding Kṛṣṇa’s amorous play, the women of the sky became bewildered;
afflicted by desire, they were struck with wonder, as was the Moon together with his attendants.
Having multiplied Himself into as many forms as there were cowherd women, He [enjoyed them].

Although the Lord delights in his own self, he sported with them in play; O dear one, out of compassion, he lovingly wiped the faces of those who were exhausted by their amorous pastimes with his most peaceful hand.

The gopīs, honoring the deeds of the Supreme Lord by means of their laughter and glances— beautified by the splendor of their cheeks and the shimmering luster of their golden earrings and locks of hair— sang of his exploits.

Accompanied by those women, whose merit consists in the joy of the touch of his hand-fingers, he dispels his fatigue through the contact of their limbs, as they rub against him with garlands crushed by their breasts and stained with saffron.

Followed by the Gandharva maidens, he entered the water like a weary lordly elephant that has broken its tethering post, being splashed about by the young women. He was thoroughly drenched by the maidens in the water.
Gazed upon with love from here and there by the laughing women, O dear one,
and honored by the denizens of celestial chariots showering flowers, he, whose delight is in himself, took pleasure there with the grace of a lordly elephant.
Then, in Kṛṣṇa’s grove, where the quarters and slopes were perfumed by breezes carrying the fragrance of flowers born of both water and land,

he wandered surrounded by throngs of female bees like a rutting elephant with its herd of females. Thus he spent his nights, which were illuminated by the rays of the moon, accompanied by groups of devoted women, for his desire was ever true.
Having internalized within himself the essence of all autumnal poetic themes and narratives, he enjoyed them in his own soul.
Śrī Parīkṣit said:
For the establishment of dharma and for the suppression of its opposite...
For the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of the universe, has indeed descended here by His partial expansion;
how then, O Brahmin, could He— who is the speaker, the creator, and the protector of the bridges of dharma— practice that which is contrary to dharma, namely, the violation of another's wife?
The Lord of the Yadus had all his desires fulfilled; why then did he perform such a loathsome act?
O observer of noble vows, please sever this doubt of ours by telling us what his intention was.
Śrī Śuka said:

A transgression of dharma and even acts of violence are seen in the case of lords; for those possessed of great splendor, such acts do not constitute a fault, just as fire consumes everything it touches.
However, one who is not a lord should never practice such things, even in thought.
One perishes through foolishness by practicing [their words] inappropriately, just as Rudra did when he consumed the ocean-born poison.
The word of the lords is true, yet it is practiced in certain ways;
therefore, a wise person should act in accordance with that which is consistent with their own word.
O Lord, for those who are free from egoism, there is no personal gain here through virtuous conduct, nor is there any misfortune through its opposite;
how much less so for all beings— be they animals, mortals, or denizens of heaven?
The sequence of auspicious and inauspicious results for the Lord and those subject to His rule belongs to Him alone;
for those who are satisfied by serving the dust of His lotus feet have all their bonds of karma shaken off by the power of yoga.
Even sages do not move about at will when they are bound; how much less can there be bondage for Him, whose very body is assumed by His own will?
[This applies] to the gopīs, their husbands, and indeed to all embodied beings.
He who moves within is the Overseer; here, through His pastimes, He assumes a body.
For the sake of favoring His devotees, He has taken on a human form and engages in such pastimes that one becomes absorbed in Him upon hearing of them.
Deluded by his illusory power, the inhabitants of Vraja did not feel envy toward Kṛṣṇa;
they considered their own respective wives to be by their own sides. When the night of Brahmā had passed, they were cheered by Vāsudeva.

Reluctantly, the cowherd women, who were dear to the Blessed One, returned to their own homes. Whoever listens with faith to this pastime of Viṣṇu with the women of Vraja, or describes it, [attains the highest goal].
Having attained supreme devotion for the Blessed Lord, the wise man quickly casts off the disease of the heart— the longing for sense objects— in no time at all.
Śrī Śuka said:
Once, during a festival for the gods, the cowherds, filled with curiosity,
set out for the Ambikā forest in carts yoked with oxen.
Having bathed there in the Sarasvatī river, they went to the omnipresent Lord Paśupati.

O King, they worshiped the Goddess Ambikā with devotion and offerings worthy of her; and with great care, they all gave cows, gold, garments, honey, and honeyed food to the brāhmaṇas, saying, "May the Goddess be pleased with us."

Having drunk water on the banks of the Sarasvatī, the highly fortunate Nanda, Sunandaka, and the others, firm in their vows, spent that night there. In that forest, a certain great serpent was extremely hungry.
By chance, a serpent approached and swallowed Nanda as he lay sleeping. Seized by the snake, he cried out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa!
This great serpent is swallowing me, my dear; deliver me, who have sought your protection!"
Hearing his cry, the cowherds rose up suddenly;
seeing that he had been seized, they became distraught and struck the serpent with firebrands.
Although being burned by the flaming torches, the serpent would not let him go.
The Blessed One, the Lord of the Sātvatas, approached and touched him with his feet. By the touch of the Blessed One’s glorious feet, his impurities were destroyed;
he abandoned his serpent body and assumed a form worshipped by the Vidyādharas.
To him, who stood there bowing with a body blazing with splendor and wearing a golden garland, Hṛṣīkeśa asked:
"Who are you, appearing so wonderful to behold and shining with such supreme beauty?"
"How was I, being helpless, brought to this loathsome state?
The serpent replied:
"I was a certain Vidyādhara known by the name Sudarśana."
Moving through the quarters in a celestial chariot, endowed with the splendor of his own physical perfection,
he laughed at the sages Virūpa and Aṅgiras out of pride in his appearance;
for having been mocked by them, he was brought to this birth by his own wickedness.
That curse was indeed made by those compassionate ones for my own benefit,
since I, with my evil destroyed, have been touched by the foot of the Teacher of the World.
Therefore, I [seek refuge] in you, the remover of fear for those who have surrendered and are terrified of worldly existence.
"I take my leave, O destroyer of all evils, for I have been liberated from the curse by the touch of Your feet. I have taken refuge in You, O Great Yogin, Supreme Person, Lord of the virtuous;
grant me permission, O God, Lord of the lords of all worlds."
O Acyuta, by the mere sight of you, I have been instantly liberated from the curse of Brahmā.
Since the utterance of your name immediately purifies all who hear it as well as oneself, what need is there to mention one who has been touched by your foot?
Having thus taken leave of the descendant of Daśārha, and having circumambulated and prostrated before him,
Sudarśana departed for heaven, and Nanda was released from his distress. Having witnessed that manifestation of Kṛṣṇa’s own divine power, [he was filled with wonder].
Then the inhabitants of Vraja, their minds filled with wonder, completed their religious observances there and returned to Vraja,
respectfully recounting those events to the King.
Once, Govinda and Rāma of wondrous prowess were wandering in the forest at night, situated in the midst of the women of Vraja,
while being charmingly sung to by those women who were bound to them by deep affection.
With their limbs well-adorned and anointed, wearing garlands and stainless garments,
they honored the onset of night as the moon and stars rose,
accompanied by the night-blooming lily-scented breeze frequented by bees intoxicated by the fragrance of jasmine.

They sang that which is auspicious for the minds and ears of all living beings, simultaneously modulating their voices through the full range of musical scales. O King, hearing that song, the gopīs were so overcome with ecstasy that they lost consciousness.
Then, while they were thus sporting at will and singing like those intoxicated, their silk garments slipping and their hair and flower-garlands disheveled,
the one known as Śaṅkhacūḍa, a follower of Kubera, arrived.

O King, while the two of them looked on, he fearlessly drove those women—who were crying out for their protector—toward the northern direction. Seeing his own followers crying out, "Kṛṣṇa! Rāma! [he continued].
Just as the two brothers, Śāla and Hasta, who were swift and cried out "Do not fear! to grant fearlessness, pursued the cattle seized by the bandit,
they quickly overtook that lowest of Guhyakas with great force.
Seeing those two arrived like Time and Death itself, he was terrified;
abandoning his women, the fool fled, desiring to save his life.
Govinda pursued him wherever he ran.
Desiring to seize that crest-jewel, Balarāma stood guarding the women;
approaching as if from no great distance, O dear one, the Lord struck off the head of that evil-minded man with his fist, along with its crest-jewel.
Having thus slain Śaṅkhacūḍa and taken his radiant jewel, he affectionately gave it to his elder sister while the women looked on. Śrī Śuka said:
When Kṛṣṇa had gone to the forest, the gopīs, their hearts following after him,
passed their days in sorrow while singing of Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes.
The gopīs said:
Where Mukunda, resting his flute upon his lower lip, with his left hand placed against his left cheek and his eyebrows dancing, plays the notes supported by his tender fingers,
the women of the celestial chariots, together with the Siddhas, perceive it and are struck with wonder and bashfulness.
Their minds surrendered to the arrows of desire, they fell into a state of delusion, forgetting their very girdles.
Alas, listen to this wonder, O women: when this son of Nanda, whose necklace laughs like steady lightning upon his chest, plays his flute, he bestows joy even upon those who are distressed.

In herds, the bulls, deer, and cows of Vraja, their minds captivated by the flute-playing, stood at a distance with morsels held between their teeth and ears pricked up; they were as motionless as figures in a painted picture.
He, with peacock feathers, flower clusters, and mineral pigments, imitated the decorations of a wrestler’s attire.
O friend, whenever Mukunda, accompanied by Balarāma and the cowherds, calls the cows,
then the rivers— having their currents broken by the breezes carrying the dust of his lotus feet—
stand with their waters motionless, their arms trembling with love like us who possess little merit.
His prowess extolled by his attendants, possessing immovable splendor like the Primeval Person (Ādi-puruṣa),
he, while wandering through the forest, would call the cows grazing on the mountain slopes with his flute. Indeed, when he was there,
the forest creepers and trees, rich with flowers and fruits, seemed to manifest Viṣṇu within themselves.

When He, the tilaka of the beautiful, took up His beloved flute, the trees— whose branches bent under the weight of His presence and whose bodies thrilled with love— rained down streams of honey; and the swarms of bees, intoxicated by the divine fragrance of the *tulasī* and the honey of the forest garlands, offered Him their deep and cherished song.
In the lake, the cranes, swans, and other birds, their hearts captivated by His beautiful songs, approached Hari; with restrained minds, eyes closed, and observing silence, they worshiped Him.
On the ridges of the mountain, the goddesses of Vraja beheld Him together with Balarāma, adorned with playful garlands and ear-ornaments.
When He, His own joy aroused by the sound of His flute, gladdens the entire world with His embrace,
the cloud— its mind apprehensive of being surpassed by that greatness— roars very softly,
raining flowers upon its friend and providing a parasol with its shade.

Your son, skilled in the various movements of the cowherds and expert in the flute, when he placed the flute to your lips, O virtuous one, produced many varieties of musical notes through his own training; hearing that at every sacrifice, the lords of the gods, led by Śakra, Śarva, and Parameṣṭhin, [were filled with wonder].
The wise, their necks and minds bowed in devotion, fell into a state of dejection as they could not ascertain the truth; yet He, whose gait was like that of a noble bull,
whose flute was praised, and who adorned His hooves with the marks of the flag, thunderbolt, lotus,
and goad, relieved the pain of the cows' hooves upon the ground of Vraja by treading softly with the petals of His own lotus feet.
As he walks, we—our hearts’ passion aroused by his playful glances—are driven into a state like that of a bird in flight;
overcome by faintness, we know not our own hair or our garments.
At times, wearing a jewel and counting his beads with a garland of beloved fragrant *tulasī*, he gazes at the cows.
Placing his arm upon the shoulder of his affectionate attendant,
he sang there where the wives of Kṛṣṇa, their hearts deceived by the sound of his resonating flute, followed Kṛṣṇa—
like does following Hari, the ocean of a multitude of virtues, having abandoned all hope for their homes.

O sinless one, your son, the delight of Nanda, sporting in the Yamunā— adorned with festive attire consisting of jasmine garlands, surrounded by cowherds and herds of cattle, and bringing joy to his friends—
was wandering about while a gentle breeze blew favorably, honoring him with the touch of sandalwood.
The hosts of demigods who were his bards surrounded him with instrumental music, song,
and offerings; affectionate toward the cows of Vraja, he was praised on the path by the elders as he drove them home at day’s end, playing his flute while his fame was celebrated by his followers.

Even with the luster of fatigue from the festival, he who was born from the womb of Devakī approaches like the moon, the king of stars, scattering the dust of his hooves upon the garlands and uplifting the eyes of all; desiring to bestow blessings upon his friends, this giver of honor wears a forest garland, his eyes slightly rolling with intoxication.

With a face as pale as the *badara* fruit, beautifying his soft cheeks with the splendor of golden earrings, the Lord of the Yadus— who moves with the gait of a king of elephants— approaches like the moon at the end of the day;
with a joyful countenance, he comes to release the cows of Vraja from their endless suffering during the day.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, in this way the women of Vraja, their hearts and minds fixed upon Him, took delight in the days as they sang of Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes, attaining great spiritual fulfillment.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said: Now, at that time, the demon Ariṣṭa in the form of a bull arrived at the cowherd settlement,
shaking the earth with his massive body and great hump as it was scarred by his hooves.
Bellowing most fiercely, scratching the earth with his hooves,
raising his tail, and tearing up the embankments with the tips of his horns,
he passed dung and urine here and there with fixed eyes.
O dear one, by his harsh bellowing, the embryos of cows and men fell prematurely and indeed miscarried out of sheer fear; and the clouds would enter his hump,
mistaking it for a mountain peak.
Beholding him with his sharp horns, the cowherd women and the cowherds were terrified;
the cattle fled in fear, O King, abandoning the herd, and they all sought refuge in Govinda, crying out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa!"
The Blessed One, seeing that the cowherd village had fled in fear,
comforted them with the words, "Do not fear," and then challenged the demon Vṛṣāsura:
"O lowest of men, what is the use of these cowherds and cattle who have been terrified by you, O fool?"
"Upon me, the Teacher, you wicked and evil-minded ones such as yourself!"—
shouting thus and provoking Ariṣṭa with the sound of his palms, Acyuta, Hari, threw his broad arm around his friend's shoulder and stood there.
Thus provoked, Ariṣṭa, scratching the earth with his hoof,
his tail raised and whirling like a cloud, rushed angrily toward Kṛṣṇa;
he stood before Acyuta with the tips of his horns thrust forward and his bloodshot eyes fixed on him.
Having cast him aside with a sidelong glance, he rushed forward swiftly like a thunderbolt released by Indra;
then the Blessed One, seizing him by the two tusks, drew him back eighteen steps, just as one elephant repels a rival elephant.
Cast off by the Blessed One, he rose up again and rushed forward in haste,
his entire body perspiring and sighing heavily, faint with rage.
As he charged, He seized him by the horns, stepped upon him with His foot, and threw him down to the ground.
He squeezed him as if wringing out a wet garment and struck him with his tusk;

he fell down, vomiting blood, discharging urine and excrement, and tossing his feet about with unsteady eyes. Then, as he suffered the agony of the abode of Nirṛti, the gods scattered flowers and praised Hari.

Having thus slain the bull-demon Ariṣṭa while being praised by the twice-born, Kṛṣṇa— whose deeds are miraculous— entered the cow-pasture with his companions, a festival for the eyes of the gopīs. 10.36.15–16.1.
Then the blessed Nārada, who has the vision of the gods, said to Kaṃsa:
"The daughter of Yaśodā is actually the daughter of Devakī, and Kṛṣṇa as well;
and Rāma, the son of Rohiṇī, was carried away by Vasudeva out of fear."
Those two were indeed entrusted to his friend Nanda, by whom those men had been slain.
Upon hearing this, the Lord of the Bhojas, his senses agitated by anger,
seized a sharpened sword with the intent to kill Vasudeva.
Having been dissuaded by Nārada, Kaṃsa learned of his own death at the hands of those two sons;
he then bound them, along with his wife, with iron fetters. When the celestial sage had departed, Kaṃsa addressed Keśin.
"Kill Rāma and Keśava! Thus he dispatched [the messengers].
Then the King of the Bhojas, having summoned Muṣṭika, Cāṇūra, Śala, Tośalaka, and others, as well as his ministers and elephant-keepers, spoke to them.
"O heroes Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika, listen to this:
it is said that the two sons of Ānakadundubhi, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, are staying in Nanda’s cowherd settlement; therefore, my own death has indeed been indicated [to me] by them."
"When you two have arrived here, they shall be slain with the skill of wrestlers.
Let various platforms be constructed surrounding the wrestling arena,
so that all the citizens and country-folk may witness the spontaneous combat."

"O noble minister, let the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa be brought by you to the gate of the arena; slay my two enemies with him. Let the ritual of the bow-sacrifice be commenced on the fourteenth day according to the prescribed rules."
"Let them slaughter the sacrificial animals for the bountiful King of Beings! Having thus commanded, he who was skilled in the management of affairs summoned the bull of the Yadus,
took Akrūra by the hand with his own, and then spoke to him.
"O patron of charity, please show me your friendly favor with due respect.
Among the Bhojas and Vṛṣṇis, there is no one found to be more beneficial than you.
Therefore, O gentle one, I have taken refuge in you to accomplish this weighty task."

Just as the powerful Indra attained his own purpose by taking refuge in Viṣṇu, go now to the cowherd settlement of Nanda; there the two sons of Ānakadundubhi are staying. Bring them here on this chariot without delay.
"It was indeed ordained for me by the gods who take refuge in Vaikuṇṭha that my death should come from you;
therefore, bring them here along with the cowherds headed by Nanda and their offerings.
Once they have been brought here, I shall have them killed by an elephant that is like Death itself."
If he is released from that, then I shall have him struck down by wrestlers who are like lightning bolts.
Once those two are slain, I will slaughter their kinsmen— the Vṛṣṇis, Bhojas, and Daśārhas— led by Vasudeva, who will be consumed by grief.
And my father Ugrasena, who was old yet desirous of the kingdom,
his brother Devaka, and whoever else were my enemies— thereafter, O friend, this earth [was mine].
It will become free of thorns.
Jarāsandha is my elder, Dvivida is my dear friend,
and Śambara, Naraka, and Bāṇa have placed their friendship in me alone.
"By means of them, having slain the kings who side with the gods, I shall enjoy the earth.
Having understood this, quickly bring here the two children Rāma and Kṛṣṇa for the purpose of witnessing the bow-sacrifice and to behold the splendor of the Yadu city.
Śrī Akrūra said:
O King, your desire for the cleansing of your own faults is indeed noble;
yet one should remain equanimous toward success or failure, for destiny is the means by which results are brought about.
People form lofty desires even when they are thwarted by fate; nevertheless, they remain subject to joy and sorrow. Yet, I shall carry out your command.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus instructed Akrūra and dismissed his ministers,
Kaṃsa entered his own house, and likewise Akrūra went to his own abode.
Śrī Śuka said:
But Keśī, a great horse sent by Kaṃsa, swift as thought, tearing up the earth with his hooves,
[rushed toward Him] amidst a mass of clouds and celestial chariots shaken by his mane.
Making the entire sky terrifying with its neighing,
that [demon] was frightening his own Gokula; the Blessed One [perceived him] by those neighs, which caused the clouds to tremble like hair.
Seeking him in battle, the leader challenged him; he roared like the king of beasts.
Having perceived him approaching with his sacrifice toward the sky, he [the lion] turned his face toward him.
Drinking him in as it were, the exceedingly intolerant one rushed forward;
difficult to approach, with fierce speed and impossible to overcome, he struck the lotus-eyed Lord with his feet.

Having deceived him, Adhokṣaja, seizing him with his two arms in anger and whirling him around by the feet, cast him down with contempt at a distance of a hundred bow-lengths, as the son of Tārkṣya leaves behind a serpent; he then stood firm. Having regained consciousness, he rose up again in rage.
Opening his mouth wide, Keśin rushed swiftly at Hari; smiling, He [Hari] thrust His upper arm into the demon's mouth,
just as one would insert a snake into its hole.
The teeth of Keśin fell away upon being touched by the arm of the Blessed One, like [metal] that has been touched by glowing fire; and the arm of the Great Soul entered his body.
Just as a disease grows when neglected, so he grew;
with his breath obstructed by Kṛṣṇa’s expanding arm, tossing his legs about,
his limbs perspiring and his eyes rolling, he fell lifeless upon the ground, voiding excrement.

O King, having effortlessly struck down his enemy, the mighty-armed Lord— unmoved by pride and praised by the gods who showered him with rains of flowers— drew back his arm from the body of the demon, which resembled a karkaṭikā fruit,
while the celestial sage Nārada, the foremost of the devotees of the Lord, approached him.
In private, he spoke these words to Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are untiring:
"O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable soul, Lord of Yoga, Sovereign of the Universe,
Vāsudeva, Abode of all, Foremost of the Sātvatas, O Master!"
You are the Self of all beings, like the one light within pieces of wood;
hidden, dwelling in the cave of the heart, the witness, the Great Person, the Lord.
Having first taken refuge in Yourself by means of Your own self, You created the modes of nature through Your illusory power (*māyā*).
By means of them, you, the Lord whose resolve is ever true, create, consume,
and sustain this world; as such, you have descended for the destruction of the Daityas, Pramathas, and Rakshasas who burden the earth, and for the protection of the virtuous.
"By good fortune, this Daitya in the form of a horse has been slain by you with ease— he at whose neighing the gods, terrified, abandon heaven.
[And you have likewise subdued] Cāṇūra, Muṣṭika, other wrestlers, and the elephant."
"O All-pervading Lord, on the day after tomorrow I shall see Kaṃsa slain;
following that, the slaying of Śaṅkha, Yavana, and Mura, as well as of Naraka,
the seizing of the Pārijāta tree, and the defeat of Indra."
The marriage of the hero’s daughters, characterized by the bride-price of his own prowess;
the liberation of Nṛga from his curse, O Lord of the World, at Dvārakā;
and the acquisition of the Syamantaka jewel together with his wife.
The restoration of the dead son to the Brāhmaṇa from his own abode,
the subsequent slaying of Pauṇḍraka and the burning of the city of Kāśī,
and the destruction of Dantavakra and the King of Cedi at the great sacrifice;

Whatever other heroic deeds you perform while residing in Dvārakā, I shall witness them; they are to be sung by poets on earth. Now, regarding those [deeds] of yours which will destroy this very world in the form of Time—
I shall behold the destruction of the Akṣauhiṇī armies by Arjuna’s charioteer—
he who is a mass of pure consciousness, established in his own nature,
for whom all purposes are fulfilled, and whose desires are never in vain.
We take refuge in the Blessed One, by whose own splendor the flow of the qualities of *māyā* is eternally ceased;
we take refuge in You, the Lord, who are self-supported and who, by Your own *ātma-māyā*, have fashioned all particular conceptualizations.
"I bow down to the leader of the Yadus, Vṛṣṇis, and Sātvatas, who has now assumed a human form for the sake of divine play.
Śrī Śuka said:
"In this way, the sage, the foremost of the devotees, [praised] Kṛṣṇa, the lord of the Yadus."
Having prostrated and received permission, he departed, for him the festival of that vision had begun.
The Blessed Lord Govinda, having slain Keśin in battle,
protected the cattle with his joyful cowherds, bringing happiness to Vraja.
Once, while they were tending their cattle on the mountain ridges, they engaged in a game of hide-and-seek under the pretext of being thieves and herdsmen.
Among them, O King, some were thieves and some were herdsmen.
And some there, acting like rams, wandered about free from all fear.
Vyoma, the son of Maya, a master of great illusion, wearing the guise of a cowherd,
carried away many of those who were acting like rams, for he was mostly behaving like a thief.

Having thrown them into a mountain cave, the great asura carried them away one by one and blocked the entrance with a boulder; only four or five remained. Perceiving that deed of his, Kṛṣṇa, the refuge of the virtuous, [acted].
As he was leading the cowherds away, he seized a wolf with his might, as Hari seizes a boar.
Assuming his own form, which resembled the king of mountains, the powerful one desired to release himself, but being distressed by the grip, he was unable to do so.
Seizing him with his two arms and throwing him down upon the surface of the earth,
Acyuta killed that beast-slayer while the gods in heaven looked on; then, having burst open the cave’s entrance, he brought the cowherds out from their distress.
Being praised by the gods and the cowherds, He entered His own Gokula.
Śrī Śuka said:
And the high-minded Akrūra also spent that night in the city of Madhupurī.
Having stayed there, he mounted his chariot and set out for Nanda’s Gokula. As he traveled on the road, the illustrious one, having attained supreme devotion for the lotus-eyed Lord, reflected thus:
"What auspicious deed have I performed, or what supreme austerity have I practiced,
or what worthy gift have I given, that today I shall behold Keśava?
I consider this vision of the One of Excellent Fame to be difficult for me to attain."
Just as the chanting of the names of Brahman is possible for one born as a *śūdra* whose mind is attached to sense objects,
so too may there be a vision of Acyuta even for me, though I am most base;
for only rarely does someone, being swept away by the turbulent river of worldly existence, ever cross over.
"Today my inauspiciousness has perished and my birth has become fruitful, since I bow down to the lotus feet of the Blessed One, which are the object of meditation for yogis.
Alas, Kaṃsa has today bestowed a great favor upon me; sent by him, I shall behold the lotus feet of Hari."
The darkness that was difficult to cross before has been crossed by those for whom You have manifested an incarnation, by the luster of the circle of Your toenails;
You who are worshipped by the gods beginning with Brahmā and Bhava,
by the goddess Śrī, and by the sages together with the Sātvatas.

Wandering in the forest with his cowherd companions for the sake of tending the cows, I shall surely behold Him whose cheeks and nose are marked by the saffron from the breasts of the gopīs, and whose lotus-like eyes are reddened by His smiling glances.
The deer indeed circumambulate the face of Mukunda, which is covered by his curly locks.
Even today, when Viṣṇu has assumed human form by His own will to remove the burden of the earth,
the direct perception of Him, the abode of loveliness, shall surely not be without fruit for my eyes.
He who is the witness, free from the sense of "I," by whose own splendor the delusion of duality between the unreal and the real has been dispelled;
he who, through his own *māyā*, is perceived within the dwellings of living beings by means of the vital breaths, senses, and intellects fashioned for himself by that very perception;
he whose names, mixed with descriptions of his qualities, activities, and incarnations, are most auspicious and destroy all misfortunes when uttered.
Those who breathe, beautify, and indeed purify the world—those who are detached from them are considered as beautiful as a corpse.

And he, having descended into the lineage of the Satvatas, the protector of his own bridge and the bestower of peace upon the foremost of the immortals, dwelt in Vraja spreading his glory; that Lord, whose auspiciousness is complete, is sung of by the gods.
But today he has surely assumed that form which is the refuge of the great, the teacher, the delight of the three worlds, a magnificent festival for the eyes, and the desired abode of Śrī.

"I shall see my beautiful mornings approaching. Then, having immediately descended from the chariot of the two Lords, I— though I am certain that the feet of the Supreme Person, which are held in mind by yogis for their own attainment, are worthy of worship— bow down to them and to these forest-dwelling friends of theirs.
May the All-pervading Lord place His own lotus-hand— granting freedom from fear against the speed of the serpent of Time— upon the head of me who have fallen at the base of His feet.
Where Kauśika and Bali, having offered worship to those men who were agitated and seeking refuge, attained the lordship of the three worlds;
or where, during his pastimes, he dispelled the fatigue of the women of Vraja with his touch, which was fragrant like the saugandhika lotus.
The infallible All-Seeing One, who knows the inner and outer workings of the mind, will not regard me as an enemy, even though I have been sent as Kaṃsa’s messenger.
The Knower of the Field beheld me with his stainless eye, even as I stood at the base of His feet with palms joined in reverence; He gazed upon me with a smile and a moist, compassionate glance.
Immediately, with all his sins cast away, free from doubt and filled with intense joy,
he will embrace me with his two mighty arms— me, his dearest friend and kinsman, who have no other deity.
"For at that very moment my self is made a sacred ford and my bondage consisting of karma is dissolved; therefore,
O Akrūra, having obtained the touch of his limbs, the one of great fame will say to me as I bow with joined palms, 'O dear one!'"
"Then we were merely bearers of birth by that Great One; fie upon His birth, for He did not even deign to acknowledge us!
To Him there is no one most dear or best friend, nor anyone unpleasant, hateful, or even to be disregarded."
Nevertheless, He favors His devotees in whatever manner they approach Him, just as the celestial wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpa-vṛkṣa*) grants the needs of whoever relies upon it.

Furthermore, the best of the Yadus, smiling, embraced His elder brother who was bowing down and took him by his joined palms; having led him into the house and honored him with all hospitality, He questioned him regarding what Kaṃsa had done to their kinsmen.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, while his son was thus meditating upon Kṛṣṇa along the road, Akrūra reached Gokula by chariot as the sun set behind the western mountain.

He saw in the cowherd settlement the footprints of Him whose stainless foot-dust is honored by the crowns of all the world-protectors— footprints that were objects of wonder upon the earth, marked with the signs of the lotus, barleycorn, elephant-goad, and so forth. At the sight of them, his agitation increased due to the joy of that vision.
With his hair standing on end and his eyes filled with tears of love,
he leaped down from the chariot and fell prostrate among them,
exclaiming, "Oh, these are the dust-particles from the feet of the Lord!"
For embodied beings, this much is the ultimate goal: having abandoned hypocrisy, fear, and grief,
to behold Kṛṣṇa and Rāma in Vraja while they have gone out for milking the cows, through the sight of His marks and by hearing of Him, according to the instruction of Hari.
Wearing yellow and blue garments, with eyes like autumn lotuses,
they were youthful, dark and white respectively, the abodes of Śrī, possessed of mighty arms, with beautiful faces and exquisite forms, and having the prowess of elephants in rut.
Adorning Vraja with their feet marked by the signs of the banner, thunderbolt, goad, and lotus, those two great-souled ones, whose glances were compassionate and smiling,
engaged in noble and charming play, wearing garlands and forest wreaths.
With their limbs anointed with holy fragrances, having bathed and wearing stainless garments,
the two primordial beings, Pradhāna and Puruṣa— the causes and lords of the universe—
have descended as Balarāma and Keśava through their own portions for the sake of the world.
O King, making the quarters of the sky free from darkness by their own radiance,
like a mountain of emerald and silver overlaid with gold,
Akrūra, overwhelmed with affection, quickly leaped down from the chariot.
He fell like a staff at the feet of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
his eyes clouded with tears of joy from the sight of the Lord,
his limbs covered in horripilation due to intense longing; O King, he was unable to speak of his own name.
The Blessed One, intending him for that purpose, drew him close and embraced him with his hand marked by the sign of the chariot wheel, being pleased and affectionate toward those who bow before him;
and the high-minded Saṅkarṣaṇa also embraced him as he bowed down.
Taking him by the hand with his own, he led him home along with his younger brothers; then,
having asked after his welfare and offered him an excellent seat,
he washed his feet according to the prescribed rite and presented the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
Having offered a cow to the guest and having respectfully massaged his weary feet,
the powerful lord, with faith, presented him with abundant and pure food.
When he had eaten, Rāma, the knower of the supreme dharma, spoke to him with affection.

With garments from the sacrifice, perfumes, and garlands, Nanda again bestowed supreme delight upon them; having honored them, he asked: "O scion of the Daśārhas, how do you remain here while Kaṃsa lives, like birds in the care of a butcher?"
"That wicked man, who thirsts for life, slew the children of his own sister while she was crying out;
how indeed can we consider the welfare of those who are his progeny?
Thus was Nanda most hospitably honored with such truthful and pleasant words.
Akrūra, having been thus questioned, cast off the fatigue of the journey.
Śrī Śuka said: Seated comfortably upon a couch, he was honored by Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
On the way, he obtained all the desires that he had formed;
for when the Blessed One, the abode of Śrī, is pleased, what is there that cannot be attained? Nevertheless, O King, those who are solely devoted to Him do not desire anything at all.
Having finished his evening meal, the Blessed Lord, the son of Devakī,
asked His friends about Kaṃsa’s conduct and what else he intended to do.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O dear one, you have come at an auspicious time; welcome! May it be well with you all.
Are our own kinsmen and relatives free from misfortune and disease? Why do you ask after our welfare while the malady of the lineage is increasing?"

O dear one, because of Kaṃsa— who was known as our maternal uncle— great sin has been committed by us toward our own kinsmen and their offspring; for it is on his account that our sons have died and those two noble parents have suffered imprisonment.
"By good fortune, O gentle one, the sight of you, my own kinsmen, which I have long desired, has been granted to me today. Tell me, dear child, the reason for your arrival.
Śrī Śuka said:
Questioned by the Blessed One, Mādhava described everything:
his persistent enmity toward the Yadus and his attempt to kill Vasudeva;
as well as the message he had been sent with and the purpose for which he himself had been dispatched as a messenger.
Having heard what was said by Nārada regarding his own birth from Ānakadundubhi, and having heard the words of Akrūra, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, the slayers of enemy heroes,
laughed and learned from their father Nanda that this had been ordained by the King.
He also commanded the cowherds: "Let all the products of the cows be collected; take the offerings and let the wagons be yoked.
Tomorrow we shall go to the city of Madhu and bestow our delicacies upon the king."
"We shall see a truly great festival; indeed, the people of the countryside are departing.
Thus did Nanda-gopa have it proclaimed by his servants throughout his own cowherd settlement. Upon hearing this, those gopīs became deeply distressed.
Some women, their facial luster withered by sighs born from the heartache caused by Akrūra’s departure to lead Rāma and Kṛṣṇa back to the city,
had their silk garments, bracelets, and hair-knots slipping loose; while others likewise appeared distressed.
Others, whose entire mental functions had ceased through meditation upon Him,
did not perceive this world, as if they had entered their own spiritual realm;
while yet others remembered Śauri, moved by His affectionate smiles.
The women were utterly enchanted by his words, which touched their hearts with their wonderful phrasing;
by his most graceful gait, his gestures, his affectionate smiles and glances; and by his jokes that dispel sorrow and his unrestrained deeds.
Thinking of Mukunda, terrified and distressed by the prospect of separation, the gopīs—
meeting together in groups, their faces bathed in tears and their hearts fixed on Acyuta— spoke.
The Śrī-gopīs said:

"O Creator, you have no compassion anywhere; having joined embodied beings together with friendship and affection, you now separate them before their goals are achieved. Your sport is useless, like the behavior of a child, you who display [yourself] with dark locks of hair covering [your face]."
Mukunda’s face, with its beautiful cheeks and prominent nose,
made lovely by a trace of a smile that dispels all sorrow— you have made it invisible; you have done what is not good.

Though you are cruel, you are known by the name Akrūra; alas, like an ignorant man, you take away from us the very eye with which [we behold] the entirety of the beauty of creation in this single spot.
We have seen Your form, O enemy of Madhu;
yet the son of Nanda, whose friendship is as fleeting as a moment, does not look upon us, alas, for we are distressed by our own deeds.
Having abandoned their homes, kinsmen, children, and husbands, they had truly attained the state of being His maidservants;
now that He was their new beloved,
the night surely dawned with happiness and the city women’s blessings became realized.
Those women who shall drink the wine of the sidelong glances and smiles of the Lord of Vraja as he enters their mouths—
Mukunda, by means of his honey-sweet speech, will captivate their hearts; though he is wise and independent, he becomes subject to them.
"But how will that weak woman return to us?
Today, as he wanders with his rustic, modest smiles and amorous gestures, he will surely become the object of the glances of the Dāśārhas, Bhojas, Andhakas, Vṛṣṇis, and Sātvatas."
Those who behold the son of Devakī on the road— the great festival, the beloved of Śrī, the abode of all virtues—
will find that for one such as this, who is utterly merciless and exceedingly cruel, the name "Akrūra" (the Non-Cruel) has become quite unbecoming;
for he will lead away from the path, without having consoled the deeply grieving people, the one dearer than the dearest.

"This man of unyielding intellect has mounted his chariot, and these intoxicated cowherds are following him in haste. The elders have neglected us, and fate today acts against us. Let us go together and restrain Mādhava; what would our family elders and kinsmen do for us?"
For those whose wretched minds have been devastated by fate, it is difficult to abandon even for half a moment the company of Mukunda; [for them],
there is the assembly of the rāsa dance, consisting of his affectionate, playful smiles, charming mantras, amorous glances, and embraces.
"O Gopīs, we have been led away as if by a single moment, yet this night without Him has become an eternity;
how indeed shall we cross over this insurmountable darkness? He who, at the close of day, surrounded by His infinite friends, [returned] to Vraja..."
Entering [the city] with cowherds, his locks and garland dusted with the pollen from their hooves,
sounding his flute and captivating the mind with his smiles and sidelong glances— how indeed shall we exist without him?
Śrī Śuka said:
Speaking thus, the women of Vraja, deeply distressed by separation and with their minds fixed on Kṛṣṇa, cast aside all shame and wept aloud, crying, "O Govinda! O Dāmodara! O Mādhava!"
While the women were thus weeping as the sun had risen,
Akrūra, having performed the preliminary rites of friendship and other rituals, urged the chariot forward.
Then Nanda and the other cowherds followed him with their wagons.
Taking many offerings consisting of jars filled with cow's milk,
the gopīs, deeply enamored, followed their beloved Kṛṣṇa and stood waiting,
longing for a response from the Blessed One.
Seeing them thus grieving at the time of his departure, the best of the Yadus consoled them with affectionate messengers, saying,
"I shall return. [He departed] as long as the banner was visible and as long as the dust of the chariot remained.
With their minds fixed on following him, they appeared like figures in a painting;
having lost all hope regarding Govinda’s return,
they turned back and spent their days free from sorrow, singing of his beloved deeds.
O King, the Blessed Lord also arrived, accompanied by Rāma and Akrūra,
in a chariot with the speed of the wind, to the Kālindī river which destroys all sins.
Having sipped water there and drunk the pure water that shone like a gem, he [performed his ablutions].
Having approached a grove of trees, Rāma entered the chariot. Akrūra, having taken leave of the two of them and having set the chariot down,
went to a pool of the Kālindī and performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rites.

Having immersed himself in that water and chanting the eternal Brahman, Akrūra beheld those very two, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, together. "How are these two sons of Ānakadundubhi here, standing upon the chariot? he wondered.
"Are they perhaps not in the chariot? he thought, and emerging, he looked;
there too, they were seated exactly as before. He then submerged himself again, wondering, "Is my vision of them in the water false?"
Furthermore, there he beheld the Lord of Serpents being praised by Siddhas,
Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and Asuras with bowed necks—
the god who possesses a thousand heads and a thousand crested hoods.

He was clad in blue garments, white with blossoming lotuses, and stood as if made of white peaks; upon his lap sat a peaceful four-armed Person, dark as a rain-cloud, dressed in yellow silk, with eyes as red as lotus petals.
With a beautiful and serene face, a charming smile and gaze,
fine eyebrows and nose, lovely ears, and beautiful cheeks with reddish lips; with long, thick arms and the splendor of broad shoulders and a high chest.
With a neck like a conch-shell, a deep navel, and an abdomen marked with folds like tender leaves;
with broad hips, a wide pelvis, and thighs like the trunks of elephants; endowed with a pair of beautiful knees and a pair of lovely shanks.
His lotus feet shone with nine petals— the toes and thumbs— encircled by the radiance of the multitude of reddish nails upon his high ankles;
and he was adorned with a crown, bracelets, armlets, and anklets set with clusters of most precious gems.
He was resplendent with a waist-thread, a sacred thread, necklaces, anklets, and earrings; he held a lotus in his hand and bore the conch, discus, and mace;
the Śrīvatsa mark adorned his chest, he wore the shining Kaustubha gem, and was garlanded with forest flowers.
[He was surrounded] by assemblies headed by Sunanda and Nanda, by Sanaka and the others,
by the lords of the gods such as Brahmā and Rudra, by the nine most excellent twice-born ones,
and by the supreme devotees headed by Prahlāda, Nārada, and the Vasus.
He was being praised with distinct utterances by those of pure soul—
by Śrī, Puṣṭi, Gīr, Kānti, Kīrti, Tuṣṭi, Ilā, Ūrjā, Vijayā,
Vidyā, Avidyā, Śakti, and Māyā— and was attended by them all.

Beholding him, the Sātvata was exceedingly pleased and filled with supreme devotion; with his hair standing on end, his eyes moistened by his spiritual emotion (bhāva), he praised the Supreme Being with a voice faltering with emotion, summoning his inner strength.
Having bowed his head with humility and joined his palms in reverence,
Śrī Akrūra slowly spoke: "I bow down to you, Nārāyaṇa, the primordial and imperishable Person, the cause of the cause of all."
From the interior of the lotus born from Your navel, Brahmā appeared, from whom this world arose:
earth, water, fire, air, ether, the mahat-tattva, the ego, the mind, the senses,
all objects of the senses, and all the gods— all these causes of the universe are Your limbs, O Lord.

These—Aja and the others—do not know Your true nature, for they have grasped the Self as the non-Self; Aja is bound by the qualities of the Unborn (Māyā), and thus he does not know Your true nature, which transcends those qualities.
The yogis truly worship You, the Great Person, the Supreme Lord.

O virtuous ones, some twice-born performers of Vedic sacrifices worship you through the threefold knowledge (*trayi-vidyā*), along with the self (*adhyātman*), the elements (*adhibhūta*), and the divine powers (*adhidaiva*),
by means of extensive sacrifices under various names of the gods.

Some, having renounced all ritual actions and attained tranquility, being wise, worship You— the embodiment of knowledge— through the sacrifice of knowledge. Others, whose selves are purified by the prescribed injunctions, [worship You].
Those who are absorbed in you indeed worship you, who possess many forms yet are one in form; others worship you alone, whose nature is Śiva, according to the path taught by Śiva,
through the various distinctions of many teachers, O Blessed One.
Everyone indeed worships you, the Lord who consists of all the gods. O Lord, even those who are devotees of other deities, though their minds are directed elsewhere—
just as rivers originating from mountains are filled by the rain-clouds, O Lord.
Just as rivers flow from all sides into the ocean, so do all destinies ultimately enter You.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities of Your material nature (prakṛti); indeed, all beings—from Brahmā down to the immovable plants—are woven upon these qualities of nature.
Salutations to You, whose vision is unattached; salutations to the Self of all, the witness of all intellects.
This flow of the qualities (guṇas) is produced by ignorance.
The [universe] proceeds within the forms of gods, humans, animals, and selfs.
Fire is Your mouth; the earth is Your feet; the sun is Your eye; the sky is Your navel; and the directions are Your ears.
The sky is Your head, O Lord of gods; the oceans are Your arms; the Maruts are Your abdomen; and the vital breath and strength are ordained as Your power.
The trees and medicinal herbs are Your body hairs, and the plants are Your hair on the head.
The clouds are Your bones and nails; the mountains are Your eyelids; day and night are Your closing and opening of the eyes; and Prajāpati is Your penis, while rain is considered to be Your semen.
O Imperishable Self, O Supreme Person, within You are fashioned the worlds together with their guardians, teeming with many living beings;
just as aquatic creatures are contained within water, or gnats within an udumbara fruit, so are they within Your mind-made form.
Indeed, whatever forms You assume here for the sake of sport—
With their sorrows wiped away by those [beings], the worlds joyfully sing Your glory:
"Obeisance to You, the Causal Fish who dwells in the ocean of dissolution;
obeisance to You, the Horse-headed One, the death of Madhu and Kaiṭabha."
Obeisance to the vast Akūpāra, the sustainer of Mount Mandara;
obeisance to the one in the form of a boar, who sported in lifting up the earth. Obeisance to you, the wonderful lion, who removes the fear of the world of the virtuous.
Salutations to You, the Dwarf, who strode across the three worlds;
salutations to the Lord of the Bhṛgus, the cutter down of the forest of arrogant Kṣatriyas;
salutations to You, the best of the Raghus, the bringer of Rāvaṇa’s end.
Salutations to You, Vāsudeva; salutations to Saṅkarṣaṇa;
salutations to Pradyumna and Aniruddha, the Lord of the Sātvatas.
Salutations to the pure Buddha, who deludes the Daityas and Dānavas.
Obeisances to You in the form of Kalki, the slayer of the kṣatriyas who are mostly barbarians.
O Blessed One, this world of living beings is deluded by Your illusory energy; seized by the false notions of "I" and "mine," it wanders upon the paths of karma.
O All-pervading Lord, I wander like a fool among my body, children, home, wife, wealth, and kinsmen— which are like dreams— perceiving them as real;
for I possess a perverted mind regarding that which is impermanent, non-self, and suffering.
Delighting in dualities and enveloped by darkness, I do not know what is truly dear to my own self.
Just as an ignorant man leaves behind water and pursues a mirage produced by it because of its deceptive appearance, so too have I turned my back upon You.

"I am one of feeble intellect; my mind, struck down by desire and action, cannot be restrained as it is carried here and there by the turbulent senses. Therefore, I have come to your feet—that which is difficult for the wicked to attain."

And I consider that, O Lord, such a thing occurs only through Your grace; for when a person’s liberation from the cycle of worldly existence is at hand, O Lotus-navelled One, their mind becomes fixed upon You through the practice of true devotion.
Obeisance to the one who is pure consciousness alone, the cause of all perceptions;
to the Brahman who is the Lord of the Person (Puruṣa) and Pradhāna, possessing infinite power. Obeisance to You, Vāsudeva, the abode of all beings.
“O Hṛṣīkeśa, obeisances unto You! O Lord, protect me who have sought refuge in You.
Śrī Śuka said:
While he was thus offering praise, the Blessed Lord manifested His form within the water.
Kṛṣṇa withdrew [the illusion] once more, as an actor withdraws his performance;
and he too, seeing that it had vanished, emerged quickly from the water,
performed all his necessary duties, and returned to the chariot in amazement.
Hṛṣīkeśa asked him: "What wonderful thing have you seen on earth, in the sky, or in the water, that we perceive you to be so? Śrī Akrūra replied:
Whatever wonders exist here on earth, in the sky, or in the water—all those reside in You, the Soul of the Universe.
What remains unseen for me, who beholds all? For in You, the source of all wonders, everything exists—on earth, in the sky, or in the water.
"O Brahmin, what wonder have I seen here while beholding you? Having said this, the son of Gāndinī urged the chariot forward;
he brought Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa to Mathurā at the close of day.
O King, as they proceeded along the road, the villagers gathered here and there,
and upon seeing the two sons of Vasudeva, they were so filled with joy that they could not take their eyes off them.
Just then, the inhabitants of Vraja, headed by Nanda the cowherd, appeared before them.
Having reached the garden of the city, they remained waiting;
then the Blessed Lord, the Master of the Universe, approached them and, taking the hand of the humble Akrūra with His own hand, spoke as if smiling.
"May you enter the city and the house first, along with the vehicle;
we, however, shall unyoke [the animals] here and then behold the city.
Śrī Akrūra said:
"O Lord, I shall not enter Mathurā separated from you two.
O Master, you ought not to abandon me, your devotee, O lover of your devotees! Come, let us go to our homes; O Adhokṣaja, make them have a protector."

O best of friends, together with Your elder brother, the cowherd boys, and Your companions, purify our homes— those of us who maintain the household fire— with the dust of Your feet, by the purity of which the ancestors, the gods, and those who maintain the sacred fires are fully satisfied.
Having washed his pair of feet, the great Bali became worthy of praise;
he obtained incomparable sovereignty as well as that goal which belongs to those who are single-mindedly devoted.
The pure waters used for washing his feet purified the three worlds.
O Śarva, those sons of Sagara who went to heaven were placed upon Your head;
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, whose hearing and chanting are meritorious, O Nārāyaṇa, best of the best of the Yadus, O You of excellent fame, salutations be unto You!
The Blessed Lord said:
"I shall come to your home accompanied by my noble brother; having slain the enemy of the Yadu dynasty, I will bestow what is dear to my friends."
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, Akrūra, appearing somewhat dejected, entered the city; having reported his actions to Kaṃsa, he went to his own home.

Then, in the afternoon, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Saṅkarṣaṇa and surrounded by cowherds, entered Mathurā, desiring to see it. He beheld that city with its lofty gateways of crystal and its massive golden doors and arches.
It had copper-colored walls and moats that were difficult to approach, and was adorned with delightful gardens and groves;
it was embellished with golden crossroads, mansions, pleasure-parks, rows of shops, assembly halls, and palaces,
where the roofs and altars were set with lapis lazuli, diamonds, spotless sapphires, corals, pearls, and emeralds.
The city resounded with the cooing of pigeons and the cries of peacocks entering through the latticed windows and the openings of the pavements;
its streets, marketplaces, roads, and crossroads were sprinkled with water and strewn with flower garlands, sprouts, parched grain, and rice.
It was further adorned with full water-pots smeared with yogurt and sandalwood paste, and with rows of flowers and lamps accompanied by leafy branches.

The two sons of Vasudeva entered that city, whose gates and houses were beautifully adorned with clusters of plantains, betel-nut trees, banners, and silk streamers; surrounded by their companions and following the path of kings,
the women of the city gathered in haste to see them, and, eager for the sight of the prince, they climbed onto the rooftops of their mansions.
Some had their garments and ornaments turned upside down; others had forgotten one of their pairs [of earrings or anklets], leaving them with only a single earring or a single anklet.

Some, having anointed one eye but not the second, were eating while others, full of festive excitement, were discarding that [ointment]; some were being massaged, while others, having failed to bathe, were sleeping;
and mothers, having risen and heard the sound [of the drum], were nursing their infants and putting them aside.

The lotus-eyed Lord, possessing the gait of a rutting lordly elephant, captivated their minds with his bold, playful smiles and glances, bestowing upon their eyes a festival of the Self who is the Beloved of Śrī;
for they had repeatedly seen and heard of him, and their hearts now rushed toward him.
Having received honor from the glances of His smiling nectar-like eyes as they gazed upon them,
and having embraced Him who is the embodiment of bliss— Him whom they had previously perceived only through their vision—
their skin thrilled with joy, and they cast off the mental anguish caused by their enemies, O subduer of foes.
Mounted upon the rooftops of the palaces, their lotus-faces blossoming with joy,
the women showered Balarāma and Keśava with flowers,
curds, unbroken grains of rice, water-vessels, garlands, perfumes, and other offerings.

The twice-born there, filled with joy, honored them in various ways; and the citizens said: "Aha! What great austerity must the gopīs have practiced, since they behold these two who are the great festival of the world of men?"
Seeing a certain dyer, a washerman, approaching, the elder brother of Gada requested from him his most excellent washed garments:
"O dear one, give us two garments suitable for those who deserve them."
"Supreme welfare will come to you as a giver; there is no doubt about this.
Thus entreated by the Lord, who is complete in every respect, that servant of the king—extremely arrogant and provoked to anger—replied with reproach.

"Such garments as these, suited for one who constantly wanders the mountain forests, you always wear; why have you become so arrogant that you desire royal possessions? Go away at once, you fools! Do not pray for such things if you wish to live."
"Royal families indeed bind, kill, and plunder one who is arrogant.
While he was boasting thus, the son of Devakī became enraged and,
with the tip of his hand, struck off the washerman's head from his body.
All his attendants, having cast aside their garments and purses, fled in every direction along the path; yet Acyuta took the clothes for himself.
Having dressed themselves in those garments dear to them, Kṛṣṇa and Saṅkarṣaṇa likewise departed.
Having distributed some of the remaining [cloths] to the cowherds and having laid others upon the ground,
the weaver was then pleased and fashioned garments for the two of them from multicolored cotton fabrics, providing them with appropriate ornaments.
Adorned with various marks and attire, Kṛṣṇa and Rāma shone like two young elephants on the day of the full moon, one white and the other black.
With him [the sage] pleased, the Blessed Lord granted him his own form.
And [they bestowed] supreme fortune in the world, along with strength, sovereignty, memory, and the senses.
Then the two went to the abode of Sudāmā, the garland-maker.
Seeing them, he rose up and bowed his head to the ground.

Having brought seats for the two of them, he performed worship with water for the feet (*pādya*), respectful offerings (*arghya*), and other honors, as well as garlands, betel, and ointments, for the two of them along with their followers.
He said: "O Lord, our birth has become meaningful and our lineage has been purified."
The ancestors, gods, and sages are indeed pleased with my arrival; for you two are truly the supreme cause of the entire universe,
descended here by your portions for the sake of its welfare and prosperity.

Indeed, there is no partiality in the vision of you two, the friends and the Self of the universe, who are equal toward all beings and who likewise favor those who worship you. Therefore, command me, your servant: "What shall I do for you?"
"O King of kings, thinking, 'This is indeed a supreme favor for me that you have appointed me [to this task],' Sudāmā, with a joyful heart,
gave a garland fashioned from excellent, fragrant flowers."
Adorned by them and filled with joy, Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, together with their followers,
granted boons to him who had bowed down and sought refuge, for they were givers of boons.
He, in turn, chose unwavering devotion toward Him alone, the Soul of all.
"Friendliness toward His devotees and supreme compassion toward all living beings"— having granted him this boon, as well as prosperity that increases his lineage,
strength, long life, fame, and splendor, He departed along with His elder brother.
Śrī Śuka said:

Then, as Mādhava was walking along the royal road, he saw a young, hunchbacked woman of beautiful countenance carrying a vessel of fragrant body-unguents; the bestower of delight smiled and questioned her as she passed by.
"Who are you, O lady of beautiful thighs? And whose is this ointment, O woman? Tell us truly. Give this excellent body-ointment to the two of us; from that, your own welfare will soon follow.
The Sairandhrī said:
"O handsome one, I shall be a maidservant approved by Kaṃsa; for I am named Trivakrā, skilled in the art of applying unguents,
and I am highly favored by the Lord of the Bhojas through my own charms."
"Except for you two, who else among them is worthy of that? Having been captivated by your forms, grace, sweetness, smiles, conversation, and glances,
he gave both of you this thick ointment."

Then, with their bodies colored by that cosmetic paste which shone with hues other than their own natural skin tone and had attained its highest excellence, the two of them appeared beautifully adorned.
The gracious Lord [then beheld] the hunchbacked Trivakrā, whose face was lovely.
Desiring to straighten his mind and demonstrating the fruit of spiritual vision,
Acyuta pressed down on his forefeet with his feet, grasped his chin with both hands turned upward with the fingers extended, and drew himself up into the state of the supreme self.
With limbs as straight as a reed and possessing large hips and breasts,
she instantly became a most excellent woman through the touch of Mukunda. Then, endowed with beauty, virtue, and magnanimity, she spoke to Keśava.
Pulling at the edge of his upper garment, she, smiling and with passion awakened in her heart, said:
"Come, O hero, let us go home; I cannot bear to leave you here. Be gracious to me, whose mind has been ravished by you, O bull among men."
Thus entreated by the woman, Kṛṣṇa, while Rāma looked on,
glanced at the faces of the cowherds and, smiling, said to her:
"O fair-browed one, I shall come to your home, which destroys the mental anguish of men."
"O you who have accomplished our purpose, you are the ultimate refuge for us who are like travelers without homes.
Having dismissed her with these honeyed words, he proceeded along the merchant's roads on his way,
and was honored by his brothers with various offerings, betel, garlands, and perfumes.
From the agitation caused by seeing and remembering Him, the women were not even aware of themselves;
their garments, braids, and bracelets fell away, leaving them like figures in a painting.
Then Acyuta, inquiring after the citizens, [sought] the location of the bow.
Having entered it, he beheld a wondrous bow, like that of Indra,
guarded by many men, honored, and possessed of supreme splendor;
though being restrained by those men, Kṛṣṇa took up the bow by force.

With his left hand, the Lord of Wide Strides playfully drew the strung bow and, while the men looked on, snapped it in the middle in an instant like a stalk of sugarcane, as it excited their passion. As the bow broke, its sound filled the sky, heaven and earth, and all the directions.
Hearing that [sound], which filled [the air], Kaṃsa was seized with terror;
and his guards, along with their followers, becoming enraged and acting as assassins, surrounded him, desiring to seize him, crying out, "Seize him! Kill him!"
Then, beholding those men of evil intent, Balarāma and Keśava became enraged; taking up their bows, they shattered them into pieces and struck them down.
Furthermore, having slain Bala, who had been dispatched by Kaṃsa, they then [emerged] from the entrance of the hall.
Having gone out, they wandered about joyfully, beholding the splendors of the city.
Observing that wondrous valor of theirs, the inhabitants of the city considered their brilliance, boldness, and form to be those of the two supreme gods.
While the two of them were wandering at their own pleasure, the sun went to its setting;
Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, surrounded by cowherds, departed from the city toward Śakaṭa.
Those gopīs who, distressed by separation upon Mukunda’s departure, had offered true prayers for blessings, now became like Madhupurī itself.
While they were beholding the splendor of the limbs adorned by the Person (the Lord), Śrī, having abandoned her other suitors, desired them as her husbands.
Having eaten and been served milk-rice, the two of them, whose pair of feet had been washed,
spent that night happily, knowing what Kaṃsa intended to do.
But Kaṃsa, having heard of the breaking of the bow and the slaughter of his guards and his own army, and having witnessed the supreme prowess of Govinda and Rāma,
became terrified; the evil-minded one suffered from long sleeplessness and perceived ill omens.
He spoke many things in both ways regarding the acts of the messengers of death:
the invisibility of his own head even though a reflection was present,
and likewise the doubling of the luminaries even when there was no second object.
Perceiving holes in shadows, hearing the sound of breath, perceiving gold in trees, not seeing one's own footprints;
embracing a ghost in a dream, riding a donkey, and despairing.
Even one who might wear a garland of *nalada* grass, be anointed with oil, and go about naked;
or others likewise situated— whether dreaming or awake—
one who sees such things becomes terrified of death and finds no sleep due to anxiety.

When the night had dawned, O descendant of Kuru, and the sun had risen from the waters, Kaṃsa indeed caused a great festival of wrestling matches to be held. Men decorated the arena, and trumpets and drums were sounded.
The platforms were adorned with garlands, banners, cloths, and arches;
upon them, the citizens and country folk, led by the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas,
as well as the kings, took their seats according to their pleasure.

Surrounded by his ministers, Kaṃsa sat upon the royal throne in the midst of the circle of provincial lords, his heart burning with anguish, while musical instruments were being played accompanied by the rhythmic clapping of wrestlers.
The proud Mallas, well-adorned and accompanied by their teachers, arrived together at the assembly hall— Cāṇūra, Muṣṭika, Kūṭa, Śala, and Tośala— as well as others, delighted by the beautiful music.
The cowherds, headed by Nanda Gopa, being summoned by the King of the Bhojas and having presented their offerings, sat down together upon a single platform. Śrī Śuka said:

Then Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, O scorcher of foes, having performed their purificatory rites and hearing the sound of the wrestlers' drums, approached to see the spectacle; having reached the entrance of the arena, they beheld the elephant stationed there.
Kṛṣ� urged on by Ambaṣṭha, Kṛṣṇa beheld Kuvalayāpīḍa. Tying his lower garment and smoothing back his curly locks,
Śauri spoke to the elephant-driver with a voice as deep as the roar of a cloud:
"O Ambaṣṭha, Ambaṣṭha! Give us the way; depart without delay!
If you do not, I shall send you today, along with your elephant, to the abode of Yama.
Thus rebuked, the enraged Ambaṣṭha goaded his angry elephant.
He urged that elephant, which resembled Yama, the ender of time, toward Kṛṣṇa; charging at him, the lordly elephant seized him with its trunk by force.
Released from the trunk, he struck the elephant and hid himself in its feet.
Enraged and unable to see him, he whose vision was directed toward his sense of smell seized Keśava with his trunk; but He, exerting great force, emerged from it,
dragging the extremely powerful elephant by its tail for a distance of twenty-five bows.
Just as Suparṇa effortlessly drags a serpent, Acyuta dragged him about with ease; as he was whirled around from left to right,
he reeled like a young child being spun by a cow-calf.
Then, having approached the elephant face-to-face and struck it with his hand, he ran away;
yet, being touched at every step, he caused the beast to fall.
As it was running, it fell to the ground out of exhaustion and rose up suddenly.
Thinking that he had fallen, the enraged lord of elephants struck the earth with his tusks; his own prowess having been thwarted, he was filled with extreme indignation.
Urged on by his mahouts, he rushed toward Kṛṣṇa in a fit of rage.
Approaching him as he was rushing forward, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana seized his hand with His own hand and cast him down upon the ground; having struck him down,
He stepped upon him with His foot as easily as a lion does.
Having uprooted the tusk, Hari struck the elephant and its keepers with it.
Abandoning the dead elephant, he entered [the city] with the tusk in his hand,
its tip resting upon his shoulder and marked by drops of blood and ichor.
With drops of perspiration sprouting upon their lotus-like faces,
Baladeva and Janārdana, armed with excellent weapons like elephant tusks, entered the arena accompanied by a few cowherds, O King.
He was a thunderbolt to the Mallas, the best of men to human beings, and Cupid incarnate to women; he was a kinsman to the cowherds, a punisher of wicked kings, and a child to his own parents;
he was death to the Lord of the Bhojas, the cosmic Virāṭ to the ignorant, and the supreme reality to the yogis.
O King, known as the supreme deity of the Vṛṣṇis, Kṛṣṇa entered the arena accompanied by his elder brother; seeing that even those two invincible ones had slain Kuvalayāpīḍa,
