Kaṃsa was then deeply agitated in his mind.

Those two long-armed ones, having entered the arena, shone with their various costumes, ornaments, garlands, and garments, like two actors wearing excellent attire; they captivated the minds of those who gazed upon them with their splendor, O King. Seeing those two Supreme Persons, the people seated on the platforms—the citizens and the country-folk—were struck with wonder.
With eyes and faces overflowing with the surge of great joy, they drank in his face with their eyes without satiety;
as if drinking with their eyes, licking with their tongues,
smelling with their nostrils, and embracing with their arms.
They spoke to one another exactly as they had seen and heard it; as if reminded by the beauty, qualities, sweetness, and majesty of that form, they said,
"These two are indeed the direct manifestations of the Blessed Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa."
Having descended here by His partial expansion into the household of Vasudeva,
He was indeed born of Devakī and taken to Gokula;
dwelling there in concealment during this time, He grew up in the home of Nanda.
By him Pūtanā was brought to her end, as were the Dānava Cakravāta,
the two Arjunas, Guhyaka, Keśin, Dhenuka, and others of that sort;
by him the cows along with their keepers were delivered from the forest fire.
The serpent Kāliya was subdued, and Indra was rendered free of pride;
with a single hand, he held aloft the best of mountains for seven days,
and Gokula was protected from the rains, the winds, and the thunderbolts.
The gopīs, beholding His face with its ever-joyful, smiling gaze,
crossed over various miseries with delight as they entered His hermitage;
they declared, "By Him, this lineage of Yadu has become exceedingly renowned."
Protected by him, he shall obtain fortune, glory, and greatness.
And this elder brother of his, the illustrious lotus-eyed Rāma,
is he by whom Pralamba was slain, as well as Vatsaka, Baka, and the others.
While the people were speaking thus and the musical instruments were sounding,
Cāṇūra addressed Kṛṣṇa and Rāma and spoke these words:
"O son of Nanda, O Rāma, you two are esteemed as heroes."
Hearing that they were skilled in wrestling, the King summoned them, desiring to see them;
for subjects who act for the pleasure of their king find prosperity through thought, deed, and speech, whereas otherwise, it is the opposite.
The cowherds, ever joyful like those tending calves,
graze the cows while playing at wrestling in the forests;
therefore, O friends, let both you and we do what is pleasing to the King.
"O King, all beings are propitiated by you, for you consist of all beings.
Having heard that, Kṛṣṇa spoke words appropriate to the place and time,
welcoming them as he considered wrestling to be his own desired sport.

"O Lord of the Bhojas, we and even these forest-dwellers shall always do what is pleasing to you; that would be our greatest favor. We are but children; let us play as is fitting with those of equal strength."
"Let there be a wrestling match; may no unrighteousness touch the assembly of wrestlers.
Cāṇūra said:
"You are neither a child nor a youth; you are Balarāma, the best among the strong."
"He by whom an elephant, possessing the strength of a thousand elephants, was slain as a mere sport—against him you two, being powerful, must now fight; there is no injustice in this.
O Vārṣṇeya, display your prowess against me, while Muṣṭika fights with Bala."
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus resolved his intention, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana,
the son of Rohiṇī, then approached Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika.
Binding hand to hand and foot to foot,
they dragged each other with force, desiring victory; likewise,
elbow to elbow and knee to knee.
Head struck head and chest struck chest as they struck one another; with whirling, hurling,
embracing, and throwing down, and with advancing and retreating, they obstructed one another.
By means of lifting up, raising, shaking, and setting down one another, the two, desiring to conquer each other, performed feats that diminished their own strength;
all the women gathered there watched that battle, which was characterized by such displays of relative strength and weakness.
O King, they spoke to one another in groups, full of compassion: "Alas, this is a great unrighteousness on the part of these members of the royal assembly,
who seek a battle between the strong and the weak while the king looks on."

Where are these two wrestlers, whose every limb is as hard as adamant and who resemble the lords of mountains; and where are these two youths, whose limbs are exceedingly delicate and who have not yet reached full maturity?
Indeed, a transgression of dharma will surely occur for this assembly.
One should never remain where unrighteousness prevails.
A wise man should not enter an assembly, mindful of the faults of its members; by failing to speak or by speaking falsely, a man incurs sin.
Behold the lotus-face of Kṛṣṇa as he leaps about his enemy, drenched with drops of perspiration like a lotus bud sprinkled by water. Do you not see the face of Rāma, with its eyes slightly reddened?
[He spoke] to Muṣṭika with indignation, beautified by a smile and agitation:
"Blessed indeed are the lands of Vraja, since this Ancient Person (Purāṇa-puruṣa), concealed in human form and wearing forest garlands, [dwells there]."
Tending the cows along with Balarāma and playing his flute,
He whose feet are worshipped by Śiva and Lakṣmī wanders about for sport.
What austerity must the gopīs have performed, that they beheld His form?
With their eyes, they drink that essence of loveliness— which is unsurpassed, not produced by anything else, ever-renewed, and difficult to attain—
the singular abode of fame, fortune, and sovereignty.

Blessed are the women of Vraja, whose minds are devoted to Him and who sing of Him while milking, threshing, churning, smearing [the floor], swinging, rocking the cradle, bathing the infant, weeping, sprinkling, and cleansing; they, with throats choked by tears,
have their hearts carried away by the Lord of Wide Strides as He departs from Vraja in the morning and enters it in the evening.
Hearing his flute playing in harmony with the lowing of the cows,
those women of great merit quickly emerged onto the path and beheld him with a smiling face and compassionate glances.
While the women were speaking thus, O bull of the Bharatas, the Lord Hari, the master of yoga, set his mind on slaying the enemy.
Hearing the words of the women, which were filled with fear, and seeing them distressed by grief for their son out of maternal affection, [the two of them remained there].
The two parents grew distressed at the strength of their two sons, who were unaware of it.
Just as Acyuta and his opponent fought with various methods of wrestling,
so too did Balarāma and Muṣṭika fight one another.
With the blows from the Lord’s limbs, as harsh as the crushing of a thunderbolt,
Cāṇūra’s body was shattered and he repeatedly fell into exhaustion.
Then, with the speed of a hawk, he sprang up and clenched both his hands into fists.
Enraged, he struck the Blessed Vāsudeva on the chest;
yet Hari did not waver from that blow, like an elephant struck by a garland.
Seizing Cāṇūra by the arms, Hari whirled him around many times.
He dashed him violently to the surface of the earth, his life-breath exhausted;
with his ornaments, hair, and garland disarrayed, he fell like the banner of Indra.
In the same way, Muṣṭika was likewise struck first by His own fist.
Struck violently by the palm of the powerful Balabhadra,
he trembled, tormented and vomiting blood from his mouth;
lifeless, he fell upon the surface of the earth like a tree struck down by the wind.
Then, O King, as the peak approached, Rāma, the best among strikers,
effortlessly struck it with his left fist with utter disdain;
at that very moment, Śala’s head was struck by Kṛṣṇa’s forefoot.
Toshalaka split in two and both fell down.
When Cāṇūra, Muṣṭika, Kūṭa, Śala, and Toshalaka had been slain,
all the remaining wrestlers fled, seeking to save their lives.
Drawing the cowherd boys as their companions and mingling with them, the two of them sported about;
while the musical instruments were being played, they leaped about, their anklets tinkling. All the people rejoiced at the deeds of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.

Except for Kaṃsa, the eminent brāhmaṇas and the saintly persons cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! When the chief wrestlers had been slain and the Bhojas had fled, the King of the Bhojas silenced his own musical instruments and spoke these words.
"Drive out from the city those two sons of Vasudeva who act wickedly! Seize the wealth of the cowherds and bind the evil-minded Nanda!
Furthermore, let the foolish Vasudeva, that most wretched of men, be put to death immediately!"
His father Ugrasena and his followers were likewise on the side of the enemy. While Kaṃsa was thus boasting, the Imperishable Lord became enraged;
leaping up with agility, he swiftly ascended the high couch.
Beholding Death approaching him,
the wise one rose suddenly from his seat and seized his sword and shield.
As he moved swiftly through the air, brandishing the sword in his hand, now to the right and now to the left like a hawk, [the Lord struck him down].
He of unbearable and fierce splendor seized him by force, just as the son of Tārkṣya seizes a serpent;
having grabbed him by the hair while his crown was shaking, he threw him down from the high platform onto the arena floor.
Then, above him, the lotus-navelled Lord himself—the refuge of the universe and self-dependent—fell down.
While the world looked on, Hari dragged that deceased man across the ground like an elephant;
O King, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! was then uttered by all the people.
He who had always been anxious in mind, whether drinking, eating, walking, sleeping, or breathing, [now saw] that Lord.
He beheld the one whose weapon is the discus before him; from that very direction, he attained that same form which is so difficult to obtain.
His eight younger brothers, Kaṅka, Nyagrodhaka, and the others, rushed forward in great rage, seeking to take revenge upon their brother.
Then Rohiṇī’s son,
raising his iron club, struck those who were so fiercely intent on battle, like a lion slaying cattle;
meanwhile, the drums resounded in the sky and the manifestations of Brahmā, Śiva, and the other gods celebrated.
Scattering flowers over him, the women, filled with joy, praised him and danced.
O great king, their wives, distressed by the death of their friend,
arrived there, beating their heads and with eyes full of tears.
Embracing their husbands who lay upon the hero’s bed, the women lamented with melodious voices, repeatedly shedding tears of grief:
"Alas, O Lord! O Beloved! O Knower of Dharma! O Compassionate One, who art kind to the helpless!"
"With you slain, we are as good as slain, along with our homes and progeny.
O bull among men, bereft of you as its lord, this city does not shine, just as we do not, now that our festivals and auspicious rites have ceased."
You have committed a terrible act of hostility toward innocent beings;
O friend, because of that, you have been brought to this state. What peace can one who harms living beings ever find?
For He is indeed the source and the dissolution of all beings here.
"And the protector who disregards him never prospers in happiness anywhere.
Śrī Śuka said:
"The Blessed One, the creator of the worlds, having comforted the royal women,"
He established for those who had been slain that which is called the worldly funeral rite;
then, having liberated both his mother and father from their bonds,
Kṛṣṇa and Rāma paid obeisance to them, touching their feet with their heads.
Devakī and Vasudeva, recognizing their two sons as the Lords of the universe, embraced them after they had offered their salutations, feeling no doubt whatsoever.
Śrī Śuka said:
Knowing that his parents had understood the truth, the Supreme Person, the bull among men,
spread his own illusion which deludes all people, thinking, "Let it not be so. Then,
accompanied by his elder brother, he approached his parents and spoke with words of consolation.
Bowing down with humility and affectionately addressing them as "Mother" and "Father," he said respectfully:
"O Father, even though we two sons were constantly longing for you, our childhood, boyhood, and youth never passed away from you."
Ours, who were struck down by fate, did not obtain a dwelling in your presence—
that joy which children living in their father’s house find when they are cherished. For from you was born and nourished this body, the source of all our well-being.
A mortal does not attain fulfillment for his parents even in a hundred years if he,
as their son, fails to provide for them with his own person and wealth throughout his lifetime; indeed, after death, such a one is made to eat his own flesh.
One who is capable but fails to provide for his mother, father, aged wife, virtuous spouse, infant son,
teacher, a learned brāhmaṇa, or one who has sought refuge, dies while still breathing.
Because Kaṃsa’s mind was constantly agitated by this thought, we did not provide for those two.

"These days of yours have passed in vain, for you did not offer us worship. Therefore, dear father and mother, you ought to forgive us, who were dependent on another and failed to serve you while you were greatly afflicted by that evil-hearted one."
Śrī Śuka said:

Thus, by the words of Hari, the Soul of the Universe who had assumed a human form through his illusory power (*māyā*), the two of them were enchanted; lifting him onto their laps and embracing him, they experienced great joy.
Drenching one another with streams of tears and bound by the fetters of affection,
O King, their throats choked with sobs and their minds bewildered, they said nothing at all.
Having thus consoled his parents, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, [proceeded].
He made his maternal grandfather Ugrasena the king of the Yadus and said to him,
"O great king, you ought to command us and your subjects that,
due to the curse of Yayāti, we must not sit upon the royal throne."
While I, your servant, am waiting upon you, the gods and others bring tribute to you with bowed heads; how much more so, then, other kings?
[I have brought] all my own kinsmen and relatives from every direction, who were distressed by the fear of Kaṃsa.
The Creator of the Universe, having honored and comforted the Yadus, Vṛṣṇis, Andhakas, Madhus, Dāśārhas, Kukuras, and others who were emaciated by living in foreign lands,
settled them in their own homes, satisfying them with wealth.
Protected by the arms of Kṛṣṇa and Saṅkarṣaṇa, their desires fulfilled,
those perfected ones rejoiced in their homes, freed from the fever of worldly anxiety through their devotion to Kṛṣṇa and Rāma;
day after day, they joyfully beheld the lotus face of Mukunda.
It was eternally joyful, glorious, and filled with compassionate, smiling glances.
There, even those who were aged became young again, endowed with exceeding strength and vigor,
as they repeatedly drank the nectar of Mukunda’s lotus face through the dice.
Then, O King of kings, the Blessed Lord, the son of Devakī, and Saṅkarṣaṇa approached Nanda and, embracing him, spoke as follows:
"O father, we have been nourished and cherished exceedingly by you two, who are so affectionate toward us."
For the love for one's own children is indeed greater than that for one's parents;
he is a father and she is a mother who nourish like their own sons those infants abandoned by relatives who are incapable of providing sustenance and protection.

"Go now to Vraja, my dear; we shall come to see your kinsmen who are pained by affection, having first ensured the happiness of our friends. Having thus consoled Nanda and the inhabitants of Vraja, the Lord Acyuta departed.
He respectfully honored them with garments, ornaments, base metals, and other gifts.
Thus addressed, Nanda, overwhelmed with affection, embraced them both;
with eyes filled with tears, he returned to Vraja along with the cowherds.

Then, O King, the son of Śūra had the sacramental rites for his two sons performed duly by the family priest and the brahmins. To them he gave as sacrificial fees cows adorned with golden necklaces and well-decorated ornaments.
Having honored those cows, adorned with silken garlands and accompanied by their calves,

the high-minded [Akrūra] gave them away, recollecting how they had been taken unrighteously by Kaṃsa on the very day of the birth-stars of Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, which he himself had previously offered mentally.
Then, having received the purificatory rites and attained the status of the twice-born, those two of excellent vows undertook the Gāyatra vow from Garga, the preceptor of the Yadu clan;
they were the source of all branches of knowledge, omniscient, and lords of the universe.
Concealing their stainless knowledge, which was not attained through any other means, by means of human activities,
they then desired to dwell in the house of a preceptor and approached Sāndīpani, the son of Kāśya, who resided in Avanti-pura.

Having approached their teacher with self-control, those two, who were honored like gods, practiced toward him a faultless conduct out of devotion. The best of the twice-born was pleased with them because of their pure disposition and faithful service.
The Guru taught him all the Vedas along with the Upaniṣads, as well as the science of archery together with its secret doctrines, the codes of dharma, the paths of logic,
and likewise the science of metaphysics and the sixfold science of statecraft.
O King, those two best among the foremost of men, the initiators of all branches of knowledge, mastered all sixty-four arts with a single recitation,
remaining diligent for sixty-four days and nights.
O King, the two of them invited their teacher to accept his fee for the instruction;
and the twice-born one, O King, having observed their wondrous majesty, conceived a thought that was superhuman.
Having consulted with his wife, he chose the dead child at Prabhāsa from the great ocean. Saying "So be it," the two great chariot-warriors then mounted their chariot.
Having reached Prabhāsa, those two of unbounded prowess approached the shore and sat down for a moment; the Ocean,
recognizing them, brought an offering for them.
The Blessed One said to him: "Let that son of your preceptor be given back quickly—he who was swallowed here by you as a great wave while he was but a child. Śrī Samudra replied:

"O Lord, I did not take it; rather, it was the great Daitya Pañcajana, an asura who dwells within the waters, O Kṛṣṇa, who took it while assuming the form of a conch. Having heard this, the Lord immediately [set out].
Having entered the water and slain him, he did not see the child within his belly;
taking the conch shell produced from that body’s limbs,
he returned to his chariot and then proceeded toward Yama’s beloved city named Saṃyamanī.
Having arrived, Janārdana, accompanied by Halāyudha, blew his conch shell.
Hearing the roar of the conch, Yama, the restrainer of living beings,
performed a grand worship for the two of them, augmented by devotion.
Bowing down before Kṛṣṇa, who dwells within the hearts of all beings, he said:
"O Viṣṇu, what may we do for you two, who are divine sports appearing as human?
The Blessed Lord replied:
"O Great King, bring here the son of my preceptor, who has been brought by his own karma; do so while honoring my command. Saying "So be it," the two best of the Yadus brought the preceptor's son.
Having given [the gift] to their own teacher, they said to him again, "Choose [another boon].
The venerable teacher said:
"O child, the fee for the teacher has been fully paid by you both."

"What desire could possibly remain unfulfilled for one who has you as his guru? Go to your own homes, O heroes; may your fame be purifying. May the Vedic hymns remain unfailing for you both in this world and the next."
Thus permitted by their preceptor, O dear one, they arrived at their own city on a chariot with the speed of the wind and a roar like that of a rain-cloud;
and all the subjects rejoiced upon seeing Rāma and Janārdana.
Not seeing him for many days, they were like those who have lost and then recovered their wealth.
Śrī Śuka said:
"The foremost counselor of the Vṛṣṇis, the beloved friend of Kṛṣṇa..."
Bṛhaspati’s disciple Uddhava was truly the most excellent in intelligence; once,
Hari— the remover of the distress of those who have surrendered— taking by his hand the hand of that most beloved and single-minded devotee, spoke to him.
"Go to Vraja, O gentle Uddhava, and bring joy to our two parents;
release the Gopīs from the anguish of separation from Me by means of My messages.
Their minds are fixed on Me, their life-breaths are parched for Me, and they have renounced all concern for their bodies for My sake."

I support those who have abandoned worldly duties and, with their minds, have reached me alone as their beloved, dearest Self; for my sake, I sustain them. Those women of Gokula [longed] for me, their most beloved, even though I was far away.
O dear one, remembering [you], my cowherd women— who are my very self— are bewildered, overwhelmed by the longing of separation;
they sustain their lives with great difficulty, somehow or other,
through the messages concerning your return.
Śrī Śuka said: O King, having been thus addressed, Uddhava, respectfully taking his master’s message,
mounted his chariot and set out for Nanda’s cowherd settlement.
The glorious Lord arrived at Nanda’s cowherd settlement as the sun was setting;
his vehicle remained concealed by the dust raised from the hooves of the cattle entering the fold,
while the place resounded with the bellowing of powerful bulls fighting for the sake of the cows in heat.
It was adorned with white calves leaping here and there under the weight of their udders as their mothers ran after them,
and it resounded with the sounds of milking cows and the music of flutes.
It was graced by cowherd women, beautifully adorned, who sang of the auspicious deeds of Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa,
and by cowherds who were devoted to the worship of fire, the sun, guests, cows, brahmins, ancestors, and the gods.
It was made delightful by incense, lamps, garlands, and cow-pen dwellings;
on all sides it was filled with flowering forests resounding with the songs of flocks of birds,
and adorned with clusters of lotuses crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks.
Having approached him as he arrived— the beloved follower of Kṛṣṇa—
Nanda, filled with joy, embraced him and honored him with the thought that he was Vāsudeva himself.
Having fed him with the finest food, he settled him comfortably upon a couch.
Having relieved his fatigue by massaging his feet and other services, he inquired:
"O noble one, is our friend, the son of Śūra, well? Is he living happily, blessed with children and the like, liberated, and faithful to his friends?"
By good fortune, the wicked Kaṃsa has been slain along with his followers by his own evil deeds— he who always hated the Yādavas, the virtuous ones devoted to righteousness.
Does Kṛṣṇa even remember us— his mother, his well-wishers, and his friends?

"Will Govinda come to the cowherds, the cow-pen, his own kinsmen, the cows, Vṛndāvana, and the mountain, even for a single glance at his own people? If so, then we shall behold his face, with its beautiful nose and eyes smiling with gentle grace."
They were protected from forest fires, wind and rain, and from bulls and serpents—
those insurmountable forms of death— by the Great-Souled Kṛṣṇa, as he remembered their heroic deeds and his own playful side-long glances.

O dear one, our every action has become slackened by your laughter and speech; as we gaze upon the sporting grounds adorned with the footprints of Mukunda, which include rivers, mountains, and forest regions, our minds attain oneness with them.
"I believe that Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, the two supreme among the gods, have arrived here for the great purpose of the deities, just as Garga had foretold;
they are like Kaṃsa, who possessed the strength of ten thousand elephants, or like the two wrestlers and the lordly elephant."
He slew them with ease, as a lion slays beasts; he broke the great, powerful bow with a single hand, like an elephant-king snapping a palm staff, and held up the mountain for seven days.
By whom Pralamba, Dhenuka, Ariṣṭa, Tṛṇāvarta, Baka,
and other Daityas— who had conquered both gods and demons— were slain here with ease;
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, as Nanda repeatedly recollected these things, his mind became deeply attached to Kṛṣṇa; overcome by an outpouring of love, he remained silent in great longing.
Yaśodā, for her part, [recollected] the deeds of her son as they were being described.
Hearing this, she shed tears as her breasts overflowed with milk out of affection.
Observing such supreme love for the Lord Kṛṣṇa in Nanda and Yaśodā, Uddhava joyfully spoke to Nanda.
Śrī Uddhava said:
O bestower of honor, you two are surely the most praiseworthy among all embodied beings here,
since such a disposition has been fixed upon Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of the entire universe.
For these two, Rāma and Mukunda, are the seed and the womb of the universe—the Puruṣa and the Pradhāna. These two ancient ones preside over the distinct knowledge within all beings.
When a person, at the time of separation from life, fixes his impure mind upon them for even a moment—

Having swiftly cast off the accumulation of karma, one becomes composed of Brahman, sun-colored, and attains the supreme goal. Therefore, O Great-souled ones, direct your constant devotion toward that Nārāyaṇa, the cause of all selves, who assumes a mortal form for a specific purpose. What further duty remains for you two?
In no long time, Acyuta,
the Lord and Master of the Sātvatas, will come to Vraja and bring joy to his parents after slaying Kaṃsa, the enemy of all the Sātvatas, in the midst of the arena.
"Whatever Kṛṣṇa has said to you upon coming here, he will make that come true.
Do not grieve, O highly fortunate ones; you shall behold Kṛṣṇa nearby.
He dwells within the hearts of all beings, like light within fuel."
For Him who is free from pride, there is no one dear and no one unpleasant; He is neither superior nor inferior, for He is equal toward all, even toward the unequal.
To Him there is no mother, no father, no wife, and no children or others.

He has no sense of "mine," nor does he regard others as "other"; he has no body, nor even birth, nor any action in this world among the various wombs of the existent, the non-existent, or their mixture.
Even so, for the sake of sport, he manifests himself for the protection of the virtuous.
Though devoid of qualities, the unborn Lord assumes the qualities of goodness, passion, and ignorance; though transcending them, He creates, protects, and destroys while sporting with them,
just as the earth appears to spin when seen by one suffering from vertigo.
In that mind which acts as the agent, the Self is traditionally regarded through the notion of "I" as if it were the agent.
This Lord Hari is not merely the son of you two;
for He is the Self of all, the father, the mother, and the Supreme Lord.
Whatever has been seen or heard—whether past, present, or future;
whether stationary or moving; whether great or small—there is no entity whatsoever that can be described apart from Acyuta.
He alone is everything, having become the Supreme Self.
O King, as they were thus conversing, that night passed for Nanda and Kṛṣṇa’s follower.
Then the gopīs arose, lit the lamps, worshipped the household deities, and churned the *dadhi*.
Those ropes, shimmering with gems as bright as lamps, were pulled by their arms adorned with bracelets and garlands;
their hips, breasts, necklaces, and earrings swayed, while their faces—reddened with saffron on their cheeks—were illuminated by the luster of their ornaments.
As the women of Vraja sang aloud to the lotus-eyed Lord, their sound reached the very heavens.
The sound of the churning of the curd, which dispels the inauspiciousness of the quarters, was mingled with that [sound].
When the sun had risen and the Blessed One had appeared at Nanda’s gate, the inhabitants of Vraja,
seeing the chariot made of refined gold, asked, "Whose is this?"
"Has Akrūra arrived— he who accomplishes Kaṃsa's purpose, by whom the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa was taken to the city of Madhupurī?
What will he accomplish for us, as a means of repayment to our master who is well-pleased?"
Then, while the women were still speaking, Uddhava arrived having completed his daily rites.
Śrī Śuka said:
Seeing him, the attendant of the Fire-god, the women of Vraja...
With long arms and eyes like fresh lotuses,
wearing yellow garments and a garland of lotuses, his lotus-face was radiant as he moved his earrings.

Greatly amazed, they all surrounded him with eager curiosity, wondering: "Who is this of such extraordinary appearance? From where does he come, and to whom does he belong—he who bears the attire and ornaments of Acyuta?"

Having recognized him as a messenger from the Lord of Ramā, they— bowing with humility and having honored him well with shy smiles, glances, kind words, and other gestures— asked him in private as he sat upon his seat, for he was one who took refuge at the lotus feet of the One of Excellent Renown (Uttama-śloka).
We know you, O Lord of the Yadus, to have arrived as an attendant;

you have been sent here by your master out of a desire to do what is pleasing to his parents. Otherwise, we would not perceive anything in the cowherd settlement that would be worthy of remembrance for him.
The bond of affection among kinsmen is very difficult to relinquish, even for a sage;
friendship with others is based on self-interest and lasts only as long as that interest persists,
just as men behave toward women or as bees toward flowers.
Prostitutes abandon a man who has no wealth; subjects abandon a king who is incapable;
those who have completed their studies abandon their teacher; and officiating priests abandon one who has given them their sacrificial fees.
Birds abandon a tree whose fruit is gone, and guests, having eaten, abandon a house.
"The deer have burned the forest," and "the paramours have enjoyed the devoted wife"—
thus did the gopīs speak of Govinda, their speech, body, and mind entirely absorbed in Him;
and when Uddhava, the messenger of Kṛṣṇa, arrived, they abandoned all worldly concerns.
Singing of his beloved deeds and weeping, their modesty cast aside as they repeatedly recalled those acts he had performed in his youth and childhood;
one of them, seeing a honeybee, meditated upon her union with Kṛṣṇa.
Having dispatched a messenger sent by her beloved, she spoke these words:
The Gopī said:
"O honey-gatherer, O kinsman of gamblers, do not touch the foot of my co-wife!"
May the Lord of Spring grant his favor to us— the women who are jealous of him— whose beards are stained by the saffron from the garlands crushed between their breasts;
for in the assembly of the Yadus, you act as his messenger, appearing in such a state of imitation.
Having once made us drink his own intoxicating nectar of the lips,
one such as you has immediately abandoned us like withered flowers; how indeed does Lakṣmī continue to serve the lotus-feet of that very person?

Alas! My mind has indeed been stolen away by the praises of the Lord of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka). O six-legged one, why do you sing so much here about the ancient Lord of the Yadus before us, who are without homes?
Let the friends of Vijaya’s companions sing of that association; for those beloved women, having allayed the pain of their breasts, provide whatever is desired.
What women in heaven, on earth, or in the netherworld are difficult for him to attain?
What are we compared to the prosperity of one who serves the dust of the feet of Him whose playful expansion of eyebrows is accompanied by a charming, deceptive smile?
Furthermore, the title "Uttamaśloka" belongs indeed to the side of the wretched.

Place your foot upon my head; I know you, who are skilled in conciliation, for you have come as an envoy from Mukunda with fourfold overtures. Here, I am one whose offspring, their offspring, and other worlds have all been surrendered by me through my own deeds.
With a corrupted mind, he released [his weapon], thinking, "What indeed can be negotiated with this man?
Like a hunter following the ways of a fowler, he pierced the lord of monkeys; conquered by a woman, he disfigured his wife, who was driven by desire.
He who, like a crow, devoured even Bali while devouring Bali; enough then with friendship with the dark one, for his stories are difficult to abandon—
those drops of nectar for the ears which are the playful deeds performed by him.
Having their dualities shaken off by eating but once,
those wretched ones suddenly abandon their homes and families;
many such birds here wander about, practicing the life of mendicants.

Faithful like deer hearing the cry of a peacock, yet ignorant like those who mistake the call of a woodpecker for the truth, we have repeatedly beheld this intense touch of his nails, which was like the realization of the sacred *ṛta*.
"O counselor of the pain of love, let some other news be told!
Dear friend, have you come again, sent by my beloved? Choose a boon; what do you desire? You are worthy of my respect, my dear."
"How can you lead us here to the side of one for whom the pairs of opposites are difficult to abandon?
O gentle one, that bride Śrī always dwells together upon your chest.
Alas, does the noble son not dwell now even in the city of Madhu?"
O gentle one, he remembers his father’s house and his kinsmen, the cowherds;
will he ever at some time speak of us, his maidservants, or place his arm, fragrant with aloe-wood, upon our heads?
Śrī Śuka said: Then Uddhava, having heard this, spoke these words to the gopīs, consoling them with the dear messages of Kṛṣṇa, as they were longing for a vision of Him.
Śrī Uddhava said:
Oh, you have attained your ultimate goal; you are honored by the world, for your minds have been thus offered unto the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva.

Indeed, devotion to Kṛṣṇa is accomplished through charity, vows, austerity, fire-offerings, chanting, study of the scriptures, self-restraint, various other auspicious means, and other excellent practices;
may such unsurpassed devotion toward the Lord of Excellent Fame be attained by you.
By good fortune, devotion— which is difficult even for sages to attain—
has been set in motion. By good fortune, you have abandoned sons, husbands, bodies, kinsmen, and homes, and have chosen the Supreme Person known as Kṛṣṇa.
"O highly fortunate ones, you have been authorized to possess exclusive devotion to Adhokṣaja; through this separation, you have performed a great service to me.
Listen now to my dear message, which shall bring you happiness."
"O auspicious one, I have come taking him with me as a secret messenger for my husband.
The Blessed Lord said:
"For you, there shall never be any separation from Me in any way whatsoever."
Just as the elements— ether, air, fire, water, and earth— exist within all beings,
so too do I, the substratum of the mind, vital breath, elements, senses, and the modes of nature.
By my own self, within my very self, I create, destroy, and sustain myself.
By the power of His own *māyā*, which consists of the elements, the senses, and the modes of nature,
the Self— which is composed of knowledge, pure, distinct, and untouched by the modes—
is perceived through the functions of *māyā* as deep sleep, dreaming, and waking.

One should restrain those senses by which one might contemplate sense-objects falsely, like one awakened from a dream; thus, remaining vigilant, he attained [the goal]. This is the limit of all sacred tradition: the Yoga and Sāṅkhya systems for the wise.
Renunciation, austerity, self-control, and truthfulness flow toward me like rivers reaching the ocean;
yet, that I remain far away from your dear eyes is for the sake of drawing your minds closer to me through the longing of meditation upon me.

Just as the mind of women remains occupied with their beloved even when he is far away, it does not do so for me when I am close at hand within the range of their vision; rather, having fixed their entire mind upon me, they are freed from all other mental fluctuations.
Constantly remembering me, you shall before long come to me—
those auspicious women who, while I was sporting with them in this forest at night, remained in Vraja without having attained the *rāsa* dance; by reflecting upon my prowess, they have reached me.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus heard the instructions given by their beloved, the women of Vraja were filled with joy; their memories awakened by his message, they spoke to Uddhava.
The gopīs said:
"By good fortune, Kaṃsa, the evildoer who brought calamity upon the Yadus, has been slain along with his followers.
By good fortune, Acyuta now remains well, having attained all his goals through those who have reached him."
O gentle one, does the elder brother of Gada bring delight to the women of the city,
honored by their affectionate, bashful, smiling, and noble glances? For he is an expert in the nuances of love and is dear to the city's women.
One should not be bound by his words when one is overwhelmed by delusions;
O virtuous one, does Govinda ever remember us in some context,
amidst the midst of assemblies of city women during their casual conversations?
Does he remember those nights when,
in Vṛndāvana— so beautiful with night-lotuses, jasmine, and the moon—
he delighted in the rāsa dance assembly where his beloveds’ anklets tinkled?
Will He whose charming stories are praised by us— the scion of the Daśārhas— ever come here to revive us, who are scorched by our own self-inflicted grief,
with His very limbs, just as Indra revives the forest with rain-clouds?
"Why has Kṛṣṇa come here, having obtained the kingdom and slain his enemies,
having married the daughters of the lords of men, and being delighted and surrounded by all his friends?
What concern have we forest-dwellers, or others, with that Great Soul?"
What purpose could there be in serving the Lord of Śrī, whose desires are already fulfilled and who has perfected his own self?
For even Piṅgalā, a woman of loose conduct, said that supreme happiness lies in freedom from desire;
yet, despite knowing this, our longing for Kṛṣṇa remains difficult to overcome.
Who would dare to abandon the consciousness of the One of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka),
from whose limbs the Goddess of Fortune (Śrī) never departs even against His will?
These rivers, mountains, forest regions, cows, and the sounds of the bamboos [all bear witness].
O Lord, these deeds performed by Kṛṣṇa with Saṅkarṣaṇa as his companion remind us again and again of the son of Nanda-gopa; alas,
we are simply unable to forget those footprints of His, which are the very abode of Śrī.

O Lord, O Lord of Ramā, O Destroyer of the Suffering of the Lords of Vraja! How can we forget Him, whose minds have been captivated by His graceful gait, His noble smiles, His playful glances, and His honey-sweet speech? How can we forget Him? O Lord, O Lord of Ramā, O Destroyer of the Suffering of the Lords of Vraja! How can we forget Him? O Lord, O Lord of Ramā, O Destroyer of the Suffering of the Lords of Vraja! How can we forget Him? O Lord, O Lord of Ramā, O Destroyer of the Suffering of the Lords of Vraja! How can we forget
"O Govinda, lift up Gokula, which is submerged in an ocean of suffering!
Śrī Śuka said:
Then, by Kṛṣṇa’s messages, they were freed from the fever of separation.
Having realized that the Self was Adhokṣaja, they honored Uddhava;
he dwelt there for several months, dispelling the grief of the gopīs and delighting Gokula by singing the stories of Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes.
For as many days as Uddhava dwelt in Nanda’s cowherd settlement,
those days seemed like mere moments to the inhabitants of Vraja because of their news of Kṛṣṇa;
he spent his time observing the rivers, forests, mountain valleys, and flowering trees.
Reminding Kṛṣṇa [of his love], Hari’s servant took delight among the inhabitants of Vraja. Having seen such bewilderment of the gopīs' selves due to their absorption in Kṛṣṇa,
Uddhava, supremely pleased, bowed down to them and sang this.
These cowherd women on earth, who have taken up bodies as the ultimate [objects of love], have fixed their hearts' affection solely upon Govinda, the Self of all;
they long for that which even sages and we ourselves desire, out of fear of worldly existence.
What need has he for births in the families of the Brahmins, who relishes the nectar of the infinite stories [of Kṛṣṇa]?
Where are these women wandering in the forest, corrupted by infidelity? And where is this deep-rooted devotion to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self?
Indeed, the Lord directly bestows the highest good even upon the ignorant who worship Him, just as the king of medicines, when consumed, acts as a cure;
yet this favor is not for the sake of the Goddess Śrī, whose love for His limbs is absolute.
How could the celestial women, though possessing the fragrance and luster of lotuses, ever compare to those beloved ladies of Vraja who,
during the rāsa festival, had their necks grasped by his staff-like arms and received his blessing?
O, may I become even a mere shrub, creeper, or herb in Vṛndāvana for those who enjoy the dust of their feet— those who, having abandoned their own kin and the path of the noble, have followed them.
They took refuge at the feet of Mukunda, which are sought after by the Vedas;
those feet which are indeed worshipped by Śrī and by the gods beginning with Brahmā whose desires are fulfilled,
and even by the lords of yoga within their own souls during the rāsa dance assembly.
They dispelled their distress by embracing and pressing to their breasts that lotus-foot of the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa which had been placed there;
I perpetually revere the dust of the feet of the women of Nanda’s cowherd settlement.
The singing of whose stories concerning Hari purifies the three worlds.
Śrī Śuka said:
Then, having taken leave of the gopīs, as well as Yaśodā and Nanda, [he departed].
Having addressed the cowherds, the descendant of Daśārha, intending to depart, mounted his chariot.
As he emerged, Nanda and the others approached him with various offerings in their hands; moved by affection, they spoke to him with eyes full of tears.

May our mental functions take refuge at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa; may our speech consist of uttering His names; and may our bodies be engaged in bowing down to Him and other such acts, even as we wander here and there by the will of the Lord.
"May our delight be in Lord Kṛṣṇa through auspicious practices and acts of charity.
O King, thus honored by the cowherds with devotion to Kṛṣṇa,
Uddhava returned once more to Mathurā, which was protected by Kṛṣṇa.
Having prostrated before Kṛṣṇa, he spoke of the intensity of the devotion of the inhabitants of Vraja;
then he presented the offerings to Vasudeva, Rāma, and the King.
Śrī Śuka said:
Then the Blessed One, the soul of all and the seer of all, having understood [her intent],
went to the house of the Sairandhrī— who was tormented by desire— desiring to do what was pleasing to her;
it was richly furnished with costly utensils and provided with every means for the gratification of desire.
Adorned with strings of pearls, banners, canopies, couches, and seats,
as well as fragrant incense, lamps, garlands, and perfumes, she,
upon seeing him approaching, rose immediately from her seat in a state of great agitation.
Just as [the gopīs] had approached Acyuta and honored him with seats and other offerings,
so too Uddhava, honored for his saintliness, sat upon the ground after touching the seat. Kṛṣṇa also quickly entered his costly bedchamber, following the customs of the world.
Having adorned herself with bathing powders, ointments, fine silken garments, ornaments, garlands, perfumes, betel, and the nectar of wine,

she approached Mādhava with bashful, playful, smiling, and amorous glances. Summoning his beloved— who was apprehensive due to the modesty of their first union— with his hand decorated by a bracelet, he spoke.
Taking her bed and settling Rāma upon it, he took his delight with her, who was purified by even a mere trace of the merit from applying fragrant unguents;
she, while smelling his chest and her own breasts heated by the god of love, as well as his eyes, wiped away their afflictions with the touch of his infinite feet.
Embracing with both arms her beloved, who was the very embodiment of bliss and stood between her breasts, she cast off her exceedingly long-lasting torment.
Thus, having attained that Lord, the master of liberation, who is so difficult to reach, she—
"O dear one, alas, this unfortunate woman has requested this by offering her body-unguents:
'O most beloved, stay here with me for a few days;
enjoy yourself, O lotus-eyed one, for I cannot bear to part from your company.'"
Having granted her a boon according to her desire and having honored her, the Giver of Honor, the Lord of All, returned with Uddhava to His own opulent abode,
after she had fully propitiated Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords, who is difficult to please.
That person of poor intellect who, due to a lack of discernment, chooses that which is grasped only by the mind is truly deluded.
Then the Lord Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Rāma and Uddhava, went to Akrūra’s residence,
desiring to do something for his pleasure.
Seeing those best of men, his own kinsmen, from a distance,
he rose up with great joy, embraced them,
and greeted them; he bowed down to Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, and was likewise saluted by them.
O King, having offered them seats according to the prescribed rites, he honored them— who had accepted their places— by bearing on his head the water for washing their feet,
and by presenting them with respectful offerings, divine garments, perfumes, excellent garlands, and the finest ornaments.
Having honored them by bowing his head and massaging their feet as they sat upon his lap, Akrūra, humbled by humility, spoke to Kṛṣṇa and Rāma:
"By good fortune, the sinful Kaṃsa has been slain along with his followers; this lineage [is yours]."
By you two, we have been rescued from this miserable and endless suffering and have been made to flourish.
You two are the Pradhāna and Puruṣa, the causes of the universe and identical with the universe;
apart from you two, there is nothing else, neither superior nor inferior.
O Brahmin, having entered this universe created by Himself through His own potencies, He moves in manifold ways, becoming the object of both scripture and direct perception.
For just as the elements, beginning with earth, appear in various forms within all beings, both moving and stationary, according to their respective sources.

Thus, you, the absolute one, who are self-born and independent of any other, manifest yourself in many ways. By means of your own potencies—the qualities of *rajas*, *tamas*, and *sattva*—you create, maintain, and dissolve the universe.
Yet you are not bound by the actions resulting from those qualities; for you, whose nature is pure knowledge, what cause for bondage could there ever be?
Because the limiting adjuncts such as the body and so forth are not established [as real], there can be no birth for the Self, nor can there be any differentiation.

Therefore, neither bondage nor liberation can belong to You; indeed, there is no lack of discernment in You. This ancient path of the Vedas was proclaimed by You for the welfare of the world whenever it was needed.

At that time, you would have been oppressed by the wicked paths of heresy; yet now, O Lord, you who possess the quality of pure goodness (*sattva*) have descended here into the house of Vasudeva with a portion of yourself to remove the burden of the earth.
By slaying hundreds of akṣauhiṇī divisions of kings who were portions of asuras, he spreads the fame of his own lineage; O Lord, our dwellings today are indeed most fortunate.

O Adhokṣaja, You who are the embodiment of all gods, ancestors, spirits, humans, and deities; You whose water for washing the feet purifies the three worlds— You, the Teacher of the Universe, have entered [this world].
What wise person other than You would seek refuge elsewhere—
You who are dear to Your devotees, whose word is truth, who are a well-wishing friend, and who are grateful;
for You grant all the desires of the friends who worship You?
Even for Yourself, there is neither increase nor decrease; by good fortune, O Janārdana, You have been perceived here by us—
You whose state is difficult to attain even for the lords of the gods and the masters of yoga.
"Quickly cut the cord of delusion regarding our sons, wives, wealth, kinsmen, home, body, and so forth— this illusion of yours.
Thus was the Blessed Lord Hari worshipped and praised by his devotee.
Smiling, as if to bewilder him with his words, the Blessed Lord spoke to Akrūra:
The Blessed Lord said: "You are our teacher, our paternal uncle, and always our praiseworthy kinsman."
We, indeed, are your subjects— worthy of protection, nourishment, and compassion; for those like you, O highly fortunate ones, who are the most worthy of honor,
are always to be served by men desiring their own welfare, not the gods.
For holy places are not made of water, nor are the gods made of clay or stone;
the saintly purify others merely by their sight, whereas those [other sites] do so only after a long time.
Therefore, you, who desire to bring about our welfare, are indeed the most excellent among our friends.
"Go to Hastināpura for the sake of inquiring about the Pāṇḍavas.
We have heard that when their father had passed away, the children, together with their mother and deeply afflicted by grief,
were brought to their own city by the king and are living there."

Among those sons of his brothers, the king, the son of Ambikā, being of feeble intellect and blinded by sight, surely does not behave with impartiality, for he is under the sway of his wicked son. Go now and find out whether his conduct is right or wrong.
"Having understood this, we shall act in such a way that there may be well-being for our friends.
Having thus instructed Akrūra, the Blessed Lord Hari, the Supreme Controller,
then departed for his own abode together with Saṅkarṣaṇa and Uddhava.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having gone to Hāstinapura, which was marked by the fame of the lord of the Pauravas,
he saw there the son of Ambikā (Dhṛtarāṣṭra), along with Bhīṣma, Vidura, and Pṛthā.
Having duly approached Bāhlīka with his son, Bhāradvāja along with Gautama,
Karṇa, Suyodhana, the son of Droṇa, the Pāṇḍavas, and other friends,
the son of Gāndinī met with his kinsmen.
Questioned by them regarding the welfare of his friends, he himself inquired after their own well-being;
desiring to know the conduct of the king— who was of evil intellect, meager merit, and a follower of the will of the wicked— he resided there for several months.
Unable to endure the splendor, vigor, strength, heroism, humility, and other virtuous qualities [of the Pāṇḍavas], as well as the affection of the subjects for the sons of Pṛthā,
the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra plotted and carried out various unseemly acts, such as the administration of poison.
Pṛthā and Vidura related everything to him;
then Pṛthā, approaching her brother Akrūra who had arrived,
spoke to him with eyes brimming with tears, remembering her place of birth.

O gentle one, do my parents, my brothers, my two sisters, my nephews, my daughters-in-law, and my friends still remember us? And does the venerable Kṛṣṇa, my brother, the refuge of all and the lover of his devotees, remember us?
The lotus-eyed Rāma will remember his father’s sister’s sons;
he will comfort me with his words as I grieve in the midst of my rivals like a doe among wolves, and he will care for the children who are deprived of their father.
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, great yogin, soul of the universe, creator of the world! O Govinda, protect me, who have taken refuge in you and am sinking down with my children.
I see no other shelter for men than your lotus feet.
To those who fear the cycle of birth and death and the Lord who grants liberation—
salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the pure, the Brahman, the Supreme Self,
the Lord of Yoga, and Yoga itself; I have come to You for refuge.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, thus remembering her own kin and Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the universe,
your great-great-grandmother wept in deep sorrow.
Akrūra, who shared equally in her sorrow and joy, and the highly illustrious Vidura,
consoled Kuntī with reasons for the birth of her sons. As he was about to depart, he approached the king, who was distressed by his longing for a son.
In the midst of his friends, he spoke words prompted by affection for his kinsmen.
Akrūra said:
"O son of Vicitravīrya, you who increase the glory of the Kurus!"
Now that your brother Pāṇḍu has passed away, you have ascended the throne;

by protecting the earth with righteousness and pleasing the subjects with your virtuous character, and by conducting yourself with impartiality toward your own kin, you shall attain prosperity and fame.
Otherwise, by acting differently in this world, you will be censured and go to darkness.
Therefore, maintain equanimity toward both the Pāṇḍavas and your own sons.
Furthermore, there is no permanent dwelling here for anyone with anyone else.
O King, what use is even one's own body, much less a wife, children, and so forth?
A living being is born alone, and alone indeed it perishes.
Alone it experiences the fruits of its good deeds, and alone those of its evil deeds.
Those of small intelligence seize the wealth accumulated through unrighteousness under the pretext of providing for their dependents,
just as leeches suck up water. He who nourishes such people by means of unrighteousness according to his own judgment is a fool.
Life, wealth, children, and the like depart, leaving one who has failed to achieve his purpose;
having themselves taken away one's merit, they abandon the person who knows nothing of true value. Failing to accomplish his goal and turning away from his own duty, he enters the blinding darkness.
"Therefore, O King, seeing this world as a dream, an illusion, and a mental construction, restrain yourself by means of the self; be equanimous and peaceful, O Lord.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
O Lord of Charity, although you speak such auspicious words,
I am not satiated by them, just as a mortal is never satiated by nectar.
Nevertheless, O gentle one, these truthful and pleasant words do not remain in my fickle heart.
Just as a flash of lightning from the clouds is unpredictable, so too is the affection of the Lord for His son;
what man indeed can subvert the decree of the Lord? He who has descended into the lineage of Yadu for the purpose of removing the earth's burden.

Salutations to Him whose method of inscrutable play is difficult to comprehend, who, having created this universe by His own Maya of unfathomable path, differentiates the modes of nature while entering into them.
To the Supreme Lord, who causes one to traverse the wheel of worldly existence,
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus understood the intention of the king, that Yādava...

Permitted by his friends, he returned again to the city of the Yadus and related to Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa the conduct of Dhṛtarāṣṭra toward the Pāṇḍavas, O descendant of Kuru, regarding which matter he himself had been sent.
Śrī Śuka said: O bull of the Bharatas, Asti and Prāpti, the two queens of Kaṃsa,
when their husband had died, went to their father’s house, afflicted by grief.
They informed their grieving father, Jarāsandha, the King of Magadha,
of everything that had caused their own widowhood.
Hearing those unpleasant tidings, the king was filled with sorrow and indignation.
He made a supreme effort to rid the earth of the Yādavas;
surrounded by twenty-three *akṣauhiṇīs*,
he besieged Mathurā, the capital of the Yadus, from every direction.
Beholding that army, which was like the ocean overflowing its shores, and seeing his own city besieged by it and his people overwhelmed with fear,
the Blessed Lord Hari, who had assumed a human form for a specific purpose, reflected thus.
In accordance with the requirements of that place and time, I shall fulfill the purpose of my own incarnation:
"I will indeed slay this Balarāma, who has been placed upon the earth as a burden,
brought here by the King of Magadha and under the control of all subordinate monarchs."
"Accompanied by an *akṣauhiṇī* of soldiers, horses, chariots, and elephants,
the King of Magadha must not be slain, for he will again exert his military power.
It is for this purpose that I have descended to remove the burden of the earth."
For the protection of the virtuous and for the destruction of others,
another body is assumed by me for the sake of preserving dharma; indeed, at times when unrighteousness prevails, a body is manifested even for its suppression.
While Govinda was thus meditating, two chariots, possessing the splendor of the sun, immediately appeared from the sky along with their drivers and equipment;
and by his mere will, his ancient, divine weapons also arrived.
Having seen those [omens], Hṛṣīkeśa then spoke to Saṅkarṣaṇa:
"O Noble One, O Lord, behold the calamity that has befallen the Yadus who have you as their protector!
Here comes your chariot and your beloved weapons."
"O Lord, this birth of ours was indeed for this purpose, to bring happiness to the virtuous;
now remove the burden of the earth known as the twenty-three armies.
Having thus consulted together, the two scions of the Daśārha clan, clad in armor, mounted their chariots and departed from the city.
Richly equipped with their own weapons and surrounded by a small force, the two went forth.
Having emerged, Hari, with Dāruka as his charioteer, blew his conch shell;
thereupon, terror and trembling seized the hearts of the enemy armies.
Beholding them, the King of Magadha said: "O Kṛṣṇa, you lowest of men!
Out of shame, I do not wish to fight with you alone, a mere child.
Indeed, O dull-witted one, I will not fight with you while you are protected; go, you slayer of your own kin!"
"O Rāma, if you have the resolve, fight and summon your courage;
or else, casting off this body severed by my arrows, go to heaven—slay me!
The Blessed Lord said:
"Heroes indeed do not boast; they simply demonstrate their prowess.
"O King, we do not heed the words of one who is afflicted and about to die.
Śrī Śuka said:
Jarā’s two sons, approaching the two Mādhavas with a vast flood of troops, overwhelmed those two powerful ones along with their armies,
vehicles, banners, horses, and charioteers— just as the wind covers the sun and fire with clouds and dust.
Their chariots were marked by the emblems of Garuḍa and the palm tree.
Failing to perceive the combat between Hari and Rāma,
the women, who had taken refuge on the city walls, the turrets, the palaces, and the gate-towers, were overcome with fainting, afflicted by grief.

Hari, beholding his own army— which was worshipped by both gods and demons— repeatedly tormented by the exceedingly fierce rain of arrows from the enemy’s cloud-like ranks, strung his excellent bow Śārṅga and,
taking arrows from his quiver, fixed them upon it.
Drawing back and releasing volleys of sharp arrows,
he struck down chariots, elephants, horses, and infantrymen,
appearing like a continuous circle of fire.
Elephants fell by the hundreds with their frontal globes split open; horses had their necks severed by arrows;

chariots were deprived of their horses, banners, drivers, and warriors; and infantrymen had their arms, thighs, and necks lopped off. Rivers of blood flowed by the hundreds from the limbs of men, elephants, and horses being hacked to pieces.
With arms for serpents, human heads for tortoises, and elephants, islands, and horses for crocodiles;
with thighs and shanks for fish, human hair for moss, bows for waves, and weapons for thickets;
terrifying with the whirlpools of swords and featuring stones and pebbles in the form of excellent great jewels and ornaments.
In that battle, those weapons, which brought fear to the timid and inspired joy among the high-minded,
were hurled at one another by Saṅkarṣaṇa, whose splendor is immeasurable, as they struck down their arrogant enemies with the club.
That army, protected by the Lord of Magadha, was as terrifying as a sea of burning coals, difficult to cross and seemingly endless.

The supreme pastimes of Vasudeva’s two sons, the lords of the universe, which bring about the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the three worlds, were brought to an end by Him who possesses infinite qualities and acts according to His own will through His divine play.
It was no wonder that he subdued the opposing side;
nevertheless, it is described as such because He conformed to the ways of mortals.
Rāma seized the immensely powerful Jarāsandha, who was deprived of his chariot.

Like a lion overpowering a lion with its might, Govinda restrained the surviving warrior of the slain army as he was being bound with Varuṇa’s and human nooses, though he had already struck down his enemies, desiring to accomplish a specific purpose through him.
Released by the two Lords of the World, he was ashamed yet honored by the heroes;
having resolved to perform austerities, he was restrained on the road by kings with words whose meanings were purifying, though their expressions were ordinary.
This defeat of yours by the Yadus was brought about by the bondage of your own karma; when all his armies had been slain, King Bārhadratha,
disregarded by the Blessed One, departed for Magadha with a heavy heart.
Mukunda, his strength unimpaired and having crossed the ocean of the enemy's forces,
was showered with flowers by the gods and greeted by the people of Mathurā,
who were free from anxiety and joyful in heart.
While his victory was being sung by Sūtas, Māgadhas, and bards,
conchs and dundubhi drums resounded, as did kettledrums and various musical instruments, along with lutes,
flutes, and mṛdaṅga drums, as the Lord entered the city.
The road was sprinkled with water, filled with joyful people, and beautifully adorned with banners; it resounded with the chanting of the Vedas and was decorated with festive arches,
while he was showered by the women with garlands, curd, unbroken grains, and sprouts.
Beholding the infinite wealth brought from the battlefield, adorned with the ornaments of heroes, the Lord, looking upon it with affection through eyes overflowing with love,
directed that everything be delivered to the King of the Yadus.
In this manner, seventeen times over, the King of Magadha, possessing an army of that many *akṣauhiṇīs*, fought with the Yadus protected by Kṛṣṇa;
yet the Vṛṣṇis, through the splendor of Kṛṣṇa, exhausted that entire force.
When his own armies had been slain, the king was abandoned by his followers and fled from his enemies; meanwhile, during that interval before the eighteenth battle was to come,
a heroic Yavana, sent by Nārada, appeared.
Having arrived at Mathurā with thirty million Mlecchas, he besieged it;
for in the world of men, he was without rival. Hearing that the Vṛṣṇis were his equals, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Saṅkarṣaṇa, saw him and reflected.
"Alas! A great calamity has befallen the Yadus from both sides:
today this Yavana of immense strength besieges us; and today, tomorrow, or the day after, the King of Magadha will also arrive."
"If the son of Jarā comes while we two are fighting him,
that powerful one will either slay our kinsmen or carry them off to his own city;
therefore, today we shall construct a fortress, difficult for even bipeds to penetrate."

Having deliberated there, saying, "Let us reassure our kinsmen and have the Yavana slain," the Blessed One caused a city twelve *yojanas* in extent to be built within the ocean, complete with all wonders.
There, indeed, the craftsmanship and artistic skill of Tvaṣṭṛ were visible,
with its streets, crossroads, and lanes constructed according to the proper layout,
and endowed with gardens of celestial trees and creepers, as well as various wonderful groves.
With golden peaks touching the heavens, with crystal watchtowers and gateways,
with silver and copper-roofed chambers adorned with golden jars,
with houses of gold topped with jewels, and with courtyards of great emeralds;
Built with the houses and turrets of the Vāstoṣpatis,
crowded with people of the four castes, and shining with the residences of the Yadu deities,
Mahendra sent Sudharmā and the Pārijāta tree to Hari.
And where a mortal who is situated is no longer joined with mortal attributes;
where Varuṇa [rides] eight horses of a single dark-blue hue, white, and swift as thought;
and where the Lord of Treasures [Kubera] possesses his own eight self-arisen treasures as the guardians of the world.
O King, when the Lord had descended to the earth, all those who had been granted sovereignty by Him for their own success returned everything to Hari;
there, Hari, having led all the people away by the power of His yoga, [established them in His realm].
BhP 10.50.057/3–5: Being thus addressed by Rāma, the protector of the subjects, Kṛṣṇa, wearing a garland of lotuses and unarmed, went forth from the city gate.
BhP 10.51.001/0: Śrī Śuka said:
Beholding him as he emerged, appearing like the rising moon—
most beautiful to behold, dark-complexioned, clad in yellow silk garments,
with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest and the radiant Kaustubha gem resting upon his bare neck.
He possessed four arms, broad and long, with eyes as reddish as a fresh lotus;
he was eternally joyful, glorious, with beautiful cheeks and a pure smile,
bearing a lotus-face adorned with shimmering makara-shaped earrings.
"He must indeed be Vāsudeva, for he is a person marked with the Śrīvatsa,
four-armed, lotus-eyed, wearing forest garlands, and exceedingly beautiful;
by these characteristics described by Nārada, he cannot be anyone else."
"Armed with nothing but my feet, I shall fight this man who is likewise unarmed," having thus resolved, the Yavana pursued him as he fled with his back turned,
desiring to seize him who was difficult even for yogis to attain.
At every step, the Lord of the Yavanas was led far away by Hari, who showed him mountain caves as if he were within his very grasp;
yet, for one born in the Yadu clan, such flight is not fitting.
Thus reviling him as he pursued, he whose sins had been destroyed did not catch up with him;
even though thus reviled, the Blessed One entered a mountain cave,
and he too, having entered there, beheld another man lying down.
Thinking, "Surely he has brought me here from afar and now lies here like a saint," the fool struck Acyuta with his foot.
Rising up after having slept for a long time, he slowly opened his eyes.
Looking around in all directions, he saw him standing at his side;
O descendant of Bharata, by the glance of that enraged one,
he was instantly consumed by the fire born of his body and reduced to ashes in an instant.
The King said:
O Brāhmaṇa, who was that man, to whom did he belong, and what was his prowess?
Why did that destroyer of the Yavanas enter the cave with his disciple, and what was his splendor?
Śrī Śuka said:
Born in the lineage of Ikṣvāku as the son of Māndhātṛ, he was a great soul known as Mucukunda, devoted to the brāhmaṇas and true to his promise.

Requested by the hosts of gods, led by Indra, who were terrified of the asuras, he protected them for a long time against those demons. Having obtained Guha as the protector of heaven, they then spoke to Mucukunda.
O King, desist from this hardship of protecting us;
O hero, having abandoned the world of men and your kingdom whose thorns have been removed,
all your desires have been renounced as you protect us.
Your daughters, queens, kinsmen, ministers, counselors, and subjects—all who were your contemporaries—are no longer here; they have been swept away by Time.
Time is more powerful than the powerful; it is the Lord, the Blessed One, the imperishable.
He drives forth all creatures for his sport, just as a cowherd drives his cattle. Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—with the sole exception of liberation from us today;
for he alone is the Lord, the inexhaustible Blessed Viṣṇu.
Thus addressed, that highly illustrious one, having offered salutations to the gods,
lay down within the cave, overcome by the sleep granted by the Lord.
When the Yavana had been reduced to ashes, the Blessed One, the bull among the Sātvatas, [arose].
He revealed Himself to the wise Mucukunda.
Beholding Him, dark as a rain cloud, clad in yellow silk garments,
with the Śrīvatsa mark upon His chest, and resplendent with the shining Kaustubha gem;
He had four arms and was radiant with the Vaijayantī garland;
his face was beautiful and serene, adorned with shimmering makara-shaped earrings. He was a sight to behold for the world of men, his eyes filled with affectionate smiles.

The king, whose great intelligence was humbled by the other's splendor, questioned him who possessed the noble prowess of a maddened lion in his prime; overcome by that brilliance, he timidly spoke to him who was as invincible as fire.
Śrī Mucukunda said:
Who are you that have arrived here in this forest within a mountain cave, wandering on foot with feet like lotus petals upon the thorny ground?
What indeed is the splendor of those who possess splendor— is it the Lord Fire,
or the Sun, or the Moon, or the Great Indra, or another world-protector?
O God, I consider you the bull among men, the supreme among the three gods of the gods.

O bull among men, just as a lamp dispels the darkness within a cave with its radiance, you have dispelled the darkness of our hearts; O best of men, if it pleases you, please tell us the truth regarding your birth, your deeds, and your lineage, for we are eager to hear it.
"But we, O tiger among men, are the descendants of Ikṣvāku, mere kṣatriyas. O Lord, I am known as Mucukunda, the son of Yuvanāśva.
Exhausted from staying awake for a long time, my senses were overcome by sleep."
"I was lying here in this secluded place at my pleasure when I was surely awakened by someone; even he has certainly been reduced to ashes by his own very sin.
Immediately thereafter, you, the illustrious subduer of enemies, were perceived."
"Because of Your unbearable splendor, we are unable to look upon You extensively. O illustrious one, Your power has been diminished; You are worthy of honor by all embodied beings.
Thus addressed by the king, the Blessed Lord, the creator of all beings, [replied].
Laughing, the Blessed Lord replied with a voice as deep as the roar of a thundercloud: The Blessed Lord said:
"O dear one, my births, deeds, and names are indeed thousands in number."

Indeed, because they are infinite, even I am unable to enumerate them. At one time, I measured out the earthly dust particles with my vast births; yet my births, characterized by their qualities and activities, can never be fully recounted.
O King, even the supreme sages, though they recount my births and activities occurring throughout the three periods of time, do not reach their end. Nevertheless,
O dear one, listen now as I describe those pertaining to the present day.
Requested by Viriñca in the past for the protection of dharma and for the destruction of the demons who were becoming a burden to the earth,
I have descended into the Yadu clan in the home of Ānakadundubhi.
Indeed, they call me Vāsudeva, the son of Vasudeva;
for Kālanemi has been slain, as have Kaṃsa, Pralamba, and my other enemies.
And this Yavana, O King, has been consumed by your sharp glance.

I, who am affectionate toward my devotees, have come to this cave for the sake of showing you favor, having been previously entreated by you many times. O royal sage, choose boons; I shall grant you all your desires.
"Once I have become gracious, no person shall ever again deserve to grieve for me.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having been addressed thus, Mucukunda, filled with joy, bowed to him and spoke.
Having realized that Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Lord and recollecting the words of Garga,
Śrī Mucukunda said:
"O Lord, this person is deluded by Your illusory energy (māyā) and, perceiving only what is worthless, does not worship You."
Deceived by their own delusion, both woman and man become attached to the home, which is the source of suffering though they seek happiness;
O sinless one, having somehow obtained this rare human birth here, free from defects and without effort, people remain thus.
One of wicked intellect does not worship Your lotus feet,
like a beast fallen into the blind well of domestic life.
O Unconquered One, this time of mine has passed fruitlessly, while I, the lord of the earth, was intoxicated by the pride of sovereign power and royal splendor.
With the intellect identifying with the mortal body, I was attached to my children, wife, treasury, and lands through endless anxieties;
and regarding this body, which is like a jar or a wall,
I was firmly established in the pride of thinking, "I am a king."
Surrounded by divisions of chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry,
he wandered the earth with great arrogance, disregarding you; he was heedless due to intense anxiety over his duties, and his greed for sense objects had increased to the point of longing.
Vigilant, you suddenly pounce like a serpent licking its prey upon a mouse— the Ender—
though formerly you moved about in chariots adorned with gold or on rutting elephants, known by the title "God among Men."
By that same insurmountable Time, Your body—
now designated as ordure, worms, and ashes—
is cast away; yet You, having conquered the circle of the quarters, possess a form beyond the material elements, seated upon an excellent throne, and worshipped by equal kings.
O Lord, a man is led like a pet animal among women in their homes for the sake of sexual pleasure;
though he performs rituals with great dedication to austerity, desisting from enjoyment and offering them with that expectation,
he is not fit for happiness, for his thirst increases further with the thought, "May I become a sovereign once again."
O Acyuta, when liberation from worldly existence occurs for a person wandering in saṃsāra, then there is association with the saintly;
and when there is association with the saintly, then one's mind is directed toward You, the Supreme Lord, the goal of the righteous, both high and low.
O Lord, I consider that You have bestowed Your grace upon me by the mere chance of my release from the entanglements of kingship.

O Lord, I desire no other boon than service at Your feet— the boon most sought after by the destitute— which is prayed for by saintly kings who, desiring to enter the solitary forest, practice the life of solitude.
For who, O Hari, having propitiated You, the giver of liberation, would choose as a boon that which binds the self?
Therefore, O Lord, having cast aside from all sides those blessings that are bound to the qualities of *rajas*, *tamas*, and *sattva*,
I go unto You— the stainless, quality-less, non-dual, supreme Person, who is pure consciousness alone. For long I have been afflicted here by misfortune and tormented by regrets.
O Giver of Refuge, O Supreme Self, I am thirsty, my six enemies are unsubdued, and I have found no peace; somehow I have approached Your lotus feet—
protect me, who have come for shelter, O Lord, from fearlessness, truth, and freedom from sorrow.
The Blessed Lord said: O great king, sovereign of the whole earth, your intellect is stainless and exalted,
since it has not been thwarted by desires even though you were tempted with boons.
Know that your being enticed by boons was for the sake of vigilance;
the intellect of those who are single-mindedly devoted is never disturbed by blessings.
[This is unlike] the minds of non-devotees who strive with breath-control and other such practices.
"O King, one whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are not exhausted is seen to rise again;
therefore, wander the earth as you desire, with your mind absorbed in me. May such devotion toward me remain yours forever, never-failing."
O King, you who remained established in the dharma of a kṣatriya killed living beings through hunting and other such means;
now, being composed and taking refuge in Me, abandon that sin through austerity.
In your next birth, O King, you shall be the most excellent friend of all beings.
"Having become the best of the twice-born, you shall indeed come to me alone.
Śrī Śuka said:
"O dear one, having been thus favored by Kṛṣṇa, that descendant of Ikṣvāku [departed]."
Having circumambulated and bowed down to him, he emerged from the mouth of the cave;
beholding the small mortal beings, the animals, and the plants and trees,
and realizing that the Kali Yuga had arrived, he departed toward the northern direction.
Endowed with austerity and faith, steadfast, free from attachment and liberated from doubt,
he concentrated his mind upon Kṛṣṇa and entered Gandhamādana.
Having reached Badarī-āśrama, the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, he settled there.
Enduring all dualities and tranquil, he propitiated Hari through austerity. Then the Blessed Lord returned to the city besieged by the Yavanas,
and having slain the Mleccha forces, he brought their wealth to Dvārakā.
While the cattle were being led away by men impelled by Acyuta,
Jarāsandha arrived with twenty-three armies;
and the two Mādhavas beheld the impetuous onset of the enemy host.
O King, having assumed human behavior, they fled swiftly,
abandoning their abundant wealth; though fearless, they acted like those terrified by fear, traveling many yojanas on foot with their bare feet.
Seeing the two of them fleeing, the powerful King of Magadha, who was unaware of the true power of the Lords, laughed and pursued them with his chariot divisions.
Having fled a great distance, they became exhausted and climbed a lofty mountain.
O King, knowing that [the two demons] were hidden on the mountain named Pravarṣaṇa, where the Lord constantly rains, and being unable to find their location,
he set fire to the mountain from all sides, discharging flames with fuel.
Then, springing up with speed from the burning slope that was eleven yojanas high, those two best of the Yadus fell down to the earth below,
unseen by the enemy and his followers.
O King, having returned again to their own city which was surrounded by the ocean as a moat, the King of Magadha,
falsely believing that Balarāma and Keśava had been burned,
summoned his great army and marched toward the Magadhas.
The illustrious Raivata, lord of Ānarta,
being urged by Brahmā as previously described, gave his daughter Raivatī to Bala;
O best of the Kurus, the Blessed Lord Govinda also married her.
At her svayaṃvara, having violently overpowered King Śālva and others who sided with the King of Cedi, he took Vaidarbhī, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka and the very embodiment of the Goddess of Fortune,
just as the son of Tārkṣya [Garuḍa] carried away the nectar while all the worlds looked on.
The King said:
"I have heard that the Blessed One married Rukmiṇī, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka, who has a beautiful countenance,
according to the rākṣasa rite."
O Blessed One, I wish to hear how Kṛṣṇa, of immeasurable splendor,
conquered the King of Magadha, Śālva, and others, and won the maiden. O Brahmin, the sacred stories of Kṛṣṇa are like honey, removing the impurities of the world.
"Who indeed could ever be satiated while hearing these eternally fresh accounts, O knower of what has been heard?
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
"There was once a great king named Bhīṣmaka, the sovereign of Vidarbha."
