He had five sons and one daughter of beautiful countenance. Rukmin was the eldest, followed by Rukmaratha, Rukmabāhu, Rukmakeśa, and Rukmamālin; this virtuous Rukmiṇī was his sister.
Having heard of Mukunda’s beauty, prowess, virtues,
and splendor being sung by those who had come to her home, she considered him a suitable husband; he was the refuge of her intellect, auspicious marks, generosity, beauty, character, and qualities.
And Kṛṣṇa set his mind on marrying a suitable wife. O King, although his kinsmen desired to give their sister to Kṛṣṇa, Rukmī, an enemy of Kṛṣṇa, dissuaded them and instead chose the King of Cedi.

Having understood that, the princess of Vidarbha, her eyes reaching to her ears and her mind deeply distressed, reflected for a moment and quickly dispatched a certain trusted brahmin to Kṛṣṇa. Upon arriving at Dvārakā, he was ushered inside by the gatekeepers.

He saw the Primal Person seated upon a golden throne; having seen him, that God who is devoted to the Brahman descended from his own seat, and after seating him, he honored him with the same hospitality as he would offer himself to the inhabitants of heaven.
When he had finished eating and was rested, the refuge of the virtuous approached him and,
touching his feet with his hand, asked him without distraction:
"O best of the foremost of the twice-born, is your dharma, which is esteemed by the elders, proceeding well?"
For one whose mind is always contented, life proceeds without excessive hardship.
When a brāhmaṇa lives satisfied with whatever he may have,
not falling away from his own duty, that very state becomes for him the cow of plenty that fulfills all desires.
Even the lord of the gods, if dissatisfied, repeatedly attains various worlds;
yet even one who possesses nothing, if satisfied, sleeps with all his limbs free from feverish distress.
[One should honor] the brāhmaṇas who are satisfied with their own gains, the saintly ones who are the greatest friends to all beings.

I repeatedly bow my head in reverence to those who are free from ego and are peaceful. O brāhmaṇas, is all well with you? Indeed, that king under whom the subjects dwell happily while being protected is dear to me.
"From where have you come, having crossed this difficult path here by your own will?
Tell us everything, if it is not a secret; what service may we do for you?
Thus was the Brahmin questioned by the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
With a body assumed through divine play (*līlā*), he described everything to him.
Śrī Rukmiṇī said:
"O most beautiful in the world, having heard your qualities from those who hear them..."

O Acyuta, as my shameless mind enters into You— You who remove the distress of the limbs through the openings of the ears, and whose form is the attainment of all goals for those possessing sight through the eyes— [I am filled with joy].

O Mukunda, what noble-minded girl of good family, character, beauty, learning, youth, wealth, and station would not choose you as her husband— you who are equal to herself? Who, being wise and of good lineage, would not choose you?

O Nṛsiṃha, at the proper time, please ordain for me that husband who delights the minds of the world of men; O Lord, you have indeed been chosen by me as my husband, and I have surrendered myself to you— act accordingly here, O All-pervading One.
O lotus-eyed one, let not the King of Cedi touch the portion belonging to the hero, like a jackal approaching the offering of the lord of beasts. [May he not touch] the merit of public works,
sacrifices, gifts, observances, vows, the gods, and the brahmins.
Enough with the worship of gurus and other such rites; if the Supreme Lord, the Highest Ruler, the elder brother of Gadā, is propitiated, may He Himself come and take my hand,
and not others such as the son of Damaghoṣa.
Tomorrow, on the occasion of the marriage of the unconquered one, you shall go to Vidarbha protected and surrounded by the commanders of the armies;
having forcibly crushed the forces of the lords of Cedi and Magadha.
"Marry me according to the rite of a *rākṣasa*, for my dowry is valor;
I am one who moves within the inner apartments. How can you marry me without having slain my kinsmen? I shall tell you the means."
On the previous day, there was a great festival for the family deity,
at which the new bride would go outside to visit Girijā;
bathing in the dust of whose lotus feet great souls [attain purification].
O lotus-eyed one, I long for your grace just as the Lord of Umā longs to destroy his own darkness; if I should not obtain it,
I would give up my life-breaths, emaciated by vows, though it might take a hundred births.
The brāhmaṇa said:
"O God of the Yadus, these secret messages have been brought by me;
having reflected upon them, let that which is to be done here be performed immediately thereafter."
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard the message of the princess of Vidarbha, the joy of the Yadus took her hand in his own and,
smiling, spoke as follows.
The Blessed Lord said:
"In that same way, my mind is fixed upon him, and I find no sleep at night.
I know that Rukmī, out of hatred, prevented my marriage."
"I shall bring her here after crushing those lowest of kings in battle— she who is devoted to me and possesses faultless limbs, like a flame of fire from fuel.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having ascertained the auspicious constellation for Rukmiṇī’s wedding, Madhusūdana said to his charioteer, "Dāruka, let the chariot be yoked at once.
And he [prepared it] with the horses Śaibya, Sugrīva, Meghapuṣpa, and Balāhaka.
Having brought forward the yoked chariot, he stood before him with palms joined in reverence.
Ascending the chariot and causing the twice-born man to mount, Śauri traveled from Ānarta to Vidarbha in a single night by means of horses of swift gait.

That king, the lord of Kuṇḍina, being driven by the power of affection for his son, had various preparations made while intending to give his daughter to Śiśupāla. He had the city’s streets, roads, and crossroads swept clean and sprinkled with water.
It was adorned with variegated banners, flags,
and archways; it was graced by men and women wearing stainless garments and ornaments, garlands, perfumes, and wreaths, and by magnificent houses fumigated with aloe-wood incense.
O King, having duly honored the ancestors, the gods, and the brahmins according to the prescribed rites,
he fed them as was appropriate and had auspicious benedictions recited.
Then [he presented] the maiden, who was well-bathed, possessed beautiful teeth, and had the auspicious marriage-thread and ornaments placed upon her.

The best of the twice-born adorned her with a pair of fresh garments and the finest ornaments; then, with the mantras of the Sāma, Ṛg, and Yajur Vedas, they performed the protective rite for the bride.
Meanwhile, the domestic priest, learned in the Atharva Veda, offered oblations to pacify the influence of the planets.
The king, the best among those who know the ordinances, gave gold, silver, garments, and sesame seeds mixed with molasses, as well as cows, to the Brahmins.
In this manner, King Damaghoṣa, the lord of Cedi, [bestowed gifts] upon his son.
He had everything appropriate for a festive occasion performed by those skilled in mantras; surrounded by armies consisting of herds of rutting elephants, chariots adorned with golden garlands,
and throngs of infantry and cavalry, he went toward Kuṇḍina.
The lord of Vidarbha approached him, honored him,
and with joy settled him in a specially prepared residence.
There were Śālva, Jarāsandha, Dantavakra, and Vidūratha.
Thousands of followers of the King of Cedi, such as Pauṇḍraka and others,

who were enemies of Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, arrived there prepared to secure the maiden for the King of Cedi, thinking: "If Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Balarāma and the other Yadus, should come here, he might carry her off."
With their minds firmly resolved, "We shall fight him united," all those kings arrived with their entire forces and vehicles.
Having heard of this exertion of the hostile kings, the blessed Lord Rāma...

Fearing a quarrel over the abduction of the maiden, and overwhelmed with brotherly affection, he set out for Kuṇḍina in haste with a great force of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, intent on seizing Kṛṣṇa alone.
The daughter of Bhīṣma, of beautiful form, longing for the arrival of Hari and seeing no sign of his return, then reflected upon the brahmin:
"Alas! My marriage has been postponed by three watches of the night, I who am so lacking in merit."
"The lotus-eyed Lord does not come; I do not know the reason for this.
Even that brahmin who brought my message has not returned to this day.
Could it be that he, whose soul is faultless, saw something loathsome in me?"
"Surely he has not exerted himself to take my hand;
for the Creator is not favorable to me, an unfortunate woman, nor is Maheśvara. Or perhaps the goddess Gaurī, Rudrāṇī, Girijā, Satī, has turned her face away."
While the young woman, her mind stolen by Govinda, was thus reflecting, she,
who knew the right time, closed her eyes which were clouded with teardrops.
O King, while the daughter-in-law was waiting in this manner for the arrival of Govinda—
The left thigh, arm, and eye of him who spoke so pleasantly throbbed. Then, directed by Kṛṣṇa, that very best of the twice-born beheld the princess, the queen who moved within the inner apartments.
Perceiving him to have a joyful countenance and a composed mind,
the virtuous Lakṣaṇā, who was skilled in reading signs, questioned him with a pure smile.
He informed her that he had arrived and described the joy of the descendant of Yadu.
And regarding the taking of the Self as one's teacher, the word of truth was spoken.
Having learned that he had arrived, the princess of Vidarbha, her mind filled with joy,
bowed to the Brahmin, seeing no other object of affection for him.
Upon hearing that they had arrived, eager to witness the marriage of his daughter,
he approached Rāma and Kṛṣṇa with the sounding of musical instruments and offerings of worship;
having presented them with the madhuparka, he offered spotless garments.
He honored their desired offerings according to the prescribed rites;
having prepared a magnificent residence for the two of them along with their armies and followers, the high-minded king extended hospitality to them as was fitting.
Thus, he honored all the assembled kings according to their prowess, age, strength, and wealth, and with every desirable object.
Upon hearing that Kṛṣṇa had arrived, the inhabitants of the city of Vidarbha [prepared for his reception].
Having arrived, they drank in his lotus-face with their eyes like cupped hands;
Rukmiṇī alone is worthy to be his wife, and no other. He too, of faultless soul, is a husband suited for the daughter of Bhīṣmaka.

"Whatever slight good deed we have performed, may the Creator of the three worlds, being pleased by it, bestow his grace; may Acyuta take the hand of the princess of Vidarbha. Thus spoke the citizens, bound by the strands of their love.
The maiden, protected by guards, went from the inner apartments to the temple of Ambikā;
she went forth on foot to behold the lotus-feet of Bhavānī.
And she meditated perfectly upon the lotus-feet of Mukunda.
Restraining her speech, she was accompanied by her mothers and surrounded by her female companions;
she was protected by brave royal soldiers clad in armor with weapons raised,
while mṛdaṅgas, conchs, paṇavas, tūryas, and bherīs were sounded.
Thousands of courtesans offered various kinds of offerings and oblations;
the wives of the twice-born, beautifully adorned with garlands, perfumes, garments, and ornaments, sang praises; and singers and musicians played their instruments.
Sūtas, Māgadhas, and bards followed, surrounding the bride.
Having reached the queen’s chamber, she washed her lotus-like feet and hands; then, purified and tranquil, she approached the presence of Ambikā.

The elderly wives of the brahmins, who were well-versed in the sacred injunctions, paid homage to that young girl, the daughter of Bhava and the consort of Bhava, accompanied by her husband. "O Ambikā, I perpetually bow down to you, the auspicious one, together with your own offspring."
"May the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa be my husband; may He grant His approval.
[She offered worship] with water, scents, unbroken grains, incense, garments, garlands, ornaments, various offerings and oblations, and distinct rows of lamps.
Likewise, he honored the wives of the brahmins who were accompanied by their husbands with salted cakes,
betel, necklaces, fruits, and sugarcane.
Those women gave him the remnants and bestowed blessings upon him.
He offered obeisances to those goddesses, and the bride accepted the remaining ones.
Then, having abandoned her vow of silence, she emerged from Ambikā’s chamber,
taking hold of her handmaid with a hand adorned by a jeweled seal-ring.
She was like a divine illusion that deludes even the wise—a woman of slender waist, her face adorned with earrings;
dark-complexioned, with a jeweled girdle fastened upon her hips, her breasts beginning to manifest, and her eyes made suspicious by her curling locks of hair;
she possessed a pure smile, and the jasmine buds of her teeth were turning crimson from the glow of her lips, which were as radiant as the *bimba* fruit.
Seeing her walking with the graceful gait of a swan, adorned with the splendor of tinkling, exquisite anklets,

those assembled heroes— renowned and yet tormented by the love-sickness she had aroused in their hearts— were utterly bewildered. Upon beholding her, those kings, their minds captivated by her noble laughter and bashful glances, cast aside their weapons.
Confused, those mounted on elephants, chariots, and horses fell upon the earth under the pretext of departing, as she was offering her own beauty to Hari.
As she thus slowly moved her trembling lotus-buds, she watched for the arrival of the Blessed One.
Pushing aside her curls with the nails of her left hand, she looked at the kings who had arrived with sidelong glances, and then she beheld Acyuta.
While his enemies looked on, Kṛṣṇa carried off that princess as she was attempting to mount her chariot;
having placed her upon the chariot marked with the emblem of Garuḍa, Mādhava, disregarding the circle of kings,
then departed slowly with Balarāma at his head, like Hari taking his share from among jackals.
The proud enemies, headed by Jarāsandha, could not endure that humiliation and the destruction of their fame; they cried out,
"Alas, shame on us, whose wealth was our glory, now snatched away by this wielder of the bow!"
The cowherds were carried off by lions like deer; thus [it was].
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, all of them, highly incensed and clad in armor, mounted their mounts.
Surrounded by their respective forces and wielding their bows, they pursued him. O King, seeing those [demons] attacking, the leaders of the Yādava army stood facing them, twanging their own bows.
Skilled in weapons, they released showers of arrows from the backs of horses, the shoulders of elephants, and the seats of chariots, just as clouds pour down water upon mountains.
Seeing her husband’s army covered by those torrents of arrows, the slender-waisted woman [lamented].
With eyes overwhelmed by fear, she looked at his face with shame;
the Blessed One, smiling, said: "Do not be afraid, O fair-eyed one;
this enemy force shall perish this very moment by your hands."
Unable to endure that prowess of theirs, the heroes Gada, Saṅkarṣaṇa, and the others struck down horses, elephants, and chariots with iron arrows. The heads of the chariot-warriors,
horsemen, and elephant-riders fell upon the earth.
There were millions of heads adorned with earrings, crowns, and turbans;
hands holding swords, maces, and bows; as well as trunks, thighs, feet, and the heads of horses, mules, elephants, camels, donkeys, and mortals.
Their armies being slaughtered by the Vṛṣṇis who were desirous of victory,
the kings, led by Jarāsaṃdha, turned their backs and fled;
they approached Śiśupāla, who was as distressed as one whose wife had been carried off.
With their splendor vanished, their enthusiasm gone, and their faces parched, they spoke:
"O tiger among men, O King, cast off this despondency;
the ultimate certainty regarding what is pleasant and unpleasant is not seen among embodied beings."
Just as a wooden puppet woman is made to dance by the will of a magician,
so too this [individual soul], dependent on the Lord, strives for pleasure and pain.
For seventeen days, indeed, he was defeated in battles by Śauri.
With twenty-three armies, I conquered a single supreme foe;
nevertheless, I neither grieve nor rejoice at any time,
knowing that the world is driven away by Time joined with Destiny.
Even now, we who are all leaders of the hosts of heroes have been defeated by the insignificant Yadus protected by Kṛṣṇa;
our enemies have triumphed while Time follows its own course.
"Then we shall be victorious when the time is favorable.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus enlightened by his friends, the King of Cedi departed for his city with his followers.
Those kings who remained after the slaughter returned each to their own city.
But the powerful Rukmī, hating Kṛṣṇa, could not endure his sister’s marriage to a Rākṣasa;
surrounded by an akṣauhiṇī of troops, he pursued Kṛṣṇa from behind.
Rukmin, indignant and highly agitated, while all the kings were listening,
the mighty-armed one, clad in armor and equipped with his bow, made this vow:
"Without slaying Kṛṣṇa in battle and without bringing back Rukmiṇī..."
"I shall not enter Kuṇḍina; I tell you this as the truth.
Having spoken thus, he mounted his chariot and quickly said to the charioteer:
"Drive the horses to where Kṛṣṇa is; there let my battle take place."
Today, with my sharpened arrows, I shall destroy the pride of prowess of that evil-minded cowherd by whom my sister was forcibly abducted;
he is a fool who boasts while ignorant of the true measure of the Lord.
With a single chariot, he called out to Govinda, "Stay! Stay!
Then, drawing his bow very firmly, he struck Kṛṣṇa with three arrows and said, "Wait a moment here, you disgrace of the Yadu clan!"
"O crow, where will you go after stealing my sister like a sacrificial oblation?
O dull-witted one, today I shall take away the pride of you, a deceitful and treacherous warrior—
before you lie slain by my arrows, release my daughter!"
Smiling, Kṛṣṇa cut the bow and pierced Rukmin with six arrows;
he struck the four horses with eight, the charioteer with two, and the banner with three.
Taking up another bow, Rukmin pierced Kṛṣṇa with five arrows.
Struck by those showers of arrows, Acyuta cut down his bow; the Imperishable One took up another, and he too he severed.
[The opponent then took up] a club, a sharp-edged spear, a trident, a shield, a sword, a javelin, and a lance.
Whatever weapon he took up, Hari cut all of that to pieces.
Then, leaping down from his chariot with sword in hand and desiring to kill,
he rushed at Kṛṣṇa in fury like a moth toward a flame.
As he was rushing forward, [Kṛṣṇa] cut his sword and shield into pieces as small as sesame seeds with his arrows;
then, intent on slaying Rukmin, he took up a sharp sword. Seeing his brother’s attempt to kill him, Rukmiṇī was overwhelmed with fear.
Falling at her husband’s feet,
the virtuous Śrī Rukmiṇī spoke piteously:
“O Lord of Yoga, O immeasurable Soul, O God of gods, O Lord of the universe!
"O mighty-armed one, O auspicious one, you ought not to kill my brother.
Śrī Śuka said:
With her limbs trembling from terror and her throat choked with grief as her mouth was parched, she spoke thus.
Taking hold of his feet, the compassionate Lord returned, while he wore a golden garland that had slipped from his neck due to his dejection.
Binding that evildoer with a cloth, He disfigured him by shaving off his beard and hair.
Meanwhile, the heroic Yadus crushed the wondrous enemy army, just as elephants trample a lotus pond.
Approaching the presence of Kṛṣṇa, they saw Rukmī there in such a state,
nearly dead. Seeing him thus, the all-pervading Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa,
out of compassion, released the bound Kṛṣṇa and spoke to him.
"O Kṛṣṇa, this which you have done is improper and loathsome to us:
the shaving of your beard and hair, your disfigurement, and the slaughter of a friend. Do not be envious of us because of your brother's disfigurement."
There is no one else who bestows happiness or suffering, since a person experiences the fruits of his own actions.
Even a kinsman guilty of a crime deserving death does not merit execution by a kinsman;
he has already been destroyed by his own fault—why should he be slain again?
This is the duty of Kṣatriyas ordained by Prajāpati;
for it is more terrible than that by which even a brother might slay his own brother—
[the duty] regarding kingdom, land, wealth, women, honor, and splendor.
Out of pride or for some other reason, those blinded by the intoxication of wealth indeed revile You;
for this is the perverse intellect of the ill-disposed toward all beings, that like an ignorant man, You consider what is always harmful to Your friends to be beneficial.

The delusion of selfhood in men arises through the divine illusory power (māyā) regarding those who identify the body as the self— thinking, "This one is a friend," "That one is an enemy," and "This one is neutral. For there is indeed only one Supreme Self for all embodied beings.
Just as light and the sky are perceived as manifold by the deluded,
so too this body— composed of material elements, vital breaths, and qualities, and subject to birth and death—
is superimposed upon the Self through ignorance, causing the embodied soul to wander in saṃsāra.
There is no conjunction or disjunction of the Self with anything else, for it exists as that which is real;
this is established by its being the cause of such perceptions, just as the sun is known through its light and form.
Birth and other such states belong only to the body; they never pertain to the Self.
Just as there is no death for the moon other than its phases, nor is there a dark new-moon day (kuhū) apart from them;
so too, just as one lying down experiences oneself, sense objects,
and their fruits even though those objects are unreal, in that same way the ignorant man attains worldly existence (bhava).
"Therefore, O lady of pure smiles, having dispelled with the knowledge of reality this grief born of ignorance— which withers and deludes the self— be established in your own true state.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus enlightened by the Lord Rāma,
the slender lady cast off her despondency and steadied her mind through her intellect.
Her strength and luster destroyed by her enemies, she was left with nothing but her life-breath remaining.
Remembering the disfigurement [of his son] and with his own desires frustrated,
he built a great city named Bhojakaṭa for his residence.
Having failed to kill Kṛṣṇa and having failed to bring back his younger sister, the evil-minded one remained there.

Having declared, "I will not enter Kuṇḍina," the Blessed One dwelt there in anger. O best of the Kurus, having thus defeated the rulers of the earth, he brought the daughter of Bhīṣmaka to his city and married her according to the prescribed rites.
O King, at that time there was a great festival in every house throughout the city of the Yadus for those whose devotion was directed solely toward Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Yadus;
both men and women were joyful, adorned with polished jewel-earrings.
They presented wedding gifts for the two bridegrooms who were dressed in variegated garments;
that city of the Vṛṣṇis was adorned with raised Indra-banners and archways featuring wonderful garlands, cloths, and jewels.
At every gate it shone with auspicious objects arranged there—
full water-jars, incense of aguru, and lamps—
while the paths were sprinkled by rutting elephants who called out to their beloved kings.
Adorned with plantains and betel-nut trees brushed by elephants at the gates,
the Kurus, Sṛñjayas, Kaikeyas, Vidarbhas, Yadus,
and Kuntis rejoiced together as they ran about in excitement.
Having heard the account of the abduction of Rukmiṇī being sung here and there,
the kings and princesses were filled with great wonder. O King, in Dvārakā, the inhabitants of the city experienced immense joy.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī, united with Rukmiṇī and Ramā,
Śrī Śuka said:
Kāma, who is a portion of Vāsudeva, had previously been burnt by the wrath of Rudra.
In order to obtain a body once more, he entered into that very same [seed] again; he was born of the princess of Vidarbha from the potency of Kṛṣṇa,
renowned as Pradyumna, who was in every way not inferior to his father.
Śambara, who could assume any form at will, having abducted that infant less than ten days old,
recognized him as his enemy and cast him into the ocean, departing for his own home. A powerful fish swallowed him along with others.
Encircled by a great net and captured by fishermen,
they brought him as a gift to Śambara. Having led this wonder to the kitchen, the cooks cut it with a sharp knife.
Having seen the child within her womb, they reported it to Māyāvatī;
Nārada then related everything to her, whose mind was filled with doubt—
the truth concerning the child’s birth and his entry into the belly of the fish.
And she was the illustrious Rati, the wife of Kāma;
awaiting the rebirth of her husband whose body had been consumed by fire,
she was appointed by Śambara to prepare rice for the cook.
Perceiving the child to be Kāmadeva himself, he then felt affection for that infant. In no long time, that son of Kṛṣṇa attained full youth and,
while the women gazed upon him, aroused their amorous agitation.

She, Rati, approached her husband—who had eyes as broad as lotus petals, long arms, and was the most beautiful in the world of men—approaching him with love and amorous gestures, while her eyebrows were raised with a bashful smile, O dear one. Then the Blessed Lord, the son of Kṛṣṇā, said to her: "O Mother, your mind is directed elsewhere."
"Having transgressed the conduct due to a mother, you behave like a lustful woman.
Rati said:
"You are the son of Nārāyaṇa, who was carried away from your home by Śambara."
"I am your authorized wife, Rati, and you, O Lord, are Kāma.
This demon Śambara cast you into the ocean before ten days had passed;
a fish swallowed you, and from its belly you have now been recovered, O Lord."

Slay this one, O invincible one—this enemy of yours who is difficult to overcome and who knows a hundred illusions; slay him with your own illusions, such as those that cause delusion. Your mother grieves for you like a female osprey whose offspring has perished.
Distraught with affection for her son, wretched and as distressed as a cow deprived of her calf,
Māyāvatī spoke thus and bestowed upon the high-souled Pradyumna the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*), which destroys all illusions.
He approached Śambara and challenged him to combat;
casting insults at him that were difficult to endure, he stirred up strife.
Thus reviled by those harsh words, he was like a serpent struck by a foot.
With mace in hand, his eyes copper-red with indignation, he rushed forth;
brandishing his mace with speed, he hurled it at the high-souled Pradyumna and let out a roar as harsh as the crash of a thunderbolt.

O King, as that mace was falling upon him, the blessed Pradyumna, filled with rage, warded off the opponent's mace with his own and hurled it back at the enemy. He, for his part, resorted to the illusory power of the Daityas, as shown by Maya.
The asura, stationed in the sky, released a rain consisting of missiles upon the son of Kṛṣṇa;
being thus afflicted by that shower of missiles, the great chariot-warrior, the son of Rukmiṇī,
[invoked] the Great Knowledge (Mahā-vidyā) whose nature is pure goodness (sattva), which crushes all illusions.
Then the Daitya unleashed hundreds of Guhyakas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasīs; the son of Kṛṣṇa (Pradyumna) destroyed them all.
Raising his sharp sword, he [struck] him who was wearing a crown and earrings.
By his power, he severed from Śambara’s body the head, which had a copper-colored beard;
while being showered with heaps of flowers by the gods in heaven who were offering praises,
he was led through the sky by his wife, who traveled through the air, to his city.

O King, like a flash of lightning entering a cloud, he entered the excellent inner apartments crowded with hundreds of women along with his wife. Seeing him, dark as a rain-cloud and clad in yellow silk garments, [the women were filled with wonder].
Seeing Kṛṣṇa with long arms, copper-colored eyes, a beautiful smile,
and a lovely face, his lotus-like countenance adorned by dark, curling locks of hair,
the women were overcome with bashfulness and hid themselves here and there.
Having observed the women with a slight, slow, and somewhat embarrassed air,
they approached, joyful and greatly amazed, along with their jewel among women.
Then, seated there, was the princess of Vidarbha, whose eyes reached to her ears and who spoke so sweetly.
Her breasts overflowing with milk from maternal affection, she did not remember her lost son and wondered:

"Who indeed is this man, a jewel among men? To whom does he belong, or by whom was this lotus-eyed one carried in her womb? And who is she by whom he was obtained, or by whom was she herself obtained?"
"My own son was also lost, having been taken from the maternity chamber;
if a boy of similar age and appearance is alive somewhere,
how has he attained such a resemblance to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow?"
"By his form, limbs, gait, voice, smile, and glances,
he must surely be that very child who was held by me in my womb;
for my affection for him is great, and my left arm throbs."
While Vaidarbhī was thus deliberating, the son of Devakī,
the Lord of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka), arrived at the home of Devakī and Ānakadundubhi.
Although the Blessed One, Janārdana, already knew the matter, he remained silent.
Nārada related everything, beginning with the abduction of Śambara;
having heard that great wonder, the women of Kṛṣṇa’s inner apartments rejoiced as if he had returned from the dead after many years of being lost.
Devakī and Vasudeva, as well as Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and the women—
those two couples and Rukmiṇī— embraced him and attained great joy.
Upon hearing that Pradyumna had returned from being lost, the inhabitants of Dvārakā rejoiced.

"Aha! By good fortune, the boy has returned as if from the dead! they cried out in joy, for his mothers—whose own husbands were like fathers to him—had repeatedly served him with feelings of intimacy rooted in secret passion.
It is not at all surprising that the eyes should be drawn toward the reflection of the form of the Abode of Ramā;
how much less so toward Kāma, the object of memory, or other women?
Śrī Śuka said:
Having committed an offense, Satrājit himself offered his own daughter to Kṛṣṇa along with the Syamantaka jewel. Śrī Rājā said:
O brāhmaṇa, what did Satrājit do that he incurred the enmity of Kṛṣṇa?
From where did he obtain the Syamantaka jewel, and for what reason was his daughter given to Hari?
Śrī Śuka said:
Sūrya was the supreme friend of his devotee Satrājit;
being pleased with him, he gave him the Syamantaka jewel, and he was well-pleased with it.
Wearing that jewel upon his neck, he shone like the sun.
O King, having entered Dvārakā, he was not perceived because of his splendor.
Seeing him from afar, their vision stolen by that brilliance, the people,
suspecting it to be the sun, informed the Lord who was playing with dice.
O Nārāyaṇa, homage be unto you, O wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace;
O Dāmodara, O lotus-eyed one, O Govinda, O delight of the Yadus!
O Lord of the world, here comes the sun, desiring to behold you.
Stealing away the eyes of men with his wheel-like rays,

the sun of fierce heat indeed searches for your path throughout the three worlds, O bull among the gods; yet now, O Lord, having learned that you are hidden among the Yadus, the Unborn One comes to see you.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard the words of the child, the lotus-eyed Lord laughed and said,
"O Satrājit, this is not the sun-god shining with his jewel."
Satrājit entered his own opulent home, where auspicious rites had been performed,
and placed the jewel in the temple of the gods along with the brāhmaṇas.
O Lord, day after day, he produced eight bhāras of gold.
Famine, pestilence, calamities, serpents, mental anxieties, diseases, and inauspicious things do not exist where that jewel, when worshipped, resides; nor do deceitful persons exist there.
Once, Śauri (Kṛṣṇa) requested that jewel from someone for the sake of the King of the Yadus.
Desiring wealth and not considering the refusal of his request,
Prasena once fastened that highly radiant jewel around his neck,
mounted his horse, and went out into the forest to hunt deer.

Having killed Prasena along with his horse and snatched the jewel, Keśarī was slain by Jāmbavān as he was entering the mountain, who desired the jewel. He, too, made the jewel a plaything for the Prince within the cave.
Not seeing his brother, his brother Satrājit was consumed with grief;
"My brother has likely been killed by Kṛṣṇa and has gone to the forest wearing the jewel around his neck"— hearing this, the people whispered it from ear to ear.
Having heard that ill repute clinging to himself, the Blessed One set out upon the path of Prasena,
accompanied by the citizens, to wipe it away. Seeing Prasena and his horse slain by a lion in the forest, [he proceeded further].
And the people saw him slain upon the mountain ridge by the bear;
then the Blessed One, leaving his subjects outside, entered alone the terrifying cave of the king of bears, which was shrouded in blinding darkness.
There, seeing that most precious jewel which had been made into a child's toy,
he resolved to seize it and stood near the children.
Seeing that unprecedented man, the nurse cried out as if terrified.
Hearing that, Jāmbavān, the best among the strong, rushed forward in anger;
he fought with that Blessed One, his own master,
thinking him to be an ordinary man, for he was ignorant of his true majesty.
A tumultuous duel took place between the two who were desirous of victory,
fought with weapons, stones, trees, and their arms like two hawks competing for meat; that lasted for twenty-eight days with their mutual blows of the fists.
His limbs and great thighs crushed by the incessant impact of Kṛṣṇa’s fists— hard as the strike of a thunderbolt— day and night without rest,
his strength exhausted and his body perspiring, he spoke to him, utterly amazed.
I know you to be the vital breath, the vigor, the endurance, and the strength of all living beings;
you are Viṣṇu, the ancient Person, the source of all, and the supreme Lord. For you are the creator of the creators of the universe, and that which exists within all created things.
Time is the lord of all that measures, and the Supreme Self is likewise the self of all selves;
yet by the casting of even a slight glance from His eye, with its rising wrath, the ocean— with its agitated crocodiles and whales— was made to reveal its path.
"A bridge has been built, Laṅkā has been illuminated by his own glory,
and the heads of the Rākṣasas, pierced by his arrows, have fallen upon the earth.
Thus spoke Acyuta to the king of the bears, who had gained full knowledge of the situation.
O great king, the Lord, the son of Devakī,
whose eyes are like lotuses, touched that devotee with His auspicious hand and,
out of supreme compassion, spoke to him in a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
"O Lord of Bears, we have come here to this cave for the sake of the jewel;
by means of this jewel, may he wipe away the false accusation against himself.
Having been addressed thus, [the bear] joyfully [gave] his own daughter, the maiden Jāmbavatī.
He offered that jewel to Kṛṣṇa as a mark of honor.
Not seeing the exit of Śauri who had entered the cave,
the people waited for twelve days and, being distressed, returned to their own city.
Having heard that Kṛṣṇa had not emerged from the cave, Queen Devakī, Rukmiṇī, Ānakadundubhi, their friends, and their kinsmen grieved;
and the inhabitants of Dvārakā, being distressed, cursed Satrājit.
They worshipped the goddess Durgā at Candrabhāgā for the sake of attaining Kṛṣṇa.
Through their worship of the Goddess, Hari appeared there with his wife, having granted them their desired blessings and fulfilling their purpose, bringing them great joy.
Having perceived Hṛṣīkeśa, who was like one returning from death,
along with his wife Maṇigrīva, everyone experienced a great festival of joy.
Then, having summoned Satrājit into the assembly hall in the presence of the king, [they spoke].
Having announced his arrival, the Blessed One presented the jewel to him;
and he, overcome with extreme shame, took the gem and, with his face cast downward, went to his home feeling remorse for his own sin.
Reflecting upon that very sin which had overwhelmed him with a powerful agitation, he thought:
"How shall I cleanse the dust from my soul? How may Acyuta be propitiated? What should I do so that it may be well for me, and people do not curse me?"
To that short-sighted, petty, foolish man who is greedy for wealth, I shall give my daughter, a jewel among women, as well as a precious gem.
This is the proper means; there is no other way for his pacification.
Having thus resolved with his intellect, Satrājit himself took up his auspicious daughter and the jewel, and offered them to Kṛṣṇa;
the Blessed One then married that Satyabhāmā according to the prescribed rites.
Though she was entreated by many, she who was endowed with the virtues of good character, beauty, and magnanimity, the Blessed One said: "O King, we do not accept the jewel;
let it remain with you, a devotee of the gods, and we shall likewise partake in its fruit."
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Although Govinda already knew the facts, upon hearing that the Pāṇḍavas had been burned,
he went to the Kurus along with Rāma to perform the funeral rites for Kuntī.
Approaching Bhīṣma, Kṛpa, Vidura, Gāndhārī, and Droṇa,
they both, sharing the same grief, cried out, "Alas, what misery!
O King, having found this opportunity, they spoke to Śatadhanvan.
Why are Akrūra and Kṛtavarman not seized? And why does Satrājit, having promised us this jewel of a maiden, now reject us and give her to Kṛṣṇa— why does he not follow his own brother?
Thus, his mind divided by those two, that most wicked and sinful man, whose life was spent, killed Satrājit while he lay down out of greed,
even as the women cried out and wailed like those who are helpless.
Having killed the animals like a butcher and taken the jewel, he departed.
And Satyabhāmā, seeing her father slain, was overcome with grief;
crying out, "O father! O father! she lamented, "Alas, I am ruined," falling into a state of delusion.
Having cast the dead body into a vat of oil, he went to Hastināpura;
there, he informed Kṛṣṇa, who already knew the facts, of his father’s murder.
O King, having heard that, the two Lords, conforming to the ways of the human world, followed him.
"Alas! What supreme misery is ours! they cried out, shedding tears and lamenting.
Then the Blessed Lord, accompanied by his wife and his elder brother, returned from there to the city and set about slaying Śatadhanvan in order to recover the jewel.
He too, perceiving that [Kṛṣṇa] had made his effort, became afraid and, desiring to save his life, requested Kṛtavarmā for assistance; and he replied:
"I shall not show disrespect toward the two lords, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa."
Who indeed could find peace by practicing wickedness toward those two?
Kaṃsa, along with his followers, has perished because he was deprived of his fortune through hatred for them;
and Jarāsandha has been rendered chariotless after seventeen battles.
Having been rejected, he then requested Akrūra to act as his rear-guard;
he too replied: "What wise man would oppose the power of these two lords, who sportively create, protect, and destroy this universe?"
The deluded creators of the universe do not understand the activity of Him who,
as a seven-year-old child, playfully uprooted a mountain with one hand and held it like a young boy holding a mushroom.
Salutations to that Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa of wondrous deeds;
salutations to the infinite one, the primordial being, the immutable Self.
Having been thus rejected by Him as well, Śatadhanvan [took] the great jewel.
Having placed the horse there, he mounted it and departed; it traveled a hundred *yojanas*.
O King, Rāma and Janārdana, having mounted their chariot bearing the banner of Garuḍa, followed the betrayer of his preceptor on horses of great speed.
In the grove at Mithilā, having released the fallen horse,
Kṛṣṇa also ran after him in fury as he fled on foot; the Lord, likewise on foot, pursued that pedestrian with His sharp-edged discus.
Having severed his head with his discus, he searched the two garments for the jewel.
Having returned without having found the jewel, Kṛṣṇa said to his elder brother:
"Śatadhanu has been slain in vain; the jewel is not there."
Then Balarāma said: "Surely that jewel has been placed with some man by Śatadhanvan; go to the city and search for it.
As for me, I wish to see the King of Videha, who is most dear to me."
O King, having spoken thus, the son of Yadu entered Mithilā.
Seeing him, the King of Mithilā rose up suddenly with a joyful heart and honored Him— who was worthy of honor— with offerings according to the prescribed rites.
The Lord dwelt in that city of Mithilā for several years,
honored by the high-souled Janaka, who was filled with affection;
thereafter, at the proper time, Suyodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, learned the art of the mace.
Having arrived at Dvārakā, the all-pervading Lord Keśava, who acts for the benefit of his beloved, informed his dear wife of the death of Śatadhanvan and the failure to recover the jewel.
Thereafter, he indeed caused the funeral rites for his deceased kinsman to be performed.
Together with his friends, the Blessed One performed whatever rites were necessary for the journey; meanwhile,
having heard of the slaughter of Śatadhanu,
Akrūra and Kṛtavarman, trembling with fear, fled from Dvārakā, the very cause of their departure.
While Akrūra was away, misfortunes indeed befell the inhabitants of Dvārakā—
bodily afflictions, mental agonies, and frequent calamities caused by gods and elemental forces.
Thus some teachers point out, having forgotten what was previously stated.
"How could an ill omen have occurred in the abode of the sage's dwelling?
While the god did not send rain, the Lord of Kāśī gave his daughter Gāndinī to Śvaphalka who had arrived there; thereafter, it rained upon the land of Kāśī."
"His son was Akrūra, who possessed such power that wherever the Lord sent down rain, there were neither calamities nor pestilences.
Having heard these words of the elders, [Uddhava said: "This much alone is not the cause here."
Having reflected thus, Janārdana summoned Akrūra;
and after honoring him, addressing him, and engaging in pleasant conversation,
he who knows the hearts of all spoke with a smile.

"O Lord of Gifts, the illustrious Syamantaka jewel was indeed deposited with you by Śatadhanvan; this has been known to us even before. Since Satrājit is childless, his daughter's sons shall take it."

Having delivered the inheritance, offered the water and rice-balls, and discharged his remaining debts, [the elder brother] nevertheless found it difficult for others to hold; let this jewel remain with you, O lady of virtuous vows.
However, my elder brother does not fully trust me regarding this jewel.
"O illustrious one, show yourself and bring peace to your kinsmen!
Your sacrifices, with their golden altars, continue today without interruption.
Thus entreated by the *sāman* chants, the son of Śvaphalka [offered] the jewel.

Having covered it with his garment and shown the Syamantaka jewel, which possessed a luster equal to the sun, he gave it to his kinsmen to clear his reputation; then the lord, having wiped away the stain from himself by means of the gem, returned it to him once more.
But whoever reads, hears, or remembers this narrative of the Lord Viṣṇu, the Sovereign, which is rich in heroic power, removes sin, and is most auspicious;
Having cast off ill-repute and sin, he attains peace.
Śrī Śuka said:
Once, the Supreme Person (Kṛṣṇa) went to see the Pāṇḍavas who were residing in Indraprastha.
Having gone to Indraprastha, the glorious one, surrounded by Yuyudhāna and others, was seen by the sons of Pṛthā as they arrived; Mukunda, the Lord of all, having come,
the heroes rose up simultaneously, like the vital breaths rising when the chief life-force returns.
Embracing Acyuta, their sins destroyed by contact with his limbs,
those heroes gazed upon his face with its affectionate smile and attained great joy;
they did so after performing the salutation of his feet on behalf of Yudhiṣṭhira and Bhīma.
Then, having embraced Phālguna and being saluted by the two Yamas,
the faultless Draupadī, bashful as a newlywed bride, approached slowly and paid her respects to Kṛṣṇa as he sat upon a supreme seat.
In the same way, Sātyaki, honored and saluted by the sons of Pṛthā, sat down upon a seat;
and others, having been honored, sat around him in attendance. Having approached Pṛthā, he offered his salutations and was embraced by her with eyes moistened by the depth of her affection.
Having inquired after the welfare of his father’s sister along with her daughter-in-law, and having likewise questioned his kinsmen,

he was addressed by her as she remembered those many sufferings and perceived the self as the remover of suffering; her throat was choked and her eyes were filled with tears due to the agitation of her love.
"At that very moment, all was well with us; we were made to have a protector by you.
O Kṛṣṇa, remembering our kinsmen, my brother has been sent by you.
For you, whose self is the friend of the entire universe, there is no delusion regarding self or others."
"Nevertheless, abiding in their hearts, You eternally destroy the afflictions of those who remember You.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Supreme Lord, I do not know what auspicious deed I have failed to perform."
"Difficult to behold even for the masters of yoga, yet seen by us who are of dull intellect"—
thus was the Lord entreated by the King during the months of the rainy season,
bringing joy to the eyes of the inhabitants of Indraprastha.
Once, Vijaya, having mounted his chariot marked with the monkey-banner,
took up the Gāṇḍīva bow and two quivers of inexhaustible arrows;
equipped for battle along with Kṛṣṇa, he set out to roam the great forest.
The slayer of enemy heroes entered that place teeming with many predatory beasts and wild animals;
there he pierced with arrows tigers, boars, buffaloes, ruru deer,
śarabhas, gavayas, rhinoceroses, antelopes, rabbits, and porcupines.
When the auspicious festival day had arrived, the servants led those sacrificial animals to the king.
Meanwhile, overcome by thirst and exhausted, Bibhatsu went to the Yamunā.
Having sipped water there and drunk the pure liquid, the two great chariot-warriors [rested].
The two Kṛṣṇas beheld the maiden of beautiful appearance as she was wandering;
having approached that woman of noble hips, fine teeth,
and lovely face, Phālguna, sent by his friend, questioned that most excellent of women.
"Who are you? To whom do you belong, O lady of beautiful hips? From where have you come, and what do you wish to do?
I think you desire a husband; tell me everything, O beautiful one.
Śrī Kālindī replied:

"I am the daughter of the god Savitṛ, and desiring a husband, I have undertaken supreme austerity for Viṣṇu— the most excellent, the giver of boons. O hero, I choose no other husband than him, the abode of Śrī."
May that Blessed Lord Mukunda, the refuge of the helpless, be pleased with me.
Known as Kālindī, I dwell in the waters of the Yamunā, having constructed a dwelling for myself by my father until the vision of Acyuta.
Thus did Guḍākeśa speak to Vāsudeva; he too, knowing the situation, placed her upon his chariot and approached the King of Dharma.
At that very moment, Kṛṣṇa was commanded by the Pārthas to perform a most wonderful deed.
He had a wonderful city constructed by Viśvakarman;
while residing there, the Blessed One, desiring to do what was pleasing to his own people,
acted as Arjuna’s charioteer in order to give the Khāṇḍava forest to Agni.
O King, Agni, being pleased, gave to Arjuna a bow, white horses, a chariot,
two inexhaustible quivers, and armor impenetrable by weapons.
And Maya, having been rescued from the fire, presented a palace to his friend.
In that place, Duryodhana had experienced the delusion of perceiving water as dry land;
permitted by him and cheered on by his friends,
he returned once more to Dvārakā, surrounded by Sātyaki and others.
Then, during the most auspicious month of Kārttika and under a highly meritorious constellation, he who was the supreme source of blessing for his own people married Kālindī,
bestowing upon them the highest bliss.
[He also took] Vindhyā and Anuvindhyā from Āvanti, who were followers of Duryodhana.
At the *svayaṃvara*, Kṛṣṇa prevented his own sister from being given to him as she was attached to him;
O King, Kṛṣṇa then forcibly carried off Mitravindā, the daughter of his father’s sister Rājādhidevī, while the kings looked on.
In Kośala there was a king named Nagnajit who was exceedingly righteous.
O King, he had a daughter named Satyā, also known as Nāgnajitī.
No kings were able to marry her without first conquering seven bulls.

Hearing that those wicked men— who possessed sharp horns, were extremely difficult to overcome, and could not endure the scent of his prowess— were to be won by a bull, the Blessed Lord, the Master of the Sātvatas,
went to the city of Kauśalya surrounded by a great army.
The lord of Kośala, delighted, honored him with rising from his seat, offering a seat, and other marks of profound respect; being thus welcomed and gratified,
the princess, beholding the desired boon arrived, fell in love with the Lord of Ramā.
"May this fire grant my prayer that he be my husband, provided that the vow I have maintained has been true—
[the vow] whose lotus-feet Śrī, Brahmā,
Śiva, and the world-protectors bear upon their heads."

By what means may that Blessed Lord, who assumed a playful body out of a desire to protect the boundaries established by Himself, be pleased with me? O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the universe, he spoke again regarding how He might be worshipped.
"What little service can I, a mere trifle, perform for You who are filled with the bliss of Your own Self?
Śrī Śuka said:
Having accepted the seat, the Lord, being delighted, spoke to him.
With a voice as deep as a thundercloud, the Blessed Lord, smiling,
spoke to the descendant of Kuru:
"O King, begging is censured by the wise for a noble warrior who abides in his own duty."
Nevertheless, out of a desire for your friendship, I beg you for your daughter; indeed, we do not have to pay a bride-price.
The King said:
O Lord, who else here could be a more suitable suitor for your daughter than you?
"O bull among the Sātvatas, although Śrī dwells eternally upon the body of Him who is the sole abode of all qualities,
we previously made an agreement for the purpose of testing the prowess of men, desiring a bridegroom for our daughter."
"O hero, these seven bulls are difficult to tame and impossible to restrain;
by them, very many princes have been broken with mangled limbs. O delighter of the Yadus, it is only right that they should be subdued by you alone."
"O Lord of Śrī, you are the desired suitor for my daughter.
Having heard these terms, the Lord girded His loins and,
dividing Himself into seven forms, effortlessly subdued them all in play.
Having bound them with ropes, Śauri— whose pride was broken and whose vigor destroyed—
dragged them about as if in play, like a child dragging wooden dolls.
Then, filled with wonder and joy, the king gave his daughter to Kṛṣṇa.
The Lord, the Master, accepted her according to the prescribed rites, as she was a worthy match for him.
And the king’s wives, having obtained Kṛṣṇa as their beloved husband for their daughter,
experienced supreme bliss, and a great festival took place.
Conchs, kettledrums, and large drums resounded, accompanied by songs, instrumental music, and the blessings of the twice-born;
men and women were overjoyed, adorned with fine garments, garlands, and ornaments.
The Lord gave ten thousand cows as a wedding gift.
Three thousand young women, adorned with golden neck-ornaments and fine garments; nine thousand elephants; chariots a hundred times more numerous than the elephants;
horses a hundred times more numerous than the chariots; and men a hundred times more numerous than the horses.
Having placed the royal couple upon the chariot, the King of Kośala, his heart overflowing with affection, escorted them along with a vast army.
Hearing this, the kings blocked the path as he was leading away the maiden.

In former times, their prowess broken by the bulls among the Yadus, those [enemies] were exceedingly difficult to withstand; yet Arjuna, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow who acts for the welfare of his kin, warded off the multitudes of arrows they discharged like a lion driving away small animals.
Having accepted his dowry and returned to Dvārakā with Satyabhāmā,
the Blessed Lord, the bull among the Yadus and son of Devakī, took pleasure with her.
He then married Bhadrā, the daughter of Śrutakīrti and the sister of his father’s paternal aunt.
Kṛṣṇa took as his wives Kaikeyī, who had been given to him by his brothers Santardana and the others,
and Lakṣmaṇā, the daughter of the lord of Madra, who was endowed with auspicious marks;
he alone carried them away at her own choosing, just as Suparṇa carried away the nectar.
Kṛṣṇa had thousands of other wives of this same kind;
having slain Bhauma, he brought those women of beautiful appearance from his confinement.
Śrī Rājā said: How was Bhauma killed by the Blessed One, and by whom were those women [rescued]?
"Tell us this feat of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, by which they were restrained.
Śrī Śuka said:
"By Indra, whose parasol had been taken away and whose kinsman Kuṇḍala had been seized..."
Informed of Bhauma’s activities by the one residing on the stolen mountain of the gods (Indra),
he, mounted upon Garuḍa together with his wife, went toward the city of Prāgjyotiṣa—
a place made difficult of access by mountain fortresses, weapon-fortresses, and the dangers of water, fire, and wind.
He shattered with his mace the mountains and the fortresses protected by weapons that were surrounded on all sides by tens of thousands of Mura’s terrible and firm nooses;
likewise, he destroyed fire, water, and wind with his discus, and the nooses of Mura with his sword.
With the blast of his conch, Gadādhara shattered the fortifications and pierced the hearts and minds of the wise;
having heard the sound of Pāñcajanya, which was as terrifying as the thunderbolt at the end of an eon.
The five-headed Daitya Mura, who had been lying in the water, rose up;

raising his trident, he was difficult to behold, with a fierce luster like the fire of the sun at the end of an eon. As if swallowing the three worlds with his five mouths, he rushed toward the son of Tārkṣya like a serpent.

Brandishing his trident with speed, he hurled it at Garuḍa and roared with his five mouths. Filling heaven and earth, all the directions, the sky, and the great shell of the cosmic egg, that massive weapon fell upon Garuḍa; then Hari, by his power, split it into three pieces with two arrows.
He struck him in the face with arrows, and he too, in his rage, hurled a mace at him.
As that mace came flying toward him in the fray, the elder brother of Gada shattered it into a thousand pieces with his own mace.
Then, as the unconquered one rushed forward with his arms raised, [Balarāma] effortlessly severed his heads with his discus.
Deprived of life, his head severed, he fell into the water like a mountain whose peaks have been lopped off by the splendor of Indra.
His seven sons, distressed by the slaughter of their father and filled with indignation at seeking vengeance, rose up;
they were Tāmra, Antarikṣa, Śravaṇa, and Vibhāvasu.
Vasu, Nabhasvān, Aruṇa, and the seventh,
Pīṭha— placing the commander of the army at their head, they went forth in battle with weapons grasped, dispatched by Bhauma.

Enraged, they discharged arrows, swords, maces, spears, double-edged blades, and tridents at the Unconquerable One; however, the Blessed Lord, whose prowess is unfailing, cut that mass of weapons into pieces as small as sesame seeds with his own arrows and sent those leaders,
headed by Pīṭha, to the abode of Yama.
With his head, thighs, arms, feet,
and armor severed by the discus and arrows of Acyuta, Naraka, the son of the Earth, likewise drove away his own troops.
Seeing him standing upon Garuḍa with his wife, Durmarṣaṇa advanced with elephants born from the ocean, their temples flowing with rut.
Like a dark cloud accompanied by lightning above the sun,
he discharged a *śataghnī* weapon at him,
and all the warriors simultaneously struck him as well.
Then the Lord, the elder brother of Gada,
with sharp, feathered arrows of various plumages, cut down the arms, thighs, heads, necks, and bodies of that earthly army.
At that very moment, O best of the Kurus, Hari destroyed the horses and elephants; and whatever weapons and missiles were discharged by the warriors,
he severed each one individually with three sharp arrows.
Carried by Suparṇa, who struck down the elephants with his two wings, the elephants, being slaughtered by the heavy-bodied bird with its beak, wings, and talons,
fled in distress toward the city; Naraka, however, continued to fight.
Seeing his own army routed and tormented by Garuḍa, Bhauma struck him with a spear; however, because it was repelled like a thunderbolt,
he did not tremble when pierced by it, like an elephant struck by a garland.
With his efforts rendered futile, Bhauma took up a trident to slay Acyuta;
even before he could release it, Hari, while Naraka was mounted upon an elephant, struck off his head with his discus whose rim was as sharp as a razor.
Adorned with earrings and a beautiful crown, he shone brilliantly as he lay fallen upon the earth.
"Ha! Ha! Excellent! cried the sages and the lords of the gods, as they honored Mukunda by scattering flower garlands over him.
Then the Earth approached Kṛṣṇa and [offered] the two earrings.
Upon him, who was radiant with refined gold and jewels, he placed a Vaijayantī forest garland,
as well as a parasol and a great gem belonging to the son of Pracetas.

Then, O King, with palms joined in reverence and a mind inclined toward devotion, the goddess Earth bowed down and praised the Lord of the Universe, who is worshipped by the best of gods. The Earth spoke:

Obeisances to You, O Lord of the lords of gods, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace; obeisances be to You, O Supreme Self, who assumes forms according to the desires of Your devotees. Obeisances to the one whose navel is a lotus; obeisances to the one garlanded with lotuses.
Obeisances to the lotus-eyed one; obeisances to you whose feet are like lotuses. Obeisances to you, the Blessed One, Vāsudeva, Viṣṇu;
obeisances to you, the Supreme Person, the primordial seed, and perfect consciousness.

Obeisances unto You, the unborn progenitor of this universe, the Brahman of infinite power, the Self of the high and the low, the Self of all beings, the Supreme Self. O Lord, as the unborn one desiring to create, You indeed [manifest] the intense [power].
O Lord of the world, You manifest as unconditioned *tamas* for the cessation [of the world], and as *sattva* for its maintenance;
You are Time, Pradhāna, and Puruṣa, the Supreme.
"I am water, light, air, and space; the elements, the gods, the mind, and the senses;
the agent, the Mahat, and all that is moving and unmoving—O Blessed One, this is a delusion regarding You, the non-dual.
This son of his, terrified, has approached Your lotus feet, which remove the suffering of those who seek refuge.
"Protect him; place your lotus-hand upon his head, for it removes all sins.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus entreated by the Earth with words accompanied by devotion, the Blessed One, bowed down by her humility—

Having granted them freedom from fear, Hari entered the palace of Bhauma, which was endowed with every prosperity. There, Hari beheld eleven thousand six hundred maidens of royal lineage who had been brought there by Bhauma after he had overpowered their kings.
Seeing that best of men enter, the women were utterly infatuated;
they chose in their minds their desired husband, who had been brought to them by destiny. "May this man be my husband; may the Creator grant his approval."

Thus, with their hearts fixed on Kṛṣṇa through their devotion, all of them were sent separately to Dvāravatī, dressed in well-cleansed, stainless garments. He dispatched them with human-carriages, great treasuries, chariots, horses, and vast wealth.
Keśava dispatched sixty-four swift, white elephants from the lineage of Airāvata, each possessing four tusks;
having gone to the abode of the lord of the gods, he gave the earrings to Aditi.
Honored by the lord of the thirty gods and by Mahendrāṇī along with her beloved,
and urged by his wife, he uprooted the Pārījāta tree and, having placed it upon Garuḍa,
brought it to the city after defeating the gods led by Indra.
Established as an ornament for the garden of Satyabhāmā’s house,
bees followed from heaven, greedy for its fragrance and nectar;
bowing with the tips of their crowns and touching the feet of Acyuta, the fulfiller of all purposes, they made their request.
"Alas! Siddhārtha is being defeated by this great man; fie on the ignorance and the wealth of the gods!
Then, in a single moment, the imperishable Lord assumed as many forms and took those women as his wives in various houses.
In their homes— which were free from suffering and beyond the reach of logic, and wherein all things were equal and unsurpassed— he remained,
immersed in his own desire, sporting with those women of the *ramā* class, just like any other man performing the duties of a householder.
Thus, having obtained the Lord of Ramā as their husband, those women...
Even Brahmā and the other gods do not know His path,
yet they have joyfully and incessantly followed Him with ever-increasing love,
their laughter, glances, fresh unions, conversations, and shyness all manifesting their devotion.
By rising to meet him, offering a seat, performing worthy worship, cleansing his feet,
providing betel, resting him, fanning him, with fragrant garlands,
by massaging his hair, and by providing a bed and bathing materials;
Even hundreds of female servants performed service for the Lord.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Once, while the Teacher of the World was seated comfortably upon his own couch, [the sages approached him].
The daughter of Bhīṣmaka attended upon her husband with fans along with her female companions.
He who, as the Lord, creates, devours, and protects this universe by his mere sport—
he, the unborn, has indeed been born among the Yadus for the protection of his own laws.
In that inner chamber, which was resplendent with a canopy from which hung shimmering strings of pearls and adorned with lamps made of jewels,
as well as garlands of jasmine flowers humming with swarms of bees;

O King, with the stainless rays of the moon entering through the lattice openings, with the breeze from the Pārijāta grove fragrant with the scent of the garden, and with incense smoke produced from aloe-wood issuing forth from the lattice apertures;
She approached the Lord of the worlds, her husband, as he sat comfortably upon a white couch covered with an excellent rug, which resembled the foam of milk;
she took from the hand of a female companion a fly-whisk with a jeweled handle.

With that [fan], the goddess fanned the Lord and performed service to him; making the sound of her jeweled anklets as she moved toward Acyuta, she shone with her hand holding a fan, while wearing rings and bracelets.

Beholding her, the personified Śrī, whose necklace was reddened by the saffron of her breasts hidden within the hem of her garment, and who wore a most excellent girdle upon her hips, he perceived that she had no other refuge.
To her, whose form was a fitting match for his body assumed in sport,
Hari— pleased and smiling, with locks, earrings, a breast-jewel, and a necklace upon his neck—
spoke the nectar of his radiant smile.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O princess, you have been desired by kings who possess the majesty of the world-protectors—
men of great power, endowed with splendor, and exalted by their beauty, generosity, and strength."
Why did you reject us— those seekers who had arrived, though they were as intoxicated by lust as the King of Cedi and others—
and instead bestow [the hand] upon those unequal to us, sons of our brother and father? O fair-browed one, why did you choose them who, fearing the kings, have fled for refuge to the ocean?

O fair-browed one, women who have taken the path of those men whose hostility has been provoked by the powerful, who have mostly abandoned their royal thrones, and who have entered the world beyond the reach of the visible path, generally fall into despair.
"We are eternally destitute of possessions, and I am dear to those who are destitute. Therefore, O slender-waisted one, the wealthy generally do not worship me.
"For those two [parents], wealth, birth, sovereignty, appearance, and status were equal to their own."
"Marriage and friendship between those who are high and low never occur anywhere.
O daughter of Vidarbha, failing to perceive this and lacking long-term foresight,
you have chosen us— who are devoid of virtues— merely because we were praised by mendicants in vain."
"Therefore, O best of women, accept a bull among Kṣatriyas who is truly worthy of yourself,
by whom you shall obtain your desires made true both in this world and the next.
"The kings headed by the rulers of Cedi, Śālva, Jarāsaṃdha, and Dantavakra..."

"O lady of beautiful thighs, Rukmī, your elder brother, and others likewise hate me; O blessed one, you have been brought here by me to dispel the pride and arrogance of those who are blinded by the intoxication of their own prowess and who seek to diminish my splendor."
"We are indeed indifferent; we have no desire for women, children, or wealth.
We are fulfilled by the attainment of the Self, remaining inactive like a light within our two bodies.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having said this much, the Blessed One, who destroys her pride because she considers herself inseparable from him as if he were her own beloved, ceased speaking.
Thus, the Goddess heard something never before heard— a disagreeable thing— from her own dear Lord, the Master of the Three Worlds.
Hearing this, she became terrified, a trembling arose in her heart, and weeping, she fell into a state of endless anxiety.

With her well-formed feet, whose beauty was the crimson glow of her nails, she scratched the ground; drenching her breasts, which were smeared with saffron, with tears darkened by collyrium, she stood with her face cast down, her speech choked by extreme sorrow.

From her hand, whose grip on the fan had loosened due to bracelets slipping off because her intellect was destroyed by extreme suffering, fear, and grief, the fan fell; and the body of her, whose mind was distraught, suddenly began to faint.
Like a plantain tree shaken by the wind, she scattered her hair;
seeing that, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa, being compassionate, felt pity for his beloved who was unaware of the maturity of her laughter, which was the very bond of her love.
Quickly descending from the couch and raising her up, the four-armed Lord gathered her hair and wiped her face with his lotus-hand;
he wiped away the tears from her eyes and the stains of grief from her breasts.
O King, embracing her with his arm— she who was devoted to no other object—

the Lord, who knows how to offer consolation, compassionately comforted that wretched woman; for he, the refuge of the virtuous, saw that her mind was wandering due to the intensity of her laughter, though she did not deserve such a state.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Princess of Vidarbha, do not be resentful toward me; I know you to be devoted to Me.
O lovely lady, out of a desire to hear your words, I acted thus in jest."
To behold His face, with its lower lip quivering from the intensity of love, its outer corners reddened by side-long glances, and the slopes of His beautiful eyebrows knit together—
this indeed is the supreme gain for householders living in their homes.
"O timid, passionate woman, let us go on our journey with playful jests by means of my beloved.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having been thus consoled by the Blessed One, the princess of Vidarbha...

Having understood those joking words, she abandoned her fear of being separated from her beloved; O descendant of Bharata, looking at the face of the Blessed One, the bull among men, she spoke with a side-glance beautiful and affectionate with a bashful smile.
Śrī Rukmiṇī said:
"O lotus-eyed one, it is indeed as you have said; for you are truly incomparable to the all-pervading Lord.

Where is the Blessed One, the sovereign of the three worlds, who delights in his own glory? And where am I, whose nature is composed of the modes of material nature and whose feet are grasped only by the ignorant?"
O Urukrama, it is true that the Self, who is the mere witness, dwells within the ocean of the material modes as if out of fear of them;
yet You, whose eternal form is manifest, have entered into conflict with the multitude of wretched senses.
The state of kingship, which is blinding darkness, has been cast off by Your servants;
for those sages who relish the nectar of Your lotus feet,
the path is not obscured, whereas it is indeed difficult for beast-like kings to discern.
Since the activity of the Lord is as if supernatural, so too is Your activity, O Infinite One;
and those who follow You are likewise.
Indeed, You are "possessing nothing," for there is nothing that exists apart from You.
To You, whom even the devourers of offerings— beginning with Brahmā—
bring tribute, those who subsist on the vital breaths and are blinded by wealth do not know You to be their own end.
You are the most beloved even of the gods who consume offerings, and they, too, belong to You.

O Lord, you are indeed the embodiment of all human goals and the very essence of the fruit of their attainment; for those wise ones who renounce everything out of desire for you, a gathering of yours is most fitting, O All-pervading One.

O Lord of inconceivable power, you have been chosen by me as the Self and the giver of selfhood to all worlds— He who is not subject to the pleasure and pain of a man and woman in union, and who is praised by sages who have laid aside the rod of punishment.

Having abandoned the blessings of the lotus-born Brahmā and the lords of heaven, which were destroyed by the force of Time set in motion by your eyebrows— O elder brother of Gada, how could others [be spared] from the dullness of speech when even kings [fell]?
Having put them to flight with the sound of Your Śārṅga bow, You seized me,
O Lord, just as a lion seizes his own portion from the herd of animals;
out of fear of them, I have sought refuge in the ocean.
O lotus-eyed one, desiring which Vainya, the crest-jewel of kings, as well as Nāhuṣa, Gaya, and others were born, abandoned their sovereign kingdoms and entered the forest.
Why do they sit here, following your path and yet sinking down? What other refuge could one seek than the fragrance of your lotus feet, which,
made resonant by the prayers of the virtuous, grants liberation to all people?

O Abode of Virtues, disregarding You— the abode of Lakṣmī— the mortal woman whose vision was obscured by material interests chose me, who am a source of great fear; yet I have now sought refuge in You, the Lord of the worlds, who are my worthy match.

May Your feet, which fulfill all desires both in this world and the next, be my refuge as I wander through the cycles of existence; for You indeed come to the aid of one who worships You, granting liberation from falsehood.
O Acyuta, may those kings whom you have designated become her [sons],
yet let them be like donkeys, oxen, dogs, cats, and servants within the houses of women,
such that they do not come near the root of her ear.
Your stories are sung in the assemblies of Śiva and Brahmā;
yet within [this body] is covered by skin, beard, body hair, nails, and head hair,
and filled with flesh, bone, blood, worms, feces, phlegm, bile, and wind.
A woman who does not inhale the nectar of your lotus feet is a deluded one whose mind clings to a corpse while it is still alive;
O lotus-eyed one, let there be for me devotion to your feet.

When you, who find delight in the Self and perceive Me as non-different from it, look upon Me with a mind whose passion has been increased by the means for its own advancement— that indeed is the supreme compassion You have for us.
O Madhusūdana, I do not consider your words to be false;
for it is likely that even a maiden’s mother might occasionally find pleasure [in such things],
and the mind of even a married woman who has become unchaste turns toward ever-new [objects of desire].
"A wise man should not support an unchaste woman; by supporting her, he falls from both worlds.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O princess, you have been deceived by those who desired to hear this virtuous account."

"O beautiful lady, everything that I have spoken which you have repeated is indeed the truth. Whatever desires you wish for me, though I am free from desire, they shall be yours forever, O auspicious one, for you are my exclusive devotee."
O sinless one, I have perceived your love for your husband and your devotion as a faithful wife,
since even when your mind was being shaken by my words, it was not drawn away from me. Those who worship me in the state of a married couple through austerity and the observance of vows—

Those whose souls are possessed by desire, deluded by my *māyā*, O proud lady, do not seek me— the Lord of liberation— once they have attained me; instead, they desire only worldly prosperity and its master.
Those men who do not serve me are unfortunate, for even in hell they find no relief; yet for them, hell is actually a pleasant association because it consists of material objects.
By good fortune, O mistress of the household, you have repeatedly performed service toward me—which liberates one from worldly existence—despite the efforts of the wicked.

O proud lady, I have never seen in my home a devoted wife like you, who at the time of your own wedding— though women who seek only their own lives and indulge in deceit are exceedingly difficult to satisfy and harbor most wicked desires.
Disregarding the kings who had arrived, you sent away my secret messenger, the twice-born, after he had heard my noble discourse;
and you brought about the disfigurement of my brother, who was defeated in battle.
And during the festival of the wedding procession, and likewise at the gambling match,
you did not say anything at all when suffering arose from the fear of separation from us because you could not endure it; by that, we have been conquered by you.
The messenger you dispatched to obtain me was well-instructed in counsel;
yet, finding me delayed, he has concluded this place to be empty and wishes to abandon this body,
which is fit for no other purpose.
"May that remain with you; we rejoice in it.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, through these amorous conversations, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of the Universe, [remained].

Delighting in his own self, Hari, the teacher of the world, took pleasure with Ramā while imitating the ways of the human world; likewise, the Lord remained in the houses of other women as if he were a householder, observing the duties of a married man.
Śrī Śuka said:
Each one of them gave birth to ten sons, who were as excellent as their father in every personal perfection.
Seeing Acyuta standing there, never leaving their home, the princesses each regarded him as her own most beloved; those women did not know his true nature.
He possessed a face like the interior of a beautiful lotus, long arms, and large eyes.

Bewildered by the Lord’s charming speech, which was accompanied by affectionate smiles and glances full of rasa, the women were unable to win over the mind of the all-pervading Blessed One with their own amorous gestures.

His sixteen thousand wives were captivated by the glances of his smiles, which revealed his inner emotions, and by those skilled in the arts of love who employed the secret charms of amorous gestures from his arched eyebrows; they were further pierced by the arrows of the bodiless god of love.
Whose senses they were unable to disturb with their own instruments—
having thus obtained as their husband the Lord of Ramā, those women,
though even Brahmā and the other gods do not know His path.
They attended upon Him with joy, their hearts overflowing with ever-increasing affection,
longing for His fresh union with smiles, glances, and laughter;
they rose to meet Him, offered Him a seat, honored Him with excellent worship, and washed His feet.
With betel, rest, fanning, perfumes, and garlands; with the massaging of hair, providing beds, bathing, and offerings—
even hundreds of maidservants performed service for the Lord.
Of those wives of Kṛṣṇa who were previously mentioned as having ten sons each, eight were his principal queens; I shall now describe their sons, beginning with Pradyumna:
Cārudeṣṇa, Sudeṣṇa, and the heroic Cārudeha.
Sucāru, Cārugupta, and another named Bhadracāru,
as well as Cārucandra, Vicāru, and Cāru as the tenth—
these were the sons born to Rukmiṇī from Hari, none of whom were inferior to their father; Pradyumna was the foremost among them.
Bhānu, Subhānu, Svarbhānu, Prabhānu, Bhānumat, Candrabhānu, Bṛhadbhānu, Atibhānu as the eighth,
Śrībhānu, and Pratibhānu— these were the ten sons of Satyabhāmā.
Sāmba, Sumitra, Purujit, Śatajit, Sahasrajit,
Viyaya, Citraketu, Vasumān, Draviḍa, and Kratu—
these sons of Jāmbavatī, headed by Sāmba, were highly esteemed by their father.
Vīra, Candra, Aśvasena, Citragu, Vegavān, Vṛṣa,
Āma, Śaṅku, Vasu, and the illustrious Kunti were the sons of Nagnajitī.
Śruta, Kavi, Vṛṣa, Vīra, Subāhu, Bhadra, and Ekala [were the sons of Kunti].
Śānti, Darśa, Pūrṇamāsa, and the younger Somaka were born of Kālindī; Praghoṣa, Gātravan, Siṃha, Bala, Prabala,
and Ūrdhaga were the sons of Mādrī, as were Mahāśakti, Sahas, Ojas, and Aparājita.
Vṛka, Harṣa, Anila, Gṛdhra, Vardhana, Unnāda,
Mahāman, Pāvana, Vahni, and Kṣudhi were the sons of Mitravindā;
and Saṅgrāmajit, Bṛhatsena, Śūra, Praharaṇa, and Arijit [were the sons of Satyabhāmā].
Jaya, Subhadra, Vāma, Āyu, and Satyaka were born of Bhadrā;
Dīptimat, Tāmratapta, and others were the sons of Rohiṇī from Hari. From Pradyumna, the mighty Aniruddha was born of Rukmavatī.
O King, in the city of Bhojakaṭa, he begot [sons] upon the daughter of Rukmin named Revatī;
O monarch, these men had sons and grandsons by the millions,
and there were sixteen thousand mothers of those born of Kṛṣṇa’s lineage.
The King said:
How did Rukmī give his daughter to the son of his enemy in battle? Having been humiliated by Kṛṣṇa, he was waiting for an opportunity to kill him.
