O learned one, tell me this: the mutual marriage of the two enemies—
past, future, and present, beyond the reach of the senses, remote, and concealed— for yogis perceive all things perfectly.
Śrī Śuka said:
At the *svayaṃvara*, the God of Love himself, united with his body, was chosen by her;
having defeated the assembled kings in battle from a single chariot, he carried her away.
O King, although Rukmī, having been insulted by Kṛṣṇa, remembered his enmity,
he gave his daughter to his sister’s son, doing what was pleasing to his sister;
for the powerful Rukmī was the son of Kṛtavarman.
He married the large-eyed maiden Cārumatī; indeed, although Rukmī was bound by enmity, he gave his granddaughter Rocanā to Hari’s grandson Aniruddha out of a desire to please his sister.
Knowing that such a marriage was unrighteous, yet bound by the cords of affection for her,
O King, at that auspicious occasion Rukmiṇī, Balarāma, Keśava,
Sāmba, Pradyumna, and the others went to the city of Bhojakaṭa.
When that marriage ceremony had concluded, the arrogant kings, headed by the King of Kaliṅga, said to Rukmī: "O King, defeat Balarāma at dice;
for although he is unskilled at dice, his addiction to it is great."
Thus addressed, Rukmi summoned Balarāma and played dice with him.
There, Rāma took up a stake of a hundred, a thousand, and ten thousand;
however, Rukmi defeated him there, and the King of Kaliṅga laughed at Bala.
Baring his teeth and laughing loudly, Halāyudha could not tolerate that;
then Rukmin took a stake of one hundred thousand, which Balarāma won there.
Resorting to deceit, Rukmin said, "I have won."
Agitated by wrath like the majestic ocean on a full-moon day, his naturally reddish eyes glowing with intense fury, he took up the stake of one hundred million;
yet Rāma, resorting to a trick, defeated him according to the rules of the game.
"Let these judges declare that I have won," Rukmī said;
then a voice from the sky spoke: "The wager has been won by Balarāma alone. By his word alone, according to dharma, Rukmī speaks falsely."
Disregarding her, the King of Vidarbha, impelled by wicked kṣatriyas and driven by fate,
spoke while mocking Saṅkarṣaṇa:
"You cowherds who roam the forest are certainly not experts in dice."
"Kings play with dice, but those like you do not play with arrows.
Thus insulted by Rukmin and mocked by the kings, he became enraged; raising his iron club, he struck him in that assembly of heroes.
Having swiftly seized the King of Kaliṅga at the tenth step, he,
enraged, knocked out his teeth with those very teeth which had been bared in laughter.
Others had their arms, thighs, and heads shattered, and were drenched in blood.
The kings fled in fear, overwhelmed by the force of Balarāma.
When his brother-in-law Rukmī had been slain, Hari said nothing— neither good nor bad—
to Rukmiṇī and her army, O King, out of fear of breaking their affection.

Then, having placed Aniruddha along with Sūryā upon the excellent chariot, Rāma and the other Daśārhas set out from Bhojakaṭa for Kuśasthalī; they had achieved all their goals by taking refuge in Madhusūdana.
The King said:
The best of the Yadus married Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa;
there occurred a great and terrible battle between Hari and Śaṅkara.
O Great Yogin, you ought to relate all of this.
Śrī Śuka said:
Bāṇa was the eldest of the hundred sons of the high-souled Bali,
by whom the earth was given to Hari in the form of Vāmana.
His legitimate son was Bāṇa, who was always devoted to the worship of Śiva;
he was honorable, generous, wise, true to his word, and firm in his vows.
In ancient times, he ruled his kingdom in the beautiful city named Śoṇita-pura.
By the grace of that Śambhu, those immortals, like his servants,
with their thousand arms, delighted Mṛḍa with instrumental music during the Tāṇḍava dance.
The Blessed One, the Lord of all beings, the refuge, and the one who is affectionate toward his devotees—
He invited him to choose a boon, and he chose the lordship of the city.
Once, intoxicated by his own prowess, he touched the lotus-feet of Giriśa, who was seated at his side, with his crown that shone like the sun.
I bow to you, O Great God, the teacher and sovereign lord of the worlds,
the wish-fulfilling tree for men whose desires remain unfulfilled. The thousand arms granted by you have become a supreme burden to me.
"In the three worlds, I find no opponent equal to you except for you;
desiring to fight with my arms itching, I once crushed the elephants of the quarters and the mountains of the first aeon, and they too fled in fear."

Hearing that, the Blessed One became angry and said: "O fool, when your banner is broken, there shall be a battle for you with one equal to me, which will destroy your pride. Having been thus addressed, O King, the evil-minded one entered his own home delighted.
Awaiting the command of Giriśa, that fool awaited the destruction of his own virility.
His daughter, named Uṣā, experienced pleasure in a dream with the son of Pradyumna—a lover she had neither seen nor heard of before. She, the maiden, obtained union with her beloved.
Not seeing him there, she cried out, "Where are you, my beloved? and stood up in the midst of her friends, overwhelmed and deeply ashamed.
Kumbhāṇḍa was the minister of Bāṇa, and Citralekhā was his daughter.
Filled with curiosity, her friend asked her companion Ūṣā:
"O fair-browed one, whom do you seek? What is your desire? O princess, even now I do not perceive that your hand has been taken in marriage."
In a dream, I saw a certain man who was dark-complexioned with lotus-like eyes,
wearing yellow garments and possessing long arms— he who captivates the hearts of women.
Having made him drink the honey of my lips, I now seek that beloved.
"Where has he gone, having cast me, who yearned for him, into the ocean of misery?
Citralekhā said:
"I shall remove your distress, if such a person exists within the three worlds."
"I shall bring him who is the captor of your heart;
point out that boon," having said this, he drew forth the gods, gandharvas, siddhas, cāraṇas, pannagas,
daityas, vidyādharas, yakṣas, and humans as they appeared.
Among men, she depicted the Vṛṣṇis and the heroic Ānakadundubhi;
but seeing Pradyumna, she was ashamed and drew him.
Seeing Aniruddha already drawn, Uṣā lowered her face in modesty.
"Is it he? Is it he? she asked with a smile, O Lord of the Earth.
Recognizing him as the grandson of Kṛṣṇa, the yoginī Citralekhā traveled through the air, O King, to Dvārakā, which was protected by Kṛṣṇa.
There, having taken the son of Pradyumna— who was lying on a beautiful couch— as he remained absorbed in yoga,
she showed her beloved to her friends in Śoṇitapura.
And she, beholding that most handsome youth, had a face radiant with joy.
In her own home, which was difficult for men to behold, she took delight with the son of Pradyumna;
honored by him with service through most excellent garments, garlands, perfumes, incense, lamps, seats, and the like,
as well as drinks, foods, and delicacies, and through his words.
Hidden in the maidens' quarters, his senses captivated by that *ūṣā* whose affection for him had constantly increased, he did not perceive the passing days.
Thus she was enjoyed by the hero of the Yadus, her vow having been violated.
They pointed out with reasons that were difficult to refute how she had been enjoyed;
the soldiers reported, "O King, we have observed the conduct of your daughter, which brings disgrace upon the family."
"O Lord, we know of no defilement by men of our daughter— who is difficult even for us to behold— while she was protected in her home by us who never leave her side.
Thereupon, Bāṇa was deeply distressed upon hearing of the alleged defilement of his daughter.
Hurrying, he reached the maidens' quarters and beheld the leader of the Yadus—
the son of Kāma, the sole beauty of the world, dark-complexioned, clad in saffron garments, with eyes like lotuses,
long arms, and a face adorned by the luster of his earrings and locks of hair as well as by his smiling gaze.

Seeing him playing with dice with his beloved, who was full of joy, wearing a garland of jasmine flowers and saffron from her breasts clinging to his limbs, and seated before her with his arms resting upon it— Mādhava beheld him having entered [the hall], surrounded by soldiers and troops of assassins.
Raising his iron club made of *maurva* wood, he stood like Death himself with staff in hand, desiring to slay them;
just as a leader of a herd of boars strikes dogs that approach from all sides seeking to seize him, so did he strike them.
Being thus slaughtered, they fled from the palace with their heads, thighs, and arms shattered.
The powerful son of Bali, enraged, bound him with serpent-nooses as he was slaughtering his own army.
Hearing that he was bound, Ūṣā, overwhelmed by intense grief and despair, her eyes filled with tears, began to wail.
Śrī Śuka said:
O descendant of Bharata, as they did not see Aniruddha nor his kinsmen,
and as they grieved for them, four months of the rainy season passed away.
Having heard from Nārada that news of their imprisonment and the deeds performed [by the enemy], they were filled with concern.
The Vṛṣṇis, who had Kṛṣṇa as their sole deity, set out for Śoṇitapura;
Pradyumna, Yuyudhāna, Gada, Sāmba, and Sāraṇa,
along with Nanda, Upananda, Bhadra, and others, followed in the wake of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
Accompanied by twelve akṣauhiṇīs, those bulls among the Sātvatas surrounded Bāṇapura from every direction on all sides,
while the city’s gardens, walls, watchtowers, and gateways were being shattered.
Beholding them, the Lord Rudra, filled with wrath, set out with his equal army; for the sake of Bāṇa, he went forth surrounded by his sons and the Pramathas,
and having mounted his bull Nandin, he fought against Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
O King, there occurred a most tumultuous, wonderful, and hair-raising battle between Kṛṣṇa and Śaṅkara, as well as between Pradyumna and Guha; furthermore,
there was a combat between Kumbhāṇḍa and Kūpakarṇa on one side and Bala on the other.

Brahmā and the other lords of the gods, the sages, the Siddhas and Cāraṇas, the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Yakṣas came in their celestial chariots to witness the battle between Sāmba and Bāṇa, the son of Bāṇa, as well as that of Sātyaki.
Śauri [assailed] the followers of Śaṅkara— the *bhūtas*, *pramathas*, and *guhyakas*—
as well as the *ḍākinīs*, *yātudhānas*, *vetālas*, and *vināyakas*; and the *pretas*, *mātṛs*, *piśācas*, *kuṣmāṇḍas*, and *brahmarākṣasas*.
He caused [the enemy] to flee with sharp-pointed arrows discharged from his Śārṅga bow;
he employed various kinds of Piṇāka weapons against the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
but the wielder of the Śārṅga, remaining unperturbed, neutralized them with counter-weapons.
Having neutralized Brahmā’s weapon with his own Brahmā-weapon, the mountain-born weapon with the Vāyavya-weapon,
the Pārjanya-weapon with the Āgneya-weapon, and his own weapon with the Pāśupata-weapon,
he caused Giriśa to yawn by means of the Jṛmbhaṇa-weapon.
Śauri slew Bāṇa’s army with his sword,
mace, and arrows; while being afflicted on all sides by Pradyumna’s showers of shafts, Skanda, shedding blood from his limbs, fled from the battlefield on his peacock.
Kumbhāṇḍa and Kūpakarṇa fell down, struck by the club;
their armies, deprived of their leaders, fled in every direction.
Seeing his own forces being shattered, Bāṇa became exceedingly enraged.
In the battle, the chariot-warrior Bāṇa, intoxicated with the pride of combat, abandoned Satyaki and rushed toward Kṛṣṇa;
drawing his bows simultaneously, he fixed five hundred arrows upon each one,
two shafts at a time.
The Blessed Hari, the subduer of enemies, simultaneously severed those bows;
having slain the charioteer, the chariot, and the horses, he blew his conch shell.
His mother, named Koṭarā, stood there naked with her hair disheveled.
He stood before Kṛṣṇa, desiring to protect the life of his son.
Then the elder brother of Gada, turning his face away and not looking at the naked woman, remained there;
meanwhile, Bāṇa, deprived of his chariot and with his bow shattered, entered the city.
When the hosts of spirits had been put to flight, the three-headed and three-legged Jvara rushed toward the descendant of Daśārha as if burning the ten directions.
Then the divine Nārāyaṇa, seeing him, discharged [his own] Jvara.
The two fevers, one belonging to Maheśvara and the other to Viṣṇu, fought with each other.
Oppressed by force by the fever of Viṣṇu, the fever of Maheśvara cried out for help; finding no refuge elsewhere, the fever of Maheśvara was filled with fear.
Seeking refuge, with palms joined in reverence, he praised Hṛṣīkeśa.
Jvara said:
"I bow to You, the Supreme Lord of infinite power, the Self of all, the absolute, pure consciousness alone."
That which is the cause of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe—that Brahman, whose mark is Brahman, who is perfectly tranquil;
time, destiny, action, the individual soul, inherent nature, the material substance, the field, the vital breath, the self, and transformation;
the collection thereof, the continuous flow like the sprouting of seeds—this is Your illusory power (māyā). I take refuge in the negation of that.
Through various manifestations assumed merely as sport, You sustain the gods, the virtuous, and the bridges of the worlds;
You destroy those who follow the wrong path by acting with violence. This birth of Yours is for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth.
I am tormented by Your unbearable, fierce, and exceedingly violent heat, like a fever that is both pacifying and agonizing.
"Embodied beings suffer as long as they do not serve the root of my feet, being bound by their desires.
The Blessed Lord said:
"I am pleased with you, O Three-headed one; let the fear of my fever depart from you."
"He who remembers our conversation shall have no fear from you. Having been addressed thus, the fever of Maheśvara bowed to Acyuta and departed;
Bāṇa, however, mounted his chariot and went forth to fight Janārdana.
Then, O King, the Asura, wielding various weapons with his thousand arms,
being extremely enraged, discharged arrows at the wielder of the discus.
As he repeatedly loosed those missiles, [the Lord] cut them down with his discus, which had a razor-sharp rim.
The Blessed One cut off Bāṇa’s arms like the branches of a great tree. While his arms were being severed, Lord Bhava,
who is compassionate toward his devotees, approached the one whose weapon is the discus and spoke to him.
Śrī Rudra said:
You are indeed the supreme Brahman, the light hidden within the Brahman consisting of speech;
whom those of pure self perceive as absolute, like the ether.
The sky is His navel, fire His mouth, water His seed,
heaven His head, the quarters His hearing, the earth His feet,
the moon His mind, and the sun His eye. He is the Self.
I am his ocean, and the lord of serpents is his belly;
the medicinal herbs are his body hairs, the clouds are his hair, Viriñca is his intellect, and the creative emission is his generative organ.
Dharma is the heart of you who are Prajāpati; indeed, you are that Supreme Person who manifests as the world.
This incarnation of yours, O Lord of unimpeded splendor, is for the protection of Dharma and for the welfare of the universe.
And all of us, empowered by you, perceive the seven worlds;

yet you alone are the primordial Person, without a second, the Fourth State, self-perceiving, the causeless cause, and the Lord. Nevertheless, for the sake of manifesting all qualities, you appear through your own *māyā* according to various transformations.
Just as the sun, though veiled by its own shadow,
illuminates both that shadow and all forms,
even so do You, though veiled by the *guṇas*, illuminate the *guṇas* themselves.
O Infinite One, those who possess qualities take You as their own lamp;
yet those whose intellects are deluded by Your māyā, being attached to children, wives, homes, and the like, rise and sink within the ocean of suffering.

Having obtained this human world bestowed by the gods, he who does not honor Your feet because his senses are unsubdued is indeed to be pitied, for he is a deceiver of himself. That mortal who abandons You— his own self, his beloved, and his Lord— is lost.
Having abandoned the nectar of immortality, he eats poison for the sake of sense-objects that lead to perverted ends.
I, Brahmā, the gods, and the sages of pure heart,
have surrendered with our whole being to You— the Self, the Beloved Lord.

To You, the cause of the world’s maintenance, its arising, and its end; who are impartial, perfectly tranquil, the friend, the self, and the deity; who are non-dual, the one, and the banner of the world-soul—[I bow].
"Let us worship the Lord for the sake of liberation from worldly existence.
O Lord, this one is my beloved, dear to me, and obedient; I have granted him freedom from fear. May that favor of yours be bestowed upon him, just as you have shown favor to the lord of the Daityas."
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Blessed One, as you have spoken, we shall do what is pleasing to you;
whatever resolve you have made is well approved by me."
"This asura, the son of Virocana, is not to be slain even by me;
a boon was granted to Prahlāda that no descendant of yours shall be killed by me.
His arms were severed by me only to subdue his pride."
The vast army has been destroyed, as well as that which was a burden to the earth;
his four remaining arms shall belong to you, and this asura, a chief among your attendants, shall be free from old age and death, having no fear from any quarter.
Having thus obtained assurance from Kṛṣṇa, the Asura bowed his head to him,
placed the son of Pradyumna upon his chariot along with his bride, and brought them forward surrounded by an akṣauhiṇī army and well-adorned with fine garments.
Placing him and his wife at the forefront, he departed, cheered by Rudra,
toward his own capital city, which was beautifully adorned with banners,
archways, and whose streets and squares were sprinkled with water.

Accompanied by the sounds of conchs, cymbals, and drums, he entered [the city] while being welcomed by the citizens, friends, and the twice-born. He who thus [describes] the victory of Kṛṣṇa and the battle with Śaṅkara—
Whoever remembers this upon rising in the morning shall suffer no defeat.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
O King, once the young princes of the Yadu clan went to a grove.
While Sāmba, Pradyumna, Cārubhānu, Gada, and the others were wandering about for recreation, they played there for a very long time; then, becoming thirsty while searching for water,
they saw a wondrous being in a well that was devoid of water.
Seeing the lizard, which resembled a mountain, their minds were filled with wonder;
moved by compassion, they made an effort to lift it up. Binding the fallen creature with leather and woven ropes, the children [tried to pull it out].
Unable to pull it out, they anxiously informed Kṛṣṇa.
Then the lotus-eyed Lord, the creator of the universe, arrived there and,
having looked at it, playfully uprooted it with his left hand.
Touched by the hand of the Lord of Excellent Renown, he immediately cast off his form as a chameleon;
possessing the beautiful color of refined gold and adorned with celestial ornaments, garments, and garlands, he became a denizen of heaven.
Although he was already wise, Mukunda questioned him in order to proclaim the cause of this transformation among the people.

"Who are you, O highly fortunate one, of most excellent form? I certainly count you as the best of gods. By what karma have you been brought to this state, O most auspicious one, though you do not deserve it? Tell us who desire to know, since you consider it appropriate for us to hear."
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus questioned by Kṛṣṇa, whose form is infinite,
the king prostrated before Mādhava with his crown, which shone like the sun, and spoke.
Nṛga said:
"O Lord, I am the king named Nṛga, the son of Ikṣvāku;
if, while the names of donors were being proclaimed, I touched your ear."
O Lord, what indeed could remain unknown to you, the witness of the self of all beings, whose vision is unimpeded by time? Nevertheless, at your command, I shall speak.
As many as there are grains of sand upon the earth, and as many as there are stars in the sky—
I gave away as many cows as there were drops of rain— milch cows, young, endowed with good character, beauty, and virtues, tawny-colored with horns like gold,
acquired by righteous means, with hooves like silver, accompanied by their calves, and adorned with fine garments, garlands, and ornaments.

I gave to those bulls among the twice-born— youths who were well-adorned, endowed with virtue and good character, maintaining their families, devoted to truth and vows, and distinguished by austerity, sacred learning, and generosity—
the gifts of cows, land, gold, dwellings, horses, elephants, maidens with female slaves, sesame seeds, silver, and beds.

Garments, jewels, furnishings, chariots, and whatever was desired—sacrifices performed and works of public charity—I offered these to a certain eminent brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, a cow belonging to someone else had strayed into my herd; not realizing it was another's, I gave that cow to the twice-born man.
As she was being led away, her owner saw her and said, "She is mine! To him, the one who had taken her claimed, "She is mine; Nṛga gave her to me.
The two Brahmins, disputing over me while seeking their own interests, spoke thus.

"Upon hearing that you are both the giver and the taker, a delusion arose within me. Having thus entreated both brahmins who were in a state of moral distress, he said, "I shall give a hundred thousand excellent cows; let this [cow] be returned."
"May you both show favor to me, your servant who lacks understanding; lift me up from this misery as I fall into the impure hell.
"O King, I do not accept [this]," the Master said, and departed.
"I do not desire even ten thousand other cows," said another, and he departed.
In the meantime, I was led by messengers of Yama to the abode of Yama. There, questioned by Yama, I spoke, O God of gods, Lord of the universe:
"O King, shall you first experience the inauspicious or the auspicious?
"I do not see an end to this gift of merit; it is like the light of the world.
"Then, O King, experience the inauspicious first," he said, and he fell.

O Lord Keśava, while falling, I then beheld myself as a chameleon; yet even now, the memory of Your servant— who is devoted to the brāhmaṇas and generous— does not fade, for I am still longing for a vision of You.
O Lord, how have You— the Supreme Self,
the Master of Yoga, who is to be contemplated by the pure hearts of those who see through the Vedas—
come directly before my eyes, O Adhokṣaja, for me whose intellect is blinded by great calamities?
O God of gods,
Lord of the universe, Govinda, Supreme Person,
Nārāyaṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, O Puṇyaśloka, Acyuta, and Immutable One— may You be my refuge here, for through You alone comes liberation from worldly existence.

"O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord, grant me leave as I depart for the destination of the gods; wherever my mind may go, may it remain fixed upon Your feet. Salutations to You, the Supreme Brahman, who exists in all beings and possesses infinite power."
"Obeisance to Kṛṣṇa, Vāsudeva, the Lord of yogas.
Having spoken thus, he circumambulated Him, touched His feet with his crown, and,
being permitted by Him, ascended a preeminent celestial chariot while the people looked on.
The Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, whose very nature is righteousness and who is the deity of the brāhmaṇas, spoke to his attendants while instructing the kṣatriyas:
"Alas, the property of a brāhmaṇa is difficult to digest; even a small amount consumed by fire [would burn it]."
How much less so for kings who consider themselves lords?
I do not consider even the *hālāhala* poison to be truly poisonous, for that has a remedy;
however, the property of a Brahmin is said to be a poison for which there is no countermeasure on earth.
Poison kills the one who consumes it, and fire is extinguished by water;

yet the fire of the sacrificial wood used for a Brahmin’s property burns the entire family to its roots. Property belonging to a Brahmin, when consumed without his permission, destroys three generations of descendants.

Those kings who, blinded by royal opulence, forcibly consume [the property of others] by power— those fools who consider the wealth of a brāhmaṇa as their own prize— do not perceive their own downfall into hell, which includes ten preceding and ten succeeding generations.
For as many grains of dust as fall from the tears of weeping brahmins who have been deprived of their livelihoods— those generous householders—
for that many years shall kings and members of royal families remain unrestrained.
Those who steal the property of Brahmins are cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hells.
Furthermore, he who seizes the livelihood of a Brahmin— whether given by himself or by another—
is born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years.
"May I not possess the wealth of the Brahmins, for by coveting it men become short-lived,
defeated, fallen from their kingdoms, and turn into harmful serpents who cause distress.
O my followers, do not bear malice even toward a Brahmin who has committed an offense."
Always offer obeisances to one who strikes you or reviles you,
just as I, being composed, regularly bow down to the brāhmaṇas;
and you too should do so, for he who acts otherwise incurs my punishment.
"For the property of a Brāhmaṇa, when stolen, casts the thief down into the depths—
even if he was unaware of it, just as the Brāhmaṇa's cow did to Nṛga.
Having thus proclaimed this to the inhabitants of Dvārakā, the Blessed Lord Mukunda [departed].
The purifier of all the worlds entered his own palace.
Śrī Śuka said:
O best of the Kurus, the Lord Balabhadra mounted His chariot.
Longing to see his friends, he set out for Nanda’s Gokula;
there he was embraced by the cowherds and cowherd women who had longed for him,
and Rāma, having saluted his parents, was greeted with their blessings.
"O descendant of Daśārha, Lord of the universe, protect us for a long time along with your younger brothers!
Having thus placed him on their laps and embraced him, they bathed him with tears from their eyes.
And he, having been saluted according to tradition by the elder cowherds with their youngest members, [honored them in return].
Then, according to their respective ages, friendships, and relationships with Him,
the cowherds approached the Lord— who was resting comfortably and seated at ease— and having come near, they questioned Him with laughter, hand-holding, and other such gestures.
Having been asked about their well-being by Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes are like lotus petals, they— having surrendered all their wealth and success to him— replied with voices faltering with love:
"O Rāma, are all our kinsmen faring well?"
"O Rāma, do you remember us, along with our wives and sons?
By good fortune the wicked Kaṃsa has been slain; by good fortune our friends have been liberated;
and by good fortune, having struck down and conquered our enemies, we have taken refuge in this fortress."
The cowherd women, filled with joy at the sight of Rāma, asked him while smiling:
"Is Kṛṣṇa, who is beloved by the women of the city, living happily?
Does he perhaps remember his kinsmen, his father, and his mother?"
Will he, the mighty-armed one, come even once to see his mother? Or will he remember us and his service to her?
[He remembers] his mother, father, brothers, husbands, sons, and sisters as well.
O Lord, O descendant of Daśārha, for whose sake we have abandoned our own kin who are so difficult to give up—
having severed our affection, he has now departed, abandoning us instantly.
How indeed could such a person not believe the words spoken by women?
How indeed could wise women accept the words of one whose mind is unstable and who is ungrateful?
They surely accept the words of that handsome man of variegated speech—
"O cowherd girls, whose passion is awakened by His smiling glances, tell us other stories; what is the use of talking about Him?
If time passes for Him even without us, it passes for us in the same way."

Remembering Śauri’s laughter, his charming speech, his beautiful glances, his gait, and his affectionate embraces, the women wept. Saṅkarṣaṇa [comforted] them with Kṛṣṇa’s messages that reached their hearts.
The Blessed One, who was skilled in various forms of conciliation, comforted them;
he dwelt there for two months, in Madhu and Mādhava,
while the Blessed Lord Rāma brought delight to the gopīs during the nights.

In the grove of the Yamunā, which was polished by the digits of the full moon and scented by the breeze carrying the fragrance of *kaumudī* flowers, He took His pleasure, surrounded and served by throngs of women;
meanwhile, the goddess Vāruṇī, sent by Varuṇa, emerged from the hollow of a tree.
As it fell, it perfumed that entire forest with its own fragrance.
Balarāma, having smelled that scent of the honey-stream brought by the wind,
approached that place and drank from it together with his women.
Being sung to by Gandharvas within a circle beautified by women,
he took delight like the lordly elephant of Indra amidst a herd of female elephants;
drums resounded in the sky and flowers rained down with joy.
Then the Gandharvas and sages praised Balarāma with hymns of his heroic deeds.
Halāyudha, his exploits being sung by women,
wandered through the forests, intoxicated and with eyes rolling in exhilaration.
Wearing a garland and a single earring, intoxicated by the Vaijayantī wreath,
and bearing a smiling lotus-face adorned with drops of perspiration like frost,
that Lord summoned the Yamunā for the sake of sporting in the water.
Disregarding his own words, thinking "I am intoxicated," the powerful Balarāma, provoked to anger, dragged with the tip of his plow the river Yamunā who had not yet arrived,
saying: "O sinful one, since you did not come when summoned by me, having shown me contempt!"
"I shall drag you, who wander at will, across [the earth] in a hundred pieces with the tip of my plow!
Thus rebuked, O King, Yamunā became terrified; trembling, she fell at the feet of the joy of the Yadus and spoke these words.
"O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, I did not know your prowess,
you by whose single portion this world is sustained, O Lord of the universe!
O Blessed One, [forgive] me, who was ignorant of the supreme nature of the Lord."
"O Soul of the Universe, O lover of Your devotees, You ought to release her who has sought refuge in You.
Thereupon, having been entreated, the Blessed Lord Balarāma released the Yamunā;
He plunged into the water with the women, like a lordly elephant with his female elephants.
Having sported as she desired, Kānti gave a garland of auspicious beauty to her who had emerged from the water and was dressed in the sky;
she then put on two blue garments and fastened a golden necklace.
O King, even today that elephant of Indra, beautifully adorned and smeared with ichor, is seen along the path drawn by the Yamunā;
it truly seems to manifest the prowess of Balarāma, whose valor is infinite.
In this way, as Rāma’s mind was captivated by the sweetness of the women of Vraja, all the nights passed for him as if they were but one while he took his delight in Vraja. Śrī Śuka said:
When Rāma had gone to Nanda’s cowherd settlement, O King,
the ignorant ruler of Karūṣa sent a messenger to Kṛṣṇa,
saying: "You are Vāsudeva, the Blessed Lord, the Master of the Universe who has descended [to earth]."

Thus incited by the children, the foolish Menā considered herself infallible; like a child-like king made by children, that dull-witted man dispatched a messenger to Kṛṣṇa, whose path is unmanifest, in Dvārakā.
The messenger, having arrived at Dvārakā, spoke the king’s message to the Lord Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes were like lotus petals, as he sat in the assembly hall:
"I, Vāsudeva, have descended alone; there is no other."

Out of compassion for all living beings, you must abandon your false pretensions. O Sātvata, cast off these emblems of ours which you wear out of delusion; come to me for refuge, or else give me battle.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard that boast of the dull-witted Pauṇḍraka,
Ugrasena and the other members of the assembly then laughed loudly.
The Blessed One spoke to the messenger in response to his joking words:
"O fool, I shall cast off those marks by which you thus boast;
O ignorant one, having covered that face, you shall be surrounded by herons, vultures, and crows."
"You shall lie there slain; you will become a refuge for dogs.
Thus the messenger delivered this entire rebuke to his master. Kṛṣṇa, having mounted his chariot, then proceeded toward Kāśī.
Pauṇḍraka, a great chariot-warrior, having learned of that effort,
quickly marched out from the city accompanied by two *akṣauhiṇīs*.
O King, the lord of Kāśī, his friend, followed as a rear-guard ally.
With three akṣauhiṇī divisions, Hari beheld Pauṇḍraka, who bore the conch, discus, sword, mace, and the Śārṅga bow, was marked with the Śrīvatsa and other signs,
wore the Kaustubha gem, and was adorned with a forest garland.
Seeing him wearing two yellow silken garments, bearing the banner of Garuḍa,
adorned with priceless crest-jewels and shimmering crocodile-shaped earrings,
and having assumed an artificial appearance identical to his own— *BhP 10.66.014–015*
Just as Hari laughed heartily at an actor on the stage, his enemies struck Hari with spears,
clubs, iron maces, javelins, double-edged swords, darts, lances, axes,
and arrows.
But Kṛṣṇa violently struck down the army of Pauṇḍraka and the King of Kāśī— consisting of elephants, chariots, horses, and foot soldiers— with his mace, sword, discus, and arrows.

Just as at the end of a yuga the consumer of oblations [fire] devours all creatures separately, so did that battlefield shine— strewn with chariots, horses, elephants, lions, donkeys, and camels mangled by the enemy— as a source of joy for the wise and a fierce playground for the Lord of Beings.
Then Śauri said to Pauṇḍraka: "O Pauṇḍraka, those weapons which you spoke of to me through the words of your messenger, I shall discharge them at you;
and I shall cause you to relinquish that name which you have falsely assumed, O fool."
"I seek refuge in you today, if I do not desire further combat. Having thus spoken, and having deprived Pauṇḍraka of his chariot with sharp arrows,
he severed his head with his discus, as Indra [severs] the peak of a mountain with his thunderbolt.
Likewise, having severed the head from the body of the Lord of Kāśī with his feathered arrows,
he caused it to fall upon the city of Kāśī, like the wind scattering a lotus bud.
Thus, Hari slew the envious Pauṇḍraka along with his companions.
Entering Dvārakā while the perfected ones (*siddhas*) sang the nectar of his stories, he—
whose every bond was eternally destroyed by meditation on the Lord,
O King— bore the very form of Hari and became absorbed in Him.

Seeing the head with its earrings fallen at the king’s gate, the people wondered, "What is this? Whose face is it? Having learned that it was the head of the King of Kāśī, the queens, sons, and kinsmen [gathered].
And the citizens, O King, cried out, "Alas! Alas! Our protector is slain!
Sudakṣiṇa, his son, having performed the funeral rites for his father, vowed: "Having slain the slayer of my father, I shall pay him due honor."
Having thus resolved within himself, he, along with his preceptor, worshipped Maheśvara with excellent sacrificial fees and supreme concentration.
Pleased by this, the omnipresent Lord, in the sacred field of Avimukta, granted him a boon.

He chose as his desired boon the means for the slaughter of his father’s killer: "Serve the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire together with Brahmins acting as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) according to the ritual of *abhicāra*; and let that fire be surrounded by the *pramatha* demons."
"Employed against one who is unrighteous (abrahmaṇya), he will accomplish his resolve. Having been thus instructed, the practitioner performed the malevolent rite (*abhicāra*) against Kṛṣṇa.
Thereupon, Fire arose from the sacrificial pit in a personified form, most terrifying.
With his hair and beard glowing like heated copper, his eyes emitting sparks of charcoal,

his fierce fangs bared, his eyebrows knitted into a staff-like frown, and his mouth cruel, he licked the corners of his lips with his own tongue; naked, he brandished his three-pointed flaming trident.
With his feet, which were as large as palm trees, shaking the surface of the earth,
he rushed toward Dvārakā, surrounded by spirits and scorching the directions.
As he approached, burning with the fire of his malevolent magic, the inhabitants of Dvārakā—
Beholding him, they all collapsed like deer in a forest fire;
overcome with fear as the Blessed One was playing with dice in the assembly hall, they cried:
"Save us! Save us, O Lord of the three worlds, from the fire that is burning the city!"

Having heard that distress of the people and seeing the trepidation of his own followers, the Lord, the refuge of all, laughed and said, "Do not fear; I am your protector. The omnipresent witness of the interior and exterior of everything [neutralized] the sorcery of Maheśvara.
Having understood this, for the purpose of thwarting it, he commanded the discus standing at his side.
That Sudarśana, resembling ten million suns, blazing with the splendor of the fire of universal dissolution,
then scorched the sky, the quarters, heaven and earth, and the fire itself with its own brilliance— Mukunda’s weapon, the Discus.
O King, that *kṛtyā* fire, its power neutralized by the energy of the weapon of the Discus-wielder,
retreated with its face shattered;
having reached Vārāṇasī, it approached Sudakṣiṇa.
The malevolent incantation performed by him consumed the people along with the officiating priests;
and the discus of Viṣṇu entered Vārāṇasī, which was filled with marketplaces, assembly halls,
and temples, crowded with gate-towers, watchtowers, and storehouses, and abounding in treasuries, elephants, horses, chariots, food, and grain.

Having burned the entire city of Vārāṇasī, Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana discus returned once more to the side of Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless. Any mortal who causes others to hear this account of the prowess of the Lord of Excellent Fame [attains the highest goal].
Or, being composed in meditation, one who hears [this] is liberated from all sins.
The King said: I desire to hear further of Rāma, whose deeds are wonderful.
Regarding what else the Lord of the infinite and immeasurable did,
Śrī Śuka said:
There was a certain monkey named Dvivida who was a friend of Naraka.
Then that powerful monkey, the minister of Sugrīva and brother of Mainda,
seeking to repay his friend’s kindness, set fire to cities, villages, mines, and cowherd settlements, causing a general upheaval throughout the kingdom.
In some places, uprooting mountains, he pulverized the lands with them—
especially the Ānarta region where Hari, the slayer of Mura, resided.
In other places, standing in the midst of the ocean, he lifted its waters up with his two arms.
Possessing the strength of ten thousand elephants, he submerged entire regions along the coastal shores;
having broken the trees of the hermitages of the foremost sages,
that wicked one defiled the sacrificial fires with his excrement and urine.
Arrogant, he cast men and women into mountain caves and valleys and covered them with boulders, like a weaver trapping a worm in its cocoon;
thus he oppressed the lands and corrupted the wives of noble families.
Having heard that most charming song, he went to Mount Raivataka;
there he beheld Rāma, the lord of the Yadus, wearing a garland of lotuses,
his every limb beautiful to behold, standing in the midst of a throng of women.
Having drunk the wine of Varuṇa, his eyes were unsteady with intoxication as he sang;
his body was radiant, like an elephant in rut.
A wicked monkey, perched upon a branch, shook the trees.
Displaying himself, he made a "kilakila" sound;
seeing the audacity of that monkey, the young wives of Baladeva— naturally fickle and fond of laughter— burst into laughter.
The monkey [Hanumān] treated them with contempt by raising his eyebrows and turning his face away,
while showing his own anus to them as he was being watched by Rāma;
then Balarāma, the best among strikers, became enraged and struck him with a stone.
Having deceived the pressing-stone, the monkey took the jar of wine and, laughing, playfully tossed it about while provoking his anger; then,
having shattered the jar, the wicked one forcefully struck at his garments.
Having treated them with contempt, the powerful one, arrogant with pride, acted perversely. Seeing his insolence and the lands afflicted by him,
the enraged [Lord] took up his mace and plow, desiring to slay the enemy.
The immensely powerful Dvivida, having raised a śāla tree with his hand,
approached with speed and struck Balarāma on the head with it;
but Saṅkarṣaṇa, like a mountain, [received] him as he fell upon his head.
The powerful one received him and struck him with Sunanda;
with his brain crushed by the club, he shone with a stream of blood like a mountain with red chalk after a blow, unconcerned by the injury.
Again, having hurled another [missile] and stripped it of its feathers by his might, Balarāma, highly incensed, struck him with it; but he cut that one into a hundred pieces.
Then, with yet another, he struck him in anger, and he too he cut into a hundred pieces.
Thus fighting with the Lord, who repeatedly broke him again and again,
he dragged trees from all sides and made the forest treeless. Then,
filled with indignation, he released a rain of rocks upon Balarāma.
The wielder of the club effortlessly pulverized all of that with ease.
Then the lord of monkeys, clenching his palm-tree-like arms into fists,
approached the son of Rohiṇī and crushed his chest with them.
The lord of the Yādavas also, casting aside the club and the plow with his two arms, struck him in the collarbone in a rage; he fell down vomiting blood.
As he fell, the mountain shook along with its peaks and its forest trees.
O tiger among the Kurus, Parvata was carried away by the wind like a boat upon the waters;
meanwhile, in the sky, there arose the sounds of "Victory!", "Obeisances!", and "Well done! Well done!
from the gods, Siddhas, and lords of sages who were showering flowers.
Having thus slain Dvivida, who brought calamity upon the world,
the Blessed One entered His own city while being praised by the people.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī and conqueror in assembly, abducted Duryodhana’s daughter Lakṣmaṇā while she was at her *svayaṃvara*. Enraged, the Kauravas said, "This boy is ill-mannered."
"Having disregarded our daughter who was unwilling, he has carried her off by force.
Bind this ill-behaved man! What can the Vṛṣṇis do? They enjoy the earth which was given to us and increased through our favor."
"If the Vṛṣṇis hear that their son has been captured and come here,
they will become humble and attain peace, like vital breaths well-restrained when their pride is broken.
Thus spoke Karṇa, Śala, Bhūri, Yajñaketu, and Suyodhana.
Encouraged by the elders of the Kurus, they began to fight with Sāmba.
Seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra pursuing him, the great chariot-warrior Sāmba took up his beautiful bow and stood alone like a lion.

Desirous of seizing him and shouting "Stay! Stay!", those angry archers, led by Karṇa, approached and overwhelmed him with their arrows. Thus was that joy of the Yadus struck down by the Kurus, O best of the Kurus.
The inconceivable child could not tolerate that, like a lion toward small animals;
brandishing his beautiful bow,
the hero pierced all six car-warriors, beginning with Karṇa, simultaneously and individually with as many arrows.
With four [arrows] they struck his four horses, and with one each they struck the charioteers and the great archer who was the car-warrior; they thus honored that feat of his.
But those four [archers] deprived him of his chariot by striking his four horses.
One struck down his charioteer, while another cut his bow;
having bound him and deprived him of his chariot in battle, the victorious Kurus entered their own city with the prince and his daughter amidst great difficulty.
Having heard that which was spoken by Nārada, O King, they became filled with wrath;
urged on by Ugrasena, they made preparations against the Kurus. But Rāma, having consoled those preeminent Vṛṣṇis who were already equipped for battle, [restrained them].
He who removes the impurity of the Kali age did not desire strife between the Kurus and the Vṛṣṇis;
he departed for Hastināpura by means of a chariot with the splendor of the sun,
surrounded by Brahmins and family elders like the moon by the planets.
Having gone to Hastināpura, Rāma stationed himself in the outer grove and sent Uddhava to Dhṛtarāṣṭra out of a desire to know his intentions.
He [Uddhava], having paid homage to the son of Ambikā (Dhṛtarāṣṭra), as well as to Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Bāhlīka...
And he spoke to Duryodhana according to the prescribed rites regarding Rāma’s arrival.
Hearing that their dearest friend Rāma had arrived, they were exceedingly joyful;
having honored him, they all went out to meet him with auspicious offerings in their hands.
Having approached him according to the prescribed rule, they offered him a cow and the guest-offering (arghya).
Among them, those who knew his power bowed their heads to Balarāma.
Having heard that their kinsmen were well, and having inquired after their welfare and health, [he greeted them].
Then Rāma spoke these words without hesitation to one another:
"Having heard with undistracted minds what Ugrasena, the lord of the earth and your sovereign master, has commanded, carry it out without delay."
"Since you many have, by unrighteous means, bound this single righteous man after defeating him, I nevertheless forgive that act out of a desire for the unity of my kinsmen.
These words were consistent with his own power, swelling with heroism, valor, and strength.
Hearing this from Baladeva, the Kurus became enraged and said:
"Aha! This is a great marvel brought about by the course of time, which is so difficult to overcome—that a mere sandal indeed seeks to ascend the head adorned with a crown!"
These Vṛṣṇis, bound by kinship through marriage and sharing our beds, seats, and meals, have been elevated to equality with us, having been granted royal thrones by us.
They were provided with yak-tail whisks, a conch shell, and a white parasol.
He uses our crown, throne, and bed out of disregard for us;
enough of these royal insignia for the Yadus, who are like nectar to those who oppose their benefactor, as it is to serpents!
Alas, the Yādavas, who were once nurtured by our favor, now issue commands today, devoid of shame.
"How could even Indra seize what was not given by the Kurus— by Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Arjuna, and the others— any more than a jackal might take prey from the jaws of a lion?
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
O bull among the Bharatas, those vulgar men, their pride swollen by the wealth of their kinsmen,
having shouted foul and indecent words at Rāma, entered the city. Having seen the depravity of the Kurus and heard their unspeakable insults, Acyuta—
Uttering these words, agitated by anger, difficult to look upon, and laughing repeatedly, he said:
"Surely the wicked, puffed up with various kinds of pride, do not desire peace;
for them, punishment is the means of pacification, just as a club is for cattle."
"Aha! Having gradually pacified the highly agitated Yadus and the enraged Kṛṣṇa, I have come here desiring peace for them. Yet these wretched ones are dull-witted and take delight in quarreling."

Disregarding me, those arrogant men repeatedly spoke these harsh words: "Ugrasena is certainly no lord; he is merely the chief of the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas, whose commands even Indra and the other world-protectors obey."
He by whom the Sudharmā hall is entered and the celestial tree Pārijāta is brought and enjoyed— he indeed is not worthy of a formal seat.
He whose pair of feet the Goddess Śrī herself, the sovereign of all, directly serves.
Indeed, that Lord of Śrī does not deserve the royal paraphernalia of a human king,
for the dust of His lotus feet is held upon the finest crowns by all the guardians of the worlds and is the most sacred of all holy places.
Brahmā, Śiva, and I myself are but portions of his portion;
and we, along with Lakṣmī, bear his royal throne for a long time— where indeed could the Vṛṣṇis enjoy this fragment of earth given by the Kurus?
"We are merely sandals, while you are the heads yourselves"—
alas, who could endure such harsh and incoherent words from those intoxicated by power, like madmen full of pride? Who indeed would instruct them?
Filled with indignation, thinking, "Today I shall rid the earth of the Kauravas," he rose up grasping his plow as if burning the three worlds;
with the tip of his plow, he tore open the city named after the elephant.
Enraged and intending to strike, he dragged [the city] into the Gaṅgā;
seeing the city falling into the Gaṅgā like a tossing boat,
the Kauravas were seized with alarm.
Desiring to live, they went for refuge to Him alone, together with their families;
placing Sāmba and Lakṣmaṇa at their head, they stood before the Lord with palms joined in reverence.
"O Rāma, O Rāma, support of all! We do not know Your true power."
O Lord, you ought to forgive the transgression of us fools who possess perverted intellects.
You alone are the supportless cause of the maintenance, creation, and dissolution of the worlds;
for they say that the worlds are playthings for you as you sport.

O Infinite One, O thousand-headed one, you alone support this circle of the earth upon your head through your divine play; and at the end, having withdrawn the universe into your own self, you remain as the non-dual, solitary remainder. Your anger is for the sake of instructing all beings, not out of hatred nor out of envy.
O Blessed One, you who uphold the quality of goodness (*sattva*) and are intent upon the preservation of the world;
obeisance to You, the Self of all beings, the imperishable wielder of all powers! O Architect of the Universe, let there be obeisance to You; we have come to You for refuge.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus propitiated by those who had surrendered, who were agitated and trembling with tearful eyes, Balarāma was well-pleased and granted them fearlessness, saying, "Do not fear."
Duryodhana gave as a dowry sixty-year-old elephants, twelve hundred thousand horses,
and six thousand gold chariots possessing the brilliance of the sun.
The Lord, the bull among the Sātvatas, being affectionate toward his daughter, accepted all of that— including a thousand maidservants with golden necklaces—
and departed together with his son, his daughter-in-law, and his friends, who greeted him with joy.
Then Halāyudha entered his own city and,
having met with his kinsmen whose hearts were full of affection, he related everything concerning the leaders of the Yadus.
In the midst of the assembly hall among the Kurus, his own deeds [were recounted];
even today, this city, rising high to the south of the Gaṅgā, clearly indicates the prowess of Rāma.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard that Naraka had been slain and that Kṛṣṇa alone had married so many women, Nārada desired to witness that.

"How wonderful! How is it that with a single body he simultaneously and separately married sixteen thousand women in their respective homes? Thus filled with curiosity, the celestial sage came to Dvāravatī to see for himself.
It resounded with the songs of flocks of birds in the flowering groves and gardens;
its lakes were strewn with blooming blue lotuses, day-lotuses, white lilies,
and water-lilies, and were filled with the loud cries of swans and cranes.
It was graced with nine hundred thousand palaces made of crystal and silver,
resembling great emeralds and adorned with gold and jewels;
it was beautiful with its well-divided streets, roads, crossroads, marketplaces, halls, assembly houses, and temples.
Its paths, courtyards, streets, and thresholds were sprinkled with water, and the heat was warded off by fluttering banners and flags.
Within it stood the magnificent inner apartments, honored by the lords of all the celestial realms,
wherein the artisan Tvaṣṭṛ had displayed his craftsmanship in its entirety for the sake of Hari.
There, he entered the great residence of the wives of Śauri, which was adorned with sixteen thousand mansions and supported by pillars of coral and excellent slabs of lapis lazuli.
With walls made of sapphire and a floor of unblemished luster, with canopies fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ from which hung strings of pearls,
and with seats and couches made of ivory and adorned with the finest jewels.
O dear one, it was adorned by female servants wearing golden neck-chains and fine garments,
and by men clad in tunics, turbans, excellent clothes, jewels, and earrings;
the darkness was dispelled by the radiance of clusters of gem-lamps upon the variegated gables where peacocks perched.
Where, seeing Him emerging with His eyes [anointed] by the thick smoke of burning aloe-wood incense, they dance while shouting out, mistaking Him for a rain cloud;
in that place, together with His wife— who was accompanied by thousands of maidservants of equal virtue, beauty, age, and attire— He sported at every moment.
The brahmin saw the Lord of the Sātvatas being fanned with a yak-tail whisk having a golden handle;
beholding him, the Blessed One’s splendor suddenly arose.
Descending from his couch, he who is the most excellent among all upholders of dharma bowed his head, adorned with a crown, at the pair of feet [of the Lord] and,
with palms joined in reverence, took his place upon his own seat.
Having washed his feet, he took that water upon his own head;
for even though he is the greatest teacher of the universe and the Lord of the virtuous,
the title "God of the Brahmanas" (Brahmaṇyadeva) is truly appropriate for him according to his qualities.

Having worshipped that very one— the foremost of gods and sages— according to the prescribed rite, the ancient sage Nārāyaṇa, the friend of Nara, [honored] his very foot-wash water, which is the source of all sacred fords.
Having addressed him with measured, nectar-like, and sweet speech, he said: "O Lord, what may we do for the Blessed One?
Śrī Nārada said:
O All-pervading Lord, Master of all the worlds, it is not at all surprising that you show friendship toward all people and exercise restraint over the wicked;
for this serves the ultimate welfare of the world through the preservation of its stability.

O Lord of wide renown, through Your own incarnation, we have clearly perceived Your pair of feet, which grant liberation to all people and are meditated upon in the hearts of Brahmā and others of unfathomable wisdom.

"Contemplating him as the support for crossing over the pit of saṃsāra, I wander; please favor me so that my remembrance [of you] may remain. Then, that Nārada entered another house, the home of Kṛṣṇa’s wife.

O dear one, having been honored with supreme devotion through rising to greet him, offering a seat, and other such services, [Nārada] beheld the Lord of the lords of yoga playing at dice there with his beloved, Uddhava, out of a desire to manifest his *yoga-māyā*.
He was questioned by one who was ignorant, as it were: "When did you arrive?
"What indeed can be done by those like us, who are incomplete, for those who are already complete?
Nevertheless, O Brāhmaṇa, tell us; make this birth of ours auspicious."
Filled with wonder, he rose and went silently to another house;
there too he beheld Govinda fondling his infant sons.
Then, in yet another house, he saw him making preparations for bathing.
He saw him offering oblations into the sacrificial fires arranged for the ritual, performing the five great sacrifices (*pañcamakha*),
feeding the twice-born, and in another place eating the remnants; in yet another place he saw him seated at the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*), muttering prayers with his speech restrained.
In one place he saw the elder brother of Gada moving about with sword and shield on the paths of the swordsmen; elsewhere he saw him wandering among horses, elephants, and chariots;
and in another place he saw him reclining on a couch while being praised by bards.
In one place he was consulting with his ministers, such as Uddhava and others; in another, he was engaged in water-sports surrounded by the women of the harem;
and elsewhere, he was bestowing well-adorned cows upon the foremost of the twice-born.

Sometimes he was listening to the Itihāsas and Purāṇas and auspicious hymns; sometimes he was laughing with his beloved at home during a humorous conversation; and sometimes he was practicing virtue, wealth, and pleasure in various places.

Somewhere Keśava was seen meditating alone while seated, beyond the reach of material nature; elsewhere he was serving his elders with devotion, desires, enjoyments, and worship; and in another place he was making war with some and peace with others.
In another place, he was with Rāma contemplating the welfare of the virtuous,

considering at the proper time the marriage of his sons and daughters to suitable spouses according to the injunctions, providing them with brides and bridegrooms of equal status along with abundant riches.
Having witnessed the great festivals for the departure and initiation of his children—
festivals at which the worlds were filled with wonder— the Lord of the masters of yoga was seen by some performing sacrifices to all the gods with magnificent rites.

In one place, he was fulfilling his religious duties through the construction of ponds, gardens, and monasteries; in another, having mounted a Sindhu-bred horse, he was hunting deer fit for sacrifice,
surrounded by the foremost of the Yadus.

Seeing the Lord of Yoga moving about in various places— among the inner apartments, the palace, and other locations— disguised by unmanifest signs within those various conditions, Nārada, desiring to know His true nature, then spoke to Hṛṣīkeśa as if smiling.

Having observed the manifestation of Your yogic power (yoga-māyā) in the manner of one who has assumed human form, we now understand that Your yogic power is difficult to perceive even for masters of illusion; yet, O Soul of the Lord of Yoga, it has become manifest through our service to Your feet.
"O Lord, grant me permission; I shall wander through the worlds drenched in Your glory, singing aloud of Your pastimes that purify the universe. The Blessed Lord said:
"O Brahmin, I am the speaker of dharma, its performer, and its approver;
I abide in this world teaching it to people—my son, do not grieve.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, as he was practicing the purifying duties of householders,
she beheld him alone, present in every house,
for that was the great manifestation of the yoga-māyā of Kṛṣṇa of infinite prowess.
Having gazed upon him again and again, the sage was struck with wonder and filled with curiosity.
Thus, having been properly honored by Kṛṣṇa— who, though his soul was devoted to the goals of wealth, desire, and duty— was pleased and departed while constantly remembering Him alone.
Thus, following the path of humanity, Nārāyaṇa, who has assumed His potencies for the sake of the world's manifestation,

took delight, O dear one, among sixteen thousand excellent women, who were filled with bashfulness, affectionate glances, and laughter— He who is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.
O dear one, he who sings of, hears, or approves of the deeds of Hari— which have no other object—
will surely possess devotion for the Blessed One, the path to liberation.
Śrī Śuka said: Then,
as dawn approached, the wives of the cowherds, distressed by separation and with their necks gripped by their husbands, cursed the crowing cocks.
The birds warbled as if they were bards awakening Kṛṣṇa; while the bees sang, never ceasing due to the breezes from the Mandāra groves,
the princess of Vidarbha could not bear that moment of extreme splendor for even a brief instant.
Due to the separation from her embrace, she had moved to the space between the arms of her beloved;
then, having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and sipped water, Mādhava,
with his senses serene, meditated upon the Self beyond darkness.
The one who is self-luminous, non-dual, immutable, eternally free from all taint by its own nature,
known as Brahman, whose manifestation and cessation are characterized by its own potencies— having thus bathed in the pure water according to the prescribed rite, [he beheld that Brahman].
Having put on his two garments as prescribed by ritual tradition,
the seventh son performed the twilight prayers and other rites;
with his speech restrained, he offered oblations into the fire and chanted the sacred Veda.
Having attended upon the rising sun and offered libations to his own vital constituents (kalās),
and having worshipped the gods, sages, ancestors, elders, and brāhmaṇas, the self-possessed one [presented] cows with golden horns, auspicious, and adorned with strings of pearls.

Day after day, he gave to the adorned brāhmaṇas a herd upon a herd of milk-yielding cows— each with her calf, well-clothed, and having silver-tipped hooves— along with linen garments, deerskins, and sesame seeds.

Having offered obeisances to the cows, brāhmaṇas, deities, elders, gurus, and all living beings in every respect— those who are the sources of his own being— he touched auspicious objects and adorned himself,
he who is the ornament of the world of men.
With his own garments, ornaments, divine garlands, and ointments, he honored clarified butter, the mirror, the bull, the twice-born, and the deities,
as well as the desires of all the classes of people dwelling within the city and the inner apartments.
Having gratified the subjects with their desired objects, he returned their greetings; having first distributed garlands, betel, and ointments to the brahmins,
he then personally employed his friends, ministers, and wives.
Then the charioteer, having brought forward a most wonderful chariot yoked with horses such as Sugrīva and others, bowed down and stood before him;
thereupon, taking the charioteer’s hands in his own, he ascended it.
Accompanied by Sātyaki and Uddhava, like the sun rising over the eastern mountain,
he was gazed upon by the women of the inner apartments with glances of bashful love;
released with difficulty, he went forth with a smile, stealing their hearts.
Surrounded by all the Vṛṣṇis, he entered the assembly hall named Sudharmā, wherein,
O dear one, those who are seated find no trace of the six waves of worldly existence.
Seated there upon a supreme throne, the Lord shone with his own radiance, illuminating the quarters of the sky.
Surrounded by the Yadus, those lions among men, that best of the Yadus shone like the moon, the lord of the stars, amidst the hosts of constellations in the sky.
There, O King, the ministers approached the Lord with various humorous sentiments; the masters of actors performed, and the female dancers presented their individual *tāṇḍava* dances.
To the sounds of mṛdaṅgas, vīṇās, murajas, flutes, cymbals, and drums,
the sūtas, māgadhas, and bards danced, sang, and offered praise.
There, certain seated brāhmaṇas who were exponents of the Veda spoke.
They recounted the stories of former kings of virtuous fame; then,
O King, a man of unprecedented appearance arrived there,
announced by the doorkeepers and ushered into the presence of the Blessed One.
Having offered salutations with joined palms to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord,
he reported to him the suffering of the kings arising from their imprisonment by Jarāsandha,
as well as those kings who had not submitted during his conquest of the quarters.
Having been forcibly confined within Girivraja by him,
twenty thousand kings spoke:
"O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, O immeasurable Soul, O destroyer of the fear of those who have sought refuge!"
We, whose intellects are divided and who are terrified by worldly existence, seek refuge in you.
The world is intent on improper actions and is negligent regarding what is wholesome;
it is occupied with its own duties as proclaimed by you, which consist of the worship of you.

Salutations to that powerful one who instantly cuts away the hope for life here; to Him, the Unblinking One, be homage. In this world, Your Lordship, the Lord of the universe, has descended by a portion of Yourself.
O Lord, is there someone else besides You who transgresses Your command for the sake of protecting the virtuous and restraining the wicked?
Or do people simply experience the results of their own actions? We do not know this.
O Lord, royal happiness is like a dream, dependent on others;
we carry its burden with constant fear, as if bearing a corpse.
Abandoning that, may we attain within ourselves the bliss obtained effortlessly through You.
We, who are exceedingly wretched, suffer here due to Your illusory power;
therefore, O Lord, whose pair of feet removes the grief of those who bow before You,
release us who are bound by the fetters of karma known as Magadha.
He who alone possessed the prowess of ten thousand elephants and kings of the earth,
yet remained confined in his palace like a lion in a cage;
he who was indeed struck by you with your exalted discus nineteen times.

O Unconquered One, having indeed defeated you of infinite prowess in battle, that arrogant one, intoxicated by a single victory, now oppresses your subjects who are devoted to the world of men; therefore, O Lord, provide a remedy for this.
The messenger said:
"Thus restrained by the King of Magadha and longing for a vision of you, they have sought refuge at the soles of your feet; O Lord of the distressed, let welfare be bestowed upon them."
Śrī Śuka said:
While the king’s messenger was speaking thus, the celestial sage of supreme effulgence appeared,
bearing a mass of tawny matted locks like the sun.

Seeing him, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the lords of all worlds, rose with his courtiers and followers and joyfully saluted him with his head bowed. Having honored him according to the prescribed rites, he offered him a seat.
He spoke with truthful words, satisfying the sage with faith:
"Is it not indeed a great virtue for the Blessed One, as he wanders through the worlds, that today the three worlds are free from fear?"
"Indeed, nothing in these worlds governed by the Lord is unknown to you. Therefore, we ask you about what the Pāṇḍavas intend to do.
Śrī Nārada said:
O All-pervading Lord, we have witnessed Your illusory power many times, which is difficult to overcome, as well as the power of the creators of the universe who possess such power.

O Earth-portion, it is no wonder to us that You move among living beings with Your own potencies, like fire whose radiance is concealed. Who is capable of truly understanding Your activity as You create and withdraw this universe by means of Your own *māyā*?
Salutations to You, whose nature is distinct from Your own manifestations;

I take refuge in You, who, through Your divine pastimes (*līlāvatāra*), kindled the lamp of Your own glory to deliver the transmigrating soul— from whom liberation is unknown— from this body that brings only misfortune.
Nevertheless, let me announce this sacred vow, which is a mere imitation of the world of men:
the son of Pāṇḍu, the devoted grandson of my paternal aunt, intends to perform for you the Rājasūya, the sovereign of all sacrifices.
O King, you who desire the supreme state of Brahmā, please grant your approval for this.
At that most excellent sacrifice, O Lord, the gods and others,
as well as illustrious kings, will assemble, desiring to behold you.
O Lord, those who dwell near you—who are composed of Brahman—are purified by hearing, chanting, and meditating upon you; how much more so, then, for those who behold you and touch you?
Your stainless fame is celebrated in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld.

And upon the earth, O auspiciousness of the world, Your foot-water spreads as a canopy across the quarters; it is known as Mandākinī in heaven, Bhogavatī below, and here on earth as Gaṅgā, purifying the entire universe.
Śrī Śuka said: While they were there, each defending their own side out of a desire for victory,
Keśava, smiling, addressed his servant Uddhava with these skillful words.
The Blessed Lord said:
You are indeed our supreme eye, our well-wisher, and the knower of the true meaning of counsel.
Therefore, speak here of what is to be performed; we have faith in it and shall carry it out.
Thus addressed by his master, who is all-knowing, Uddhava— acting like one who is simple-minded— placed the command upon his head and replied. Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard what was thus spoken by the celestial sage, the high-minded Uddhava, having ascertained the opinion of the assembly members as well as that of Kṛṣṇa,
spoke. Śrī Uddhava said:
O Lord, as was stated by the sage: "You must provide assistance to your sister's son who is about to perform a sacrifice, and you must protect those seeking refuge;
O All-pervading One, you who have conquered all quarters of the earth, you must perform the Rājasūya sacrifice."
Therefore, O son of Jarā, victory in both matters is my considered opinion;
for by this very means, a great benefit will accrue to us as well,
and you shall gain glory, O Govinda, as you release the bound kings.
That King Durviṣaha was indeed equal in strength to ten thousand elephants;
he could not be defeated by any other strong men except for one of equal power to Bhīma. He must be conquered in single combat (*dvairatha*), for he is accompanied by a hundred *akṣauhiṇī* divisions.
The Brāhmaṇī will never refuse when entreated by the Brahmins;
therefore, Vṛkodara, assuming the guise of a Brahmin, should go and beg from her.
He will undoubtedly slay him in a duel in your presence.
Hiraṇyagarbha and Śarva are merely the instrumental causes for the creation and dissolution of the universe by You, the Supreme Lord; they are the effects of Your formless Time.
O performer of pure deeds, the goddesses sing of You within their homes.
The kings achieved the slaughter of their own enemies and their own liberation;
the cowherd women obtained the Lord of Elephants; Janaka’s daughter and her parents attained refuge; and so did the sages and we ourselves.
"O Kṛṣṇa, the slaying of Jarāsandha will serve your many purposes; indeed, through the ripening of past deeds, your desired sacrifice is now at hand.
Śrī Śuka said:

O King, the celestial sage Nārada, the elders of the Yadu clan, and Kṛṣṇa themselves honored these words of Uddhava, which were auspicious in every respect and infallible. Then the Blessed Lord, the son of Devakī, gave the command to depart.
Having taken leave of his servants, headed by Dāruka and Jaitra, and having dismissed his elders, his harem, and his sons along with their attendants, the Lord,
O slayer of enemies, took leave of Saṅkarṣaṇa and the King of the Yadus.
He ascended his own chariot, which bore the banner of Garuḍa,
as it was brought by the charioteer; then he was surrounded by his own army, led by commanders of chariots, elephants, infantry, and cavalry, and formidable in appearance.
With the sounds of mṛdaṅgas, bherīs, ānakas, conchs,
and gomukhas resounding through all directions, he departed;
and with their sons, the wives of excellent vows followed their husband Acyuta in golden palanquins drawn by men and horses.
Clad in excellent garments, ornaments, ointments, and garlands, and well-guarded by men with swords and shields in their hands, they were accompanied by men,
camels, cows, buffaloes, donkeys, mules,
carts, female elephants, and the women of the retinue.
Well-adorned with mats, huts, blankets, garments, and other equipment, they set out from all sides,
accompanied by a great force featuring large banners, cloth canopies, parasols, and chowries.
With excellent weapons, ornaments, crowns, and armor,
and with divine rays, he shone with a tumultuous roar like the ocean with its agitated *timiṅgila* fish and waves.
Then the sage, honored by the Lord of the Yadus, bowed to him and, placing him in his heart, departed through the air.
Having heard of his resolve and having received the offerings of hospitality, his senses were filled with bliss from the sight of Mukunda;
the Blessed One, gladdening the royal messenger with his speech, spoke these words.
"Do not fear; may it be well with you, O messenger; I shall slay the King of Magadha.
Thus addressed, the messenger departed and spoke to the kings exactly as he had been told. Desiring liberation, they too awaited an audience with Śauri.
Having crossed the Ānartas, Sauvīras, and Marus, Hari passed through Vinaśana;
he traversed mountains, rivers, cities, villages, cow-pens, and mines.
Then, having crossed the Dṛṣadvatī, Mukunda reached the Sarasvatī.
Then, having passed through Pañcāla and Matsya, he arrived at Śakraprastha.
Hearing that he, who is difficult for men to behold, had arrived,
Ajātaśatru was filled with joy and went out to meet him, accompanied by his teachers and surrounded by his friends.
Amidst the sound of singing and musical instruments and the great resonance of Vedic recitation,
he approached Hṛṣīkeśa with reverence, just as the vital breaths approach the life-force.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa, the son of Pāṇḍu’s heart was moistened with affection.
Then, having seen her beloved after a long time,

the king— whose sins were destroyed— embraced Ramā’s stainless abode, the body of Mukunda, again and again with both arms; with tears in his eyes and his body bristling with joy, he attained supreme bliss, forgetting the delusions of the world.
Embracing his maternal cousin, Bhīma was filled with bliss and, smiling, his senses were overwhelmed by tears of love.
The twins and Arjuna also joyfully embraced Acyuta, their best friend, as their tears flowed profusely.
He was embraced by Arjuna and saluted by the twins.
Having offered salutations to the brāhmaṇas and the elders as was appropriate, he, though himself honored, paid honor to the Kurus, Sṛñjayas,
and Kaikayas; and to the sūtas, māgadhas, gandharvas, bards, and courtiers.
With mṛdaṅgas, conchs, kettledrums, lutes, small drums, and gomukhas,
the brāhmaṇas praised the lotus-eyed Lord, danced, and sang.
Thus surrounded by his friends, he who is the crest-jewel of those of virtuous fame—
Being thus praised, the Blessed One entered the decorated city,
whose streets were sprinkled with the ichor-water of elephants and adorned with variegated banners, golden arches, and full water-jars.
It was resplendent with men and young women who were purified by their very souls and adorned with new silk garments, ornaments, garlands, and fragrances;
and in every house, the latticed windows were filled with offerings and brightly burning lamps.

He beheld the capital of the Kuru king, adorned with houses that were beautiful with wafting incense, graced with fluttering banners, and endowed with golden jars upon their summits and large silver pinnacles.
Hearing that he had arrived— the vessel for the drinking of the eyes of men—
the women immediately abandoned their household chores and their husbands on the beds, the knots of their hair and silk garments loosened by their eagerness.
On that royal road, which was densely crowded with elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers, young women went out to see him;
having learned that Kṛṣṇa was there with his wife, they climbed onto the roofs of their houses.
The women scattered flowers and embraced him in their minds;
with smiles and glances, they offered him a most welcome reception.
Having seen him on the road, the wives of Mukunda spoke thus.
What improper act could these stars perform, accompanied as they are by the moon,
when the Lord who is the crown of all beings, with His noble smile, spreads a festival for the eyes through even a fraction of His playful glance?
Approaching Him here and there with auspicious offerings in their hands,
the leading guilds of the citizens, their sins destroyed, performed worship for Kṛṣṇa;
and Mukunda was greeted with affection by the women of the inner apartments, whose eyes were wide with joy.
Approached with great haste, he entered the royal palace.
Upon seeing her brother’s son Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the three worlds, Pṛthā was filled with joy; rising from her couch along with her daughter-in-law, she embraced him.
Having respectfully brought Govinda, the Lord of the gods of gods, into his home,
the king, overwhelmed with joy, did not know what to do in the matter of worship. Kṛṣṇa offered salutations to his father’s sister and to the wives of his elders.
O King, he himself was greeted with salutations by Kṛṣṇā and his sister; then, urged by his mother-in-law, Kṛṣṇā paid homage to all the wives of Kṛṣṇa,
as well as Rukmiṇī, Satyā, Bhadrā, and Jāmbavatī.

The King of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) comfortably settled Janārdana with Kālindī, Mitravindā, Śaibyā, the virtuous Nāgnajitī, and whatever other women had arrived, providing them with garments, garlands, ornaments, and the like.
Accompanied by Phālguna, he gratified the Fire-god with the Khāṇḍava forest— along with its armies, followers, horses, and wives, and in ever-new ways—
and having liberated Maya, he caused him to build a divine assembly hall for the king.
Desiring to do what was pleasing to the king, He dwelt there for several months,
traveling about on His chariot accompanied by Phālguna and surrounded by soldiers.
Śrī Śuka said:
Once, while seated in the midst of the assembly hall, Yudhiṣṭhira was surrounded by sages, brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, his brothers,
teachers, elders of the clan, and kinsmen, relatives, and friends.
While they were still listening, he addressed them and spoke this.
Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Govinda, by means of the Rājasūya, the king of sacrifices, [the waters] are purifying."
"I shall worship Your opulences; therefore, O Lord, please fulfill that for us.
Those pure ones who constantly circumambulate Your sandals, meditate upon them as the destroyer of all inauspiciousness, and chant their praises—"
O Lotus-navelled One, those who desire no other blessings, O Lord, find liberation from worldly existence through You;
therefore, O God of gods, [I seek] Your lotus feet.
O Lord, let this world behold here the power of devotion; demonstrate the ultimate fate of both those who worship you and those who do not, among the Kurus and the Sṛñjayas.
O Brahman, for You who are the Self of all, who perceive all equally, and whose experience is Your own bliss, there can be no notion of "self" versus "other.
Your grace flows to those who serve You, just as it does from a celestial wish-fulfilling tree.
"The success resulting from service is in accordance with that service; there is no deviation in this matter.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O King, O crusher of enemies, you have rightly resolved."
O Lord, by this auspicious sacrifice of yours, your fame shall pervade the worlds;
it is desired by the sages, the ancestors, the gods, our friends,
and indeed by all living beings— this sovereign of sacrifices.

"Having conquered all kings and brought the earth under your control, O King, gather all the necessary materials and perform the great sacrifice. These brothers of yours, O King, are born from portions of the world-protectors."
