"I am conquered by you, who possess self-mastery—I who am difficult to defeat for those of undisciplined soul. No one in this world, not even a god, can surpass me in splendor, fame, fortune, or opulence; how much less a mere king?"
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard the song of the Blessed Lord, he was delighted, his lotus-like face blossoming;
he then dispatched his brothers, empowered by the splendor of Viṣṇu, on their conquest of the quarters.
He assigned Sahadeva to the southern quarter along with the Sṛñjayas;
Nakula to the western quarter; Savyasācin (Arjuna) to the northern quarter;
and Vṛkodara (Bhīma) to the eastern quarter, together with the Matsyas, Kekayas, and Madrakas.

Having conquered those kings by their prowess, those heroes brought back vast wealth from all directions for Ajātaśatru, who was about to perform a sacrifice, O King. Hearing that Jarāsaṃdha was unconquered, Hari meditated upon the king.
He spoke of that very means which Uddhava had previously mentioned:
"O dear one, Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and Kṛṣṇa— these three, assuming the marks of Brahmins—
went to Girivraja, where the son of Bṛhadratha resided."
Having arrived at the time for receiving guests at their homes, those kṣatriyas, appearing in the guise of brāhmaṇas, requested alms from that householder who was devoted to the brāhmaṇas.
"O King, know us to be guests who have come from afar seeking your favor."
Therefore, may you be blessed; grant us that which we desire.
What is unbearable for those who practice forbearance? What is an improper act for the wicked?
What is there that the generous should not give? And who is a stranger to those who perceive all with equanimity?
He who, though capable, does not himself accumulate eternal fame— which is worthy of being sung by the virtuous— by means of this impermanent body, is indeed to be pitied and called wretched.
Hariścandra, Rantideva, Śibi, Bali, and those who lived by gathering grains (uñchavṛtti)— [all attained such fame].
The hunter, the pigeon, and many others indeed attained the eternal through the impermanent.
Śrī Śuka said:
By their voices, their forms, and even by their forearms scarred by the bowstring...
Recognizing them as kinsmen of the royal order whom he had seen before, he reflected:
"These are indeed kinsmen of the royal order who bear the marks of Brahmanas;
I shall give to them even my own self, though it is so difficult to abandon."
Indeed, the stainless fame of Bali is heard spread throughout the quarters,
even though he was deprived of his sovereignty by Viṣṇu under the guise of a brāhmaṇa;
likewise [the fame] of Indra, who desired to seize the fortune from Viṣṇu when the latter appeared in the form of a twice-born.
Even though he knew [the truth], the king of the Daityas gave away the earth even while being restrained, thinking:
"What purpose is there for a kinsman of the Kṣatriyas who lives merely for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa? What great fame is gained by this perishing body, rather than by it remaining alive?"
Thus the noble-minded one spoke to Kṛṣṇa, Arjuna, and Vṛkodara:
"O brāhmaṇas, let your desire be chosen; I shall grant it to you, even my own head.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Indra among kings, grant us battle, if you so intend it, in single combats.
We Kṣatriyas have arrived seeking war, desiring nothing else.
This is Vṛkodara Pārtha, and this indeed is his brother Arjuna."
"Know me, Kṛṣṇa, the son of their maternal uncle, to be your enemy.
When he had been informed thus, the King of Magadha laughed loudly and, filled with indignation, said: "O fools, then I grant you battle!"
"I will not fight with you, for you are a coward whose prowess has failed in battle;
having abandoned your own city of Mathurā, you have sought refuge in the ocean.
But this one is my equal in age, yet he lacks sufficient strength and is not my match."
"Arjuna shall not be the warrior; Bhīma is my equal in strength.
Having said this, he gave a great mace to Bhīmasena, took a second one himself, and went out from the city.
Then, on level ground, those two heroes, intoxicated by battle, locked together and struck one another with maces as formidable as thunderbolts;
they moved in various circles, both to the left and to the right.
As they moved about, their battle shone like that of two actors on a stage;
then, O King, as their maces were hurled like the tusks of two elephants, there arose a crackling sound resembling the crash of a thunderbolt.
As those two clubs were brought down by the speed of their arms,
they struck one another upon the shoulders, hips, feet, hands, thighs, and collarbones, shattering them like the branches of a tree struck by the sun’s rays.
Like two blazing elephants engaged in combat,
as their maces thus struck one another, the two heroes among men, filled with rage, crushed each other with their own fists that felt like iron.
As those two struck each other like two elephants, there arose a sound from the clashing of their palms, harsh as a thunderclap or a lightning bolt;
for those two, who were equal in training, strength, and vigor, continued thus to strike one another.
O King, the battle between those two of undiminished speed was without distinction;
Hari, knowing that birth and death belong to the enemy and that life is subject to old age,
strengthened Pārtha with his own splendor and reflected thus.

Having reflected upon the means for slaying his enemy, he whose vision was unfailing showed [the way] to Bhīma by a sign, as if tearing apart a branch. Understanding that, the great-souled Bhīma, the best among strikers, [acted].
Seizing the enemy by the feet, he threw him down upon the ground;
treading on one foot with his own foot and grasping the other with both arms,
he tore him apart from the anus like a great elephant tearing a branch.
The subjects beheld two halves, each possessing one foot, thigh, testicle, hip, back, breast, shoulder, one arm, eye, eyebrow, and ear;
and a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose when the Lord of Magadha was slain.
Jayanta and Acyuta embraced Bhīma and honored him;
then the Blessed One, the creator of beings, the Lord of immeasurable soul, consecrated Sahadeva, his son, as the sovereign of the Magadhas.
He liberated the kṣatriyas who had been imprisoned by the King of Magadha.
Śrī Śuka said:
Twenty thousand and eight hundred [warriors] were captured after being defeated in battle.
Emerging from the mountain valley, soiled and clad in dirty garments, emaciated by hunger, their faces parched and wasted by their confinement,
they beheld Him who is dark as a rain cloud and dressed in yellow silk.
He bore the Śrīvatsa mark, had four arms, and eyes as reddish as the interior of a lotus; his face was beautiful and serene, adorned with shimmering makara-shaped earrings;
he held a lotus in his hand and was distinguished by a mace, a conch, and a discus.
Adorned with a crown, necklaces, bracelets, a waist-string,
and armlets, his neck shone with a magnificent gem, and he was draped with a forest garland;
[the people] seemed to drink him in with their eyes and lick him with their tongues.
As if smelling with their two nostrils and as if embracing with their arms,
they— whose sins were destroyed— bowed their heads at the feet of Hari;
their exhaustion from confinement was dispelled by the joy of beholding Kṛṣṇa.
With palms joined in reverence, the kings praised Hṛṣīkeśa with these words.
The kings said:
"Obeisances to You, O Lord of the lords of gods, the imperishable remover of the distress of those who have sought refuge!"

"O Kṛṣṇa, protect us who have surrendered to You, for we are weary of this terrible cycle of worldly existence. O Madhusūdana, we do not harbor any ill-will toward this King of Magadha; rather, O Lord, it is Your very grace that these kings have been deprived of their kingdoms."
O King, a ruler intoxicated by the pride of royal power and sovereignty does not find what is truly beneficial;
deluded by your māyā, he considers transient prosperities to be permanent. Just as children imagine a mirage to be a reservoir of water.

O Lord, having thus failed to understand Your transformative illusory power (*vaikārikī māyā*), we previously spoke of it as a material reality; with our vision lost through the intoxication of prosperity, we vied with one another out of a desire for conquest.
Utterly merciless toward our own subjects and intoxicated by pride, we disregarded even Death himself who stood before us.

O Kṛṣṇa, those very fortunes of ours, which were once agitated by Your profound speed and enduring prowess in the form of Time, have now had their pride destroyed through Your compassion; we remember Your feet.
Furthermore, we do not desire a kingdom that is like a mirage, nor this body which is a constant source of pain and falls away.
O All-pervading Lord, we long to worship that which is the fruit of ritual action after death and which delights the ears;
please instruct us in that means by which the remembrance of Your lotus feet may never cease, even for those wandering here in this world.
"Obeisances again and again to Kṛṣṇa, Vāsudeva, Hari, the Supreme Soul, Govinda, who destroys the suffering of those who bow down to Him. Śrī Śuka said:
Being praised by the kings whose bonds had been released, the Blessed One,
O dear one, who is the refuge of all, spoke to them with a compassionate and gentle voice.
The Blessed Lord said:

"O kings, from this day forward, may firm devotion toward Me—the Self, the Lord of all—arise within you; indeed, your prayer has been granted. By good fortune, O kings, you who speak the truth have resolved upon this."
Behold the intoxication of pride born of wealth and power, which drives men to madness: Haihaya, Nahuṣa, Veṇa, Rāvaṇa, Naraka,
and others— these lords of gods, demons, and men were all cast down from their positions due to the arrogance of their prosperity.
"O sages, having understood this— that the body and so forth are produced and are subject to end—
worship Me with sacrifices and, being disciplined, protect your subjects according to dharma. Continuing the lineages of progeny, [regard] happiness and misery, existence and non-existence."
Enjoying whatever comes to you as it arrives, with your minds fixed on Me, you shall wander about;
indifferent to the body and its like, delighting in the Self, and firm in your vows,
you shall properly entrust your minds to Me and, in the end, attain Me, the Brahman.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus instructed the kings, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, the sovereign of the universe,
appointed men among them to perform the task of bathing the women.
O descendant of Bharata, he had Sahadeva perform the worship with garments, ornaments, garlands, and ointments befitting a king;
having bathed them well and adorned them, he fed them with excellent food.

Honored by Mukunda with various enjoyments such as betel and other royal luxuries, those kings, adorned with polished earrings and liberated from their suffering, shone like planets at the end of the rainy season.
Having placed them upon chariots drawn by excellent horses and adorned with jewels and gold,
and having gratified them with kind words, he sent them back to their own countries. Thus were they liberated from their distress by the high-souled Kṛṣṇa.

They departed, meditating upon Him alone and the deeds of the Lord of the universe. They recounted to the subjects those exploits of the Great Person exactly as the Blessed One had commanded, and they carried them out without weariness.
Having caused Jarāsandha to be slain by Bhīmasena, Keśava,
accompanied by the two sons of Pṛthā and honored by Sahadeva, set forth.
Having gone to Khāṇḍavaprastha, they, having conquered their enemies, blew their conch shells.
Gladdening their own friends and bringing misery to their enemies,
the inhabitants of Indraprastha, hearing that, were delighted in heart;
they considered the King of Magadha subdued, and the king [Yudhiṣṭhira] had his desires fulfilled.

Then, having paid homage to the king, Bhīma, Arjuna, and Janārdana reported everything that they themselves had accomplished. Having heard that he was favored by Keśava, Dharmarāja [was filled with joy].
Shedding drops of tears of joy, he said nothing out of love.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, King Yudhiṣṭhira [heard] of the slaying of Jarāsandha by the Lord...
Having heard of that power of Kṛṣṇa, he was delighted and said to him.
Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Those who are the teachers of the three worlds, all the lords of the worlds—"

Having obtained that which is so difficult to attain, they carry Your command upon their heads; yet You, O lotus-eyed Lord, bear the command of those who consider themselves masters over the wretched— a most extreme mockery.
For the splendor of the one, non-dual Brahman, the Supreme Self, does not increase or diminish through actions, just as that of the sun does not;
O Mādhava, O Unconquered One, [the thought] "I am yours" or "you are mine" does not truly apply to Your devotees.
"The notion of 'you' and 'mine' is a distorted perception like that of animals.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having spoken thus, at the time prescribed for sacrifice, he chose the qualified officiating priests.
Permitted by Kṛṣṇa, Pārtha [invited] the Brahmins who were exponents of the Veda:
Dvaipāyana, Bharadvāja, Sumantu, Gotama, Asita,
Vasiṣṭha, Cyavana, Kaṇva, Maitreya, Kavaṣa, and Trita.
Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Sumati, Jaimini, Kratu, Paila, Parāśara, Garga, Vaiśampāyana,
as well as Atharvan, Kaśyapa, Dhaumya, Rāma Bhārgava, and Āsuri.
Vītihotra, Madhucchandas, Vīrasena, Akṛtavraṇa,
as well as others such as Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Kṛpa,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra with his sons, and the high-minded Vidura were invited.

O King, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and all the kings along with their subjects arrived there, desiring to witness the sacrifice. Then those Brāhmaṇas [prepared] the sacrificial ground with golden plows.
Having ploughed that ground according to the traditional injunctions, they initiated the king;
indeed, their implements were made of gold, just like those of Varuṇa in ancient times.
Indra and the other guardians of the worlds, together with Viriñci and Bhava, performed the rites.
The Siddhas and Gandharvas with their hosts, the Vidyādharas and Mahoragas, the sages, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, birds, Kinnaras, and Cāraṇas,
as well as the kings and the queens from all quarters, were summoned.
The kings indeed assembled for the Rājasūya sacrifice of the son of Pāṇḍu;
being free from pride, they considered it most fitting that he, a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, should perform it.
O great king, the priests, possessing divine luster, officiated for the monarch.

On the day of the Soma extraction, the protector of the earth, being perfectly composed, duly honored the sacrificial priests and the presiding masters of the assembly— those highly fortunate ones— with the Rājasūya sacrifice according to the prescribed rules, just as the immortals did for Pracetas.
The members of the assembly, deliberating on who was worthy of the foremost honor for the *sadasya* position, could not reach a decision due to their lack of consensus; then Sahadeva spoke:
"Indeed, the Lord Acyuta, the Master of the Sātvatas, deserves preeminence."
He indeed is all the deities, as well as place, time, wealth, and so forth; He is the essence of this entire universe, and the sacrifices have Him as their essence.
Fire, the oblations, the mantras, Sāṅkhya, and Yoga—all have Him as their ultimate goal.
He alone is without a second; this entire world has Him as its essence.
O noble ones, the unborn Self, resting in Himself, creates, sustains, and destroys by His own power. It is by His glance that He brings forth the various activities here in this world.
Whatever this entire world strives for as its highest good, characterized by dharma and other virtues—
for that reason, let the most worthy of honor be offered to the Great Kṛṣṇa;
for in this way, there would be worship both of all beings and of one's own self.
"To Kṛṣṇa, who has become the self of all beings, who perceives nothing else,
who is peaceful and complete— one desiring the infinity of what is given should offer [this gift].
Having spoken thus, Sahadeva, knowing the majesty of Kṛṣṇa, became silent.
Hearing that, all those most excellent men praised him, saying, "Excellent! Excellent!
Having heard what was uttered by the twice-born and having understood the inner heart of the members of the assembly, the king, pleased and overwhelmed with affection, honored Hṛṣīkeśa.
Washing his feet with water that purifies the world,
he— along with his wife, younger brothers, ministers, and family— joyfully bore it upon his head;
and he honored him with garments of yellow silk and highly precious ornaments.
Having offered worship, his eyes filled with tears, he was unable to look upon him.
Seeing him thus honored, all the people with palms joined in reverence cried out, "Obeisances! Victory! and fell prostrate; showers of flowers rained down upon him.
Having heard this, the son of Damaghoṣa rose from his seat; filled with indignation at the description of Kṛṣṇa’s virtues,
the impatient man raised his arm and spoke thus to the assembly.

Fearlessly uttering harsh words against the Blessed Lord, he said: "The Lord is Time, which is impossible to overcome; such is the truth-bearing Vedic revelation. Even the intellect of the elders is led astray by the words of children."

"You are the best among those who know what constitutes a worthy recipient; do not disregard the words spoken by a child. All of you are lords of the assembly, for Kṛṣṇa is deemed worthy of this honor.
[He honors] those who maintain austerity, knowledge, and vows, whose impurities have been destroyed by wisdom."

Passing over the supreme seers established in Brahman, who are honored by the guardians of the worlds, and even the lords of the assembly— how can this cowherd, a disgrace to his family, deserve such honor? He is like a crow that covets the sacrificial cake.
Devoid of caste, stage of life, and family lineage, excluded from all religious duties,
acting according to his own whims, and lacking in virtues— how could he deserve worship?
For Yayāti’s lineage has been cursed by the virtuous and cast out.
How can one who is constantly addicted to useless drinking deserve worship? Having abandoned the regions frequented by Brahman-sages, these people, devoid of spiritual luster,
have taken refuge in the inaccessible ocean and are oppressing the subjects like bandits.

Thus, with his auspiciousness destroyed, he spoke such inauspicious words; yet the Blessed One said nothing at all, just as a lion ignores the howling of a jackal. Hearing that unbearable blasphemy against the Blessed One, the members of the assembly were distressed.
Covering their ears, they went forth in anger, cursing the King of Cedi;
for he who hears the censure of the Blessed Lord, or that of His devotees,
and does not depart from there, falls away from his merit and goes to a lower state.
Then the sons of Pāṇḍu, along with the Matsyas, Kaikayas, and Sṛñjayas, rose up in anger with weapons uplifted,
desiring to slay Śiśupāla.
Thereupon, the King of Cedi, remaining unperturbed, seized his sword and shield.
O descendant of Bharata, while he was reviling the kings who were supporters of Kṛṣṇa in the assembly,
the Blessed Lord rose up, restrained his own followers, and in his wrath himself struck off the head of the attacking enemy with his razor-edged discus.
A great clamor then arose when Śiśupāla was slain;
his followers, the kings, fled seeking to save their lives.
The light arising from the body of the King of Cedi entered Vāsudeva.
While all living beings looked on, she fell from the sky to the earth like a meteor.
With a mind inflamed by enmity accumulated over three lifetimes, he meditated upon her; for absorption in an object is indeed the cause of worldly existence.

The sole sovereign gave abundant sacrificial fees to the officiating priests and their assistants; having honored them all according to the prescribed rites, the King of kings performed the avabhṛtha bath.
Having thus completed the sacrifice of the king, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the masters of yoga, departed.
Requested by his friends, he dwelt there for several months; then, having taken leave of the king— who though unwilling to let him go—
Lord Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, departed for his own city accompanied by his wife, ministers, and companions.
I have related that narrative to you in great detail,
including the repeated births of the two residents of Vaikuṇṭha resulting from the curse of the brahmins.
King Yudhiṣṭhira, having bathed at the concluding purificatory rite of the Rājasūya sacrifice, [proceeded].
In the midst of the assembly of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, he shone like the king of the gods. Honored by the king, all the denizens of heaven, men,
and sky-goers departed for their own abodes with joy, praising Kṛṣṇa and the sacrifice.

Except for the wicked Duryodhana, the Kali-age personification and disease of the Kuru lineage, who could not endure seeing that flourishing prosperity of the son of Pāṇḍu? He who shall recite this deed of Viṣṇu, beginning with the slaying of the King of Cedi—

By witnessing the liberation of the king and the sacrificial canopy, one is released from all sins. The King said: O Brahmin, having seen that great success of the Rājasūya sacrifice of Ajātaśatru, all the god-like kings who had assembled there rejoiced.
"O Blessed One, we have heard that all the kings, along with the sages and the gods—with the sole exception of Duryodhana—were present there; please tell us the reason for this.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
At the Rājasūya sacrifice of your high-souled grandfather,
his kinsmen were bound by affection as they attended upon him.
Bhīma was the superintendent of the kitchen, and Suyodhana was the superintendent of the treasury.
Sahadeva was appointed to the task of worship; Nakula to the procurement of materials; Arjuna to the service of the teacher; Kṛṣṇā to the washing of the feet;
Draupadī to the serving of food; and the high-minded Karṇa to the distribution of gifts.
Yuyudhāna, Vikarṇa, Hārdikya, Vidura and others,
the sons of Bāhlīka such as Bhūri and others, and those such as Santardana—
these were all appointed at that time to various tasks during the great sacrifice.

O King of kings, they proceeded with the desire to do what was pleasing to the monarch, toward the officiating priests, the members of the assembly, the many learned scholars, and their dearest friends,
honoring them with their own offerings, kind words, and ritual fees.
And when the son of Cedi had entered the feet of the Lord of the Sātvatas,
they then performed the ritual ablution (*avabhṛtha-snāna*) in the celestial river,
accompanied by the sounds of mṛdaṅgas, conchs, paṇavas, dhuṇdhurīs, ānakas, and gomukhas.
At the concluding bath festival (*āvabhṛtha-utsava*), various musical instruments resounded;
joyful female dancers danced, and singers sang in groups.
The resonance of their lutes, flutes, and hand-claps reached unto the heavens.
Adorned with golden garlands, the kings set forth on elephants, chariots, and horses, accompanied by well-equipped warriors bearing variegated banners and the tips of flags;
they were the Yadus, Sṛñjayas, Kāmbojas, Kurus, Kekayas, and Kośalas.
Making the earth tremble with their armies, preceded by those who were hastening forward,
the members of the assembly, the officiating priests, and the best of the twice-born offered great sounds of Vedic chanting;
meanwhile, the celestial sages, ancestors, and gandharvas praised them while showering down flowers.
Men and women, beautifully adorned with perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and garments, sported with various flavors, anointing and sprinkling one another with oils,
milk, scented water, turmeric, and thick saffron.
The courtesans, smeared with unguents themselves, anointed the men as they sported;
guarded by their attendants, they went forth to obtain this [pleasure],
just as goddesses in heaven travel in excellent celestial chariots.
Being sprinkled by their maternal cousins and friends,
they shone with faces blossoming from bashful smiles; they, in turn,
sprinkled their brothers-in-law and friends with water from leather bags.
With their garments wet, their bodies, breasts, thighs, and waists exposed,
and with their flower garlands falling from their loosened braids due to their longing,
they stirred the minds of those impure in intellect with their graceful movements.
Mounted upon his chariot drawn by excellent horses and adorned with golden garlands, that sovereign shone like the king of sacrifices accompanied by his wives and ritual acts;
having performed the *patnīsaṃyāja* and *avabhṛtha* rites, those priests [attended] him.
Having sipped water for purification, they bathed him in the Gaṅgā together with Kṛṣṇā.
The celestial drums resounded along with the drums of men,
while the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans showered down rains of flowers.
There, all the men belonging to the various social classes and stages of life bathed;
for even one who has committed a great sin is instantly liberated from his transgression.
Then the king, having put on two linen garments and being well-adorned, [proceeded].

Devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, the king constantly honored the officiating priests, the members of the assembly, the brahmins, and others with ornaments and garments; he likewise honored his kinsmen, relatives, kings, friends, well-wishers, and all others in every way.
All the people possessed the luster of gods, adorned with jeweled earrings, garlands, turbans, tunics, fine silken garments, and costly necklaces;
and the women were graced by pairs of earrings and clusters of anklets.
The splendor of their faces shone with golden waistbands.
Then the officiating priests of great character, the members of the assembly who were exponents of the Veda,
and the kings belonging to the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, all gathered together.
O King, the celestial sages, ancestors, spirits, and the guardians of the worlds, along with their followers,
having been honored and having taken leave of him, departed for their own abodes after witnessing the great success of the Rājasūya sacrifice of that royal sage, the servant of Hari.

They did not grow weary of praising Him, drinking it as a mortal drinks nectar. Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, distressed at the thought of Kṛṣṇa’s departure, affectionately restrained His friends, relatives, and kinsmen, as well as Kṛṣṇa Himself.
The Blessed Lord also stayed there, O dear one, acting for their pleasure;
and having sent the Yadu heroes, Sāmba and the others, back to Kuśasthalī,
the King, the son of Dharma, thus [crossed] the great ocean of his desires.
Having crossed over that which is so difficult to traverse, he became free from all distress through Kṛṣṇa.
Once, having beheld within his inner apartments the splendor of Yudhiṣṭhira— who was devoted to Acyuta— and the greatness of the Rājasūya sacrifice, Duryodhana was consumed by envy.
In Him indeed shine forth the various splendors of the lords of men, the lords of the Daityas, and the lords of the gods, fashioned by the Creator of the universe;
with these, the daughter of King Drupada attended upon her husbands.
Upon whom the King of the Kurus fixed his heart and suffered;
in whom, at that time, resided the thousand queens of the Lord of Madhu,
moving slowly with the beauty of their tinkling anklets and the weight of their hips.

In the midst of that assembly hall fashioned by Maya, the son of Dharma, the sovereign lord, sat somewhere there, his neck adorned with a necklace reddened by the saffron from his very beautiful breasts, his glorious face enriched by dangling earrings and locks of hair.
Surrounded by his followers and kinsmen, and beheld by Kṛṣṇa with His own eyes,
he sat upon a literal golden throne like Indra himself,
endowed with the splendor of the supreme office and being praised by bards.
There, O King, the proud Duryodhana, surrounded by his brothers,
entered the water wearing his crown and garland, sword in hand, brandishing it in anger;
mistaking the dry land for water, he grasped at the hem of his garment and fell upon the ground.
Deluded by the illusory power of Māyā, Bhīma laughed at him in the water as if it were dry land; O dear one, seeing this, the women and other kings laughed as well,
even though they were being restrained by the king, for they were encouraged by Kṛṣṇa.
Ashamed, with his face downcast and burning with rage, he departed in silence for the city called Gajāhvaya.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the virtuous, and Ajātaśatru became as if despondent.
The Blessed One, who desired to lift the burden of the earth, remained silent while that [demon] wandered about within His very sight.
O King, that which I was asked by you here has been related to you:
the wickedness of Suyodhana during the great Rājasūya sacrifice.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, hear now another wonderful deed of Kṛṣṇa, who had assumed a human body for his pastimes— how the lord of Saubha was slain. Śālva, the friend of Śiśupāla, arrived at the wedding of Rukmiṇī.
When Jarāsandha and the others were thus defeated in battle by the Yadus, Śālva made a vow in the hearing of all the kings:
"I shall rid the earth of Yādavas; behold my prowess!"
Having thus made this vow, O King, the deluded monarch propitiated the Lord Paśupati, the Master, by swallowing a handful of dust once every day.
At the end of a year, the Blessed One, the Lord of Umā, who is easily pleased, appeared before him.
He invited Śālva, who had come for refuge, to choose a boon.
He chose a vehicle that was indestructible by gods, asuras, humans, gandharvas, serpents, or rākṣasas; one that moved at will and was terrifying to the Vṛṣṇis.
Saying "So be it," Maya, the conqueror of enemy cities, being thus commanded by Giriśa,
constructed a city made of iron— the Saubha— and gave it to Śālva. Having obtained that vehicle which moved at will, was a mass of darkness, and was difficult to approach, he [Śālva]...
O bull of the Bharatas, remembering the enmity caused by the Vṛṣṇis, Śālva besieged Dvāravatī with a vast army and destroyed the city’s groves and gardens on all sides.
Showers of weapons fell upon the gateways with their towers, the palaces, the watchtowers, the arches, the pleasure gardens, and the finest celestial mansions;
likewise, stones, trees, thunderbolts, serpents, and showers of gravel rained down.
A fierce whirlwind arose and the quarters were shrouded in dust; thus, O King, Kṛṣṇa’s city was severely afflicted by Saubha, finding no peace,
just as the earth did not find peace when assailed by the three cities.
Seeing his own subjects being oppressed, the illustrious Lord Pradyumna,
the hero of great fame, mounted his chariot and cried out, "Do not fear!
Satyaki, Cārudeṣṇa, Sāmba, Akrūra, and his younger brother were there as well.
Hārdikya, Bhānuvinda, Gada, Śuka, and Sāraṇa,
as well as other great archers who were leaders of hosts of chariot-warriors,
went forth clad in armor and protected by chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry.
Then a tumultuous battle, hair-raising like that between the Asuras and the gods, commenced between the Śālvas and the Yadus.
And the son of Rukmiṇī [Pradyumna] countered those illusory powers of the lord of Saubha with divine weapons.
In an instant, he destroyed [the enemy] as the sun destroys the darkness of night;
with twenty-five gold-feathered,
iron-tipped arrows of straight joints, he pierced Śālva’s commander of the army.
He struck Śālva with a hundred arrows, his soldiers one by one,
the leaders with ten each, and their mounts with three each.
That was the great and wonderful feat of the high-souled Pradyumna.
Seeing him, all their own soldiers and those of the enemy honored him;
that form, which possessed many shapes yet was a single form, was visible and yet invisible—
a creation of Māyā fashioned by Maya, inconceivable to others.
Sometimes on the ground, sometimes in the sky, on a mountain peak, or in the water—
that Saubha city, revolving like a whirling circle of fire, was unstable;
wherever it was observed, there were the Saubha and its soldiers.

Then Śālva released arrows from here and there; the leaders of the Sātvatas [fought back] with shafts whose touch was like fire or the sun and which were as difficult to approach as venomous serpents.
His army being thus afflicted by those arrows discharged by his enemies, Śālva became bewildered.
Severely afflicted by the floods of weapons from Śālva’s army, the Vṛṣṇi heroes did not abandon their respective battles, desiring to conquer both worlds.
Śālva’s minister, named Dyumān, having been greatly oppressed, [attacked] Pradyumna.
Having approached with his mace and struck him, the powerful one roared;
the charioteer, the son of Dāruka, who knew the law, carried Pradyumna— the subduer of enemies whose chest had been shattered by the mace— away from the battlefield.
Regaining consciousness after a moment, the son of Kṛṣṇa (Abhimanyu) said to his charioteer:
"Alas, O charioteer, this retreat from the battle is improper;
for one born in the lineage of the Yadus is never heard of as fleeing from the field of combat."
"Without me, what indeed shall I say when I approach my parents, Rāma and Keśava, after having incurred this reproach from a charioteer of eunuch-like mind?
Having properly retreated from the battle, I must explain there what was appropriate for myself."
"Clearly my brothers' wives will laugh and say to me:
'O hero, how, how was your impotence described by others in the battle?
" The charioteer said:
"O long-lived one, O Lord, this was done by me out of knowledge of the dharma:
a charioteer should protect a warrior who has fallen into distress, and a warrior [should protect] his charioteer.
Having understood this, you were carried away by me from the battle."
"Attacked by the enemy, he fainted, struck by the mace.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having touched water for purification, he girded himself and took up his bow.
"Lead me to the side of the heroic Dyumanta," the son of Rukmiṇī said to his charioteer.
As Dyumanta was dispersing his own troops, the son of Rukmiṇī struck him down and,
smiling, pierced him with eight iron arrows.
With four arrows he struck down the four horses, with one the charioteer,
with two the bow and the banner, and with another arrow indeed his head.
Gada, Sātyaki, Sāmba, and others then struck the army of the lord of Saubha.
All the sons of Saubha fell into the ocean with their necks severed.
Thus, as the Yadus and the Śālvas struck one another,
that battle continued for twenty-seven nights— tumultuous and fierce.

Having been summoned by the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira), Kṛṣṇa went to Indraprastha. Then, when the Rājasūya sacrifice had concluded and Śiśupāla had passed away, he took leave of the elders of the Kurus, the sages, and Pṛthā along with her sons.
Beholding extremely terrible omens, he went to Dvāravatī and said: "I have arrived here accompanied by my noble kinsmen;
surely the kings who side with the King of Cedi will destroy my city."
Having witnessed that slaughter of his own people and having observed the protection of the city,
as well as the *saubha* and King Śālva, Keśava spoke to Dāruka:
"O charioteer, quickly drive my chariot to the presence of Śālva."
"You must not be alarmed; this king of Saubha is a master of illusion.
Having been thus addressed, Dāruka mounted the chariot and urged it forward.
Then everyone—both their own people and the enemy—beheld Aruṇa’s younger brother entering [the city].
And Śālva, seeing that the lord of his army was nearly destroyed,
hurled a spear of terrifying sound at Kṛṣṇa’s charioteer in the battle.
As it fell through the sky with great speed like a massive meteor, [Kṛṣṇa]—
Śauri cut through that [weapon], which was illuminating the directions, into a hundred pieces with his arrows;
and having pierced him with sixteen shafts, he struck the Saubha city as it wandered in the sky with a multitude of arrows,
just as the sun fills the firmament with its rays.
Śālva pierced the left arm of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, which held the Śārṅga bow itself;
the bow fell from his hand, and that was a marvel. A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the beings who were watching there.
Roaring loudly, the king of Saubha spoke thus to Janārdana:
"O fool, while we were looking on, you stole the wife of our friend and brother;
that heedless friend of yours was slain by you in the midst of the assembly."
"Today, with my sharpened arrows, I shall lead him— who prides himself on being unconquered—
to the state from which there is no return, if you stand before me.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O dull-witted one, you boast in vain; do you not see Death standing near? Heroes display their prowess, not by talking much.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One struck Śālva with his mace of terrifying velocity.
Enraged, he struck him on the collarbone, and he trembled, vomiting blood. When the mace returned to his hand, Śālva vanished.
Then, after a moment, a person approached Acyuta with his head bowed.
Saying, "I have been sent by Devakī," he bowed and spoke these words while weeping:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, you who are affectionate toward your father,
your father has been bound and carried away by Śālva, like a sacrificial animal by a butcher."
Having heard this unpleasant news, Kṛṣṇa, who had assumed a human nature, became dejected;
out of compassion and affection, he spoke like an ordinary man:
"How could Rāma, who is undisturbed and unconquerable even by gods and demons, [be defeated]?"
While Govinda was saying, "My powerful father has been led away by the insignificant Śālva; this is the working of destiny," the King of Saubha appeared before him and,
having brought Vasudeva along, spoke thus to Kṛṣṇa.
"This is your father, your progenitor, for whose sake you live here;
I shall kill him while you look on! If he is a lord, protect him, O fool!
Having thus reviled him, the master of illusion struck Anakadundubhi with his sword.
Having cut off his head and taken it, he entered the Saubha situated in the sky.
Then, for a moment, his natural consciousness was submerged as he remained absorbed in his own kin;
however, that noble-souled one perceived that demonic illusion, which had been dispatched by Śālva and uttered by Maya.
O royal sage, the awakened Acyuta saw neither the messenger nor his father’s corpse there in the battle;
rather, like one seeing an enemy moving through the sky in a dream, he perceived him stationed in the Saubha and prepared to slay him—
thus do the sages declare, for who would not agree?
That which contradicts Your own words, surely they do not remember;
for where are sorrow, delusion, attachment, or fear— which arise only in the ignorant—
and where are You, whose perfect knowledge, wisdom, and sovereignty remain unimpaired?

By the knowledge of the Self acquired through service to his feet, they cast off the beginningless misconception of the self; they attain their own infinite divine nature—so how could there be delusion for that Supreme One who has reached the ultimate reality?
[He struck] him, who was violently attacking with a multitude of weapons, with his own might.
Śauri, whose prowess is unfailing, pierced Śālva with arrows,
cut through his armor, his bow, and his crest-jewel,
and shattered the enemy’s Saubha city with his mace.
Shattered by the mace wielded by Kṛṣṇa’s hand, it fell into the water in a thousand pieces. Abandoning that [mace], Śālva stood upon the ground, raised his own mace, and swiftly rushed toward Acyuta.
As he charged with his mace, [Kṛṣṇa] severed his arm with a broad-headed arrow and then [severed] his wonderful discus-weapon.
Bearing a discus resembling the sun at the time of universal dissolution for the sake of slaying Śālva, Hari shone like the mountain of sunrise with the sun upon it.

With that very weapon, Hari severed the head—adorned with earrings and a crown—from the one of great illusions, just as Purandara struck Vṛtra with his thunderbolt; and then there arose from the men the cry of "Alas! Alas!"* *BhP 10.77.035–036* *Note: The asterisk indicates that the original text contains a footnote marker.*
When that wicked one had fallen and Saubha had been destroyed by the mace,
O King, kettledrums resounded in the sky, struck by the hosts of gods; meanwhile,
Dantavakra approached in a rage, seeking to avenge his friends.
Śrī Śuka said:
The evil-minded [Kamsa], while performing acts of friendship toward those who had departed for the next world— namely Śiśupāla, Śālva, and Pauṇḍraka— [acted as follows].
O great king, that single being of immense power was seen on foot, enraged, with a mace in hand, shaking the earth with his feet as he advanced.
Beholding him approaching in that manner, [the other] quickly took up his mace.
Leaping down from his chariot, Kṛṣṇa checked the Sindhu as the shore resists the ocean;
then, raising his mace, the intoxicated Karūṣa spoke to Mukunda:
"By good fortune, by good fortune, you have come today within the range of my vision!"
"O Kṛṣṇa, you are our maternal cousin, yet as a betrayer of friends you seek to kill me. Therefore, O fool, I shall strike you with my mace, which is like a thunderbolt.
Thus, O ignorant one, I who am devoted to my friends shall discharge my debt to them."
Having slain his enemy who appeared as a kinsman, just as one might destroy a disease residing within the body,
he struck Kṛṣṇa with harsh words like goads used for an elephant;
then, striking him on the head with his mace, he roared like a lion.
Though struck with a mace in battle, that scion of the Yadu dynasty did not waver;
Kṛṣṇa, for his part, struck him between the breasts with his heavy mace, Kaumodakī. With his heart pierced by the mace, he vomited blood from his mouth.
Stretching out his hair, arms, and legs, he fell lifeless upon the earth;
then, O King, as all living beings watched, a most subtle and wondrous dark light entered him, just as it did at the slaying of the King of Cedi.
But his brother Vidūratha, overwhelmed by grief for his brother,
approached with sword and shield, gasping and desiring to slay him.
As he was rushing forward, Kṛṣṇa [struck him] with His discus, which had a razor-sharp rim.
O King of kings, he severed the head, adorned with its crown and earrings.
Having thus slain Saubha, Śālva, and Dantavakra along with his younger brother— all of whom were unbearable for others— he was praised by gods and men.
His victory being sung by sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, great serpents,
Apsarases, the hosts of Pitṛs, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, and Cāraṇas,
he was showered with flowers.
Surrounded by the foremost of the Vṛṣṇis, he entered the well-adorned city.
Thus, though the Lord Kṛṣṇa, the master of yoga and the sovereign of the universe,
is never truly defeated, he appears to those with the vision of worldly beasts as one who is conquered and yet victorious.
Having heard of the Kurus' preparations for war with the Pāṇḍavas, Rāma,
remaining neutral, set out under the pretext of bathing at sacred fords.
Having bathed at Prabhāsa, he offered libations to the gods, sages, ancestors, and men.
Surrounded by brāhmaṇas, he went upstream along the Sarasvatī to Pṛthūdaka, Bindusaras, Tritakūpa, Sudarśana,
Viśāla, Brahma-tīrtha, Cakra, and the Prācī-sarasvatī.

O descendant of Bharata, he traveled along the Yamunā and the Gaṅgā to Naimiṣa, where the sages were performing a long sacrificial session (*sattra*). Perceiving that he had arrived, the sages who were conducting the long sacrifice [welcomed him].
Having greeted him according to custom, bowed down, and risen to honor him,
he— being himself honored along with his retinue and having accepted a seat—
beheld the great sage’s disciple, Romaharṣaṇa, as he sat there.
Seeing the charioteer neither rising to greet them nor offering a respectful salutation with joined palms, and observing him seated above those brahmins, Mādhava became enraged;
for this man, born of an inverse union, sits over these brahmins.
"Likewise, this evil-minded one deserves death for killing us, the protectors of dharma;
for though he was once a disciple of the blessed Ṛṣi, he studied the various dharma-śāstras along with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas in their entirety."
For one who is unsubdued, undisciplined, and vainly considers himself a scholar,
his qualities do not lead to excellence— just as those of an actor who has not conquered his own self.
Indeed, it was for this purpose that my incarnation was brought about in this world.
"Those who fly the banner of righteousness are to be slain by me, for they are greater sinners than ordinary criminals.
Having said this much, the Lord turned away from the killing of the wicked; yet, because of his compassionate nature, the Master struck him with the tip of a blade of kusha grass held in his hand.

Crying out "Alas! Alas!", all the sages, their minds distressed, said to the divine Saṅkarṣaṇa: "O Lord, an unrighteous act has been committed by you, O delighter of the Yadus, for the seat of Brahmā was offered to him by us."
Your lifespan shall last as long as you do not grow weary, until the sacrifice is completed;
for although you acted without knowing it, you have committed the slaughter of a Brahmin, since even the life-span of one such as you, a master of yoga, is subject to the constraints of destiny.

"O Purifier of the World, if you, impelled by no other, will perform this act which purifies even the murder of a brahmin for the sake of gathering the people, [it shall be so]. The Blessed Lord said:
"Out of a desire to show favor to the world, I shall perform the expiation for my killing;
let whatever rule was ordained in the first kalpa be prescribed for me.
Indeed, his lifespan, strength, and even his senses have become long-lasting."
"Whatever has been requested, accomplish that by means of your yogic power (yoga-māyā).
The sages said:
"Regarding the power of your weapon, your prowess, and even our own death..."
"O Rāma, let it be arranged in such a way that these words may become true.
The Blessed Lord said:
"It is the instruction of the Vedas that a son who is born is indeed one's own self."
"Therefore, may he who speaks for him possess long life, sensory vigor, and strength.
O best of sages, tell me what your desire is; I shall fulfill it. Or rather, O wise ones, consider how I might offer honor to one who was unaware of my presence."
The sages said:
"The son of Ilvala was a terrible Dānava named Balvala;
he would come on every lunar festival and defile our sacrificial session."
O descendant of Daśārha, destroy that evil one; that is our supreme service to you.
Then, having circumambulated the land of Bhārata-varṣa—which rains down pus, blood, feces, urine, wine, and flesh—proceed with a well-composed mind.
"By performing this for twelve months and bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), you shall be purified.
Śrī Śuka said:
Then, when a festival day arrived, a fierce rain of dust fell.
O King, Bhīma became the wind, and there was the smell of pus everywhere. Then a rain consisting of impurities was unleashed by Balvala;
it fell upon the sacrificial hall, and he was seen holding a trident.
Beholding him of massive body, resembling a heap of crushed collyrium,
with a crest and beard like molten copper, and a face marked by fierce fangs and knitted brows,
Rāma remembered his mace, the destroyer of enemy armies.
The plow and the club, which subdue the Daityas, quickly presented themselves to him.
Dragging Balvala, who moved through the sky, with the tip of his plow,
the enraged Balarāma struck the head of that violator of Brahman with his mace.

With his forehead split open and shedding blood, he fell to the earth, uttering cries of distress like a crimson mountain struck by a thunderbolt. Then the sages, having offered praises to Rāma and bestowed infallible blessings upon him, departed.
The highly fortunate ones consecrated him, just as the gods consecrated the slayer of Vṛtra;
they gave Rāma the Vaijayantī garland, which consists of unfading lotuses that are the very abode of Śrī,
as well as two divine garments and celestial ornaments.
Then, permitted by those brahmins, he went to the Kauśikī river; having bathed there, he proceeded to the lake from which the Sarayū flows. Following the current of the Sarayū, he arrived at Prayāga.
Having bathed and offered libations to the gods and others, he went to the hermitage of Pulaha;
having bathed in the Gomatī and Gaṇḍakī, he immersed himself in the Vipāśā and the Śoṇa;
and having gone to Gayā and worshipped the ancestors, he proceeded to the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Having performed ritual ablutions on Mount Mahendra, and having seen and saluted Rāma,
he then visited the Saptagodāvarī, the Veṇā, the Pampā, and the Bhīmarathī; thereafter,
having seen Skanda, Rāma proceeded to Śrīśaila, the abode of Giriśa.
In the Draviḍa country, the Lord saw the highly meritorious Veṅkaṭa mountain,
the city of Kāñcī with its lovely inner chambers, the excellent river Kāverī,
and the greatly auspicious Śrīraṅga, where Hari is ever present.
He went to Ṛṣabhadri, the sacred field of Hari, as well as to Mathurā in the south and to the ocean-setu which destroys great sins;
there, Halāyudha gave ten thousand cows to the brāhmaṇas.
[He visited] the Kṛtamālā, the Tāmraparṇī, and the Malaya mountain range.
There, having bowed down to and greeted Agastya as he sat there, and having been honored by him with blessings, he was permitted to depart and went to the ocean.
There, to the south, he beheld the goddess Durgā, known as Kanyā;
then, having reached the excellent Phālguna, where five Apsarases reside,
Viṣṇu was present there, and having bathed, he touched ten thousand cows.
Then, having traveled from there through Kerala and Trigarta,
the Blessed One reached the sacred field of Śiva known as Gokarṇa, where Dhūrjaṭi is ever-present;
and after seeing the noble Dvaipāyanī, Balarāma proceeded to Śūrpāraka.
Having touched the waters of the Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, and Nirvindhyā,
he then entered Daṇḍaka and went to the Revā, where the city of Māhiṣmatī is located.
Having touched the waters at Manu-tīrtha, he returned once more to Prabhāsa.
Having heard from the twice-born what was being told regarding the battle between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas,
and the destruction of all the kṣatriyas, he considered the burden of the earth to have been removed.
He watched as Bhīma and Duryodhana fought with their clubs in the fray.
Intending to prevent the destruction [of his lineage], the joy of the Yadus departed for Vinaśana.
Yudhiṣṭhira, however, seeing him, as did the twins and Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna,
saluted him and remained silent, wondering, "What does he wish to say here?"
Seeing both of them with maces in hand, enraged and seeking victory,
moving in various wonderful circles, he said this:
"O King, O Vṛkodara, you two are heroes of equal strength."

I consider one of you superior in strength and the other superior in training; therefore, between you two who possess equal prowess, neither victory nor defeat can be discerned here. Let this fruitless battle cease.
Bound by their mutual enmity and recollecting one another’s harsh words and evil deeds, the two did not accept those words of the king as being for his benefit; instead,
Rāma, acquiescing to what was ordained by fate, departed for Dvāravatī.
Accompanied by his joyful kinsmen, headed by Ugrasena,
he returned once more to Naimiṣa; there the sages joyfully performed for him sacrifices with all their constituent parts, whereby every obstacle was completely removed.
To them, the all-pervading Lord bestowed pure discernment,

by which they knew this entire universe within the Self and the Self as pervading the universe. Having performed his own final ablutions at the conclusion of the sacrifice, he was surrounded by kinsmen, relatives, and friends.
Clad in fine garments and beautifully adorned, he shone like the moon by its own light. Indeed,
such forms as these— countless, powerful,
infinite, and immeasurable— are possessed by him who is mortal through his own illusory power (*māyā*).
Whoever should remember the deeds of Rāma, whose actions are wonderful—
the infinite Viṣṇu— in the evening and in the morning, he shall become beloved [of Him].
Śrī-Rāja said:

O Blessed One, O Lord, I wish to hear those other heroic deeds of the high-souled Mukunda, whose prowess is infinite. O Brahmin, who indeed, having heard the excellent stories of Uttamaśloka again and again, would not be satisfied?

One who knows the distinction should desist from the pursuit of desires when they cause dejection. That is true speech by which one praises His qualities; those are true hands which perform His work; that is the true mind which remembers Him dwelling within all moving and stationary beings; and that is the true ear which hears His sacred stories.

But his head bows to that which possesses both genders; for whatever he beholds, that indeed is his eye. Furthermore, the limbs of Viṣṇu belong to those people who constantly resort to the water from His feet.
Sūta said:
Questioned by Viṣṇurāta, the blessed son of Bādarāyaṇa,
whose heart was immersed in the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, spoke. Śrī Śuka said:
Kṛṣṇa had a certain friend, a brāhmaṇa who was the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman;
he was detached from the objects of the senses, tranquil in soul, and self-controlled,
living as a householder according to whatever came to him by chance.
The wife of that man clad in rags, emaciated by hunger and likewise distressed,
approached her husband; with a withered face, trembling and sinking from poverty, that devoted wife spoke to her husband.

"O Brāhmaṇa, the Blessed One is indeed the friend of the Lord, the manifest husband of Śrī, devoted to the brāhmaṇas, the refuge of all, and the bull among the devotees. O highly fortunate one, go to him, the ultimate resort of the virtuous."
He will grant abundant wealth to you who are suffering as a householder;
the Lord of the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas now resides in Dvārakā,
and he bestows even his own self upon one who remembers his lotus feet.
"Does the Teacher of the World not favor those who pursue wealth and desire, even if they are not his most beloved?
Thus was the brahmin repeatedly entreated many times by his wife;
for the sight of Him of Excellent Renown is indeed the supreme and highest gain.
Having reflected thus in his mind, he resolved to depart.
"O auspicious lady, is there anything at home that may be offered as a gift?
Having requested it, let me take four handfuls of flattened rice from the brahmins."
Having tied them in a piece of cloth, she presented them as a gift to her husband.
Taking them, that foremost of brahmins set out for Dvārakā, reflecting, "How might I obtain an audience with Kṛṣṇa?"
Accompanied by the twice-born, the brahmin passed through three enclosures and three courtyards;
he entered the house of the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, who were followers of Acyuta’s dharma. There, the twice-born entered the residence of Hari’s sixteen thousand queens.

He entered into one [of them] who had attained the glorious bliss of Brahman. Seeing him from afar while seated upon the couch of his beloved, Acyuta rose up suddenly, approached, and joyfully embraced him with both arms.
Exceedingly delighted by the touch of his dear friend, the brahmin seer,
the lotus-eyed Lord shed tears from his eyes.
Then, having seated his friend upon a couch, he himself offered him worship.
Having offered water for washing his feet, O King, the Blessed One, the purifier of the worlds, took that foot-washing water upon his head;
he then anointed himself with divine fragrances, sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron.
Having joyfully honored his friend with fragrant incenses and rows of lamps,
and having offered him betel-leaf and a cow, he welcomed him.
[He saw] the twice-born man wearing tattered, soiled, and emaciated garments, his body covered with visible veins.
The queen herself attended upon him with a yak-tail fan; and when the women of the inner apartments saw her being honored by Kṛṣṇa of stainless fame,
they were filled with great joy and wonder that she, though a discarded woman, had been so welcomed.
"What merit has been performed by this mendicant who has shaken off all worldly ties,
who is destitute of fortune, despised in this world, and most base—
yet he who was nurtured by the Teacher of the Three Worlds, the Abode of Śrī?"
Having abandoned Śrī, who was seated upon the couch,

as the elder brother [Balarāma] embraced him, they both held each other’s hands, O King, and recited charming verses concerning themselves while they had lived together in the house of their preceptor.

The Blessed Lord said: O Brahmin, O knower of dharma, after you had completed your studies at the house of your preceptor and offered him the prescribed fee, did you, upon returning home, marry a suitable wife or not?
"O wise one, it is well known to me that your mind is generally not directed toward household life according to its desires, nor do you take great pleasure in wealth. Indeed,
some perform their duties with minds unassailed by worldly desires."
Having abandoned their divine natures for the sake of gathering the world together as I have done,
O Brahmin, do you perhaps remember our residence in the house of the guru,
from which a twice-born man, having realized that which is to be known, attains the further shore of darkness?
O dear one, he is indeed the manifest source of virtuous deeds for the twice-born in this world;
he is the primordial teacher who bestows knowledge upon those in the various stages of life (āśramas), just as I am.
Surely, O brāhmaṇa, those well-versed in the meaning of the scriptures here [know him] to be the protector of those following the system of social classes and stages of life.
Those who cross the ocean of worldly existence by means of my word or that of their guru— neither through ritual worship, progeny, austerity, nor tranquility do I,
the Self of all beings, become so pleased as I am by service to the guru.
O Brahmin, do you perhaps remember our conduct while we were living with our preceptor? Once, when we had been urged by the preceptor’s wife to fetch firewood,
we entered a vast forest during the season that is not the rainy season, O twice-born one.
A fierce wind and rain arose, accompanied by harsh peals of thunder;
the sun had set, and the quarters of the sky were shrouded in darkness.
Neither the low ground nor the riverbanks could be discerned as they were submerged in water.
In that great flood of water, we were violently struck by mighty winds and waves;
unable to discern the directions, we wandered about in the forest, distressed and holding one another's hands.
Having learned of this when the sun had risen, the preceptor Sāndīpani—
Seeking us out, the teacher found his disciples in distress.
"Alas, my dear children! For our sake you have become so deeply sorrowful;
yet the self is indeed most dear to living beings, and you have disregarded it to be devoted to me."
This indeed is the repayment to the guru that must be performed by his true disciples:
namely, the offering of all things and one's very self to the guru with a pure heart.
"O best of the twice-born, I am pleased; may your desires be fulfilled."
"May the Vedic hymns never lose their potency for me, both in this world and the next.
For those who dwell in the house of the guru, such various blessings as these arise; indeed, it is only through the grace of the guru that a person attains fullness for the sake of ultimate peace.
The venerable brāhmaṇa said: O God of gods, O Teacher of the universe, what has remained unaccomplished for us,
whose dwelling was with our guru, that you— who desire the truth— should still act?
O All-pervading Lord, for one whose body consists of the Veda (Brahman) and who is the receptacle of all auspicious things,
dwelling with teachers is an absolute mockery.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus conversing with that foremost of the twice-born, Lord Hari—
who knows the minds of all beings— smilingly spoke to him.
The blessed Kṛṣṇa, who is devoted to the brāhmaṇas, laughingly addressed his dear friend, the brāhmaṇa.
Beholding him with a glance full of love,
the Blessed Lord, who is indeed the refuge of the virtuous, spoke: "O Brāhmaṇa, what gift have you brought for me from your home?"
Even a minute thing offered by devotees with love becomes truly abundant for Me; even a vast amount offered by one who is not a devotee does not lead to My satisfaction.
He who offers Me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water with devotion—[I accept that offering].
"I eat only that which is offered with devotion by one whose self is purified"—
though addressed thus, O King, the twice-born, feeling ashamed before the Lord of Śrī,
did not offer him the handful of flattened rice, keeping his face cast down.
Perceiving directly the reason for his arrival, he who sees the Self in all beings reflected: "He did not worship me in the past out of a desire for wealth;
rather, as a friend to his devoted wife, he desires to do what is pleasing to her."
"Once he has arrived, I shall give him riches difficult even for the immortals to obtain.
Thinking thus, she herself took from the garment of the twice-born man the flattened rice tied in a cloth, while he asked, "What is this?"

"Indeed, O friend, this has been brought to me which is supremely pleasing; truly, my dear, these grains of flattened rice satisfy me in every way. Having thus eaten one handful, he took up a second to eat.
At that moment, Śrī, devoted to him, took the hand of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
"O Soul of the Universe, this much is sufficient for the perfection of all prosperity in this world or in the next; for a man, nothing else causes Your satisfaction."

Having stayed that night in the abode of Acyuta, and having eaten and drunk, the brāhmaṇa considered himself as happy as if he had gone to heaven. On the following day, he was greeted with his own blessings by the Soul of the Universe.
O dear one, returning by the same path and filled with joy, he went to his own home;
yet, having failed to obtain wealth from Kṛṣṇa, he did not ask for it himself,
but returned to his house bashfully, comforted by the vision of the Great One.

"Oh! I have witnessed the devotion to Brahmanas of the God who is the Friend of Brahmanas, in that even one as utterly destitute as I was embraced by Lakṣmī while she rested upon His chest. Where am I—a wretched sinner—and where is Kṛṣṇa, the abode of Śrī?"

"I was embraced by his arms with the words, 'O kinsman of Brahman,' and seated upon a couch favored by my beloved, like a brother; and when I was weary, I was fanned by the queen with a fly-whisk in her hand."
Honored like a god by the God of gods, the God of the brahmins, through supreme service such as massaging his feet and other attentions, he was treated with divine respect.
He is the source of heaven and liberation for men, and of all prosperity on the earth and in the lower regions.
The worship of His feet is the root of all perfections.
"Lest this poor man, having obtained wealth, become intoxicated and fail to remember Me," the Compassionate One surely did not grant me abundant riches.
Thinking thus within himself, he arrived at the vicinity of his own home,
which was surrounded on all sides by celestial chariots resembling the sun, fire, and moon,
and by various groves and gardens filled with the warbling of flocks of birds.
Abounding with blooming white water-lilies, lotuses, kahlāras, and blue lotuses, and frequented by well-adorned men and deer-eyed women, [Uddhava wondered]:
"What is this? Whose place is it? And how did this come to be?"
While he was thus reflecting, the men and women, possessing the splendor of immortals,
received that illustrious one with abundant singing and instrumental music. Hearing that her husband had arrived, his wife was filled with great joy and agitation.
She emerged quickly from the house like the goddess Śrī herself leaving her abode.
Seeing her husband, the devoted wife, her eyes filled with tears of love-longing,
closed her eyes and bowed down, embracing him in spirit and mind.
Seeing his wife radiant like a celestial goddess in her chariot,
shining in the midst of maidservants adorned with golden neck-ornaments, he was filled with wonder;
delighted, he entered his own palace accompanied by her.
It was endowed with hundreds of jeweled pillars like the palace of Mahendra;
there were couches resembling the foam of milk, made of ivory with golden coverings,
as well as beds and fly-whisks with handles of gold.
There were golden seats with soft coverings,
and radiant canopies from which hung strings of pearls;
and upon walls of clear crystal and great emeralds, [they shone].
Beholding the shining jewel-lamps and the women adorned with jewels, as well as all those abundant riches there, the Brāhmaṇa,
remaining unperturbed, reflected upon his own prosperity which was likewise without apparent cause.
"Alas! Surely this is the cause of prosperity for me, who am unfortunate and perpetually poor;
for no one other than the Lord of Great Opulence, the best of the Yadus, could possibly grant such a favor.
Indeed, even without being asked, that giver of abundant enjoyments bestows much wealth upon a suppliant in his very presence."
Like a rain-cloud, he himself beholds it; that bull among the Dāśārhas, my friend,
makes even a small gift given by himself yield great fruit,
and he makes even a trifling service rendered by a well-wisher bear abundant results.

The Great-Souled One, filled with affection, accepted this single handful of flattened rice offered by me; may I possess toward Him alone— friendship, companionship, goodwill, and servitude— in birth after birth.
For one who is attached to the Great Soul, the abode of all qualities, there arises association with His devotees.

Indeed, the unborn Lord does not bestow diverse riches, kingdoms, or opulences upon a devotee whose awakening is not long-lasting; for He Himself perceives that the downfall of the wealthy arises from pride.
Having thus resolved with his intellect, that devotee who was exceedingly attached to Janārdana enjoyed sense objects with his wife, yet he did so without being overly lustful.
[He performed this] for that Lord of gods, Hari, the Master of sacrifice and the Sovereign.
"The brāhmaṇas are the source and the deity; there exists nothing higher than them.

Thus, that brāhmaṇa, a friend of the Blessed One, having seen his own servant defeated by the Unconquered, attained His abode—the goal of the virtuous—without delay, as the bonds of his self were loosened by the force of meditation upon Him.
Having heard this devotion to Brahmanas from the God who is the friend of Brahmanas,
a person who has attained such a disposition toward the Blessed Lord is liberated from the bondage of karma.
Śrī Śuka said:
Now, once while Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa were dwelling in Dvārakā,
there occurred a very great solar eclipse, as if at the end of a kalpa.
Knowing of this, O King, the people beforehand prepared for it on all sides.
Desiring to achieve their own welfare, they went to the sacred field of Samanta-pañcaka;
it was there that Rāma, the best among those who bear arms, while making the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas,
created great lakes from the flood of the kings' blood.

And there the Lord Rāma performed sacrifices; though untouched by ritual action himself, the Lord acted in such a way as to cause the world to accept it, so that others might dispel their sins. During that great pilgrimage to sacred fords (*tīrtha-yātrā*), the people of Bhārata arrived there.
And the Vṛṣṇis— Akrūra, Vasudeva, Āhuka, and others—
as well as Gada, Pradyumna, Sāmba, and the rest, along with Sucandra, Śuka, and Sāraṇa, went to that sacred field, O descendant of Bharata, desiring to destroy their own sins.
Aniruddha remained for protection, as did Kṛtavarmā, the leader of the host;
they were accompanied by chariots resplendent as celestial mansions, horses leaping with agility,
trumpeting elephants resembling clouds, and men who shone like Vidyādharas.
Possessing great splendor, wearing golden garlands, and adorned with divine wreaths, garments, and armor, they shone upon the path like sky-dwellers accompanied by their wives.
Having bathed there, those highly fortunate ones, fasting and perfectly composed in mind, remained steadfast.
The Vṛṣṇis gave cows adorned with garments, garlands, and golden necklaces to the brāhmaṇas. Having bathed again according to the prescribed rites in the lakes of Rāma,
they gave their own food to the foremost of the twice-born, saying, "May we have devotion for Kṛṣṇa."

And having been permitted by him, the Vṛṣṇis, who had Kṛṣṇa as their deity, ate at his own hand and sat down at will beneath the feet of trees with lush shade. There they beheld the kings who had arrived— friends and relatives.
O King, [he conquered] the Matsyas, Uśīnaras, Kauśalyas, Vidarbhas, Kurus, Sṛñjayas,
Kāmbojas, Kaikayas, Madras, Kuntīs, Ānartas, and Keralas,
as well as hundreds of others belonging to his own side and those of the enemy.
Having long yearned for their friends, the cowherds headed by Nanda, and the cowherd women, they—

whose lotus-like hearts and faces were filled with the splendor of blossoming joy at the sight of one another— embraced them firmly; with tears streaming from their eyes, their skin bristling with thrill, and their speech choked with emotion, they attained supreme bliss.
And the women, beholding one another with eyes whose outer corners were bright with smiles of great affection, addressed each other, pressing their breasts—
smeared with the paste of saffron— against one another's breasts.
Having struck them with their arms, their eyes filled with tears of affection;
then, having offered salutations to the elders and being saluted in turn by the youths,
they asked after each other's welcome and welfare, and engaged in mutual conversations concerning Kṛṣṇa.
Beholding her brothers, sisters, their sons, her parents, her brothers' wives, and Mukunda, Pṛthā abandoned her grief through conversation. Kuntī said:
"Noble brother, I consider myself one who has failed to fulfill his purpose, since even in times of distress you, O most virtuous ones, did not remember my news—
neither as friends, kinsmen, sons, brothers, nor even as parents."
Those whose fate is unfavorable do not remember their own kin.
Śrī Vasudeva said:
O Mother, do not be resentful toward us, for men are but the playthings of destiny.
For the world is under the control of the Lord; it either acts of its own accord or is made to act.
O sister, tormented by Kaṃsa, we have all fled in every direction, but now, by fate, we have once again been brought back to this place.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, those kings were honored by Vasudeva, Ugrasena, and the other Yadus; they remained filled with the supreme bliss of having beheld Acyuta.
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, the son of Ambikā (Dhṛtarāṣṭra), and Gāndhārī with her sons;
likewise the Pāṇḍavas with their wives, Kuntī, Sañjaya, Vidura, and Kṛpa;
Kuntībhoja, Virāṭa, Bhīṣmaka, and the great Nagnajit.
Purujit, Drupada, Śalya, Dhṛṣṭaketu, the King of Kāśī, Damaghoṣa, Viśālākṣa, the King of Mithilā, the Kings of Madra and Kekaya,
Yudhāmanyu, Suśarmā, Bāhlīka, and others, along with their sons.
O Indra among kings, those monarchs who were devoted to Yudhiṣṭhira were filled with wonder upon beholding the form of Śauri, the abode of Śrī, together with his wives.
Then they were properly honored by Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
Filled with joy, they praised the Vṛṣṇis who were favored by Kṛṣṇa:
"O Lord of the Bhojas! You are truly the ones among men here who have attained their true birth, since you behold Kṛṣṇa again and again, who is difficult even for yogīs to see."
His fame, praised by the Vedas, is sufficient to purify this world;
so too are the water from his feet for washing and his words, which are the scripture.
Even the earth, though her fortune was scorched by Time, [was purified] by his lotus feet.
The power arising from touch showers us with all desired objects;
likewise, through seeing Him, touching Him, following in His path, conversing with Him,
sharing His bed, seat, and food, and through sexual union or kinship by birth, [the same result is attained].
In whose houses Viṣṇu himself became the cessation of heaven and liberation for you who were treading the path to hell.
Śrī Śuka said:
Nanda, learning that the Yadus had arrived there with Kṛṣṇa at their head,
came there surrounded by cowherds and those who had come in wagons, desiring to see them.
Upon seeing him, the Vṛṣṇis rejoiced, rising up like bodies regaining their life-breath.
Overcome with longing from not having seen them for so long, they embraced him tightly; Vasudeva, filled with joy yet overwhelmed by love,
embraced them while remembering the sufferings inflicted by Kaṃsa and the entrusting of his sons to Gokula.
O best of the Kurus, having embraced Kṛṣṇa and Rāma and saluted their parents, the two of them said nothing out of love, their throats choked with tears. Then,
having seated them upon their own thrones and embraced them with both arms, [the parents spoke].
And the highly fortunate Yaśodā abandoned her grief for her two sons;
then Rohiṇī and Devakī, embracing the Queen of Vraja and remembering the friendship she had shown them, spoke with voices choked with tears.
O Queen of Vraja, who could ever forget your unceasing friendship?
Even having attained the sovereignty of Indra, there is no recompense for it here in this world.
These two, who have never seen their own parents, are now the children of you both.
Having obtained nourishment, prosperity, and protection through their mutual affection, they dwelt together like the eyelids of the eyes; for those who are virtuous,
there is no distinction between "self" and "other," nor is there any fear anywhere.
Śrī Śuka said: And the gopīs, having finally attained Kṛṣṇa— the long-desired one—
cursed the eyelashes that had obstructed their vision whenever they looked at him.
Having been brought to their hearts by his glances and having embraced him fully, they all attained that state of being which is difficult even for those constantly united with Him to achieve.
The Blessed One, having approached them while they were in such a state, withdrew to a secluded place.
Embracing them and inquiring after their welfare, He spoke these words with a smile:
"O friends, do you remember us— those who, desiring to accomplish the purpose of our own kin,
went forth for a long time with minds intent on destroying the faction of our enemies?"
"Or perhaps you disregard us out of suspicion that we are ungrateful;
surely the Blessed One joins and separates all living beings,
just as the wind disperses a mass of clouds, straw, cotton, and dust."
The Creator of beings joins them together and casts them forth again in that same way.
Indeed, devotion to me leads all beings to immortality;
by good fortune, you have had such affection for me, which brings one to me.
For I am indeed the beginning, the end, the inner, and the outer of all beings;
just as space, water, earth, air, light, and women are among material things,
so too, O lady, these elements are contained within all beings by means of My own self.
"Behold both [the individual self and the Supreme] as manifest within Me, the Imperishable, the Supreme.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus were the gopīs instructed by Kṛṣṇa through this teaching on the inner self (adhyātma).
Their individual sheaths (the subtle bodies) destroyed by the remembrance of Him, they attained Him and said: "O Lotus-navelled One, we have reached Your lotus feet,
which are meditated upon in the heart by the masters of yoga possessed of unfathomable wisdom."
May that abode, which serves as the supporting hand for crossing over the pit of worldly existence, always arise in the minds of us who dwell in household life.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus shown his grace, the Blessed One— the teacher and ultimate refuge of the gopīs—
then inquired after Yudhiṣṭhira and all his well-wishers, who are imperishable.
Thus questioned by the Lord of the World and treated with great honor, they [responded].
With hearts full of joy, their sins destroyed by the sight of His feet, they replied:

"O Lord, how could there ever be anything inauspicious for those who drink with the cups of their ears the nectar flowing from Your lotus feet— which issues from the mouths of great souls and severs the forgetfulness of embodied beings regarding their true Self?"

For he is the one who, by means of his own power, has shaken off the three states created by the self; he is the undivided immersion in bliss, whose consciousness is unimpeded, and who, as the protector of the Vedas manifested in time, has assumed his yogic form.
"We bow to the one who manifests through *māyā* and whose path is that of the *paramahaṃsas*.
Śrī Ṛṣi said:
"Thus [he spoke] among the people to the crest-jewel of those whose verses are supreme..."
While they were thus offering praises, the women of the Andhakas and Kauravas gathered together and recounted among themselves various stories of Govinda;
listen as I describe to you those tales sung throughout the three worlds.
Śrī Draupadī said: "O Vaidarbhī, O blessed Acyutā; O Jāmbavatī, O Kauśalā;
O Satyabhāmā, O Kālindī, O Śaibyā, O Rohiṇī, O Lakṣmaṇā!"
"O wives of Kṛṣṇa, the Blessed Lord himself has told us this:
how He, following worldly custom, married by means of His own internal potency.
Śrī Rukmiṇī said:
While the kings had their bows raised to deliver [the boy] to the King of Cedi, He— whose foot-dust was worn as a crest by invincible warriors—
was led away like a lion from a herd of goats and sheep.
"May His feet, which are the abode of that splendor, be for my worship.
Śrī Satyabhāmā said:
"He who, by me—with a heart pained by the slaughter of my kinsmen and with limbs emaciated..."
In order to wipe away the stain of the curse, he brought [the jewel];
then, having conquered the king of the bears, he gave him the gem,
by which the terrified father ordered him to give it even to the Lord.
Śrī Jāmbavatī said:
"O wise one, knowing that this [Rāma] was his own lord and deity who had fashioned his body,
he fought with him for twenty-seven days."
Knowing this, Parīkṣit offered me worship; grasping my feet with his jewel, he said, "I am her slave.
Śrī Kālindī said:
Knowing that she was performing austerities with the desire for the touch of my feet, I approached her as a friend and took her hand; I am that very woman who used to sweep her house—
thus spoke Śrī Mitravindā.

He who, having approached me at my self-choice marriage and having defeated the kings, led me away like an elephant’s enemy leading a captive elephant to the herd; and who drove my two brothers, who had done him harm, out of his own city, the abode of prosperity.
"May I have the fortune of washing His feet.
Śrī Satyā said:
"There were seven bulls, possessed of exceeding strength and vigor, with very sharp horns."

Having swiftly subdued those challenges set by his father to test the prowess of a king, he— the slayer of the fiercely arrogant— played with them as children play with the offspring of goats, binding them.
He who, having thus defeated the kings on the road with his fourfold army, [won] me, whose bride-price was valor;

"Let there be service to Him for me.
Śrī Bhadrā said: "My father himself summoned Kṛṣṇa and gave me—whose heart was fixed on Kṛṣṇa—to him, along with an akṣauhiṇī of troops and my female companions."
