"May the touch of his feet be mine in birth after birth, for by that alone may my own welfare be attained as I am wandering through the cycle of karma.
Thus spoke Śrī Lakṣmaṇā.

O Queen, even my mind—having heard the birth and deeds of Acyuta sung repeatedly by Nārada—became fixed upon Mukunda; indeed, she who holds a lotus in her hand chose him after due reflection, having set aside the guardians of the worlds.
O virtuous lady, my father, who is affectionate toward his daughter, understood my intention.
There, the one known as Bṛhatsena devised a stratagem so that,
at the self-choice ceremony (*svayaṃvara*), the King of Matsya might be chosen by Pārtha;
for while this [king] appeared to be hidden from view, he was actually visible within the water.
Having heard this, thousands of kings, who were experts in the principles of all missiles and weapons and accompanied by their teachers, came from all directions to my father’s city;
they were all honored by my father according to their prowess and their age.
With their minds fixed on me, they took up their bows with arrows in the assembly to shoot;
some, unable to string them, cast them aside; others, having drawn the bowstring back to their ear, fell down, struck by him.
Other heroes—the Māgadhas, Ambaṣṭhas, and Cedis—strung their bows;
yet Bhīma, Duryodhana, and Karṇa did not perceive His position.
But the Matsyas, seeing what appeared like a fish in the water and knowing His true state, [perceived Him].
Pārtha, though striving, could neither cut nor even touch the arrow; then,
when those proud kṣatriyas had turned back with their pride shattered,
the Blessed One took up his bow and effortlessly strung it.
Having aimed his arrow at that fish while it was seen but once in the water,
he struck it down with the shaft as the sun stood in the *abhijit* constellation;
then the drums resounded in the sky and shouts of victory arose upon the earth.
And the gods, overwhelmed with joy, released showers of flowers.
Then I entered that arena, my feet adorned with tinkling anklets, holding a radiant garland of golden jewels.
Having put on two new garments of the finest silk,
her face showing a bashful smile, with a garland held in her braided hair, she raised her face, which was radiant with the luster of her abundant locks and earrings.
Gazing all around at the cheeks of Murāri with her cool smiles and sidelong glances, she, whose heart was enamored, slowly placed her own garland upon the shoulder of the king.
At that time, mṛdaṅgas, paṭahas, conchs, kettledrums, ānakas, and other instruments resounded; actors and dancers danced, and singers sang.
While the Blessed Lord, the Master of Maya, was thus being chosen, O King, the leaders of the royal hosts [proceeded].
O Yājñasenī, they could not endure him, for they were rivals afflicted by the arrows of love.
Then, having placed me upon a chariot drawn by four excellent horses,
he stood in the battle with four arms, equipped for combat and raising his Śārṅga bow.
Dāruka urged on the chariot with its golden fittings, O Queen,
like a lion among deer while the kings looked on;
some of those princes then endeavored to stop him on the road.
With their weapons raised, they stood ready like lions of a village against Hari;
with the volleys of arrows discharged from his Śārṅga bow, some had their arms, feet, and necks severed and fell in the battle,
while others abandoned it and fled.
Then the Lord of the Yadus entered the city of Kuśasthalī— which was exquisitely adorned with variegated archways featuring banners and cloth streamers that eclipsed the sun—
and which is celebrated both in heaven and on earth.
He entered his own abode like the sun;
my father honored his friends, associates,
and kinsmen with costly garments, ornaments, beds, seats, and furnishings.
With female servants, all manner of riches, soldiers, elephants, chariots,
and horses, he devotedly gave costly weapons to the Perfect One (Pūrṇa).
We indeed became the household slaves of that one who delights in the Self.
"Indeed, through the cessation of all attachments and by means of austerity, we have become [liberated].
The queens said:
"Having slain Bhauma along with his hosts in battle, we were imprisoned by him."

Then, knowing that we had won the daughters of the kings in the conquest of the earth, He who has all desires fulfilled led us— who were remembering Him and seeking liberation from the cycle of worldly existence— to take refuge at His lotus feet.
O virtuous lady, we do not desire sovereignty, nor lordship over heaven, nor even the status of a king;
nor do we desire the rank of a universal monarch, the position of Brahmā, or even the eternal abode of Hari— the very dust of whose glorious feet is the source of all fortune.
The women of Vraja desire to bear upon their heads the fragrance rich with the saffron from the breasts of the wielder of the mace; even the forest-dwellers, the grasses, the creepers,
the cows, and the cowherds long for the touch of the feet of that Great Soul as he tends the cattle.
Śrī Śuka said:
Then Pṛthā, the daughter of Subala, Yājñasenī, Mādhavī, the wives of the kings, and the cowherd women heard [the news].
As Kṛṣṇa, the soul of all, Hari,
was thus being addressed by the women among women and by the men among men, they were all filled with wonder at the continuous bond of affection, their eyes overwhelmed by a flood of tears.
The sages arrived there, desiring to behold Kṛṣṇa and Rāma: Dvaipāyana, Nārada, Cyavana, Devala,
Asita, Viśvāmitra, Śatānanda, Bharadvāja, and Gautama.
The blessed Rāma with his disciples, Vasiṣṭha, Gālava, Bhṛgu,
Pulastya, Kaśyapa, Atri, Mārkaṇḍeya, Bṛhaspati,
Dvita, Trita, Ekata, and likewise Aṅgiras, the son of Brahmā.
Agastya, Yājñavalkya, Vāmadeva, and others likewise;
seeing them, the kings who were previously seated,
as well as the Pāṇḍavas, Kṛṣṇa, and Rāma, suddenly rose and bowed down to those who are worshipped by the entire universe.
They all honored them in return, as did Acyuta together with Rāma,
with welcome greetings, seats, water for the feet, respectful offerings (*arghya*), garlands, incense, and ointments.
When they were seated comfortably, the Blessed One, whose body is the protector of dharma, spoke to them.
While that great assembly listened with restrained speech, the Blessed Lord said:
"Oh! We have truly borne our births; we have obtained the fruit of it in its entirety."
The vision of the Lord of Yoga is difficult even for the gods to attain;
how much more so for men of meager austerity, who perceive the deity only through their physical eyes?
[Yet for them] there is the sight, the touch, the questioning, the bowing, the worship of his feet, and so forth.
For holy places do not consist of water, nor are the gods made of clay or stone;
the virtuous purify by their mere sight,
whereas fire, the sun, and the moon and stars do not.
Neither earth, water, ether, air, speech, nor mind—
those who worship these as distinct from the Self take away their sin;
the wise destroy it by serving [the Lord] for even a moment.
He who perceives the self in this corpse composed of the three humors,
who considers his wife and others as his own, who regards the earth as worthy of worship,
and who never at any time regards water as a sacred ford— [he is truly deluded].
Among those who were knowledgeable, he himself appeared as that very bull and donkey.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus heard from the Lord Kṛṣṇa, whose intellect is unimpeded...
O brahmins, his words were difficult to follow; with their minds bewildered, they remained silent for a long time.
Then, after deep reflection, the sages, smiling, spoke to that teacher of the world regarding the Lord’s role as the one to be ruled, saying, "It is for the sake of gathering people."
The sages said:
"By whose illusory power we—who are the supreme knowers of truth and the lords of the creators of the universe—are utterly deluded;
by whose will He remains hidden even from those who seek Him—oh, how wonderful is the Lord’s inscrutable activity!"

Though effortless, the One creates, preserves, and devours this manifold universe by means of His own self, yet He is not bound—just as the earth, though possessing many names and forms through its earthly products, remains unchanged. Oh, how the conduct of the All-pervading Lord is a mere imitation!
Nevertheless, from time to time, You assume the mode of pure goodness (*sattva*) for the protection of Your own people and for the restraint of the wicked.
By Your own divine play, You, the Supreme Person, the soul of the system of social classes and stages of life, established the eternal path of the Vedas.
Through austerity, Vedic study, and self-restraint, the pure Brahman is Your heart;
therein is perceived that which is manifest, that which is unmanifest, and that which is beyond them.

Therefore, O Brahman, you honor the community of brāhmaṇas, which is the source of the scriptures for Yourself; as such, you are the foremost among those devoted to the brāhmaṇas and the abode of all that is good. Today, our birth, our learning, our austerity, and our very sight have attained their fulfillment.

Obeisances to that Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa of unimpeded intelligence, the Supreme Soul whose greatness is concealed by His own yoga-māyā, and who, having united with You— the true goal— becomes the ultimate among all auspicious things.
Those kings do not know Him, nor do the Vṛṣṇis who find delight in the One alone; they do not know the Self, Time, and the Lord, who is concealed by the curtain of His illusory power (māyā),
just as a sleeping person does not perceive the Self when viewing the reality of the material modes.
One does not know the Supreme, who is devoid of name, form, senses,

and objects; likewise, one whose mind is bewildered by the illusory power (*māyā*) through the longing of the senses for objects that are mere names and forms does not know You, due to the corruption of their memory.

Today we have beheld Your foot, which is the abode of the sacred ford that destroys the flood of sins, held within our hearts by those whose yoga has reached full maturity; for us, the sheaths of the individual soul have been shattered by the force of overflowing devotion.
"They have attained your state; now, please show favor to these devotees.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus taken leave of the descendant of Daśārha, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Yudhiṣṭhira...
"O royal sage, the sages have set their minds on returning to their own hermitages. Seeing this, the highly illustrious Vasudeva approached them,
bowed down, touched their feet, and, with great self-restraint, spoke these words.
Śrī Vasudeva said:
"Obeisances to you all, O gods! O sages, please listen;
may it be told how the removal of our karma may be achieved through action."
Śrī Nārada said:
O brāhmaṇas, this is not at all surprising that Vasudeva, desiring to know what is for his own welfare, questioned us after considering Kṛṣṇa to be but a child.
In this world, proximity to mortals is a cause for neglect;
just as one who has bathed in the Ganges might go to other waters there for purification,
so it is with those who have experienced His realization through the cycles of dissolution and creation over time.
He is not harmed by anything— neither from himself nor from another, nor by any quality whatsoever.
One might regard that Lord, whose experience is unobstructed by the flows of afflictions, karma, and the ripening of the *guṇas*, who is without a second,
and who is embraced by his own manifestations such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), as being like the sun obscured by clouds, frost, or eclipses.
Then, O King, having addressed Anasūyā’s son, the sages spoke while all the kings, as well as Acyuta and Rāma, were listening:
"This removal of the effects of past actions through [present] action has been rightly demonstrated by him."
That one should worship Viṣṇu, the Lord of all sacrifices, with faith through various rites—
this indeed is the tranquility of the mind shown by the wise through the eye of the scriptures; it is a yoga that is easy to practice and a dharma that brings joy to the self.
This is the path leading to well-being for the twice-born householder: that the Supreme Person (Puruṣa) be worshipped with pure wealth acquired through faith.
[One should abandon] the desire for wealth through sacrifices and gifts, as well as the desire for wives and children through household life.
O Lord, a wise man should, in due course of time, relinquish the desire for his own self and the desire for the world.
Having abandoned all desires for the village, all those steadfast ones went to the forest of asceticism.
O Master, a twice-born man is born with three debts: toward the gods, the sages, and the ancestors.
One who abandons those [debts] without having discharged them through sacrifice, study, and progeny shall fall;

but you, O high-minded one, are now liberated from two—the debts to the sages and the ancestors—having released the debt to the gods through sacrifices; remain free from debt, though without a refuge.
"O Vasudeva, you have surely propitiated Hari, the Lord of the worlds, with supreme devotion, since He has entered into the state of being your son. Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard those words, the high-minded Vasudeva bowed his head, propitiated them, and chose those sages as his officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
O King, those sages, being thus chosen according to dharma, [accepted] that righteous man.
In that sacred field, they caused sacrifices to be performed with rituals according to the most excellent procedures.
When the initiation for those rites had commenced, O King, the Vṛṣṇis— wearing lotus garlands, having bathed, dressed in fine garments, and being well-adorned like kings— proceeded.
And his queens, joyful, with golden coins upon their necks and wearing beautiful garments, approached the initiation hall; they were anointed and held sacrificial materials in their hands.
Mṛdaṅgas, paṭahas, conchs, kettledrums, ānakas, and other instruments resounded.
The male and female dancers danced, while the bards and panegyrists offered hymns of praise; the sweet-voiced Gandharva women sang songs accompanied by their husbands.
The officiating priests then consecrated him with water according to the prescribed rites, after he had been anointed and rubbed with unguents.

Accompanied by his eighteen wives, like King Soma surrounded by the stars, he shone resplendent— though initiated and clad in a deerskin— along with those women who were beautifully adorned with silk garments, bracelets, necklaces, anklets, and earrings.
O great king, his officiating priests (ṛtvij), dressed in garments of precious silk and accompanied by the members of the assembly (sadasyas), shone like the slayers of Vṛtra at a sacrifice.
At that time, Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa were present, accompanied by their respective kinsmen.
The Lord of Life (Brahmā) sported with his own sons and wives, accompanied by his own manifestations.
He performed sacrifices according to the prescribed rites, characterized by the *agnihotra* and other rituals—
both primary (*prākṛta*) and modified (*vaikṛta*)— to the Lord of substances, knowledge, and action.
Then, at the proper time, he gave sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) to the officiating priests (ṛtviks) as prescribed by tradition—
having adorned them, he gave cows, land, maidens, and great wealth. Having performed the Patnīsaṃyāja and Avabhṛthya rites, those great sages [departed].
The brahmins, led by the sacrificer, bathed in the Rāma-lake.
Having bathed, he gave ornaments, garments, and likewise women to the bards.
Then, having adorned himself, he honored the social classes, down to the dogs, with food.
He honored his kinsmen, along with their wives and sons, with abundant wedding gifts; and he gratified the Vidarbhas, Kośalas, Kurus, Kāśis, Kekayas, and Sṛñjayas,
as well as the members of the assembly, the officiating priests, the hosts of gods, men, spirits, ancestors, and celestial bards.
Having taken leave of the abode of Śrī, they departed for the sacrifice, praising it;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, his younger brother, the sons of Pṛthā, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Pṛthā, the twins,
the venerable Nārada, Vyāsa, and their friends, relatives, and kinsmen all went along.
Embracing their kinsmen, the Yadus, whose hearts were moistened with affection, departed for their own lands with the hardship of separation; and other people likewise went home.
But Nanda, along with the cowherds, was honored with grand hospitality.
Accompanied by Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Ugrasena, and others, Vasudeva— who is affectionate toward his kinsmen—
having easily crossed the great ocean of his desires, remained there surrounded by his friends. With a joyful heart, he touched Nanda’s hand and spoke to him.
Śrī Vasudeva said:
O brother, that bond called affection which the Lord has fashioned for men— I consider it difficult to cast off, even for heroes who are practitioners of yoga.
That this peerless friendship has been bestowed by the most excellent ones upon us, who are unworthy of such commands, and that it shall never cease to be fruitless—
this is a blessing for you, O brothers, which we did not attain since the beginning of the kalpa.
Now, our eyes blinded by the intoxication of royal splendor do not perceive the Being who stands before us.

O Giver of Honor, let there be no royal fortune for a man who desires his own spiritual welfare, for by that [fortune] one’s vision becomes so blinded that he perceives neither his own people nor his kinsmen.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, with his heart softened by affection, Ānakadundubhi wept, his eyes filled with tears as he remembered the friendship they had shared.

Nanda, however, out of love and desiring to do what was pleasing to his friend, stayed for three months with Govinda and Rāma, honored by the Yadus, thinking, "Today or tomorrow. Then, with all his desires fulfilled, he returned to Vraja along with his kinsmen.

Having accepted the dowry presented by Vasudeva and Ugrasena, as well as by Kṛṣṇa, Uddhava, Balarāma, and others— consisting of supreme ornaments, fine linen, and various priceless furnishings— he was escorted by the Yadus and departed.

Nanda, the cowherds, and the cowherd women, having cast their minds upon the lotus feet of Govinda, were unable to draw them back and departed for Mathurā. When their kinsmen had returned, the Vṛṣṇis remained with Kṛṣṇa as their sole deity.
Seeing that the rainy season was approaching, they returned once more to Dvāravatī;
there they recounted to the people the great festival of the Yadu-lord,
including the meeting with their friends and others that had occurred during the pilgrimage to the sacred fords.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said: Then, on one occasion, when his two sons had arrived and performed obeisances at his feet,
Vasudeva greeted Saṅkarṣaṇa and Acyuta with affection and spoke to them.
Having heard the words of the sages, which indicated the abode of his two sons, he—having gained confidence through their heroic deeds—addressed them with these words:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! O Mahāyogin Saṅkarṣaṇa, O Eternal One!"

I know that you two are the direct, supreme Pradhāna and Puruṣa; for whatever, by whatever means, from whatever source, of whatever, for whatever purpose, whatever it may be, and in whatever manner and at whatever time this world exists— the Blessed Lord is directly the Sovereign of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
O Adhokṣaja, O Unborn One, having entered by Yourself this manifold universe created from Yourself, You sustain it as the vital breath and the individual soul;
those powers which belong to the creators of the universe, such as the vital breaths, are Yours, the Supreme.
Because of dependence and dissimilarity, among all things that move, it is indeed the movement of these two [the wind] that is desired.
You are the luster, the heat, the radiance, and the existence of the moon, fire, sun, stars, and lightning;
you are the stability of the mountains and the earth, and you are the function and the fragrance of the earth by its very nature.
O Lord, You are the satiation and the life-giving breath of the waters, and they are Your essence;
O Sovereign, vigor, endurance, strength, movement, and motion belong to You as Vāyu.
You are the space of the quarters, the quarters themselves, the ether, and its substratum, the primordial sound.
You are the primordial sound (*nāda*), you are the syllable *oṃ*, and you are the differentiation of forms;
you are the sense organ among the senses, and you are the gods who bestow grace upon them. You are the awakening of the intellect and the true recollection of the individual soul (*jīva*).

Among beings you are the source of all beings, and among the senses you are the Taijasa (the fire-like) ego; you are the Vaikarika (the creative) ego of all conceptualizations, and the Pradhāna that underlies all latent impressions.
Among all perishable things here, you alone are the imperishable.
Just as in the transformations of a substance, the substance alone is determined to be real,
so too the qualities— sattva, rajas, and tamas—
and their functions are truly imagined within You, the supreme Brahman, by means of Your yogic power (yoga-māyā).
Therefore, these entities do not exist when they are conceptualized within You;
for You, at other times, are indeed distinct from these transformations. Within this flow of the modes, the ignorant [fail to perceive] the Self of all.

O Lord, wandering here through the cycles of birth and death due to ignorance of the subtle goal and by the force of one's own actions, I have by chance attained this human form, so difficult to obtain even in this world; yet, though it is well-suited for spiritual progress, my life has passed away while I was negligent regarding my true self-interest, all because of Your illusory power, O Sovereign.
"This one is I, these are mine, and these are my body and its progeny"—with such bonds of affection you bind this entire world.
You two, however, are not our sons; you are directly the Lords of Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
"You have indeed descended to destroy the burden of the earth and the [corrupt] kṣatriyas; thus you have spoken.
Therefore, O Friend of the distressed, today I have come to Your lotus feet, which remove the fear of worldly existence for those who have fallen into it."
Enough, enough with this craving for the senses!
Since you, who perceive the self within mortals, have conceived the thought of us as your offspring— you, the Supreme and Unborn— did you not indeed say so yourself in the maternity chamber?
In each age, You manifest Yourself as various forms for the protection of Your own dharma,
assuming them like the sky and then casting them off; O Infinite One, O Wide-Strider, who can comprehend the power of Your illusory energy?
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus heard his father’s words, the Blessed One, the bull among the Sātvatas,
bowed with humility and replied with a smile in gentle speech.
The Blessed Lord said:
O dear ones, we consider these words of yours to be consistent in their meaning,
since you have explained the collection of essential truths with reference to us, your sons.
“I, you, that noble one, and these inhabitants of Dvārakā—
all these, O best of the Yadus, are likewise to be sought within the moving and the unmoving. For the Self alone is self-luminous, eternal, distinct from the qualities, and devoid of attributes.”
He manifests Himself in many ways among the beings created by Him and fashioned from Himself—
ether, air, fire, water, and earth— according to their respective dispositions;
though He is one, He appears as manifold through manifestation, concealment, and varying degrees of presence.
Śrī Śuka said: O King, having been thus addressed by the Blessed One, Vasudeva—
his various mental constructions dissolved upon hearing this— became silent with a joyful heart.
Then there, O best of the Kurus, Devakī, having heard from her spiritual preceptor that all the gods had been brought back by her two sons, was greatly amazed;
she informed Kṛṣṇa and Rāma about her sons who had been slaughtered by Kaṃsa.
Remembering him piteously, with eyes full of tears from her distress, Śrī Devakī spoke: Śrī Devakī said:
O Rāma, O Rāma, O immeasurable soul! O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the masters of yoga!
I know you both to be the Lords of the creators of the universe, the Original Persons; indeed,
you have descended today at my request to relieve the burden of the earth, which is oppressed by kings who are deficient in goodness and who act contrary to the scriptures.
O Soul of the Universe, I have at last come to You, whose infinitesimal fraction of a fraction is said to cause the creation, dissolution, and emergence of the entire world;
for I was urged by my father long ago to take back my dead son.
They brought the teacher’s fee from the abode of the ancestors for their guru.
"O Lords of the masters of yoga, fulfill this desire of mine:
I wish to see my sons, slain by the King of the Bhojas, brought back here."
The sage said:
Thus urged by their mother, O descendant of Bharata, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa entered Sutala, having resorted to their yogic power (yoga-māyā).
Having perceived that both had entered there— the Lord who is the soul of the universe, as well as his own son— the king of the Daityas,
his heart overflowing with the joy of that vision, was utterly overwhelmed.
Rising immediately, he prostrated himself along with his lineage.
Having joyfully brought excellent seats for those two great souls, he offered them as they sat there;
and having washed their feet, he, together with his retinue, held that water, which even Brahmā and the other gods purify themselves with.
He honored those two with magnificent garments, ornaments, and unguents;
with betel, lamps, nectar-like food, and other offerings; and by surrendering his lineage, wealth, and very self.
Bearing the lotus feet of the Blessed One, Indrasena repeatedly gazed upon them with a mind overwhelmed by love.
With eyes overflowing with tears of joy, his hair standing on end, O King, he spoke in a faltering voice.
Bali said:
"Obeisances to the infinite, the great one; obeisances to Kṛṣṇa, the creator."
To the Supreme Brahman, the source of the expansion of Sāṅkhya and Yoga,
belongs this vision of yours— difficult for living beings to attain, yet not unobtainable—
which we have received by chance, even though we are of the nature of *rajas* and *tamas*.
The Daityas, Dānavas, and Gandharvas; the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Cāraṇas;
the Yakṣas, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas; and the leaders of the Bhūtas and Pramathas—all truly abide in you, whose nature is pure goodness and who are the personification of the scriptures.

We and others like us are eternally bound by enmity; some approach Him out of intense enmity, some out of devotion, and some out of desire. Yet the gods and others, though situated in close proximity, are not so intensely possessed by the quality of goodness (sattva).
O Lord of the lords of yogīs, even the masters of yoga generally do not understand this *yoga-māyā* of yours as it truly is; how then could we?
Therefore, be gracious to us, for you are sought after by those who are free from all worldly dependencies.
Having emerged from the blind well of other homes where the mind is fixed on the lotus feet of others, and having obtained my livelihood at the feet of the refuge of the universe,
I wander alone like a peaceful sage, yet accompanied by all my friends.
"O Lord of those who are to be ruled, please instruct us; O Master, make us free from sin. For a person who abides with faith in Your command is liberated.
The Blessed Lord said:
In the first interval, there were six sons of Marīci born of Ūrṇā. Seeing their son intent on sexual union, the gods laughed;
because of that, he entered an asura womb due to his despicable deed even now.
O King, those sons who were born from Hiraṇyakaśipu and carried away by Your yogic power (yoga-māyā) were born from the womb of Devakī and slain by Kaṃsa;
she grieves for them as her own children, yet they now sit here in Your presence.
"From here we shall lead them forth to dispel their mother's grief;
then, liberated from the curse, they will go to the world free from fever.
Smara, Udgītha, Pariṣvaṅga, Pataṅga, Kṣudrabhṛt, and Ghṛṇī—
"By my grace, these six shall again attain the state of the righteous," having said this and taking them with him, they were honored by Indrasena;
then, returning to Dvāravatī, they restored the sons to their mother.

Seeing those boys, the Goddess, her breasts flowing with milk from maternal affection, embraced them, took them onto her lap, and smelled their heads repeatedly; filled with joy, she suckled them at her breast, which was moistened by the touch of her sons.
Deluded by the *māyā* of Viṣṇu, by which the creation proceeds,
they drank the nectar-milk that remained after being drunk by the wielder of the mace (Gadābhṛt);
through the touch of Nārāyaṇa’s body, they attained the vision of the Self.

Having offered obeisances to Govinda, Devakī, their father, and Balarāma, they departed for the abode of the gods while all living beings looked on. Seeing that departure and arrival of the deceased, Queen Devakī—
O King, she considered it a most wonderful illusion fashioned by Kṛṣṇa. O Bhārata, such marvelous deeds of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul of infinite power, are indeed endless.
Śrī Sūta said:
He who hears this account of Murāri— whose fame is nectar— or causes it to be heard, as described by the son of Vyāsa;
It is sufficient to pierce the sins of the world; it serves as a beautiful ear-ornament for His devotees.
One whose mind is fixed on the Blessed Lord goes to that abode of security.
Śrī Rājā said:
"O Brahmin, we wish to know how Vijaya married the sister of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, who was my grandmother. Śrī Śuka said:
While wandering the earth on a pilgrimage to sacred fords, the lord Arjuna went to Prabhāsa and heard that Rāma would give his own maternal cousin to Duryodhana, and no one else.
Desiring that [wealth], he became an ascetic carrying three staffs (*tri-daṇḍin*) and went to Dvārakā;
there he dwelt for the months of the rainy season, seeking to accomplish his own purpose.
He was constantly honored by the citizens, as well as by Rāma, who did not recognize him.
Once, having brought him to his home and invited him with hospitality,
he indeed ate the alms-food offered with faith by Bala.
There, he beheld a great maiden who captivated the minds of heroes.
With eyes dilated by affection, he fixed his mind— agitated by emotion— upon her; she too, seeing him who was the very heart's desire of women, desired him,
smiling with bashful sidelong glances as she fixed her heart and eyes upon him.
Constantly meditating upon her and seeking an opportunity, Arjuna—
his mind wandering due to exceedingly powerful passion— found no peace.
During a great festival of the gods, she was seated in a chariot as it emerged from the fortress.
With the permission of his parents and Kṛṣṇa,
that great chariot-warrior took up his bow while standing in his chariot and, like a lion, put to flight the heroic and obstructing soldiers as they cried out, seizing his own allotted portion.
Hearing that, Rāma was agitated like the great ocean on a full-moon day;
having had his feet grasped by Kṛṣṇa and being consoled by his friends,
Balarāma joyfully sent bridal gifts for the bride and the bridegroom.
Great wealth, household utensils, elephants, chariots, horses, men, and women—
Śrī Śuka said:
O best of the twice-born, Kṛṣṇa had a priest known by the name Śrutadeva.
Having attained his goal through exclusive devotion to Kṛṣṇa alone, peaceful, wise,
and self-sufficient, he lived as a householder in Mithilā among the Videhas, performing his own duties with whatever provisions came to him spontaneously without effort.
Day after day, only what was necessary for his sustenance came to him by providence, and nothing more;
yet, content with that much, he performed his duties as were appropriate.
Likewise, O dear one, there was a protector of that kingdom known as Bahulāśva.
The King of Mithilā was free from the conceit of "I" and "mine," and both were dear to Acyuta.
The Lord, being pleased with them, ascended the chariot brought by Dāruka and,
together with the sages, proceeded toward Videha.
Nārada, Vāmadeva, Atri, Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Asita, Aruṇi,
I myself, Bṛhaspati, Kaṇva, Maitreya, Cyavana, and others—
O King, wherever he went, the citizens and the people of the countryside [welcomed] him.
With offerings of *arghya* in their hands, they approached him like planets approaching the risen sun;
these were the lords of Ānarta, Dhanva, Kuru, Jāṅgala, Kaṅka, Matsya,
Pāñcāla, Kunti, Madhu, Kekaya, Kośala, and Arṇa.
And other men and women, O King, drank in with their eyes his lotus-face, which possessed a noble smile and tender glances;
they did so for those [eyes] whose vision had been destroyed by darkness until then, now restored by his gaze.
Bestowing security and the vision of the ultimate goal upon the three worlds,
and hearing his own fame— which whitens the ends of the quarters and destroys all inauspiciousness—
sung by gods and men, he went slowly toward Videha.
O King, hearing that Acyuta had arrived, the citizens and the people of the countryside went out to meet him joyfully,
with offerings for his reception in their hands.
Beholding that Lord of Excellent Glory (Uttamaśloka), their faces blossomed with love.

With palms joined in reverence, they bowed to the sages whom they had heard of before; then, perceiving that the Teacher of the World had arrived to bestow His grace upon them, the King of Mithilā and Śrutadeva fell at the feet of the Lord.
The King of Mithilā and Śrutadeva, with palms joined in reverence, simultaneously invited the descendant of Daśārha along with the twice-born brahmins to offer him hospitality;
the Blessed Lord, perceiving this and desiring to do what was pleasing to both, [accepted].
He entered the house of both, unobserved by either;
then, when they had returned to their own home from afar, the high-minded Janaka, having seated them comfortably on excellent seats that had been brought for them, addressed those who were weary.
With his heart overflowing with intense devotion and his eyes moistened by tears of joy,
he bowed down to the Lord’s feet, washed them, and, carrying that water which purifies the world upon his head, he and his family honored the Lords.
Delighting those who had been satiated with food by means of perfumes, garlands, garments, ornaments, incense, lamps, water-offerings, cows, and bulls, and with sweet speech,
he gently touched the feet of Viṣṇu as they rested upon his lap, filled with joy.
Śrī Bahulāśva said:
O All-pervading Lord, You are indeed the Self of all beings, the witness, and the self-perceiving one.
Thus, You have come into our sight as we were remembering Your lotus feet.
In order to make those words of Yours true, may You become visible to our eyes;
for You have declared that neither Ananta, nor Śrī, nor the Unborn (Brahmā) are as dear to Me as My unswerving devotees.
Indeed, what man who knows this would ever abandon the lotus feet of Your own?

O You who grant Your very self to the sages who are peaceful and possess nothing; having descended into the lineage of Yadu, You have spread here upon this earth that fame which removes the sins of the three worlds for the sake of the peace of men wandering in saṃsāra.
Obeisances unto You, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa of unimpeded intelligence,
the sage Nārāyaṇa who has attained perfectly peaceful austerity. O Infinite One, please dwell for some days in our home together with the brāhmaṇas.
"Having come together with the dust of Your feet, purify this lineage of Nimi. Thus addressed by the king, the Blessed One, the creator of the worlds,
dwelt there, bringing auspiciousness to the men and women of Mithilā.

When Śrutadeva learned that Acyuta had arrived at his home, just as a father [rejoices] at the arrival of his son, he was greatly delighted; bowing down to the sages and shaking his garment, he danced indeed.
Having brought grass mats and cushions, he seated them upon them.
Having joyfully welcomed him with kind words, the noble Aṅghripa, together with his wife,
bathed himself along with his household and kin in the water from that vessel; filled with great delight, he felt as though all his heart's desires had been fulfilled.

With water containing fruits, arhaṇa, uśīra, and śivā, with fragrant clay, and with water mixed with tulasī and kuśa grass, he worshipped [the Lord] with whatever offerings were available and with food that increases the quality of goodness (sattva). He reflected: "From where has this meeting come to me, who have fallen into the blind well of household life?"
Śrutadeva approached Kṛṣṇa and His brāhmaṇa guests, who were seated comfortably after having been offered hospitality;
he was accompanied by his wife, kinsmen, and children, and he touched their feet with his head. (10.86.42–43)
Śrutadeva said: Today we have not obtained the sight of the Supreme Person, who,
having created this universe by His potencies, has entered it through His own essential nature.
Just as a person lying down, by his own mind and through his own creative power (*māyā*),
creates a supreme dream-world and enters it to manifest therein;
so do You appear to those who constantly hear, speak of, worship, and offer salutations to You.
You shine within the hearts of men who speak together with pure souls;
though dwelling in the heart, You remain exceedingly far away from those whose minds are distracted by karma.
Though ungraspable even by Your own powers, You are near to those whose nature is endowed with [discerned] qualities.

Salutations be unto You, the Supreme Self of those who know the inner self; You who are not the non-self, yet by whom death is dispelled through the realization of one's own Self; You who have attained the subtle body consisting of both the cause and the effect.
O Lord, you who have veiled and obstructed the vision of those covered by Your own *māyā*, please instruct us, Your servants; what shall we do, O God?
This is the end of the afflictions of men: that You come within the range of their sight.
Śrī Śuka said: Having heard what was thus spoken, the Blessed One, the remover of the distress of those who bow before him,
took his hand in His own hand and, smiling, spoke to him.
The Blessed Lord said:
O Brāhmaṇa, know that these sages have arrived here for the sake of showing you favor;
they traverse the worlds with Me, purifying them with the dust of their feet.

The gods, sacred fields, and holy fords gradually purify [those who visit them] over time through sight, touch, and worship— even that occurs by the grace of one most worthy of honor. Among all living beings here, the Brāhmaṇa is superior by virtue of his birth.
What need is there for austerity, knowledge, or contentment for one who is endowed with even a fraction of Me? This four-armed form is not as dear to Me as the Brahmanas;
for the Brahmin embodies all the Vedas, and I indeed embody all the gods.
Those of wicked intellect, being envious, do not understand this and thus despise me—
the Guru, the Brahmin, and their own Self— viewing me merely as an object of worship in idols and the like.
This entire universe, consisting of the moving and the non-moving, as well as those entities that are its causes, [are all myself].
"By my glance, the Brahmin holds within his mind that these are my own forms;
therefore, O Brahmā, worship these brahmin seers with faith in me. If I am thus worshipped, I am truly honored, and not otherwise by vast material opulences."
Śrī Śuka said: Thus instructed by the Lord, the King of Mithilā, together with Kṛṣṇa and the best of the twice-born,
worshiped Him with single-minded devotion and attained the destination of the righteous.
O King, having thus dwelt with His devotees and instructed them in the path of the righteous, the Blessed Lord, who is Himself devoted to His devotees, returned again to Dvāravatī.
Śrī Parīkṣit said:

O Brahman, how do the Vedic scriptures— which function through the modes of nature— directly describe that which is beyond both the manifest and the unmanifest, the Brahman who is beyond description and devoid of qualities? Śrī Śuka said:
The Lord created the intellect, the senses, the mind,
and the vital breaths of living beings for the sake of perceiving objects, for the sake of worldly existence, and for the sake of the Self’s lack of conceptualization.
Indeed, this is the Vedic Upaniṣad concerning Brahman, which was upheld by the ancients through their ancestors.
He who, possessing faith, should uphold this [teaching], shall attain peace even if he possesses nothing.
In this regard, I shall describe to you the song concerning Nārāyaṇa,
the dialogue between Nārada and the sage Nārāyaṇa.
Once, Nārada, the beloved of the Lord, while wandering through the worlds,
went to the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa to see the eternal sage— he who, indeed,
exists in this land of Bhārata for the welfare and well-being of men.
O best of the Kurus, having performed austerities endowed with righteousness, knowledge, and tranquility until the end of the kalpa,
he sat there surrounded by sages residing in Kalāpagrāma;
bowing down before him, [the king] asked this very question.
The Blessed Lord spoke this to him while the sages were listening—
this discourse on Brahman which was formerly held by the inhabitants of Janaloka. The Blessed Lord said:
In ancient times, in Janaloka, there was a Brahma-sacrifice belonging to Svāyambhuva Manu.
While you had gone to Śvetadvīpa to behold that Lord, the mind-born sages dwelling there remained with their vital seed drawn up.
The discourse on Brahman was perfectly concluded, wherein the Vedas rest;
it was there that this question which you ask me arose.
Those who were equal in learning, austerity, and character, and equal toward their own kin, enemies, and neutrals—
Some engaged in recitation, while others remained intent on listening.
Śrī Sanandana said:
Having absorbed this entire creation of his own, He lay down together with His potencies.
At the end of that [sleep], the Vedas awakened Him, the Supreme, by means of His own characteristic marks,
just as bards and dependents approach at dawn and awaken a sleeping sovereign with hymns of his glorious deeds.
The Vedic personifications of sacred knowledge said:
"Victory, victory to You! O Unconquered One, abandon the primordial nature (māyā), which is seized by the qualities of the modes.
For You are He who has, by Your own self, fully encompassed all divine opulences."
O revealer of all potencies to those who dwell within the world of moving and non-moving beings, the Veda follows You as You wander sometimes in an unmanifest form;
they understand this Great One as the Residual Reality.
Since the rising and setting of all transformations occur within You, as clay is the source of earthen forms,
therefore the seers have placed their minds, words, and deeds in You;
for how could the footsteps taken by men upon this earth ever fail to reach their destination?
O Lord of the three worlds, O destroyer of the impurities of all the worlds, by plunging into this ocean of the nectar of Your stories, Your wise devotees abandon their austerities;
how much more so those whose hearts have been shaken of the qualities of time by Your own abode?
Those who worship Your supreme abode, which is the experience of eternal bliss,
are like bellows that breathe for those who possess life-force; if they follow Your will,
the principles of Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, and the rest created the cosmic egg through Your grace.
Among the series beginning with the "consisting of food" (annamaya), You are the final one, the Person-like (puruṣavidha) lineage;
You are that which is beyond both being and non-being, and that which remains as the Truth (ṛta) within these. Those of narrow vision on the paths of the seers worship only Your belly.
O Infinite One, the heart of Aruṇi’s son is the path leading to the periphery; from there arose the small heart, and thence Your supreme abode, the head,
reaching which they do not fall again into the jaws of Death.
Entering, as it were, by way of causality into the various wombs created by Yourself,
You shine forth in degrees of intensity like fire, imitating Your own creations;
yet within these unreal forms, Your own reality remains equal and unchanging.
Those of stainless intellect, seeking the ultimate, enter into Your singular essence;
they declare that within these cities created by themselves, You— the Person who sustains all potencies— exist as the portion [of the whole], without any internal or external covering.
Having thus discerned the human condition,

the wise, placing their trust in you, worship your foot— the sower of the Vedas— which leads to liberation from worldly existence; for you have assumed a physical form on earth in order to reveal the truth of the self, which is otherwise difficult to comprehend.
O Lord, those who have exhausted themselves by circling the great ocean of the nectar of Your deeds do not desire even liberation,
having abandoned their homes through association with the swans of the lotus-clusters at Your feet.
This nest, which follows after You and contains its own kinsmen, friends,
and loved ones, moves about while You— its benefactor, beloved, and very Self— are looking on;
yet, alas, those who destroy themselves by the worship of the unreal do not find delight in it.

Driven by the latent tendencies of which they wander through bodies of wretched form in great fear, that [Supreme Being] whom sages— having restrained their breath, mind, and senses and being firmly joined in yoga— worship within the heart, even His enemies have attained upon remembering Him.

The women have their minds fixed upon the coils of the serpent-king’s hoods as their staff-like arms; we too are equal to them, for the nectar of Your lotus feet is the same for all who see with equanimity.
Alas, who in this world can truly know the beginning of Your descent, which precedes even the dissolution of the lowest birth?
From whom the Seer arose, and after whom both classes of gods followed;
at that time there was neither being nor non-being, nor both, nor the speed of time. When [that state] exists, no scripture can prevail, for he lies withdrawn within it.
Those who remember the birth of the non-existent from the existent, the death [of the existent], and the duality within the Self;
who remember the marketplace of truth and teach it with such misconceptions—
they maintain the duality that "the Person is composed of the three qualities," which is produced by ignorance.

In You, who are the essence of consciousness, that [universe] does not exist beyond You; yet, as if it were real, the threefold world appears within You, from the highest gods down to human beings. Those who know the Self perceive this entire universe as the Self, as being identical with the Real.

Indeed, they do not abandon their modifications, for gold remains identical with them; likewise, this world, which is Your own creation, has entered into You and is perceived as being of the same nature as Yourself.
Those who move about as Your attendants, because You are the abode of all beings, [do not perceive these distinctions].
They even trample upon the head of Destruction (Nirṛti) without a second thought;
with their speech, they drive away even those gods as if they were mere cattle.
Indeed, those who have established friendship with You purify themselves, whereas those who are turned away from You do not.
You are without organs of action, self-sovereign, and the bearer of the power to create all things; the gods,
together with their wives, offer you tribute and eat [the fruits of their labor],
just as the subjects of an entire earth-lord pay tribute to the creator of the universe.

O liberated one, if you were to sport with the expectation of the Supreme, then those classes of moving and non-moving beings who are subject to you would become terrified, even though they are joined to causes arising from the Unconquerable.
For there is no one who is either inferior or superior to You, the Supreme, who are like the sky— devoid of attributes and comparable to the void—
even if all embodied beings were infinite, eternal, and omnipresent.
In that case, the rule that "He cannot be commanded" is certain, and not otherwise;
for He who is the controller would not exist without being composed of that [which is to be controlled].
That which is considered equal by those who understand it is regarded as "unthinkable" (amata) due to the defectiveness of their own thinking.
The birth of the unmanifest *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* is not possible;
rather, living beings come into existence through the union of these two, like bubbles in water.
Therefore, O Supreme One, these beings exist within You through various names and qualities.

Just as all rivers dissolve into the ocean, so do all flavors merge into honey; likewise, O Lord, having understood that these men are subject to intense delusion through Your illusory power (māyā), the wise, seeking liberation from existence, fix their devotion upon You, who are beyond birth.

How can there be fear of worldly existence for those who follow You, when Your mere frown has repeatedly brought about terror even among the Three-eyed Lord (Śiva) and others who seek refuge? [O Lord,] with the senses and breath conquered, one must restrain the horse of the mind which is difficult to tame.
Those who, having abandoned the feet of the Guru, strive here to restrain the excessively fickle mind through the exhaustion of various means— though beset by hundreds of calamities—
are like merchants in the ocean who have failed to secure a helmsman and thus perish.
"O Lord who is the essence of all, while You exist, what need have men for their own kin, children, self, wife, wealth, home, land, and chariots?"— thus [the Lord spoke] to those who,
not knowing this eternal truth, wander about for the sake of pleasure in pairs.

Who indeed in this world can bring happiness to one whose own efforts have been frustrated and whose fortune has been cast away? Even those sages who are free from pride, who dwell at many holy pilgrimage sites on earth, find no peace;
yet, those whose hearts are fixed upon Your lotus feet and whose very waters are the dust from Your feet are the ones who destroy all sin.
Those who fix their minds even once upon You, the Self who is eternal bliss,
do not again resort to the abodes that carry away the essence of man.
If it is argued that this world has arisen from Being because it is "existent," then surely that is refuted by logic.

In some cases it deviates, and in others it is false; thus, for the sake of worldly transaction, this conceptual construction joined with both [truth and falsehood] is accepted through a blind tradition.
Your speech, O Lord, bewilders those dull-witted by means of Vedic hymns through its many modes of expression.
That which did not exist in the beginning, nor will it exist after this dissolution,
is measured as an interval within You, who are of a single uniform essence;
therefore, it is compared by means of various conceptual paths of material categories.
The ignorant perceive the false play of the mind as reality;
when he lies down with the unborn Māyā through her power,
enjoying the modes of nature, he then assumes a form similar to hers and, his fortune departed, undergoes death.
And you, having attained supreme fortune, cast off that [body] like a snake sheds its skin;
you, of immeasurable fortune, are magnified in your majesty endowed with the eightfold divine powers.
If the ascetics do not uproot the tangled roots of desire within their hearts—

O Blessed One, for those yogis who are addicted to the vital breaths, there is misery from both sides: You are difficult to attain by the unrighteous, yet once entered into the heart of the righteous, You are like a jewel on the neck that is forgotten;
thus they suffer from the presence of death, which has not departed, and from Your state, which they have not ascended.

One who has realized You does not perceive the connection between the qualities and defects arising from you— namely, the auspicious and inauspicious— and neither does he heed the words of embodied beings,
which follow the succession of ages and the daily flow of the lineage of those singing of the qualities.
Since you are the goal of liberation for those who carry your name upon their ears,
even the lords of heaven have not reached your end because of your infinity;
for within you are the multitudes of cosmic eggs along with their coverings.
Just as dust is blown away by the wind, so too do the Vedic scriptures,
which culminate in You and exclude all else, find their fulfillment in You alone.
The Blessed Lord said:
Having heard this instruction regarding the Self from Brahmā, the sons of Brahmā,
along with the Siddhas, then honored Sanandana, having realized their own true destination.
Thus ends the essence of all the Vedas, Purāṇas, and Upaniṣads.
O son of Brahmā, you were formerly lifted up by high-souled beings traveling through the sky; now, maintaining this instruction for the self with faith,
wander at will over the earth, which burns away the desires of men.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having thus accepted the instruction given by the sage with faith, that self-possessed sage, who was full of learning and firm in his heroic vows, spoke.
Śrī Nārada said:
Obeisances to that Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa of stainless fame,
who assumes hundreds of portions of the unborn for the sake of the non-destruction of all living beings.
Having thus bowed down to the primordial sage and his high-souled disciples,
he then went to the hermitage of my father, Dvaipāyana himself;
there he was honored by the Blessed One and accepted a seat.
He described that to him exactly as he had heard it from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, O King, has that which you asked us been described—
how the mind may move toward Brahman, who is indefinable and devoid of qualities.
He who is the beholder of this universe at its beginning, middle, and end; who is the unmanifest, the individual soul, and the Lord;
who, having created this world, entered into it, and by means of the Seer (the Veda) fashioned the bodies and governs them;
and reaching whom the one bound by latent impressions abandons the unborn material nature, just as a sleeper leaves his nest—[to Him I offer my salutations].
One should meditate constantly upon that Hari, who is fearless and whose source has been cast away through absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).
Śrī Rāja said:
Among gods, asuras, and humans, those who worship Śiva, who is inauspicious...
"Most likely those wealthy ones are merely enjoyers of riches, and not the Lord Hari, the Master of Lakṣmī.
We wish to know this, for our doubt in this matter is great.
For when two masters possess contrary natures, the destiny of those who worship them is likewise contradictory."
Śrī Śuka said:
Śiva, eternally endowed with Śakti, possesses three forms and is enveloped by the modes of nature;
thus, the ego (ahaṃkāra) is threefold: as Vaikārika, Taijasa, and Tāmasa.
From that, these sixteen transformations arose;
by taking refuge in any one of them, one attains the state of all divine manifestations.
For Hari is indeed devoid of material qualities (nirguṇa), the manifest Supreme Person (puruṣa) who transcends primordial nature (prakṛti).
He who is the all-seeing witness, by worshipping Him, becomes free from the material qualities (*nirguṇa*). When the horse-sacrifices had concluded, your grandfather, the king,
while listening to the duties of the Lord, questioned this infallible Acyuta as follows.
The Lord, the Master, being pleased with him who was intent on service, spoke to him for the sake of the supreme welfare of men— he who had descended into the lineage of Yadu. The Blessed Lord said:
Upon whomsoever I bestow grace, I shall gradually take away his wealth;
then, his kinsmen will abandon him when he is destitute and afflicted by constant sorrow. When his efforts have thus proven futile, he becomes despondent in his longing for riches.
To one who has cultivated friendship with those devoted to Me, I shall grant My grace;
by realizing that supreme Brahman— which is subtle, pure consciousness, existence, and infinite—
as one's own self, the wise man is completely liberated from the cycle of birth and death.

Therefore, people abandon me, who am so difficult to propitiate, and worship others; consequently, having obtained kingdoms and royal splendor from those easily pleased deities, they become arrogant, intoxicated, and heedless, disregarding and insulting the boons granted by me.
Śrī Śuka said:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others are masters over both cursing and bestowing grace;
however, my dear friend, it is Śiva and Brahmā who can grant curse or grace instantly, but not Acyuta.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history:
after Giriśa had granted a boon to the demon Vṛka, he fell into great distress.
There was a demon named Vṛka, the son of Śakuni, who [saw] Nārada on the road.
Seeing that the three gods were easily pleased, the evil-minded one asked them;
he said, "Run quickly to the god Giriśa, and you will achieve success—
he who is quickly pleased and quickly angered by even slight merits and faults."
Being pleased with the ten-faced Rāvaṇa and Bāṇa, who were praising him like two bards, he granted them incomparable sovereignty; yet thereafter, he fell into great distress.
Thus commanded, the Asura rushed toward him from his own body.
At Kedāra, offering his own flesh as an oblation into the mouth of Hara in the form of fire,
he failed to obtain a vision of the god; on the seventh day, out of despondency,
he cut off his head— its hair moistened by the waters of that sacred ford— with a sharp blade.

Then the Greatly Compassionate Dhūrjaṭi, like us, rose up from the fire as if it were a flame; seizing him by his two arms, he restrained him, and by that touch his form was restored once more. He said to him: "Enough with this anger! Choose a boon from me; I shall grant you whatever you desire."
"I would be pleased with the water of men who take refuge [in me]; alas, you are needlessly tormenting yourself excessively.
That most wicked one chose as his boon that which brings fear to all beings: "May whomever I place my hand upon the head die."
Having heard that, O Bhārata, Lord Rudra, appearing somewhat dejected,
laughed and said "Om," granting him [the boon] as if it were nectar to a snake. To test the efficacy of that boon, the Asura indeed struck Śambhu on the head.
Śiva began to place the mineral [poison] upon his own hand; he was terrified by what he himself had created.
Being afflicted by it, trembling and full of fear, he fled away toward the ends of heaven, earth, and the quarters, moving upward and downward.
Not knowing how to counteract it, the lords of the gods remained silent.
Then he went to Vaikuṇṭha, the radiant realm beyond darkness,
where Nārāyaṇa himself resides as the supreme goal for those who have renounced all worldly ties.
For those who are peaceful and have laid down the rod of punishment, once gone, they do not return;
seeing them thus in distress, the Blessed One, the destroyer of suffering,
approached from afar, having become a young student (*baṭuka*) through his yogic power (*yoga-māyā*).
Girdled with a belt of grass, clad in a deerskin, and holding a staff and rosary, blazing with splendor like fire, he greeted him with kusa grass in hand in a humble manner.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O son of Śakuni, you are clearly exhausted; how far have you come?
Rest for a moment, O man, for this Self is the fulfiller of all desires.
O Lord, if it is possible for us to hear what you have resolved upon," so he spoke.
"It is generally said that men, being possessed by their own self-interest, strive for their own ends.
Śrī Śuka said:
"Thus questioned by the Blessed One, who showers the nectar of his words..."
His fatigue gone, he spoke to him regarding what had been performed as previously instructed.
The Blessed Lord said:
"If it is so, then we cannot place our faith in those words."
He who, due to the curse of Dakṣa, attained the state of a Piśāca and became the king of the Pretas and Piśācas—
if you have confidence in the Teacher of the World there, O Lord of Dānavas,
then quickly place your hand upon your own head and believe.
"O bull among the Dānavas, if the word of Śambhu should somehow prove false,
then slay this speaker of untruth, so that he may not speak falsehood again.
Thus, with these various and highly refined words of the Blessed One, [he spoke].
His intellect shattered and his memory lost, the fool placed his own hand upon his head;
then, with his skull split open, he fell in an instant like one struck by a thunderbolt.
In the heavens, cries of "Victory!", "Obeisances!", and "Well done! arose.
When the wicked demon Vṛka was slain, showers of flowers fell from the sky;
the gods, sages, ancestors, and gandharvas were released, and Śiva was set free from his peril.
Then the Blessed Lord Puruṣottama spoke to the liberated Giriśa.
"Oh, O God, Great God! This wretch has been slain by his own sin.

Indeed, O Lord, what living being who has committed an offense against the great could remain safe? How much less one who has committed an offense against the Lord of the Universe, the Teacher of the World?"

Whoever thus recounts or hears this account of the liberation of Girīśa by Hari— the Supreme Soul, the manifest ocean of unmanifested powers— is liberated from the cycles of worldly existence as well as from his enemies.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, on the banks of the Sarasvatī, the sages were performing a sacrificial session (satra).
Among them, a deliberation arose as to which of the three lords was the greatest.
O King, out of a desire to ascertain this, they indeed approached Bhṛgu, the son of Brahmā.
To inform him of this, they sent [Nārada], who arrived at the assembly of Brahmā. Out of a desire to test his character, Brahmā did not offer him obeisance or hymns of praise.
The Blessed One, blazing with his own splendor, became enraged at him.
The Lord, the self-born, himself pacified within his own self the anger that had arisen toward his own son,
just as fire is extinguished by water, its own source.
Thereafter, that god Maheśvara went to Kailāsa.
Rising up with joy, he began to embrace his brother; however,
the god became enraged, thinking, "You have taken a wrong path," and with sharp eyes, he raised his trident and began to strike him down.
Falling at his feet, the goddess consoled him with her words;
then she went to Vaikuṇṭha, where the god Janārdana was lying on the lap of Śrī, and struck him on the chest with her foot.

Then, having risen from his bed together with Lakṣmī, the Blessed One, the refuge of the virtuous, descended and bowed his head to the sage. He said, "Welcome to you, O Brahmin; please sit for a moment on this seat."
O Lord, you ought to forgive us for our ignorance in having approached you;
purify me along with this world and the guardians of the worlds who have come to you,
by means of your foot-water, which makes even sacred fords holy.
"O Blessed One, today I have become the sole recipient of Lakṣmī’s favor;
prosperity shall dwell upon my chest, for my sins have been destroyed by Your feet.
Śrī Śuka said:

While Vaikuṇṭha was speaking thus with his deep and resonant voice, Bhṛgu became filled with bliss and satisfied; with eyes full of tears and longing through devotion, he remained silent for a moment,
and then returned once more to the sacrificial session of the sages who discourse on Brahman.
O King, Bhṛgu described his own experience in its entirety.
Having heard that, the sages were struck with wonder and their doubts were dispelled;
they placed even greater faith in Viṣṇu, from whom comes peace and from whom comes fearlessness.
From him comes Dharma itself, along with the knowledge and detachment that accompany it;
from him comes the eightfold sovereignty and glory that washes away the impurities of the self—
for those sages who have laid down the rod of punishment, who are peaceful, and whose minds are equanimous.
They say that for saintly persons who possess nothing, he is the supreme goal;
he whose beloved form is pure goodness (*sattva*), for whom brāhmaṇas are their chosen deities,
and whom those of subtle intellect worship without seeking rewards, being themselves peaceful.
The Rākṣasas, Asuras, and Suras are his threefold manifestations, created by his Māyā which possesses the qualities (guṇas). Among them, Sattva is the means for attaining the sacred ford (tīrtha).
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus did the Brahmins of Sarasvatī, having attained that supreme goal through service to the lotus feet of the Supreme Person, dispel the doubts of men. Śrī Sūta said:

Thus, those who fear the danger of worldly existence constantly drink with the cups of their ears this nectar of the fair renown of the Supreme Person— the fragrance of whose lotus feet is like that of the daughter of the sage.
"A traveler abandons the exhaustion of wandering on the road.
Śrī Śuka said:
"Once, in Dvāravatī, there was a young son of a brahmin's wife."

O descendant of Bharata, it is said that as soon as he was born, he touched the earth and died. Taking the dead child, the brahmin laid him at the king’s gate and, lamenting with a distressed and dejected mind, spoke these words: BhP 10.89.021/3–022/3: "O descendant of Bharata, as soon as he was born, he touched the earth and died, so they say. Taking the dead child and placing him at the king’s gate, the brahmin, wailing in distress with a dejected mind, spoke this."
"Due to the fault of the actions of that base Kṣatriya— who was a hater of Brahmins, deceitful-minded, greedy, and whose soul was devoted to sense objects— my child has met his death.
[I have brought this upon myself] by serving a king who delights in violence, is ill-behaved, and has no control over his senses."
"Subjects who are devoted [to their duties] perish, becoming impoverished and perpetually miserable.
Thus, O brahmin-sage, he recited this second verse, and likewise a third, as he stood at the king's gate singing that song.
Having overheard that [speech] once in the presence of Keśava, when the ninth child had passed away, Arjuna addressed a brāhmaṇa:
"O brāhmaṇa, is there indeed no wielder of the bow here in your residence?"
These kinsmen of royalty are indeed Brahmins performing a sacrificial session (satra);
yet those Brahmins, deprived of wealth, wives, and children, grieve there.
They are merely actors in the guise of royalty, living as mere sustainers of the breath of life.
"O Blessed One, I shall protect the offspring of you two who are here in distress. Having fulfilled my vow and cleansed of all sin, I shall enter the fire.
Śrī-Brāhmaṇa said:
Since Saṅkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Pradyumna— the best among archers—
and Aniruddha, who is without rival in battle, were unable to protect him,
how is it that you have performed this deed so difficult even for the lords of the universe?
Out of foolishness you wish to do this, but we do not believe it.
Śrī Arjuna said:
O Brahmin, I am neither Saṅkarṣaṇa, nor Kṛṣṇa, nor even the son of Kṛṣṇa (Kārṣṇi).
"Or I am Arjuna by name, whose bow is indeed the Gāṇḍīva.
Do not despise me, O Brahmin; witness my prowess in pleasing Tryambaka.
Having conquered Death in battle, I shall bring back your offspring, O Lord."
O scorcher of enemies, having been thus inspired with confidence by Phālguna, the brāhmaṇa went to his own home delighted, contemplating the prowess of Pārtha.
When the time for his wife’s delivery drew near, that best of the twice-born—
"Protect, protect my subjects from death!"— thus the distressed [Arjuna] spoke to Arjuna.
Having sipped pure water, paid homage to Maheśvara,
and called to mind his divine weapons, he strung the Gāṇḍīva bow and took it up.
He blocked the maternity chamber with arrows discharged from various weapons;
O Pārtha, he created a cage of arrows across, above, and below.
Then a son was born to the brahmin’s wife, crying repeatedly.
Instantly, he vanished from sight, traveling through the air in his physical body.
Then, in the presence of Kṛṣṇa, the brahmin spoke, censuring Vijaya:
"Behold my foolishness, I who placed my faith in the boasting of a eunuch!"
Neither Pradyumna, nor Aniruddha, nor Rāma, nor Keśava were able to protect him;
who else could have been his protector? Shame on Arjuna for his false speech! Shame on his bow that praises itself!
When the foolish and evil-minded one sought to bring back [the child] though it was possessed by a deity,
Phālguna, resorting to his knowledge, thus cursed the brahmin-sage and quickly went to Saṃyamanī, where the blessed Lord Yama resides.
Not seeing the son of the Brahmin, he then went to the city of Indra;
then to the cities of Agni, Nirṛti, Soma, Vāyu, and Varuṇa;
and with weapons raised, he traversed Rasātala, the back of the heavens (Nākapṛṣṭha), and other celestial abodes.
Then, having failed to obtain the sons of the twice-born and thus not having fulfilled his promise, he was about to enter the fire when Kṛṣṇa addressed him with a prohibition:
"I shall show you the sons of the twice-born; do not disregard yourself by yourself."
"Those men who shall establish our stainless fame," having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, together with Arjuna,
mounted his divine chariot and entered the western direction.
Having passed beyond the seven islands along with their oceans, the seven ranges of mountains, and the Lokāloka mountain, he entered the vast, profound darkness.
There, his horses Śaibya, Sugrīva, Meghapuṣpa, and Balāhaka—
O bull of the Bharatas, their paths having been lost in darkness,
the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, the sovereign of the great lords of yoga, beholding them,
hurled his own discus— which resembled a thousand suns— before him.
The Sudarśana [discus], possessing the speed of thought, entered that vast, most terrible, and dense darkness, rending it with its abundant radiance.
Just as an army is routed by Rāma’s arrow when its qualities have failed,

Phālguna beheld that darkness passing through the gateway— the path of the discus— toward the supreme light which is infinite and boundless; seeing it thus, his eyes were so dazzled that he closed both of them.
Then he entered the water, which was adorned with great surging waves driven by a powerful wind.
There, indeed, was a wondrous and most radiant palace, beautified by thousands of glittering jeweled pillars.
Within it was the wonderful Ananta, possessed of great coils.

He was resplendent with the luster of the jewels on the hoods of his thousand heads, fierce with eyes twice as large [than usual], resembling a white mountain, and possessing a dark-blue throat and tongue.
He beheld the all-pervading Lord, the most exalted of supreme persons, of great majesty, seated upon a comfortable throne for his enjoyment,
resembling a dense rain-cloud and clad in beautiful saffron-colored garments.
With a serene face and beautiful, long eyes,
his thousand locks of hair were encircled by the radiance of his crown and earrings, which were set with clusters of great jewels.
With eight long and beautiful arms, adorned with the Kaustubha gem,
marked with the Śrīvatsa, and garlanded with forest flowers; wearing a crown and earrings set with clusters of great jewels.
His thousand locks of hair were encircled by radiance; he possessed eight long and beautiful arms, was adorned with the Kaustubha gem,
bore the Śrīvatsa mark, and was draped in a garland of forest flowers.

Acyuta and Jiṣṇu, struck with awe at the sight of him, bowed down before the Infinite Self. To them, with palms joined in reverence, the Lord of the supreme sages—the Abundant One—spoke with a smile in a majestic voice:
"These two sons of a brahmin were brought by me to the earth out of a desire to see you both, for the protection of Dharma."
Having descended as partial incarnations to slay the demons who burden the earth, may you two hasten back here to my presence.
Although your desires are fulfilled, O sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa, you two preeminent ones should practice dharma for the sake of the world’s stability and its collective welfare.
Thus instructed by the Supreme Lord, those two Kṛṣṇas replied "Oṃ," bowed to the Great One, took the sons of the twice-born,
and returned with great joy to their own abode by the same way they had come.
They gave their sons to the brāhmaṇa according to his form and age.
Having beheld that Vaiṣṇava abode, Arjuna was struck with supreme wonder;
he considered whatever prowess men possess to be the result of Kṛṣṇa’s compassion.
Displaying many such heroic deeds here,
he enjoyed worldly pleasures and performed most magnificent sacrifices;
he showered all desired objects upon his subjects, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
Just as Indra, the Blessed One, established his preeminence at the appropriate time, so too did he,
having slain the most unrighteous kings and having had them executed by Arjuna and others, straightforwardly cause Dharma to prevail through Yudhiṣṭhira and his brothers.
Śrī Śuka said:
The Lord of Śrī dwelt happily in his own city, Dvārakā,
which was enriched with every prosperity and inhabited by the foremost of the Vṛṣṇis.

In those palaces, the streets were constantly crowded with women of exquisite attire and the loveliness of fresh youth, playing with balls and other toys like flashes of lightning; and with rutting elephants shedding temporal juice.
With well-adorned soldiers, horses, and chariots blazing with gold,
[he entered] that city rich in gardens and groves, where rows of flowering trees resounded on all sides with the humming of bees and the songs of birds.
He, the beloved of sixteen thousand wives, took his pleasure as their sole lord; assuming as many diverse forms as there were, he dwelt in their houses of great opulence,
which were filled with the pollen of blooming blue, white, and red lotuses and water-lilies.

The one of great glory sported, plunging into the waters of the lakes where the flocks of birds warbled and the waters were scented with pure fragrance; his limbs were smeared with the saffron from the breasts of the women who embraced him.
Being sung to by Gandharvas, while the Sūtas, Māgadhas, and bards joyfully played the mṛdaṅga, paṇava, ānaka, and lute,
Acyuta was drenched by those laughing women with showers of water.
Sprinkling [one another], he sported like the king of the Yakṣas with the Yakṣīs;
they, whose garments were soaked so that their thighs and breasts were revealed,
sprinkled him as the flowers from their large, uplifted braids fell away.
Embracing their beloved with the desire to inhale [his fragrance], they shone,
their faces radiant with the pride of awakened passion;
meanwhile, Kṛṣṇa was adorned by the garland of saffron clinging to their breasts.
With his mass of hair loosened by the immersion in play, repeatedly sprinkling the young women and being sprinkled by them in turn,
he took delight like a lordly elephant surrounded by female elephants.
Kṛṣṇa gave to the actors, the female dancers, and those who subsist on song and instrumental music— along with their wives— playthings, ornaments, and garments.
As Kṛṣṇa thus sported, [the women were captivated] by his movements, conversations, glances, and smiles.
Their intellects were indeed captivated by the jests, playful dalliances, and embraces of the women;
yet with their minds fixed solely on Mukunda, they spoke to the dull-witted [Uddhava] like madmen. Listen as I relate those words while they meditated upon the lotus-eyed Lord.
The queens said:
O female osprey, you lament; you do not sleep, for your sleep has departed.
While the world sleeps at night, the Lord remains awake, His consciousness ever protected.
O friend, just like us, has your heart perhaps been deeply pierced by the noble and playful glances of the lotus-eyed One,
that you close your eyes at night, O you who have no other kin?
O female ruddy goose, you cry out piteously; alas,
like us who have become your maidservants, you long for that garland worn upon the head of the one whose feet are cherished by Acyuta— why do you desire to bear it upon your crest?
O Ocean, you who always roar, deprived of sleep and seized by wakefulness—
have you perhaps reached this insurmountable state because your very identity has been stolen away by Mukunda? O Moon,
you have been seized by a powerful consumption.
O Moon, your darkness has been diminished by your own rays; do you not likewise diminish it?
O Mukunda, have you forgotten those words spoken by You, just as we have forgotten them, that you appear before us with your speech silenced?
"O Malaya breeze, what unpleasant thing have we done to you that you stir up passion within our hearts, which have already been pierced by Govinda’s sidelong glances?
O glorious cloud, you are surely the beloved friend of the Lord of the Yādavas."
Like us, you meditate upon Him who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, bound by love;
with an intensely longing heart, like one such as we, you shed streams of tears again and again upon remembering Him— yet that association brings you constant sorrow.
"You speak these words so dear to hear with this voice that restores the dead to life. Tell me, O sweet-throated cuckoo, what favor may I do for you today?
You neither move nor speak, O noble-minded mountain; you must be contemplating some great matter."
Alas! Do you not desire, as we do, to support with your breasts the foot of Vasudeva’s son?
Woe to us, the wives of the ocean, whose pools are parched and who are tormented by the sun; now that our beloved husband has departed, the beauty of our lotuses has been cast away.
Just as we, having failed to obtain the affectionate glance of the Lord of Madhu, have had our hearts stolen away and are greatly emaciated;
O swan, welcome! Be seated, drink the water, and tell us, dear friend, the news of Śauri.
"We know you to be His messenger; we hope that the Unconquered One is well.
Was it previously said by Him, 'What is there for us to remember, since our affection is fickle'? Why then do we worship Him?
O sweet-spoken one, speak to us of the Giver of Desires; for apart from Śrī, devotion to Him alone is the singular goal of women."
Śrī Śuka said: By performing such devotion toward Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the masters of yoga,
the wives of Mādhava attained the supreme goal.

Even merely hearing of him forcibly captivates the minds of women; how much more so for those who behold Him— the one whose strides are vast and whose glories are sung far and wide— who served Him with love by massaging His feet and other such acts?
What can be said of the austerity of those women who regarded the Teacher of the World as their husband?
Thus, practicing the dharma proclaimed by the Vedas,
the refuge of the virtuous repeatedly demonstrated that the home is the ground for the attainment of dharma, artha, and kāma.
While Kṛṣṇa was established in the supreme dharma of householders,
he had sixteen thousand principal queens and more than a hundred others;
among those women who were like jewels, eight have already been mentioned.
O King, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord whose movement is never in vain, begot ten sons by each of his wives, headed by Rukmiṇī, in due order— ten sons for each of as many wives as he had.
Among those of unrestrained prowess, there were eighteen great chariot-warriors (*mahāratha*) of noble fame; hear their names from me:
Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Dīptimān, and Bhānu.
Sāmba, Madhu, Bṛhadbhānu, Citrabhānu, Vṛka, Aruṇa, Puṣkara, Vedabāhu, Śrutadeva, Sunandana,
Citrabāhu, Virūpa, Kavi, and Nyagrodha.
O King of kings, among these sons of the enemy of Madhu, Pradyumna was the first-born; like his father, he was the son of Rukmiṇī. That great chariot-warrior married the daughter of Rukmin.
From her was born Aniruddha, endowed with the strength of a thousand elephants.
He, in turn, took as his wife the granddaughter of Rukmin and daughter of his own daughter; he was the one known as Vajra, who had survived the slaughter of the Mausala.
From him was born Pratibāhu, and Subāhu was his son.
From Subāhu came Śāntasena, and Śatasena was his son.
Indeed, those born in this lineage were never destitute nor did they have few offspring.

They were born short-lived, lacking in vigor, and devoid of devotion to the Brahmanas. O King, it is impossible to calculate the number of men born in the lineage of Yadu who performed celebrated deeds, even in tens of thousands of years.
It is heard that there were three crores, eight thousand, and eight hundred and ten teachers of the Yadu clan for the princes;
who indeed could calculate the number of those high-souled Yādavas?
There, where Āhuka dwells with ten million times ten thousand [attendants],
those most terrible Daityas who were slain in the battle between the gods and asuras have been born among men; arrogant, they oppressed the subjects.
To subdue him, the gods were commanded by Hari and descended into the lineage of Yadu;
O King, their clans numbered one hundred and one,
and the Blessed Lord Hari became their sovereign authority.
And all the Yādavas who followed him—

those Vṛṣṇis whose minds were fixed on Kṛṣṇa— grew in affection for him in every act, whether lying down, sitting, walking, conversing, playing, bathing, or other activities; they were not even aware of their own selves while he was present.

The king established a sacred ford when the celestial river, the purifier of his feet, was born among the Yadus; through him, those who were hostile or affectionate attained their true nature; for his sake, even the effort of others toward the Supreme Śrī was rendered futile;
his name, heard or uttered, destroys inauspiciousness; and by him, the dharma of the lineage was established.

It is no wonder for Kṛṣṇa, whose weapon is the wheel of time, that he has removed the burden of the earth; victorious is He who dwells among the people, who is celebrated as the son of Devakī, and who, in the assembly of the best of the Yadus, destroys unrighteousness with His own arms.
Destroying the sins of all moving and stationary beings with His beautiful, smiling, and glorious face,
He increased the god of love within the women of Vraja and the city;
thus, out of a desire to protect His own path, the Supreme Lord assumed—

One who desires to follow in the footsteps of that Supreme Lord of the Yadus should hear of His pastimes— those playful imitations suited to His various forms— and His deeds which grind away all karma.

O Mukunda, by that [devotion] which increases at every moment through hearing, chanting, and reflecting upon Your glorious narrations, a mortal attains that abode where the impetuosity of Kṛtānta is impossible to cross.
Even kings went from their villages to the forest for the sake of that which they sought.
